Work out each quantity from Table 5.2. Before you look at the email, the label is spam with probability \(\frac18\), so \(H(X) = h(1/8) = \frac18\log_2 8 + \frac78\log_2\frac87 = 0.375 + 0.1686 = 0.5436\) bits: the label is fairly predictable, because most email is ham.
If the word is absent, you are in the first column. Its only non-zero entry is ham, so the email is certainly ham and \(H(X \mid Y = 0) = 0\).
If the word is present, you are in the second column, where ham and spam each have probability \(\frac18\) out of \(\frac14\). Given the word, they are equally likely, so \(H(X \mid Y = 1) = h(1/2) = 1\) bit. Seeing the word made you more uncertain than you were before: from 0.5436 bits up to a full bit.
On average, though, the word helps. You see it absent with probability \(\frac34\) and present with probability \(\frac14\), so \(H(X \mid Y) = \frac34\cdot0 + \frac14\cdot1 = 0.25\) bits, less than \(H(X)\).
The chain rule can be checked on the same table. The word is present with probability \(\frac14\), so \(H(Y) = h(1/4) = 0.8113\), and \(H(Y) + H(X \mid Y) = 0.8113 + 0.25 = 1.0613\). That equals the entropy of the pair computed directly from the three non-zero cells \((\frac34, \frac18, \frac18)\).
Figure 5.2 draws the four numbers. The common observation (word absent) removes all uncertainty; the rare one (word present) increases it; the average goes down. That is the general pattern: conditioning reduces entropy only in expectation.






Figure 5.2: Entropy of the spam label before observing the keyword, after each of the two possible observations, and on average. The rare observation raises the entropy above \(H(X)\) (dashed line); the average falls below it.





5.3.7 Check yourself

What is the entropy of a uniformly random 4-digit PIN, and why? (There are 10,000 equally likely PINs, so \(H = \log_2 10{,}000 = 13.2877\) bits: the upper bound \(\log\lvert\mathcal X\rvert\), attained because the distribution is uniform.)
Using the chain rule, show that \(H(X, Y) \le H(X) + H(Y)\), with equality iff \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent. (\(H(X, Y) = H(Y) + H(X \mid Y)\), and \(H(X \mid Y) \le H(X)\) with equality iff independent.)

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.4 Mutual information

5.4.1 Context
How much does observing \(Y\) tell you about \(X\)? A natural answer is the drop in uncertainty it causes on average, \(H(X) - H(X \mid Y)\). This is the information gain a decision tree uses to choose a split, and the criterion many feature-selection methods use to rank features. It turns out to be a KL divergence, which makes it symmetric and non-negative, and it obeys a rule that drives a great deal of later reasoning: processing cannot create information.


5.4.2 Statement
The mutual information between \(X\) and \(Y\) is the average drop in uncertainty about \(X\) from seeing \(Y\). It can also be read as a measure of dependence: the KL divergence from the true joint distribution \(P_{XY}\) to the product \(P_XP_Y\) of its marginals, which is what the joint distribution would be if \(X\) and \(Y\) were independent. The two readings give the same number: \[I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = D\big(P_{XY}\,\big\|\,P_XP_Y\big) = \sum_{x, y}p(x, y)\log\frac{p(x, y)}{p(x)\,p(y)}. \tag{5.11}\] It follows that mutual information is symmetric, \(I(X; Y) = I(Y; X) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)\): \(Y\) tells you as much about \(X\) as \(X\) tells you about \(Y\). It is non-negative, and it is zero if and only if \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.
Sometimes a third variable \(Z\) is already known. The conditional mutual information is the same quantity computed with every distribution conditioned on \(Z = z\), then averaged over \(z\). It measures what \(Y\) adds about \(X\) beyond what \(Z\) already told you, and it is non-negative because it is an average of KL divergences: \[I(X; Y \mid Z) = H(X \mid Z) - H(X \mid Y, Z) = \sum_z p(z)\,D(P_{XY\mid z}\,\|\,P_{X\mid z}P_{Y\mid z}) \ge 0. \tag{5.12}\]
Chain rule for mutual information. What a pair \((Y, Z)\) tells you about \(X\) is what \(Y\) tells you, plus what \(Z\) adds once \(Y\) is known: \[I(X; Y, Z) = I(X; Y) + I(X; Z \mid Y). \tag{5.13}\]
Data-processing inequality. Suppose \(Z\) is computed from \(Y\) alone, possibly with fresh randomness, so that once you know \(Y\), also knowing \(X\) tells you nothing more about \(Z\). In other words, \(X\) and \(Z\) are independent given \(Y\). This is called a Markov chain and written \(X \to Y \to Z\). Then \(Z\) cannot know more about \(X\) than \(Y\) does: \[I(X; Z) \le I(X; Y). \tag{5.14}\]


5.4.3 Derivation
Mutual information is a KL divergence. The idea is to write both entropies as averages over the same pairs \((x, y)\), so that they can be combined term by term.

Start from \(H(X) - H(X \mid Y)\). The entropy \(H(X)\) is an average over \(x\), but since \(\sum_y p(x, y) = p(x)\) it can be written as an average over pairs: \(H(X) = \sum_{x, y}p(x, y)\log\frac{1}{p(x)}\). The conditional entropy is already an average over pairs, \(H(X \mid Y) = \sum_{x, y}p(x, y)\log\frac{1}{p(x \mid y)}\).
Subtract, combining the logs in each term: \(\sum_{x, y}p(x, y)\log\frac{p(x \mid y)}{p(x)}\).
Multiply the fraction inside the log by \(p(y)/p(y)\) and use \(p(x \mid y)\,p(y) = p(x, y)\): \(\frac{p(x \mid y)}{p(x)} = \frac{p(x, y)}{p(x)\,p(y)}\). The sum is now \(\sum_{x, y}p(x, y)\log\frac{p(x, y)}{p(x)\,p(y)}\), which is the definition of \(D(P_{XY}\,\|\,P_XP_Y)\).

Symmetry, non-negativity, independence. The expression at the end of step 3 does not change when you swap the roles of \(X\) and \(Y\), so \(I(X; Y) = I(Y; X)\), and running the same steps with the roles swapped gives \(H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)\). Gibbs’ inequality (Fact 2) gives \(I \ge 0\), with equality iff \(p(x, y) = p(x)\,p(y)\) for all pairs, which is the definition of independence. Since \(I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) \ge 0\), this also proves \(H(X \mid Y) \le H(X)\).
Chain rule for mutual information. The idea is to pass from knowing nothing to knowing \((Y, Z)\) through the intermediate stage of knowing only \(Y\).

By definition, \(I(X; Y, Z) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y, Z)\): the total drop in uncertainty.
Add and subtract the uncertainty at the intermediate stage, \(H(X \mid Y)\): \(\big[H(X) - H(X \mid Y)\big] + \big[H(X \mid Y) - H(X \mid Y, Z)\big]\).
The first bracket is the drop from learning \(Y\), which is \(I(X; Y)\). The second is the further drop from learning \(Z\) when \(Y\) is already known, which is \(I(X; Z \mid Y)\).

Data-processing inequality. The idea is to expand what the pair \((Y, Z)\) tells you about \(X\) in two orders. In one order, the part \(Z\) adds after \(Y\) is zero, because \(Z\) was computed from \(Y\).

Apply the chain rule with \(Z\) first and with \(Y\) first: \[I(X; Z) + I(X; Y \mid Z) = I(X; Y, Z) = I(X; Y) + I(X; Z \mid Y). \tag{5.15}\]
The Markov chain says \(X\) and \(Z\) are independent given \(Y\), so the conditional mutual information \(I(X; Z \mid Y)\) is zero (it is an average of KL divergences between identical distributions).
Hence \(I(X; Z) = I(X; Y) - I(X; Y \mid Z) \le I(X; Y)\), since conditional mutual information is non-negative.

Equality holds iff \(I(X; Y \mid Z) = 0\): once you know \(Z\), \(Y\) tells you nothing more about \(X\). Such a \(Z\) has kept everything in \(Y\) that matters for \(X\), and is called a sufficient statistic for \(X\).


5.4.4 Interpretation
Mutual information measures dependence of any kind, not only linear correlation. Two variables can have zero correlation and still be strongly dependent, as \(Y\) and \(Y^2\) are when \(Y\) is symmetric around zero. Their mutual information is positive in that case, and it is zero only under full independence.
The data-processing inequality says that no function of the data, however clever, can contain more information about the source than the data itself. Denoising, feature extraction and training a model are all processing steps. They can make information easier to use, but never larger.
Because \(I(X; Y) = D(P_{XY}\,\|\,P_XP_Y)\), every property of KL divergence in Divergences applies to mutual information. In particular, KL divergence has its own data-processing inequality there: passing two distributions through the same channel cannot increase the divergence between them. That inequality implies the one here.
Mutual information is an average over both \(x\) and \(y\). A small value can therefore hide a few outcomes in which \(Y\) reveals \(X\) completely, because those outcomes carry little weight in the average. Section 5.8 shows how far apart the average and the worst case can be.


5.4.5 Example: the keyword, then a noisy detector
In the spam table, the word reduced the uncertainty from \(H(X) = 0.5436\) bits to \(H(X \mid Y) = 0.25\) bits on average, so \(I(X; Y) = 0.5436 - 0.25 = 0.2936\) bits. The script computes the same value from the KL formula of Equation 5.11 and from \(H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)\).
Now suppose the keyword is detected by a sloppy tokenizer that gets the answer wrong with probability 0.1, whatever the email. Call its output \(Z\). A channel on \(\{0, 1\}\) that flips its input with a fixed probability is a binary symmetric channel, studied in the next section, so \(Z\) is \(Y\) passed through a binary symmetric channel with flip probability 0.1. The tokenizer looks only at the word, not at the label, so \(X \to Y \to Z\) is a Markov chain, and the data-processing inequality predicts \(I(X; Z) \le I(X; Y)\). The script finds \(I(X; Z) = 0.1668\) bits. Since \(0.1668/0.2936 \approx 0.57\), the noisy feature carries 57% of the information of the clean one: a 10% error rate in the detector costs over 40% of the information.


5.4.6 Check yourself

If \(Z = g(Y)\) for an invertible function \(g\), what is \(I(X; Z)\)? (Equal to \(I(X; Y)\). Apply the data-processing inequality to \(X \to Y \to Z\), which gives \(\le\), and to \(X \to Z \to Y\), which is also a Markov chain because \(Y = g^{-1}(Z)\) is computed from \(Z\), and gives \(\ge\).)
Can \(I(X; Y)\) exceed \(H(X)\)? (No. \(I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y)\) and \(H(X \mid Y) \ge 0\): an observation cannot remove more uncertainty than there was.)

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.5 Channels and capacity

5.5.1 Context
A channel turns an input \(X\) into a random output \(Y\): a noisy storage device, a communication link, a lossy sensor. You control the input distribution but not the noise. How much information can one use of the channel carry at best? That maximum is the capacity. Shannon’s channel coding theorem says it is exactly the rate, in bits per channel use, at which you can send data with an error probability as small as you like, using long enough codes. This chapter does not prove that theorem; it computes the capacity, which is the number the theorem is about.


5.5.2 Statement
A channel is fixed, but how much information passes through it depends on how often you send each input, the prior \(\pi\). So the capacity is the mutual information between input and output, maximized over the input prior. For a channel \(C[x, y] = p(y \mid x)\), \[\mathcal C = \max_{\pi}I(X; Y), \qquad X \sim \pi,\ Y \mid X = x \sim C[x, \cdot]. \tag{5.16}\] The binary symmetric channel \(\mathrm{BSC}(p)\) has inputs and outputs in \(\{0, 1\}\) and flips the input with probability \(p\). Its capacity is one bit, the most a binary output can carry, minus the entropy of the noise: \[\mathcal C_{\mathrm{BSC}}(p) = 1 - h(p), \tag{5.17}\] attained by the uniform input.


5.5.3 Derivation
The idea is to use the form \(I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)\): the uncertainty in the output, minus the part of it that comes from the noise. The noise part turns out not to depend on the input prior, so you only have to make the output as uncertain as possible. Let the input prior be \(q = \Pr[X = 1]\).

Use the symmetric form of mutual information: \(I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)\).
Given \(X = x\), the output equals \(x\) with probability \(1 - p\) and is flipped with probability \(p\), so \(H(Y \mid X = x) = h(p)\) for both inputs. Averaging over \(x\) gives \(H(Y \mid X) = h(p)\), whatever \(q\) is.
\(Y\) takes two values, so by the entropy upper bound \(H(Y) \le \log 2 = 1\), with equality iff \(Y\) is uniform.
The output is 1 if the input is 1 and not flipped, or the input is 0 and flipped, so \(\Pr[Y = 1] = q(1 - p) + (1 - q)p\). At \(q = \frac12\) this is \(\frac12(1 - p) + \frac12 p = \frac12\), so the uniform input makes \(Y\) uniform and the bound in step 3 is attained.
Hence \(\max_q I(X; Y) = 1 - h(p)\).



5.5.4 Interpretation
Figure 5.3 (left) shows \(I(X; Y)\) as a function of the input prior \(q\): a concave hump peaking at \(q = \frac12\) for every \(p\). Away from the peak you lose a lot. At \(p = 0.11\) and \(q = 0.2\), the output is 1 with probability \(0.2(0.89) + 0.8(0.11) = 0.266\), so \(H(Y) = h(0.266) = 0.8357\) and the channel carries only \(0.8357 - 0.4999 = 0.3358\) bits, against 0.5001 at the uniform input.
The right panel shows the capacity against \(p\). It is zero at \(p = \frac12\), where the output is a fair coin flip whatever the input, so the output is independent of the input. It is symmetric about \(\frac12\), because \(h(p) = h(1 - p)\): a channel that flips almost always is as good as one that never flips, since the receiver can flip every output back.
For channels without this symmetry, the maximum over \(\pi\) has no closed form. The Blahut–Arimoto algorithm computes it numerically, by alternately improving the prior and the receiver’s best reading of the output until neither changes. The script uses it to check Equation 5.17, and to compute two capacities in the exercises.






Figure 5.3: Left: mutual information of a binary symmetric channel as a function of the input prior, for several flip probabilities; every curve peaks at \(q = \frac12\). Right: the capacity \(1 - h(p)\) against \(p\), with the min-capacity of Section 5.7 for comparison.





5.5.5 Example: a storage medium that flips bits
A cheap storage medium flips each stored bit independently with probability \(p = 0.11\). Its capacity is \(1 - h(0.11) = 1 - 0.4999 = 0.5001\) bits per stored bit. So with good error-correcting codes you can store about one bit of data per two raw bits, with an error rate as small as you like, and by the channel coding theorem no code can do better. At \(p = 0.25\) the capacity drops to \(1 - h(0.25) = 1 - 0.8113 = 0.1887\). Since \(1/0.1887 \approx 5.3\), that is about five raw bits per data bit.


5.5.6 Check yourself

Why does the derivation not need to compute \(H(Y)\) for a general \(q\)? (Because \(H(Y \mid X)\) does not depend on \(q\), so maximizing \(I\) means maximizing \(H(Y)\), and its largest possible value 1 is attainable.)
What is the capacity of a channel whose output is independent of its input? (Zero: \(I(X; Y) = 0\) for every prior, because mutual information is zero exactly under independence.)

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.6 Min-entropy and guessing

5.6.1 Context
Shannon entropy counts the bits needed to describe a value on average. A different question is how likely you are to guess it in one try. A password chosen by a person might have high entropy, because most people choose something unusual, yet be guessed one time in ten, because one popular choice dominates. For the one-try question, all that matters is the probability of the most likely value: that is the best you can do with one guess.


5.6.2 Statement
The vulnerability of \(X\) is the success probability of the best single guess, the largest probability of any value. To put it on the same bit scale as entropy, take its negative log; that is the min-entropy: \[V(X) = \max_x p(x), \qquad H_\infty(X) = -\log V(X). \tag{5.18}\] A fair coin has \(V = \frac12\) and \(H_\infty = 1\) bit, the same as its Shannon entropy. In general, min-entropy uses the surprisal of the most likely outcome, which is the smallest surprisal, while Shannon entropy averages all surprisals. So min-entropy is never larger than Shannon entropy: \[H_\infty(X) \le H(X) \le \log\lvert\mathcal X\rvert, \tag{5.19}\] with equality in the first inequality iff \(X\) is uniform on its support, the set of values it takes with positive probability.


5.6.3 Derivation
The best single guess. If you guess \(g\), you are right with probability \(p(g)\). The best you can do is pick \(g\) with the largest \(p(g)\), so the optimal success probability is \(\max_x p(x)\).
\(H_\infty \le H\). The idea is that an average of numbers is at least their smallest value.

Every outcome has \(p(x) \le \max_{x'}p(x') = V(X)\), so its surprisal satisfies \(\log\frac{1}{p(x)} \ge \log\frac{1}{V(X)}\).
Average over \(X\): \(H(X) = \mathbb E[\log\frac{1}{p(X)}] \ge \log\frac{1}{V(X)} = H_\infty(X)\).
Equality needs every surprisal to equal the smallest one, \(p(x) = V(X)\) for every \(x\) with \(p(x) > 0\): all outcomes in the support are equally likely.



5.6.4 Interpretation
Min-entropy has a direct reading: \(H_\infty\) is the number of bits of a uniform distribution that is exactly as easy to guess as \(X\). A uniform \(k\)-bit string is guessed in one try with probability \(2^{-k}\), so a value with \(H_\infty = k\) bits is as hard to guess in one try as a uniform \(k\)-bit string, no matter how large \(H(X)\) is.
Both entropies belong to one family. The Rényi entropy of order \(\alpha\) is \(H_\alpha(X) = \frac{1}{1 - \alpha}\log\sum_x p(x)^\alpha\). As \(\alpha\) grows, the sum \(\sum_x p(x)^\alpha\) is dominated more and more by the largest probability, and as \(\alpha \to \infty\) the formula tends to \(-\log\max_x p(x) = H_\infty\). As \(\alpha \to 1\) the formula becomes \(0/0\), and its limit is Shannon’s \(H\). This parallels the family of Rényi divergences in Divergences.
For a coin, Figure 5.1 shows the gap. The min-entropy \(H_\infty = -\log\max(p, 1 - p)\) is smooth on each side of \(\frac12\) but has a kink there, where the most likely outcome switches from tails to heads, and it lies below \(h(p)\).


5.6.5 Example: a PIN with one popular choice
A uniform 4-digit PIN has \(H = H_\infty = \log_2 10{,}000 = 13.2877\) bits, and a single guess succeeds with probability \(10^{-4}\). Now suppose 10% of people choose 1234 and the rest choose uniformly among the other 9,999 PINs. The script gives two very different numbers.
The Shannon entropy is \(H = 12.4278\) bits, less than a bit below the uniform case. You can see where it comes from with the chain rule: first reveal whether the PIN is 1234, which costs \(h(0.1) = 0.4690\) bits, and then, in the 90% of cases where it is not, reveal which of the 9,999 others it is, which costs \(\log_2 9{,}999\) bits. That gives \(0.4690 + 0.9\log_2 9{,}999 = 0.4690 + 11.9588 = 12.4278\).
The min-entropy is \(H_\infty = \log_2 10 = 3.3219\) bits, because the best guess, “1234”, succeeds with probability \(0.1\), and \(-\log_2 0.1 = \log_2 10\).
The Shannon entropy says this PIN distribution is almost as good as uniform. The min-entropy says that one guess in ten succeeds. If the guesser gets one try, only the second number matters.


5.6.6 Check yourself

Which is larger for any \(X\): \(V(X)\) or \(2^{-H(X)}\)? (\(V(X)\). \(H_\infty \le H\) means \(-\log V \le H\), so \(\log V \ge -H\) and \(V \ge 2^{-H}\).)
Give a distribution on a million values whose Shannon entropy is above 10 bits but whose min-entropy is 1 bit. (Probability \(\frac12\) on one value and \(\frac12\) spread uniformly over the other 999,999. The best guess wins with probability \(\frac12\), so \(H_\infty = 1\), while by the chain rule \(H = 1 + \frac12\log_2 999{,}999 \approx 10.97\): one bit to say which half, then, half the time, the index among 999,999.)

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.7 Conditional min-entropy and min-entropy leakage

5.7.1 Context
Now the guesser sees an observation \(Y\) before guessing the hidden value \(X\), which this section calls the secret. How much does that help? The natural answer, from Smith (2009), keeps the meaning of vulnerability as a success probability: the posterior vulnerability is the success probability of the best guessing strategy that may depend on what was observed. Comparing it with the vulnerability before the observation gives the min-entropy leakage, and maximizing that over priors gives the min-capacity, the one-guess analogue of channel capacity.


5.7.2 Statement
The guesser who sees \(y\) should guess the value of \(X\) that is most likely given \(y\). Its success probability is then the average over \(y\) of \(\max_x p(x \mid y)\), and since \(p(y)\max_x p(x \mid y) = \max_x p(x, y)\), this is the sum of the largest entry in each column of the joint table. For a joint distribution \(p(x, y)\), the posterior vulnerability and the conditional min-entropy are \[V(X \mid Y) = \sum_y\max_x p(x, y), \qquad H_\infty(X \mid Y) = -\log V(X \mid Y). \tag{5.20}\] How much the observation helps is the factor by which it multiplies the chance of a correct guess, measured in bits by its log. For a prior \(\pi\) and channel \(C\), the min-entropy leakage is \[\mathcal L(\pi, C) = H_\infty(X) - H_\infty(X \mid Y) = \log\frac{V(X \mid Y)}{V(X)}. \tag{5.21}\] The leakage depends on the prior. Its largest value over all priors, the min-capacity, depends only on the channel. It has a closed form, the log of the sum of the column maxima of the channel table, and it is attained at the uniform prior: \[\mathcal{ML}(C) = \max_\pi\mathcal L(\pi, C) = \log\sum_y\max_x C[x, y]. \tag{5.22}\] It satisfies \(0 \le \mathcal{ML}(C) \le \log\min(\lvert\mathcal X\rvert, \lvert\mathcal Y\rvert)\): an observation never hurts the guesser, and it cannot multiply the chance of success by more than the number of possible secrets or the number of possible observations.


5.7.3 Derivation
Posterior vulnerability is the success of the best strategy. The idea is that the guesser’s choice for one observation does not affect its success on any other observation, so it can make the best choice column by column.

A strategy assigns a guess \(g(y)\) to each observation \(y\). It succeeds when \(X = g(Y)\), which happens with probability \(\sum_y p(g(y), y)\): the strategy picks one cell from each column of the joint table, and its success is the sum of the picked cells.
Each column can be optimized separately, since \(g(y)\) affects only the term for \(y\). The best choice in column \(y\) is the row with the largest entry. Dividing a column by \(p(y)\) does not change which row is largest, so this is also the value of \(x\) with the largest posterior probability \(p(x \mid y)\), the maximum a posteriori (MAP) guess \(\arg\max_x p(x, y) = \arg\max_x p(x \mid y)\).
So the best success probability is \(\sum_y\max_x p(x, y)\), which is Equation 5.20. Writing \(p(x, y) = p(y)\,p(x \mid y)\) gives the equivalent form \(V(X \mid Y) = \sum_y p(y)\max_x p(x \mid y)\): the average over \(y\) of the vulnerability \(V(X \mid Y = y)\) of the posterior distribution.

Min-capacity. The idea is to bound the posterior vulnerability by pulling the prior out of each column maximum, and then to notice that the uniform prior loses nothing in that step.

Write \(p(x, y) = \pi(x)C[x, y]\). In each column, the largest product is at most the largest prior times the largest channel entry: \(\max_x\pi(x)C[x, y] \le \big(\max_x\pi(x)\big)\big(\max_x C[x, y]\big) = V(X)\max_x C[x, y]\).
Sum over \(y\) and divide by \(V(X)\): \(\frac{V(X \mid Y)}{V(X)} \le \sum_y\max_x C[x, y]\), for every prior. Taking logs, \(\mathcal L(\pi, C) \le \log\sum_y\max_x C[x, y]\).
At the uniform prior \(\pi(x) = 1/\lvert\mathcal X\rvert\), the inequality in step 1 is an equality, because the constant factor \(\pi(x) = V(X)\) comes out of the max. So the bound is attained, and Equation 5.22 follows.
Range. For the upper bound, there are two ways to bound the sum of column maxima. Each column maximum is at most 1, so the sum is at most \(\lvert\mathcal Y\rvert\). Each column maximum is also at most its column sum, and all column sums together add up to \(\sum_x\sum_y C[x, y] = \lvert\mathcal X\rvert\), because each of the \(\lvert\mathcal X\rvert\) rows sums to 1. For the lower bound, fix any row \(x_0\): each column maximum is at least \(C[x_0, y]\), and these add up to 1 across the row, so the sum of column maxima is at least 1 and \(\mathcal{ML} \ge \log 1 = 0\).



5.7.4 Interpretation
Leakage is a ratio of success probabilities on a log scale: \(\mathcal L = 1\) bit means the observation doubles the chance of a correct first guess, and 2 bits means it quadruples it. That is a statement an engineer can act on, and it is why min-entropy is the usual measure in the field of quantitative information flow, which studies how much a program’s outputs reveal about its secret inputs.
Smith’s definition is not the average of \(H_\infty(X \mid Y = y)\). It averages the posterior vulnerabilities and then takes the log, \(-\log\sum_y p(y)V(X \mid Y = y)\), rather than averaging the logs, \(\sum_y p(y)\big(-\log V(X \mid Y = y)\big)\). These differ, and Jensen’s inequality (Fact 1, in the mirror version for the convex \(-\log\): the \(-\log\) of an average is at most the average of \(-\log\)) says Smith’s value is never larger. The reason to prefer Smith’s version is its meaning: it is the log of an actual success probability, that of the MAP guesser. The average of logs is not the log of any success probability.
The min-capacity is the worst case over the prior. That matters whenever you do not know the prior: a single number, computed from the channel alone, bounds the leakage for every prior. It is also cheap to compute, one maximum per column, where the Shannon capacity needs an iterative algorithm.


5.7.5 Example: walking through a small table
A secret \(X\) takes four values with prior \(\pi = (0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1)\). An observation \(Y\) takes three values, through the channel in Table 5.3.

With the observation, guess the row with the largest entry in each column (in bold): \(x_1\) on \(y_1\), \(x_2\) on \(y_2\), \(x_3\) on \(y_3\). Notice that on \(y_3\) the guesser picks \(x_3\) although the channel entry \(C[x_4, y_3] = 0.8\) is larger than \(C[x_3, y_3] = 0.5\). The guesser compares joint probabilities, not channel entries, and \(x_3\) is twice as likely as \(x_4\) a priori, which more than makes up the difference: \(0.2 \times 0.5 = 0.10\) beats \(0.1 \times 0.8 = 0.08\).

Min-capacity. The column maxima of the channel \(C\) (not of the joint table) are 0.8, 0.8, 0.8, so \(\mathcal{ML}(C) = \log_2(0.8 + 0.8 + 0.8) = \log_2 2.4 = 1.2630\) bits. Under the uniform prior, the leakage is exactly this value, and the script confirms that no prior on a grid of step 0.05 does better. Their \(-\log_2\) are 0.1293, 0.8745 and 1.0704 bits, and averaging these with weights \(p(y) = 0.35, 0.44, 0.21\) gives 0.6548 bits, larger than Smith’s 0.5995, as Jensen predicts.

5.7.6 Check yourself

What is the min-capacity of the binary symmetric channel? (\(\log_2(2\max(p, 1 - p))\): each of the two columns has maximum \(\max(p, 1 - p)\). At \(p = 0.11\) it is \(\log_2 1.78 = 0.8319\) bits, against a Shannon capacity of 0.5001. It is the dashed curve in Figure 5.3.)
Why can the min-entropy leakage for a given prior be smaller than the min-capacity? (A skewed prior already makes the best blind guess good, so the observation adds less. Here 0.7225 bits at the given prior against 1.2630 at the uniform one.)

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.8 Shannon leakage versus min-entropy leakage

5.8.1 Context
Shannon leakage, the mutual information \(I(X; Y)\), and min-entropy leakage \(\mathcal L\) both measure how much an observation reveals about a secret. They often agree. When they don’t, the disagreement is large, and it is always the same kind: a channel that reveals the secret completely on a few outcomes and nothing on the rest. Shannon leakage averages logs, so it gives those rare outcomes little weight; min-entropy leakage asks how much the guesser’s success grows, and a rare full reveal can make it grow a lot. This section works through such channels.


5.8.2 Statement
Let \(X\) be uniform on \(n\)-bit strings, and consider two families of deterministic channels, whose output is a fixed function of the input. The first reveals part of the secret every time; the second reveals all of it, but only rarely.

reveal-low(\(m\)) always outputs the lowest \(m\) bits of \(X\).
reveal-if-zero(\(j\)) outputs \(X\) itself if its lowest \(j\) bits are all zero, which happens with probability \(2^{-j}\), and a fixed symbol \(\perp\) otherwise.

For the first family both leakages equal \(m\). For the second, the Shannon leakage is about \(n\) bits times the probability \(2^{-j}\) of a reveal, plus a small term, while the min-entropy leakage is about \(n - j\) bits: \[\text{reveal-low}(m):\quad I(X; Y) = \mathcal L = m, \tag{5.23}\] \[\text{reveal-if-zero}(j),\ j \ge 1:\quad I(X; Y) = 2^{-j}n + (1 - 2^{-j})\log\frac{1}{1 - 2^{-j}}, \qquad \mathcal L = \log\big(2^{n-j} + 1\big). \tag{5.24}\]


5.8.3 Derivation
Two observations about deterministic channels make both leakages easy to compute. For Shannon leakage: the output is fixed once the input is known, so \(H(Y \mid X) = 0\) and \(I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) = H(Y)\). For min-entropy leakage: under the uniform prior, \(V(X) = 2^{-n}\), and each column of the joint table contains only entries \(2^{-n}\) (for inputs that produce that output) or 0. So each column maximum is \(2^{-n}\), and \(V(X \mid Y) = 2^{-n}\times(\text{number of distinct outputs})\). The ratio is \(V(X \mid Y)/V(X) = \text{number of distinct outputs}\), so \(\mathcal L = \log(\text{number of distinct outputs})\).
reveal-low(\(m\)). The lowest \(m\) bits of a uniform string are uniform on \(2^m\) values, so \(I(X; Y) = H(Y) = m\). There are \(2^m\) distinct outputs, so \(\mathcal L = m\).
reveal-if-zero(\(j\)).

Count the outputs and their probabilities. There are \(2^{n-j}\) strings whose lowest \(j\) bits are zero (the other \(n - j\) bits are free). Each is output as itself, with probability \(2^{-n}\). Every other string gives the output \(\perp\), which therefore has probability \(1 - 2^{n-j}\cdot2^{-n} = 1 - 2^{-j}\).
Compute \(H(Y)\) as the average surprisal. The \(2^{n-j}\) revealed outputs each have surprisal \(\log 2^n = n\), and \(\perp\) has surprisal \(\log\frac{1}{1 - 2^{-j}}\). So \(H(Y) = 2^{n-j}\cdot2^{-n}\log2^n + (1 - 2^{-j})\log\frac{1}{1 - 2^{-j}} = 2^{-j}n + (1 - 2^{-j})\log\frac{1}{1 - 2^{-j}}\).
The number of distinct outputs is the \(2^{n-j}\) revealed strings plus \(\perp\), which is \(2^{n-j} + 1\), and its log gives \(\mathcal L\).

The script checks both closed forms against the general formulas applied to the explicit channel matrices for \(n = 6\); they agree to \(7.8\times10^{-16}\), which is rounding error.


5.8.4 Interpretation
Figure 5.5 plots the two leakages against each other for \(n = 64\). The reveal-low family lies on the diagonal: Shannon and min-entropy agree. The reveal-if-zero family hugs the top-left corner: almost no Shannon leakage, almost total min-entropy leakage.
The reason is where the logarithm sits. Shannon leakage averages the log over outcomes, so an outcome of probability \(2^{-j}\) that reveals \(n\) bits contributes only \(2^{-j}n\). Min-entropy leakage takes the log of an averaged probability. The same outcome raises the guessing success from \(2^{-n}\) to more than \(2^{-j}\), because the guesser wins whenever the reveal happens, and \(\log(2^{-j}/2^{-n}) = n - j\): almost \(n - j\) bits.






Figure 5.5: Shannon leakage against min-entropy leakage for two families of deterministic channels on a uniform 64-bit secret. Revealing the low \(m\) bits gives equal leakages (diagonal). Revealing the whole secret with probability \(2^{-j}\) gives a small Shannon leakage but a min-entropy leakage close to \(64 - j\).





5.8.5 Example: two channels that Shannon ranks the wrong way
Take \(n = 64\) and compare reveal-if-zero(3), which outputs the whole secret one time in eight, with reveal-low(9).
For reveal-if-zero(3), the Shannon leakage is \(2^{-3}\cdot64 + \frac78\log_2\frac87 = 8 + 0.1686 = 8.1686\) bits. The guesser wins whenever the secret is revealed, and otherwise has one chance in \(2^{64} - 2^{61}\), so its success is just above \(\frac18 = 0.1250\); in bits, \(\log_2(2^{61} + 1)\) is 61 to many decimal places. For reveal-low(9), both leakages are 9 bits, and the guesser, knowing 9 of the 64 bits, must still guess the other 55, so it succeeds with probability \(2^{-55} \approx 2.78\times10^{-17}\). Table 5.5 puts these side by side.

By Shannon leakage, reveal-low(9) is the leakier channel. By one-guess success, reveal-if-zero(3) is worse by a factor of more than \(10^{15}\): \(0.125/(2.78\times10^{-17}) \approx 4.5\times10^{15}\). Smith (2009) used a pair of programs like these to argue that Shannon leakage is the wrong measure for one-try guessing.
The extreme case: reveal the secret only if it is all zeros. Set \(j = n\): the channel outputs \(X\) if \(X = 0\cdots0\) and \(\perp\) otherwise. For a 4-bit secret, the output reveals the secret with probability \(\frac1{16}\), so the Shannon leakage is \(H(Y) = h(1/16) = 0.3373\) bits. The min-entropy leakage is exactly 1 bit: the guesser wins if it sees \(0000\), and otherwise guesses one of the 15 remaining values, winning with probability \(\frac1{16} + \frac{15}{16}\cdot\frac1{15} = \frac2{16}\). Its success doubles from \(\frac1{16}\) to \(\frac2{16}\), and \(\log_2 2 = 1\). For a 32-bit secret the Shannon leakage falls to \(h(2^{-32}) = 7.786\times10^{-9}\) bits, and the min-entropy leakage stays at 1 bit, by the same doubling argument.
Both numbers are small, and both miss something: for the one secret value \(0000\), the channel reveals everything, \(H_\infty(X \mid Y = 0000) = 0\). Any measure that averages over the secret, Shannon or min-entropy, can hide a value that is fully exposed, because that value carries only its small share of the average. A worst-case question (“how much can the observation reveal about any single secret value?”) needs a worst-case measure, and later parts build one.


5.8.6 Check yourself

For reveal-if-zero(\(j\)) at \(n = 64\), roughly where does the Shannon leakage drop below 1 bit? (Between \(j = 6\) and \(j = 7\): the main term \(2^{-j}\cdot64\) equals 1 at \(j = 6\), where the total is just above 1 bit because of the small \(\perp\) term. That is the point labelled \(j = 6\) in Figure 5.5.)
Can a channel have min-entropy leakage 0 but positive Shannon leakage? (Yes. If the MAP guess is the same for every \(y\), as when one secret value is very likely a priori, then \(V(X \mid Y) = V(X)\), even though \(Y\) changes the posterior.)

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.9 Fano’s inequality

5.9.1 Context
Mutual information also gives lower bounds: statements that no estimator can do better than some error rate. You need these whenever you want to show that a problem is hard, rather than that a method is good. Fano’s inequality is the basic tool. It says that if \(X\) is still uncertain after seeing \(Y\), every guess of \(X\) from \(Y\) must often be wrong. The reason is that an estimator with a small error rate would leave little uncertainty: if you knew you were usually right, you would be nearly certain of \(X\).


5.9.2 Statement
Let \(X\) take values in a finite set of size \(M\), and let \(\hat X\) be any estimate of \(X\) computed from \(Y\) (deterministically or with extra randomness), with error probability \(P_e = \Pr[\hat X \ne X]\). Fano’s inequality bounds how much uncertainty a guess with this error rate can leave. Describing \(X\) given the guess takes at most two pieces: one binary piece saying whether the guess was right, worth at most \(h(P_e)\) bits, and, in the fraction \(P_e\) of cases where it was wrong, which of the other \(M - 1\) values \(X\) is, worth at most \(\log(M - 1)\) bits. So \[H(X \mid Y) \le h(P_e) + P_e\log(M - 1). \tag{5.25}\] Using \(h(P_e) \le 1\) and \(\log(M - 1) \le \log M\) gives \(H(X \mid Y) \le 1 + P_e\log M\), and solving for \(P_e\) gives the weaker but explicit form \[P_e \ge \frac{H(X \mid Y) - 1}{\log M}. \tag{5.26}\]


5.9.3 Derivation
Introduce the error indicator \(E = \mathbf 1[\hat X \ne X]\), which is 1 when the guess is wrong and 0 when it is right, so \(\Pr[E = 1] = P_e\). The idea is to compute the uncertainty of the pair \((E, X)\) given \(\hat X\), written \(H(E, X \mid \hat X)\), in two ways with the chain rule. Revealing \(X\) first makes \(E\) free; revealing \(E\) first splits \(X\)’s uncertainty into the “right” and “wrong” cases, which are easy to bound. Every entropy below is conditioned on \(\hat X\).

First order: \(X\), then \(E\). \(H(E, X \mid \hat X) = H(X \mid \hat X) + H(E \mid X, \hat X)\). Given both \(X\) and \(\hat X\), you know whether they differ, so \(E\) is determined and the last term is 0.
Second order: \(E\), then \(X\). \(H(E, X \mid \hat X) = H(E \mid \hat X) + H(X \mid E, \hat X)\).
Bound \(H(E \mid \hat X)\). Conditioning reduces entropy on average, so \(H(E \mid \hat X) \le H(E)\), and \(E\) is a Bernoulli variable with parameter \(P_e\), so \(H(E) = h(P_e)\).
Bound \(H(X \mid E, \hat X)\) by splitting on \(E\). If \(E = 0\), then \(X = \hat X\) and there is no uncertainty left. If \(E = 1\), then \(X\) is one of the \(M - 1\) values other than \(\hat X\), so its entropy is at most \(\log(M - 1)\) by the entropy upper bound. Averaging over \(E\): \(H(X \mid E, \hat X) \le (1 - P_e)\cdot0 + P_e\log(M - 1)\).
Combine steps 1–4. The two orders give the same quantity, so \(H(X \mid \hat X) = H(E \mid \hat X) + H(X \mid E, \hat X) \le h(P_e) + P_e\log(M - 1)\).
Replace \(\hat X\) by \(Y\). The estimate is computed from \(Y\), so \(X \to Y \to \hat X\) is a Markov chain, and the data-processing inequality gives \(I(X; \hat X) \le I(X; Y)\). Writing both sides as \(H(X)\) minus a conditional entropy, this is the same as \(H(X \mid Y) \le H(X \mid \hat X)\), and the bound of step 5 carries over.



5.9.4 Interpretation
The right side of Equation 5.25 increases with \(P_e\) on \([0, (M - 1)/M]\), the range from a perfect estimator to one that guesses blindly. So you can invert it numerically: the Fano bound is the smallest \(P_e\) that satisfies the inequality for the given \(H(X \mid Y)\). The script finds it by bisection, halving an interval that contains it until it is small enough.
When it is tight. Equality needs step 4 to be tight: when the guess is wrong, the true value must be uniform over the other \(M - 1\) values. The \(M\)-ary symmetric channel, which keeps the input with probability \(1 - \varepsilon\) and otherwise outputs one of the other \(M - 1\) symbols uniformly, has exactly this structure. For it, given the output, the input is the output itself with probability \(1 - \varepsilon\) and otherwise uniform over the rest, so \(H(X \mid Y) = h(\varepsilon) + \varepsilon\log(M - 1)\), and the MAP guess (the output itself) errs with probability \(\varepsilon\). Fano’s bound is exact (Figure 5.6, left).
When it is loose. If errors are concentrated on a few wrong values, \(H(X \mid Y)\) is small even when \(P_e\) is not, because the leftover uncertainty after a wrong guess is small. The shift channel, which outputs \(x + 1 \bmod M\) instead of \(x\) with probability \(\varepsilon\), has the same MAP error \(\varepsilon\) (for \(\varepsilon \le \frac12\)). But given the output, the input is one of only two values, so \(H(X \mid Y) = h(\varepsilon)\) only. At \(M = 8\) and \(\varepsilon = 0.2\), Fano’s bound is 0.2000 for the symmetric channel, equal to the MAP error, but only 0.0954 for the shift channel, against a MAP error of 0.2000 (Figure 5.6, right). The weak form Equation 5.26 gives 0.0945 and 0 respectively. For the symmetric channel, \(H(X \mid Y) = h(0.2) + 0.2\log_2 7 = 0.7219 + 0.5615 = 1.2834\), and \((1.2834 - 1)/3 = 0.0945\). For the shift channel, \(H(X \mid Y) = h(0.2) = 0.7219\) is below 1, so the weak form gives a negative number, which says nothing beyond \(P_e \ge 0\). The weak form pays for replacing \(h(P_e)\) by 1, and is useless whenever \(H(X \mid Y) \le 1\).






Figure 5.6: MAP error against Fano’s lower bound, for \(M = 8\) and a uniform \(X\), as the noise level \(\varepsilon\) grows. Left: on the symmetric channel the bound is exact. Right: on the shift channel, where errors go to a single wrong value, the bound is loose and the weak form is zero.





5.9.5 Example: how hard is a classification problem?
Eight classes and one bit. A label \(X\) is uniform over \(M = 8\) classes, so \(H(X) = \log_2 8 = 3\) bits, and you know the features \(Y\) carry at most \(I(X; Y) \le 1\) bit about it. Then \(H(X \mid Y) = 3 - I(X; Y) \ge 2\) bits. Every classifier, however it is trained, therefore has error at least the Fano bound at \(H(X \mid Y) = 2\), the \(P_e\) that solves \(h(P_e) + P_e\log_2 7 = 2\): 0.3730. The weak form gives \((2 - 1)/3 = 0.3333\).
Fano’s method for estimation. The same idea shows that estimating a parameter needs many samples. Turn estimation into identification: pick \(M\) candidate parameter values \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_M\) that are far apart, so that estimating the parameter well would identify which candidate it is. Let \(X\) be a uniformly random index, and draw \(n\) independent samples \(Y_1, \dots, Y_n\) (together written \(Y^n\)) from \(P_{\theta_X}\). If the samples carry little information about the index, Fano says no estimator can identify it, so none can estimate the parameter well. The argument has three steps.

Information adds over independent samples. Given \(X\) the samples are independent, so the chain rule gives \(H(Y^n \mid X) = \sum_i H(Y_i \mid X)\) exactly. Without conditioning on \(X\), the chain rule plus “conditioning reduces entropy” gives only \(H(Y^n) \le \sum_i H(Y_i)\). Subtracting the first from the second, \(I(X; Y^n) \le \sum_i I(X; Y_i) = n\,I(X; Y_1)\), since all samples have the same distribution.
Each sample carries at most the largest pairwise KL divergence. Let \(\bar P = \frac1M\sum_x P_{\theta_x}\) be the average of the candidate distributions, which is the distribution of \(Y_1\) when the index is random. By the KL form of Equation 5.11, \(I(X; Y_1)\) is the average KL divergence from each candidate to this average, \(\frac1M\sum_x D(P_{\theta_x}\,\|\,\bar P)\). Expanding the logs shows that for any distribution \(Q\), \(\frac1M\sum_x D(P_{\theta_x}\,\|\,Q) = \frac1M\sum_x D(P_{\theta_x}\,\|\,\bar P) + D(\bar P\,\|\,Q)\), so the average divergence to \(\bar P\) is the smallest average divergence to any \(Q\). Taking \(Q = P_{\theta_{x'}}\) gives \(I(X; Y_1) \le \frac1M\sum_x D(P_{\theta_x}\,\|\,P_{\theta_{x'}})\) for each \(x'\), and hence \(I(X; Y_1) \le \kappa = \max_{x, x'}D(P_{\theta_x}\,\|\,P_{\theta_{x'}})\).
Apply Fano. The index is uniform, so \(H(X) = \log M\) and \(H(X \mid Y^n) = \log M - I(X; Y^n) \ge \log M - n\kappa\). Putting this into Equation 5.26 gives \[P_e \ge 1 - \frac{n\kappa + 1}{\log M}. \tag{5.27}\]

With \(M = 1024\) candidates (\(\log M = 10\) bits) whose sample distributions are within \(\kappa = 0.01\) bits of each other, \(n = 100\) samples leave \(P_e \ge 1 - (100 \times 0.01 + 1)/10 = 0.8000\), and even \(n = 400\) samples leave \(P_e \ge 1 - (4 + 1)/10 = 0.5000\). Choosing the candidates well, so that they are many and far apart yet hard to tell apart, is the art of the method; Wainwright (2019) works through many cases.


5.9.6 Check yourself

If \(X\) is a deterministic function of \(Y\), what does Fano’s inequality say? (\(H(X \mid Y) = 0\), so it allows \(P_e = 0\), as it should.)
Why does step 6 of the derivation need the data-processing inequality? (Steps 1–5 only bound \(H(X \mid \hat X)\). The bound must be stated in terms of what the estimator sees, \(Y\), and the data-processing inequality says \(\hat X\) knows no more about \(X\) than \(Y\) does.)

Five lessons come out of these runs. The first is that two formulas give one number: mutual information computed as an entropy difference and as a KL divergence agree, which is a useful check on any implementation. The second is that the closed forms are right. Blahut–Arimoto, which knows nothing about the binary symmetric channel, finds \(1 - h(p)\) and the uniform input, and the leakage closed forms match the explicit matrices. The third is that vulnerability is a real success rate: the simulated MAP guesser wins at the rate \(V(X \mid Y)\) predicts. The fourth is that Shannon and min-entropy measure different things. They can rank channels in opposite orders, and neither sees a single exposed secret value. The last is that Fano’s bound is tight only when errors are spread out over the wrong values; concentrated errors make it loose.

Success of the MAP guesser

\(\mathcal L = \log V(X \mid Y)/V(X)\)
Factor by which guessing success grows


Min-capacity
\(\mathcal{ML}(C) = \log\sum_y\max_x C[x, y]\)
Attained at the uniform prior; \(\le \log\min(\lvert\mathcal X\rvert, \lvert\mathcal Y\rvert)\)


Fano
\(H(X \mid Y) \le h(P_e) + P_e\log(M - 1)\)

Rules of thumb

Shannon quantities average \(\log\) over outcomes; min-entropy quantities take \(\log\) of a best-case probability. When a rare outcome reveals a lot, the two disagree, by orders of magnitude.
Both are averages over the secret. Neither tells you how exposed a single secret value is.
To prove an estimator must fail, bound the mutual information between the unknown and the data, then apply Fano.
Processing never adds information: compute the bound on the raw observation, and it holds for everything computed from it.

Practice. Exercises for this chapter, each with a worked solution, are in the exercise book.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.1 Why this matters
Training a model means minimizing an average loss over the training set. Two questions come up every time you do it. The first is how fast the optimizer gets there. Gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent (SGD) are the workhorses, and you want to know how many steps they need, how to pick the step size, and what it costs you that the gradients SGD uses are noisy. The second is how much the answer depends on any one training example. If you replace one example and train again, does the minimizer barely move, or can it jump somewhere else entirely? The first question is about the algorithm; the second is about the problem itself, and it is the bridge to the next chapter, where a model that does not depend much on any one example is shown to generalize.
Both questions have the same kind of answer. A few constants of the loss decide everything. The first is how steep the loss can be anywhere, which is the largest size of its gradient: the Lipschitz constant \(L\). The second is how fast that slope can change as you move, which is a bound on the curvature from above: the smoothness \(\beta\). The third is how much the loss curves upward at least, a bound on the curvature from below: the strong convexity \(\lambda\). The last one belongs to the optimizer rather than the loss: how far the random gradients SGD uses scatter around the true gradient, their variance \(\sigma^2\). Every rate and every bound in this chapter is a combination of these four constants, and once you know which constant each result uses, you can tell when it applies. Table 6.1 lists the results.
The distributions behind the noise (Probability distributions) and the way averages concentrate (Concentration inequalities) are used only lightly here. This chapter is about inequalities that hold for every input, and about expectations; it never needs a tail bound.
Notation. The training data are \(n\) examples \(D = (z_1, \dots, z_n)\). The model is a parameter vector \(w \in \mathbb R^d\), and its loss on example \(z\) is \(\ell(w, z)\). The empirical risk is the average loss over the training set, \(F(w) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(w, z_i)\). A point where it is smallest is a minimizer \(w^*\), and \(F^* = F(w^*)\) is the smallest value. \(\nabla F(w)\) is the gradient, the vector of partial derivatives, which points in the direction in which \(F\) increases fastest. \(\langle a, b\rangle = \sum_j a_j b_j\) is the inner product of two vectors, and all norms are Euclidean, \(\|a\| = \sqrt{\langle a, a\rangle}\).

title: 6  Optimization
section: 6.2 Toolkit: five facts every derivation uses
text:
6.2 Toolkit: five facts every derivation uses
Every proof in this chapter tracks the distance from the current parameters to the minimizer and asks how one step changes it. The five facts below are the pieces those proofs are built from, each stated and proved once.

6.2.1 Fact 1 — A convex function lies above its tangents
A function is convex when it curves upward everywhere, with no dents. The usual way to say this is that the straight segment (the chord) between any two points on its graph never dips below the graph: for all \(w, w'\) and every mixing weight \(\theta \in [0, 1]\), the value at the mixed point is at most the same mix of the two values, \(f(\theta w' + (1-\theta)w) \le \theta f(w') + (1-\theta)f(w)\).
For a differentiable \(f\) there is an equivalent picture, and it is the one the proofs use. The tangent at \(w\) predicts the value at another point \(w'\) by starting from \(f(w)\) and adding the slope times the displacement, \(\langle\nabla f(w), w' - w\rangle\). Convexity says this linear prediction never overshoots: the graph lies above every one of its tangents, \[f(w') \ge f(w) + \langle\nabla f(w), w' - w\rangle \quad\text{for all } w, w'. \tag{6.1}\]
To see why the chord condition gives this, write the mixed point as \(w + \theta(w' - w)\), a step of size \(\theta\) from \(w\) towards \(w'\). Subtract \(f(w)\) from both sides of the chord condition and divide by \(\theta > 0\): \(\frac{f(w + \theta(w' - w)) - f(w)}{\theta} \le f(w') - f(w)\). The left side is the average slope over a short step towards \(w'\), and as \(\theta \to 0\) it becomes the slope in that direction, the directional derivative \(\langle\nabla f(w), w' - w\rangle\). That is Equation 6.1. (The other direction, from tangents to chords, is in the references.) For a concrete case take \(f(w) = w^2\) at \(w = 1\). The slope there is 2, so the tangent is \(1 + 2(w' - 1)\). At \(w' = 3\) the tangent predicts 5, and the function is 9, above it.
Here is why this matters. The fact turns a gradient, which you can compute, into a lower bound on how much higher the function is somewhere else. Every convex convergence proof uses it with \(w'\) set to the minimizer \(w^*\) and the inequality rearranged: \(\langle\nabla f(w), w - w^*\rangle \ge f(w) - f(w^*)\). In words, the gradient at \(w\) points away from the minimizer, and its component along the direction from \(w^*\) to \(w\) is at least the current error \(f(w) - f(w^*)\). So a step against the gradient makes progress towards \(w^*\) in proportion to how far from optimal you are.


6.2.2 Fact 2 — Expanding a square, and Cauchy–Schwarz
The squared length of a sum of two vectors is the two squared lengths plus a cross term, exactly as \((a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2\) for numbers. And the cross term can never be larger than the product of the lengths, because the inner product is the product of the lengths times the cosine of the angle between the vectors, and a cosine is at most 1 in size (the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality): \[\|a + b\|^2 = \|a\|^2 + 2\langle a, b\rangle + \|b\|^2, \qquad |\langle a, b\rangle| \le \|a\|\,\|b\|. \tag{6.2}\]
The first identity is what makes the SGD proofs work. One step moves \(w\) to \(w - \eta g\), where \(g\) is the gradient used and \(\eta\) the step size. The new squared distance to the minimizer, \(\|w - \eta g - w^*\|^2\), splits by the identity (with \(a = w - w^*\) and \(b = -\eta g\)) into the old squared distance, a cross term with the gradient that measures progress, and a step-length term \(\eta^2\|g\|^2\) that measures overshoot. That split is the whole SGD proof.


6.2.3 Fact 3 — Projection onto a convex set never increases distances to its points
Sometimes the parameters are kept inside a set \(\mathcal W\), such as a ball, and any step that leaves it is pulled back to the closest point of the set. This projection is \(\Pi(u) = \arg\min_{p \in \mathcal W}\|u - p\|\), the point \(p\) of \(\mathcal W\) nearest to \(u\). The fact is that pulling back can only bring you closer to every point of the set, so it never undoes progress towards a minimizer that lies in the set. This needs \(\mathcal W\) to be closed (so that a nearest point exists) and convex (so that the segment between two of its points stays inside). For every \(w \in \mathcal W\), \[\|\Pi(u) - w\| \le \|u - w\|. \tag{6.3}\]
The picture behind the proof: if \(u\) is outside the set and \(p\) is its nearest point, then any point \(w\) of the set lies “behind” \(p\) as seen from \(u\), at an angle of at least \(90°\) at \(p\). Pythagoras then makes \(u\) farther from \(w\) than \(p\) is. To make this precise, let \(p = \Pi(u)\) and \(w \in \mathcal W\). Points of the segment from \(p\) to \(w\) have the form \(p + \theta(w - p)\) with \(\theta \in [0, 1]\), and they are all in \(\mathcal W\) because it is convex. Their squared distance to \(u\) is \(h(\theta) = \|u - p - \theta(w - p)\|^2\). Since \(p\) is the closest point of the whole set, \(h\) is smallest at \(\theta = 0\), so it cannot start decreasing as \(\theta\) grows from 0: \(h'(0) = -2\langle u - p, w - p\rangle \ge 0\), which says \(\langle u - p, p - w\rangle \ge 0\). That is the obtuse angle. Now expand \(u - w = (u - p) + (p - w)\) with Fact 2: \(\|u - w\|^2 = \|u - p\|^2 + \|p - w\|^2 + 2\langle u - p, p - w\rangle\). The cross term is non-negative and so is \(\|u - p\|^2\), so \(\|u - w\|^2 \ge \|p - w\|^2\).
For the ball \(\{\|w\| \le R\}\) the projection is simple: \(\Pi(u) = u\min(1, R/\|u\|)\), which leaves \(u\) alone if it is inside and shrinks it back to the sphere of radius \(R\) if it left. Projected SGD uses this to keep its iterates in a bounded set, and Fact 3 says this costs nothing in the analysis, as long as the minimizer \(w^*\) is in \(\mathcal W\).


6.2.4 Fact 4 — Jensen: averaging inside a convex function helps
The chord condition of Fact 1 says that the value at a mix of two points is at most the mix of the values. Applying it repeatedly extends it to a mix of any number of points, which is Jensen’s inequality: for a convex \(f\) and weights \(\alpha_t \ge 0\) that add up to 1, \[f\Big(\sum_t\alpha_t w_t\Big) \le \sum_t\alpha_t f(w_t). \tag{6.4}\] (Mix the first two points, then mix the result with the third, and so on.)
The proofs need it for the following reason. They can only bound the average error over the run, \(\frac1T\sum_t (F(w_t) - F^*)\), which is not the error of any model you could hand to someone. Jensen with equal weights \(1/T\) turns it into a bound for one model, the averaged iterate \(\bar w_T = \frac1T\sum_t w_t\): its error is at most the average error.


6.2.5 Fact 5 — Unbiased gradients: the cross term averages out, the square does not
SGD does not use the true gradient \(\nabla F(w_t)\), which needs a pass over the whole training set. It uses a cheap random estimate \(g_t\), for example the gradient of one example picked at random. The estimate is unbiased: averaged over the random pick, it equals the true gradient, \(\mathbb E[g_t \mid \text{past}] = \nabla F(w_t)\). Here “past” means all the random choices made before step \(t\). Those choices determine \(w_t\), so once you condition on them \(w_t\) is a fixed vector and only the new pick at step \(t\) is random. Two consequences follow, and they explain the title of this fact.
First, an inner product of \(g_t\) with any vector \(v_t\) fixed by the past (such as \(w_t - w^*\)) behaves as if \(g_t\) were the true gradient: \(\mathbb E\langle g_t, v_t\rangle = \mathbb E\langle\nabla F(w_t), v_t\rangle\). The reason is that an inner product with a fixed vector is linear, so the conditional expectation passes inside it, \(\mathbb E[\langle g_t, v_t\rangle \mid \text{past}] = \langle\mathbb E[g_t \mid \text{past}], v_t\rangle = \langle\nabla F(w_t), v_t\rangle\); then average over the past.
Second, the squared length of \(g_t\) does not average to the squared length of the true gradient. It is larger, by the variance, the mean squared error of the estimate. This is the bias–variance split: \[\mathbb E[\|g_t\|^2 \mid \text{past}] = \|\nabla F(w_t)\|^2 + \mathbb E[\|g_t - \nabla F(w_t)\|^2 \mid \text{past}]. \tag{6.5}\] To prove it, write \(g_t\) as the true gradient plus an error, \(\nabla F + (g_t - \nabla F)\), and expand the square with Fact 2. The cross term is \(2\langle\nabla F(w_t), g_t - \nabla F(w_t)\rangle\). The first vector is fixed by the past, and the error has conditional mean zero, so by the first consequence the cross term averages to zero. The two squares remain.
A concrete case makes both consequences visible. Take three one-dimensional examples \(z = (1, 2, 6)\) and the loss \(\ell(w, z) = \frac12(w - z)^2\). The risk is \(F(w) = \frac13\sum_i\frac12(w - z_i)^2\), whose gradient is the average of the \(w - z_i\), that is \(\nabla F(w) = w - 3\), since the mean of the data is 3. At \(w = 4\), SGD picks one example uniformly at random and uses its gradient \(w - z_i\). Table 6.2 lists the three equally likely outcomes.



Table 6.2: SGD gradients for \(F(w) = \frac13\sum_i\frac12(w - z_i)^2\) at \(w = 4\), where \(\nabla F(4) = 1\).
