The hybrid bound is tight for one sample and loose afterwards, and a normal approximation shows why. The number of heads has mean \(m/2\) for the fair coin and \(m/2 + m\delta\) for the biased one, and in both cases a standard deviation of about \(\sqrt m/2\) (each flip has variance \(\frac14\) or very close to it). So the two counts are two bell curves whose centres are \(m\delta/(\sqrt m/2) = 2\delta\sqrt m\) standard deviations apart. The best test puts its threshold where the two curves cross, halfway between the means, at \(\delta\sqrt m\) standard deviations from each. Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function, \(\Phi(z) = \Pr[Z \le z]\) for \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\). The biased count lands above the threshold with probability \(\Phi(\delta\sqrt m)\) and the fair one with probability \(1 - \Phi(\delta\sqrt m)\), so the best advantage is about \(2\Phi(\delta\sqrt m) - 1\). At \(m = 100\), \(\delta\sqrt m = 0.1\) and \(2\Phi(0.1) - 1 = 0.080\); at \(m = 10{,}000\), \(\delta\sqrt m = 1\) and \(2\Phi(1) - 1 = 0.683\), the two TV values in the table. The true advantage therefore grows like \(\delta\sqrt m\), not \(\delta m\): the means of the counts separate by \(m\delta\), but each count fluctuates by about \(\sqrt m/2\). To reach a constant advantage you need \(\delta\sqrt m\) of order 1, that is about \(1/\delta^2\) samples, while the hybrid bound would allow it after \(1/\delta\).
Majority vote stalls at about \(\frac12\), because its threshold \(m/2\) sits at the centre of the fair curve instead of halfway between the two. For large \(m\) the biased count is almost surely above \(m/2\), but so is the fair count about half the time. At \(m = 10{,}000\) the biased mean is \(2\delta\sqrt m = 2\) standard deviations above \(m/2\), so the biased count clears \(m/2\) with probability about \(\Phi(2) = 0.977\), and \(0.977 - 0.5 \approx 0.48\), close to the simulated 0.481. The best test puts the threshold halfway between the two means, at \(m/2 + m\delta/2\) (Exercise 3).






Figure 8.2: Advantage of telling \(m\) flips of a coin with bias \(\frac12 + 0.01\) from fair flips: majority vote (simulation), the best possible distinguisher (exact TV distance), and the hybrid bound \(m\delta\).





8.4.6 Check yourself

Where does the hybrid lemma use that \(X\) and \(Y\) are efficiently samplable? (In step 2: \(D'\) must generate the other \(m - 1\) entries itself, in polynomial time.)
Why does the lemma need \(m\) to be polynomial? (The loss is a factor \(m\). For superpolynomial \(m\), \(\varepsilon/m\) can be negligible even when \(\varepsilon\) is not, so step 6 no longer gives a contradiction.)

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.5 Concrete versus asymptotic security

8.5.1 Context
Real systems fix \(\lambda\): AES uses 128-bit keys, not “a key of length \(\lambda\)”. A statement that holds “for all large enough \(\lambda\)” does not say whether 128 is large enough. Concrete security replaces “PPT” and “negligible” by explicit numbers.


8.5.2 Definition
Instead of “efficient” and “negligible”, concrete security names the attacker’s resources and the advantage they buy. A primitive is \((t, q, \varepsilon)\)-secure if every adversary that runs in time at most \(t\) and makes at most \(q\) queries to its oracles (the procedures the game lets it call, such as “encrypt this message for me”) has advantage at most \(\varepsilon\). Brute force over \(\kappa\)-bit keys sets the benchmark: trying \(t\) keys succeeds with probability \(t/2^\kappa\). A primitive has \(\kappa\)-bit security if, roughly, no attack does better than that: every adversary with time \(t\) has advantage at most \(t/2^\kappa\).
Security proofs then become reductions with explicit losses: “if \(A\) breaks scheme \(S\) with \((t, q, \varepsilon)\), then \(B\) breaks primitive \(P\) with \((t', q', \varepsilon')\)”. Read in reverse, this says that if \(P\) is hard to break, so is \(S\), and the losses say how much security is lost on the way. The hybrid lemma is an example with \(t' \approx t\) and \(\varepsilon' = \varepsilon/m\). A reduction is tight when \(\varepsilon' \approx \varepsilon\). A loose reduction forces larger parameters for the same guarantee, because the primitive must then be secure against advantages much smaller than the one you want for the scheme.


8.5.3 Example: what 128-bit security buys
Suppose an attacker has an exascale machine that tests \(10^{18}\) keys per second, and runs it for a year. A year is about \(3.16\times10^7\) seconds, so that is about \(3.16\times10^{25}\) keys, which is \(2^{84.7}\) keys (since \(\log_2 10 \approx 3.32\)). Each key is right with probability \(2^{-128}\), so against a 128-bit key it succeeds with probability \(2^{84.7 - 128} = 9.3\times10^{-14}\). Trying all \(2^{128}\) keys would take \(2^{128}/2^{84.7} = 2^{43.3}\) years, which is \(1.08\times10^{13}\) years. The advantage is not zero, but it is smaller than the probability of most hardware failures during the computation.


8.5.4 Example: what a \(q\)-query bound means
The next section derives that a pseudorandom permutation on \(n\)-bit blocks is also a pseudorandom function, up to an extra advantage of \(q^2/2^{n+1}\) after \(q\) queries (Equation 8.10). In words, the extra advantage is the probability that \(q\) random \(n\)-bit values contain a repeat, which grows with the square of \(q\). For a 128-bit block cipher, \(q^2/2^{129} = 2^{2k - 129}\) when \(q = 2^k\). With 16-byte (128-bit) blocks:

\(q = 2^{32}\) blocks (\(2^{36}\) bytes, 64 GiB of data): at most \(2^{64 - 129} = 2^{-65}\).
\(q = 2^{48}\) blocks (\(2^{52}\) bytes, 4 PiB): at most \(2^{96 - 129} = 2^{-33}\).
\(q = 2^{64}\) blocks: the bound reaches \(2^{128 - 129} = \frac12\) and says nothing.

So a \(q\)-query bound is a data limit. This is why block-cipher modes recommend changing keys long before \(2^{64}\) blocks: the guarantee degrades with the square of the data processed under one key.


8.5.5 Check yourself

A reduction loses a factor of \(2^{20}\) (it turns advantage \(\varepsilon\) into \(\varepsilon/2^{20}\)). If the primitive has 128-bit security, what does the scheme have? (About \(128 - 20 = 108\) bits: a scheme adversary with advantage \(\varepsilon\) gives a primitive adversary with advantage \(\varepsilon/2^{20} \le t/2^{128}\), so \(\varepsilon \le t/2^{108}\).)
Why is “\((t, \varepsilon)\)-secure” usually summarized by the ratio \(t/\varepsilon\)? (An adversary can trade time for success probability, for example by guessing a fraction of the key space: trying \(t\) of \(2^\kappa\) keys gives \(\varepsilon = t/2^\kappa\), so the ratio \(t/\varepsilon = 2^\kappa\) stays constant along that trade-off.)

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.6 Pseudorandom generators and functions

8.6.1 Context
Truly random bits are expensive to produce and to share. A short random key is cheap. Pseudorandom generators stretch a short key into a long string, and pseudorandom functions turn it into a huge table of random-looking values that can be looked up on demand. Both are defined by games.


8.6.2 Pseudorandom generators
A generator is pseudorandom if its output, on a random seed, cannot be told from truly random bits by any efficient distinguisher. Write \(U_k\) for the uniform distribution on \(\{0,1\}^k\), the strings of \(k\) bits. A deterministic, efficient \(G: \{0,1\}^\lambda \to \{0,1\}^{\ell(\lambda)}\) with \(\ell(\lambda) > \lambda\), so that the output is longer than the seed, is a pseudorandom generator (PRG) if \[G(U_\lambda) \approx_c U_{\ell(\lambda)}. \tag{8.8}\] As a game: the challenger sends either \(G(s)\) for a uniform seed \(s\), or a uniform \(\ell\)-bit string, and the adversary guesses which.
A PRG is never statistically secure. The outputs of \(G\) form a tiny subset of all \(\ell\)-bit strings, so an adversary that can check membership in that subset wins easily. The catch is that checking takes exponential time. Let \(D(y) = 1\) iff \(y = G(s)\) for some seed \(s\).

On \(G(U_\lambda)\), \(D\) always outputs 1, because the input is an output of \(G\) by construction.
There are \(2^\lambda\) seeds, so at most \(2^\lambda\) of the \(2^\ell\) strings are outputs of \(G\). On \(U_\ell\), \(D\) therefore outputs 1 with probability at most \(2^\lambda/2^\ell = 2^{\lambda - \ell}\), which is at most \(\frac12\) because \(\ell \ge \lambda + 1\).
So \(D\) has advantage at least \(1 - \frac12 = \frac12\), and by Fact 2 the TV distance is at least \(\frac12\). But \(D\) loops over \(2^\lambda\) seeds. Pseudorandomness is only a statement about efficient distinguishers.

PRGs exist if one-way functions exist (Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin & Luby 1999). In practice, stream ciphers such as ChaCha20 are modelled as PRGs.


8.6.3 Pseudorandom functions
A random function from \(\mathcal X\) to \(\mathcal Y\) is a table that assigns each input its own independent, uniform output. A keyed function \(F: \{0,1\}^\lambda \times \mathcal X \to \mathcal Y\), written \(F_k(x)\) for key \(k\), is a pseudorandom function (PRF) if no efficient adversary can tell whether it is talking to \(F_k\) with a random key or to a truly random function. Because the adversary may choose its questions, the game gives it an oracle \(O\), a box it can query, and hides behind a fair coin which function is in the box:

The challenger flips \(b\). If \(b = 0\) it samples a key \(k\) and sets \(O = F_k\). If \(b = 1\) it sets \(O = f\), a uniformly random function from \(\mathcal X\) to \(\mathcal Y\).
The adversary sends queries \(x_1, \dots, x_q\), adaptively (each may depend on earlier answers), and receives \(O(x_1), \dots, O(x_q)\).
It outputs a guess \(b'\). Its advantage is \(|\Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 1] - \Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 0]|\), the gap of Fact 1 between how often it says “random” in the two worlds.

A random function on 128-bit inputs is a table with \(2^{128}\) entries, which nobody can store. A PRF gives the same appearance from a 128-bit key. In practice the hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) is modelled as a PRF; the toy code uses HMAC-SHA256.


8.6.4 From a PRG to a PRF: the GGM tree
Goldreich, Goldwasser & Micali (1986) build a PRF from any length-doubling PRG; the construction is called the GGM tree after them. Split the PRG’s output into its two halves, \(G(s) = G_0(s)\,\|\,G_1(s)\), each as long as the seed. The idea is to use the PRG repeatedly to grow a binary tree of keys, picking the left or right half at each level according to the next bit of the input.

Start at the root with the key, \(k_\varnothing = k\).
For an input \(x = x_1x_2\cdots x_n\), walk down the tree: the node reached after the first \(i\) bits is \(k_{x_1\cdots x_i} = G_{x_i}(k_{x_1\cdots x_{i-1}})\), the left or right half of the PRG applied to its parent.
Output the leaf: \(F_k(x) = k_x\).

Proof sketch. The proof replaces the tree by random values one level at a time. Let hybrid \(H_j\) replace every node at depth \(j\) by an independent uniform string, sampled when first needed, and compute everything below it with \(G\). \(H_0\) is the real \(F_k\), and \(H_n\), where every leaf is independent and uniform, is a random function. Between \(H_{j-1}\) and \(H_j\), the only change is at depth \(j\): in \(H_{j-1}\) the nodes there are the two halves of \(G\) applied to uniform parents, and in \(H_j\) they are uniform. Each query is a path from root to leaf, with one node per depth, so a \(q\)-query adversary touches at most \(q\) parents at depth \(j - 1\). Telling \(H_{j-1}\) from \(H_j\) therefore means telling \(q\) outputs of \(G\) on uniform seeds from \(q\) uniform strings. By the hybrid lemma that costs at most \(q\) times the PRG advantage. Summing over the \(n\) levels (Fact 3): \(\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}} \le nq\cdot\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRG}}\). The full proof is in Goldreich, Foundations of Cryptography, Vol. 1, §3.6.


8.6.5 The birthday bound
Statement. Many arguments about random values fail only if two of them coincide, so you need to know how likely a coincidence is. The answer is the birthday bound: among \(q\) values there are about \(q^2/2\) pairs, each pair coincides with probability \(1/N\), so collisions become likely once \(q^2/2\) is comparable to \(N\), after about \(\sqrt N\) draws rather than \(N\). Precisely, draw \(q\) values independently and uniformly from a set of size \(N\). The probability that two of them coincide satisfies \[1 - e^{-q(q-1)/(2N)} \;\le\; \Pr[\text{collision}] \;\le\; \frac{q(q-1)}{2N} \le \frac{q^2}{2N}. \tag{8.9}\]
Derivation. The upper bound counts pairs; the lower bound computes the exact probability of no collision and bounds it with \(1 - x \le e^{-x}\).

Upper bound. There are \(\binom q2 = q(q-1)/2\) pairs, and each pair coincides with probability \(1/N\) (whatever the first value is, the second matches it with probability \(1/N\)). A collision means at least one pair coincides, so the union bound (Fact 5) gives \(\Pr[\text{collision}] \le q(q-1)/(2N)\).
Exact value. Draw the values one at a time. If no collision has happened yet, the first \(i\) values are distinct, and the \((i+1)\)-th avoids all of them with probability \(1 - i/N\). Multiplying these conditional probabilities, \(\Pr[\text{no collision}] = \prod_{i=0}^{q-1}(1 - i/N)\).
Lower bound. By \(1 - x \le e^{-x}\) applied to each factor, \(\Pr[\text{no collision}] \le \exp\big(-\sum_{i<q} i/N\big) = e^{-q(q-1)/(2N)}\), using \(\sum_{i<q} i = q(q-1)/2\). Subtracting from 1 gives the lower bound on a collision.
The 50% point. Setting \(1 - e^{-q^2/(2N)} = \frac12\) means \(q^2/(2N) = \ln 2\), so \(q \approx \sqrt{2N\ln 2} \approx 1.18\sqrt N\) (since \(2\ln 2 = 1.386\) and \(\sqrt{1.386} = 1.18\)). Collisions appear after about \(\sqrt N\) draws, not \(N\).

The two bounds are close. Write \(x = q(q-1)/(2N)\), so the union bound is \(x\) and the lower bound is \(1 - e^{-x}\). On \([0, 1]\) the curve \(1 - e^{-x}\) is concave (it bends downwards), so it lies above the straight chord joining its values at 0 and 1, which is \((1 - 1/e)x\). So when \(x \le 1\), the lower bound is at least \(1 - 1/e \approx 0.63\) times the union bound, and the union bound has the right order.
Examples. Table 8.5 gives the exact probability and both bounds for three cases. The union-bound column is \(q(q-1)/(2N)\); for the class, \(23 \times 22/730 = 0.693\).

Figure 8.3: Probability of a collision among \(q\) uniform draws from \(N = 2^{16}\) values: exact, simulated, the union bound \(q(q-1)/(2N)\) and the lower bound \(1 - e^{-q(q-1)/(2N)}\).





8.6.6 The switching lemma
A block cipher such as AES is a keyed permutation: different inputs never give the same output. It is modelled as a pseudorandom permutation (PRP), defined by the PRF game with the random function \(f\) replaced by a uniformly random permutation of \(\mathcal X\) (a random one-to-one shuffle of the inputs). Most proofs, however, want a PRF. The switching lemma bridges the gap. The only visible difference between a random function and a random permutation is that the function sometimes repeats an output and the permutation never does, so an adversary can tell them apart only about as often as \(q\) random values collide.
Statement. For any adversary making \(q\) queries, \[\big|\Pr[A^{\text{random function}} = 1] - \Pr[A^{\text{random permutation}} = 1]\big| \le \frac{q(q-1)}{2|\mathcal X|} \le \frac{q^2}{2|\mathcal X|}. \tag{8.10}\] Here \(A^{O}\) means the adversary run with oracle \(O\).
Derivation. The plan is to run both oracles from the same pre-drawn list of answers, and show they behave identically unless that list contains a repeat.

Simplify the adversary. Assume its \(q\) queries are distinct: repeating a query teaches it nothing, since both oracles answer the same question the same way every time.
Pre-sample the answers. The random-function oracle can be run by drawing \(Y_1, \dots, Y_q\) independently and uniformly from \(\mathcal X\) in advance and answering the \(i\)-th query with \(Y_i\). On distinct queries this is exactly a random function, because a random function gives each new input a fresh uniform output.
Do the same for the permutation. A random permutation answers the \(i\)-th distinct query with a value that is uniform over the \(|\mathcal X| - i + 1\) values not yet used, whatever the queries are: every unused value is the image of the new query under the same number of permutations consistent with the answers so far. So the permutation oracle can be run by pre-sampling a uniformly random sequence of \(q\) distinct values.
Compare the two. Let \(C\) be the event that the list \(Y_1, \dots, Y_q\) of step 2 has a collision. Every list has probability \(|\mathcal X|^{-q}\), so conditioning on no collision leaves every list of distinct values equally likely: exactly the permutation’s answers. Hence \(\Pr[A^{\text{RF}} = 1 \mid \neg C] = \Pr[A^{\text{RP}} = 1]\), writing \(\mathrm{RF}\) for the random function and \(\mathrm{RP}\) for the random permutation.
Bound the difference. Write \(\rho = \Pr[A^{\text{RP}} = 1]\). Splitting on \(C\), \(\Pr[A^{\text{RF}} = 1] = \Pr[C]\Pr[A^{\text{RF}} = 1 \mid C] + (1 - \Pr[C])\,\rho\). Subtracting \(\rho\) gives \(\Pr[A^{\text{RF}} = 1] - \rho = \Pr[C]\big(\Pr[A^{\text{RF}} = 1 \mid C] - \rho\big)\). The bracket is a difference of two probabilities, so its absolute value is at most 1, and the whole is at most \(\Pr[C]\).
Apply the birthday bound (Equation 8.9) with \(N = |\mathcal X|\).

The event \(C\) is defined on the pre-sampled answers, before the adversary acts, which is what makes step 4 valid for adaptive adversaries: whatever the adversary does, the answers it receives are the same list. (Bellare & Rogaway 2006 point out that a commonly given proof, which conditions on events defined through the adversary’s queries, has a gap; their “identical until bad” game-playing proof is the one above.)
Corollary. If \(F\) is a PRP with advantage \(\varepsilon\) against \(q\)-query adversaries, it is a PRF with advantage at most \(\varepsilon + q^2/(2|\mathcal X|)\). This is Fact 3 with three hybrids: going from \(F_k\) to a random permutation costs at most \(\varepsilon\), and from a random permutation to a random function at most \(q^2/(2|\mathcal X|)\).
The bound is tight. The adversary “output 1 iff two answers collide” never outputs 1 against a permutation and outputs 1 against a function with probability exactly \(\Pr[C]\). So Figure 8.3 is also the advantage of the best adversary in the switching lemma.


8.6.7 Check yourself

Why can the PRG distinguisher in the “never statistically secure” argument not be used against a real PRG? (It enumerates all \(2^\lambda\) seeds, which is not polynomial time.)
How many outputs of a 64-bit block cipher can you safely use under one key, if you want the switching term below \(2^{-20}\)? (Need \(q^2/2^{65} \le 2^{-20}\), so \(q^2 \le 2^{45}\) and \(q \le 2^{22.5}\), about 6 million blocks: a 64-bit block is too small for bulk data.)

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.7 Encryption: perfect secrecy and IND-CPA

8.7.1 Context
Encryption should hide the message. Shannon’s one-time pad hides it perfectly but needs a key as long as all the data. Computational definitions accept a negligible advantage in exchange for short keys. The definition that matters in practice, IND-CPA, has a consequence that surprises many programmers: encryption must be randomized.


8.7.2 The one-time pad and perfect secrecy
Definition. Hiding the message perfectly means that the ciphertext is no more likely to be produced by one message than by another, so seeing it tells you nothing. An encryption scheme has perfect secrecy if the ciphertext distribution does not depend on the message: for all messages \(m, m'\) and ciphertexts \(c\), \(\Pr[\mathrm{Enc}_K(m) = c] = \Pr[\mathrm{Enc}_K(m') = c]\), where \(K\) is the random key. Equivalently, seeing \(c\) does not change the probability of any message (Shannon 1949). To see the equivalence, let the message \(M\) be random with any prior, and apply Bayes’ rule: \(\Pr[M = m \mid C = c] = \Pr[C = c \mid M = m]\Pr[M = m]/\Pr[C = c]\). If \(\Pr[C = c \mid M = m]\) is the same for every \(m\), it equals its average \(\Pr[C = c]\), the ratio is 1, and the posterior equals the prior.
The one-time pad. For \(n\)-bit messages, the key \(K\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^n\) and \(\mathrm{Enc}_K(m) = m \oplus K\), where \(\oplus\) is bitwise exclusive or (XOR): each bit of the message is flipped where the key has a 1.
Derivation of perfect secrecy. Flipping a fixed message’s bits by a uniform key gives a uniform result, by Fact 4.

Fix \(m\). The map \(k \mapsto m \oplus k\) is a bijection of \(\{0,1\}^n\): applying it twice gives back \(k\), since \(m \oplus m = 0\), so it is its own inverse.
By Fact 4, \(m \oplus K\) is uniform, whatever \(m\) is: \(\Pr[\mathrm{Enc}_K(m) = c] = \Pr[K = m \oplus c] = 2^{-n}\), the same for every message.

Table 8.6 shows it for 2-bit messages: each message is sent to every ciphertext by exactly one key.



Table 8.6: The one-time pad on 2-bit messages. Each row contains every ciphertext once, so the ciphertext is uniform for every message.





Key \(K\)
00
01
10
11




Ciphertext for \(m = 01\)
01
00
11
10


Ciphertext for \(m = 10\)
10

00
01






The price. Perfect secrecy requires at least as many keys as messages. To see why, fix a ciphertext \(c\) that occurs. Decryption must work, so each key decrypts \(c\) to one message, and at most \(|\mathcal K|\) messages can produce \(c\). If there are fewer keys than messages, \(|\mathcal K| < |\mathcal M|\), some message \(m'\) never produces \(c\), while some other message does, so the ciphertext distributions of those two messages differ. And the pad must not be reused: XOR-ing two ciphertexts under the same pad cancels the pad, \((m_1 \oplus K) \oplus (m_2 \oplus K) = m_1 \oplus m_2\), and reveals the XOR of the two messages.


8.7.3 IND-CPA security
Semantic security (Goldwasser & Micali 1984) says that whatever an efficient adversary can compute about the message from the ciphertext, it could compute without the ciphertext. That is hard to work with directly, because “whatever it can compute” ranges over all functions of the message. It is equivalent to the following game, which is easier to work with: the adversary picks two messages itself, receives an encryption of one of them, chosen by a fair coin, and must say which. If it cannot beat a coin flip even for messages of its own choosing, the ciphertext reveals nothing it could use.
The IND-CPA game (indistinguishability under chosen-plaintext attack):

The challenger samples a key \(k\) and a fair bit \(b\).
The adversary may ask for encryptions \(\mathrm{Enc}_k(m)\) of messages of its choice, at any time.
It submits two messages \(m_0, m_1\) of equal length and receives the challenge \(c^* = \mathrm{Enc}_k(m_b)\).
It outputs a guess \(b'\).

The scheme is IND-CPA secure if every PPT adversary has negligible advantage \(|\Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 1] - \Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 0]|\). By Equation 8.2 the win probability is \(\frac12\) plus half of this gap, so the advantage is also \(2|\Pr[b' = b] - \frac12|\). The encryption oracle in step 2 models reality: an attacker can often get chosen data encrypted, such as a request it sends or a value it plants in a database.


8.7.4 Why encryption must be randomized
Claim. No deterministic scheme is IND-CPA secure. If encryption always maps the same message to the same ciphertext, the adversary can simply encrypt \(m_0\) itself and compare.
Attack. Ask the oracle for \(c_0 = \mathrm{Enc}_k(m_0)\), then submit \(m_0, m_1\). Output \(b' = 0\) if \(c^* = c_0\) and \(b' = 1\) otherwise. If \(b = 0\), determinism gives \(c^* = c_0\), so \(b' = 0\). If \(b = 1\), correct decryption forces \(\mathrm{Enc}_k(m_1) \ne \mathrm{Enc}_k(m_0)\) (otherwise the same ciphertext would have to decrypt to two messages), so \(b' = 1\). The adversary is always right, and the advantage is 1.
The script runs this attack against \(\mathrm{Enc}_k(m) = m \oplus F_k(0)\), a deterministic scheme built from the toy PRF. Over 20,000 games for each \(b\) the measured advantage is 1.000. The same weakness is visible without any oracle: deterministic encryption of a column of labels maps equal labels to equal ciphertexts, so the frequency of each ciphertext reveals the frequency of each label.


8.7.5 A randomized scheme from a PRF
Construction. The fix is to use a fresh pad for every encryption. Draw a fresh uniform \(r\) from a set \(\mathcal R\) and use \(F_k(r)\), a random-looking row of the PRF’s table, as a one-time pad; send \(r\) along so the receiver can recompute the pad. So \(\mathrm{Enc}_k(m) = (r,\ m \oplus F_k(r))\), and to decrypt \((r, c)\) you compute \(c \oplus F_k(r)\).
Statement. The scheme can fail in only two ways: the PRF is distinguishable from random, or the challenge reuses an \(r\) the adversary has already seen, so its pad is known. The bound adds the two. For an adversary \(A\) making \(q\) encryption queries, there is a PRF adversary \(B\), with about the same running time, such that \[\Pr[A \text{ wins}] \le \frac12 + \mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}}(B) + \frac{q}{2|\mathcal R|}. \tag{8.11}\]
Derivation.

Set up two hybrids. Hybrid 0 is the real game. Hybrid 1 is the same game with \(F_k\) replaced by a truly random function \(f\).
Hybrid 0 to 1 costs the PRF advantage. \(B\) runs the whole game for \(A\), using its own oracle in place of \(F_k\), and outputs 1 iff \(A\) wins. With oracle \(F_k\), \(B\) simulates hybrid 0; with oracle \(f\), hybrid 1. So the winning probabilities in the two hybrids differ by at most \(\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}}(B)\).
Inside hybrid 1, name the bad event. Let \(E\) be the event that the challenge’s \(r^*\) equals one of the \(q\) values \(r_i\) used by the oracle. Each \(r_i\) is independent of \(r^*\) and equals it with probability \(1/|\mathcal R|\), so by the union bound \(\Pr[E] \le q/|\mathcal R|\).
If \(E\) does not happen, the challenge is a one-time pad. Then \(f(r^*)\) is a value of the random function at a point never queried, so it is uniform and independent of everything else \(A\) sees. So \(c^* = m_b \oplus f(r^*)\) is uniform whatever \(b\) is (Fact 4), and \(A\) wins with probability exactly \(\frac12\).
Combine. Split the win on whether \(E\) happens, and bound the win probability by 1 when it does: \(\Pr[\text{win in hybrid 1}] \le \frac12\Pr[\neg E] + \Pr[E] = \frac12 + \frac12\Pr[E] \le \frac12 + \frac{q}{2|\mathcal R|}\). Add the loss from step 2.

In advantage units, \(\mathrm{Adv} = 2(\Pr[\text{win}] - \frac12)\), this is \(\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{CPA}} \le 2\,\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}} + q/|\mathcal R|\). The term \(q/|\mathcal R|\) is real, not an artefact of the proof. The script gives the adversary \(q = 16\) encryptions of \(m_0\) with 8-bit nonces (\(|\mathcal R| = 256\)); each reply \((r_i, m_0 \oplus F_k(r_i))\) reveals the pad \(F_k(r_i)\). If \(r^*\) matches one of them, the adversary removes the pad, reads the challenge, and is always right; otherwise it outputs 1. So it says 1 every time when \(b = 1\), and when \(b = 0\) it says 1 exactly when there is no match. Its advantage is \(1 - (1 - \Pr[E]) = \Pr[E]\), and since \(r^*\) misses each of the 16 independent nonces with probability \(255/256\), \(\Pr[E] = 1 - (255/256)^{16} = 0.0607\). The simulation measures 0.0605, and the bound \(q/|\mathcal R|\) is 0.0625. With 128-bit nonces the same attack has advantage below \(16/2^{128} = 2^{-124}\) for \(q = 16\).


8.7.6 Check yourself

Why does the IND-CPA game require \(|m_0| = |m_1|\)? (Ciphertext length usually reveals message length. Without the requirement, every practical scheme would be trivially broken by comparing lengths.)
In the PRF scheme, where does the proof use that \(r\) is fresh for each encryption? (In step 3: if \(r\) could repeat with high probability, \(E\) would be likely and the pad \(f(r^*)\) would be known.)

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.8 The simulation paradigm

8.8.1 Context
Encryption hides everything. Many procedures must reveal something: a participant learns its own share of a secret, or the final result, and should learn nothing else. “Nothing else” is hard to define directly, because the participant may combine what it sees in clever ways. The simulation paradigm defines it indirectly: whatever the participant sees, it could have produced by itself from what it is allowed to know (Lindell 2017 is a careful tutorial).


8.8.2 Definition
A randomized procedure gives a participant \(P\) a view \(\mathrm{View}_P(x)\): everything \(P\) sees during the run, which depends on all inputs \(x\) and on the procedure’s randomness. \(P\) is allowed to learn \(L(x)\), its leakage: for example its own input and its output. If \(P\) could fake its whole view from \(L(x)\) alone, the real view cannot contain anything beyond \(L(x)\). So the procedure reveals nothing beyond \(L\) to \(P\) if there is an efficient simulator \(S\) whose output, given only \(L(x)\), has the same distribution as the real view: \[S(L(x)) \equiv \mathrm{View}_P(x) \quad\text{for every input } x. \tag{8.12}\] Replace \(\equiv\) by \(\approx_s\) or \(\approx_c\) for statistical or computational security.
The two sides are often called the real world, where the procedure runs, and the ideal world, where a trusted party hands \(P\) exactly \(L(x)\) and the simulator fakes the rest.
Why this captures “nothing else”. Suppose some function \(g\) of the view reveals a property of \(x\). Then \(g(S(L(x)))\) has the same distribution as \(g(\mathrm{View}_P(x))\), because applying the same function to two identically distributed things gives identically distributed results, and it is computed from \(L(x)\) alone. So anything the view reveals is already revealed by \(L(x)\). Semantic security has the same shape, with \(L(m) = |m|\): the ciphertext may reveal the message’s length and nothing more.


8.8.3 Worked example: additive secret sharing
Construction. Additive sharing splits a number into random pieces that add up to it, working in \(\mathbb Z_p\), the integers \(\{0, \dots, p - 1\}\) with arithmetic mod \(p\). To share a secret \(x \in \mathbb Z_p\) among \(h\) holders, sample \(r_1, \dots, r_{h-1}\) uniformly from \(\mathbb Z_p\) and hand out \[s_1 = r_1,\ \dots,\ s_{h-1} = r_{h-1},\qquad s_h = x - (r_1 + \dots + r_{h-1}) \bmod p. \tag{8.13}\] All \(h\) shares sum to \(x\). Shares also add: if \((s_i)\) shares \(x\) and \((t_i)\) shares \(y\), then \((s_i + t_i)\) shares \(x + y\).
Statement. Any \(h - 1\) shares look like independent uniform numbers, whatever the secret is, because the one missing share is what ties them to \(x\). Precisely, any \(h - 1\) shares are independent and uniform on \(\mathbb Z_p^{h-1}\), whatever \(x\) is. The simulator for a coalition of \(h - 1\) holders, with no leakage at all, outputs \(h - 1\) independent uniform elements of \(\mathbb Z_p\), and Equation 8.12 holds with \(\equiv\): perfect security.
Derivation by counting. The plan is to show that the coalition’s shares are a one-to-one relabelling of the uniform randomness, and then apply Fact 4.

The randomness \((r_1, \dots, r_{h-1})\) is uniform on \(\mathbb Z_p^{h-1}\): each of the \(p^{h-1}\) tuples has probability \(p^{-(h-1)}\).
Fix \(x\) and a coalition that misses holder \(j\). Its shares are a function of the randomness. If \(j = h\), the coalition sees \((r_1, \dots, r_{h-1})\) itself. If \(j < h\), it sees every \(r_i\) with \(i \ne j\) together with \(s_h\), and \(r_j\) can be recovered uniquely as \(r_j = x - s_h - \sum_{i \ne j} r_i\), by rearranging the definition of \(s_h\).
Either way the map from randomness to the coalition’s shares can be undone, so it is a bijection of \(\mathbb Z_p^{h-1}\), and every tuple of shares comes from exactly one tuple of randomness (Fact 4).
So every tuple of shares has probability \(p^{-(h-1)}\), for every \(x\). That is the simulator’s output distribution.

Table 8.7 makes step 3 concrete for \(h = 2\) and \(p = 5\): the second share \(x - r\) takes each value exactly once as \(r\) runs over \(\mathbb Z_5\), for both secrets.

0






The script repeats the count exhaustively for \(h = 3\) and \(p = 5\): for every secret and every coalition of two holders, each of the 25 pairs of shares occurs for exactly one of the 25 choices of randomness.
With leakage. If the coalition also learns \(x\) (for example because the secret is later published), the simulator receives \(L = x\). It samples \(h - 1\) uniform shares and sets the last one to \(x\) minus their sum. By the statement above, this matches the joint distribution of the real shares and \(x\) exactly. This is the typical form of a simulator: random where the view is random, and consistent with the leakage where the leakage pins it down.


8.8.4 Interpretation: perfect, statistical, and broken
Reducing mod \(p\) is what makes step 3 a bijection: subtracting \(r\) wraps around, so every value is hit once whatever \(x\) is. Over the integers it fails, because nothing wraps and the range of the share moves with the secret. Take \(x \in \{0, \dots, 7\}\), \(r\) uniform on \(\{0, \dots, R - 1\}\), and the share \(x - r\) without reduction. The share is uniform on \(\{x - R + 1, \dots, x\}\), an interval of \(R\) values that moves with \(x\). For secrets \(x\) and \(x'\) the two intervals overlap in \(R - |x - x'|\) values, so \(|x - x'|\) of the \(R\) values, each with probability \(1/R\), are possible under one secret and impossible under the other. Their TV distance is therefore \(|x - x'|/R\), and by Fact 2 that is the best adversary’s advantage.
Figure 8.4 shows both cases. With \(p = 11\), the shares of \(x = 0\) and \(x = 7\) have the same flat histogram; the empirical TV distance over 100,000 shares each is 0.0045, which is sampling noise around the exact value 0. Over the integers with \(R = 16\), the supports visibly differ; the empirical TV distance is 0.4423, against the exact \(7/16 = 0.4375\). Taking \(R = 2^{3 + \sigma}\) for secrets below \(2^3\) makes the TV distance at most \(7/2^{3 + \sigma}\), which is below \(2^{-\sigma}\): statistical rather than perfect security.






Figure 8.4: Histograms of the second share for secrets \(x = 0\) and \(x = 7\). Left: reduced mod \(p = 11\), both are uniform. Right: over the integers with \(r < 16\), the support shifts with the secret.





8.8.5 Check yourself

Two of three holders combine their shares of \(x\). What do they learn? (Nothing: two shares out of three are uniform on \(\mathbb Z_p^2\) whatever \(x\) is. Only all three together determine \(x\).)
Why must the simulator be efficient? (An unbounded simulator could, in a computational setting, invert functions the participant cannot. The definition would then accept procedures whose views reveal information that is hard to compute from \(L(x)\) but easy to read from the view.)

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.9 Learning with errors

8.9.1 Context
Every primitive so far is generic. Learning with errors (LWE) is a specific hard problem, introduced by Regev (2005), with three attractions: it is as hard as worst-case lattice problems, no efficient quantum attack is known, and encryption built on it lets you add ciphertexts. Its one-line description is “linear algebra with noise”, and the noise is everything.


8.9.2 Definition
LWE hides a secret vector behind linear equations whose right-hand sides are slightly wrong. Fix a dimension \(d\), a modulus \(p\) (an integer that need not be prime), and an error distribution \(\chi\) on small integers. Pick a secret \(s\) uniform in \(\mathbb Z_p^d\), vectors of \(d\) integers mod \(p\). An LWE sample is a random vector \(a\) together with the inner product \(\langle a, s\rangle = \sum_j a_j s_j\), perturbed by a small error \(e\): \[(a,\ b = \langle a, s\rangle + e \bmod p), \qquad a \text{ uniform in } \mathbb Z_p^d,\ e \sim \chi. \tag{8.14}\] There are two versions of the problem. Search LWE asks you to find \(s\), given \(m\) samples. Decision LWE asks you to decide, given \(m\) pairs, whether they are LWE samples or uniform pairs in \(\mathbb Z_p^d \times \mathbb Z_p\).
If you can solve search, you can solve decision: find a candidate \(s\), then check whether the values \(b - \langle a, s\rangle\) are small, which they are for LWE samples and are not for uniform pairs. So decision is no harder than search. Regev shows the converse for prime \(p\) polynomial in \(d\), by guessing the coordinates of \(s\) one at a time and using the decision oracle to test each guess.
Hardness. For \(\chi\) a discretized Gaussian (a normal distribution rounded to integers) of standard deviation about \(\alpha p\) with \(\alpha p > 2\sqrt d\), Regev (2009) proves that solving LWE is at least as hard as solving worst-case lattice problems with a quantum algorithm. The lattice problems are GapSVP, the gap version of the shortest vector problem, and the shortest independent vectors problem, both to within an approximation factor \(\tilde O(d/\alpha)\) (\(d/\alpha\) up to logarithmic factors). Peikert (2009) and Brakerski, Langlois, Peikert, Regev & Stehlé (2013) give classical reductions. Treat these as cited results; the proofs are long.


8.9.3 Without noise, LWE is easy
With \(e = 0\), the samples are a linear system \(As = b\) over \(\mathbb Z_p\), where the rows of \(A\) are the vectors \(a\), and Gaussian elimination solves it from \(d\) independent equations.
Here it is with \(d = 2\), \(p = 7\) and \(s = (3, 5)\). Take \(a_1 = (1, 2)\) and \(a_2 = (3, 1)\), so \(b_1 = 3 + 10 = 13 \equiv 6\) and \(b_2 = 9 + 5 = 14 \equiv 0\).

The second equation \(3s_1 + s_2 = 0\) gives \(s_2 = -3s_1 = 4s_1\), since \(-3 \equiv 4 \pmod 7\).
Substitute into \(s_1 + 2s_2 = 6\): \(9s_1 \equiv 2s_1 = 6\), so \(s_1 = 3\) and \(s_2 = 12 \equiv 5\). Correct.

Now add the error \(e = (1, 0)\), so \(b = (0, 0)\). The same steps give \(s_2 = 4s_1\) and \(2s_1 = 0\), so \(\hat s = (0, 0)\), completely wrong. The reason is that elimination solves \(A\hat s = b = As + e\) exactly, so in general it returns \(\hat s = s + A^{-1}e\), and \(A^{-1}\) has large entries mod \(p\). Here \(A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 6\\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}\) (check: the first row of \(A\) times the first column gives \(1\cdot4 + 2\cdot2 = 8 \equiv 1\)), and \(A^{-1}(1, 0) = (4, 2)\), which shifts \(s\) to \((7, 7) \equiv (0, 0)\). A unit error is amplified into a uniformly scrambled answer.
The script does the same at \(d = 16\) and \(p = 4096\) with 32 samples. (Mod a power of two, elimination may only divide by odd numbers, the invertible ones, so it picks odd pivots.) Without noise it recovers all 16 coordinates of \(s\). With errors in \(\{-1, 0, 1\}\), it recovers 0 of 16.


8.9.4 Regev’s symmetric bit encryption
Construction. Picture \(\mathbb Z_p\) as a clock with \(p\) positions. To encrypt a bit, take an LWE sample and move its \(b\) halfway round the clock if the bit is 1. Whoever knows \(s\) can subtract \(\langle a, s\rangle\) and see whether what remains is near 0 or near halfway; the small error does not hide that. Concretely, take \(p\) even. The key is \(s \in \mathbb Z_p^d\). To encrypt a bit \(m\), draw a fresh \(a\) and \(e \sim \chi\) and output \[\mathrm{Enc}_s(m) = \big(a,\ b = \langle a, s\rangle + e + m\cdot\tfrac p2 \bmod p\big). \tag{8.15}\] To decrypt, compute \(v = b - \langle a, s\rangle \bmod p\) and output 1 if \(v\) is closer to \(p/2\) than to 0 (counting distance round the clock, so that values just below \(p\) are close to 0), that is if \(p/4 < v < 3p/4\).
Statement (correctness). Decryption is correct whenever \(|e| < p/4\).
Derivation. Removing \(\langle a, s\rangle\) leaves the error plus the encoded bit; the error is too small to move it across the decision boundary.

\(v = e + m\frac p2 \bmod p\), by the definition of \(b\).
If \(m = 0\), \(v \equiv e\) with \(|e| < p/4\), so \(v \in [0, p/4) \cup (3p/4, p)\) (a negative \(e\) wraps to just below \(p\)) and the output is 0.
If \(m = 1\), \(v = e + p/2 \in (p/4, 3p/4)\) and the output is 1.

Security, in one hybrid. Without \(s\), the pair \((a, \langle a, s\rangle + e)\) looks uniform by decision LWE, so the message is added to something that looks uniform: a one-time pad. Under decision LWE, the pairs \((a, \langle a, s\rangle + e)\) in all ciphertexts can be replaced by uniform pairs \((a, u)\). Then \(b = u + mq/2\) is uniform whatever \(m\) is (Fact 4, with the bijection “add \(mq/2\)”). So an IND-CPA adversary winning with probability \(\frac12 + \varepsilon\) yields a decision-LWE distinguisher with advantage \(\varepsilon\): it runs the game with the given pairs and outputs 1 iff the adversary wins, by the argument of step 2 in the PRF scheme.
Worked example with \(d = 3\), \(p = 4096\) and \(s = (5, 1000, 3000)\). Here \(p/2 = 2048\), and reducing mod 4096 means subtracting 4096.

Encrypt \(m = 1\) with \(a_1 = (17, 2, 1)\) and \(e_1 = -7\): \(\langle a_1, s\rangle = 85 + 2000 + 3000 = 5085 \equiv 5085 - 4096 = 989\), so \(b_1 = 989 - 7 + 2048 = 3030\). Decrypting, \(v = 3030 - 989 = 2041\), which is 7 from \(p/2 = 2048\): the output is 1.
Encrypt \(m = 1\) with \(a_2 = (1, 1, 1)\) and \(e_2 = 12\): \(\langle a_2, s\rangle = 4005\), so \(b_2 = 4005 + 12 + 2048 = 6065 \equiv 1969\).



8.9.5 Adding ciphertexts, and the noise budget
Statement. Because everything in a ciphertext is linear in \(a\), the error and the encoded bit, adding ciphertexts adds all three. The bits add mod 2, since two half-turns round the clock are a full turn, and the errors pile up. So the componentwise sum of ciphertexts of \(m_1, \dots, m_k\) is a ciphertext of \(m_1 \oplus \dots \oplus m_k\) with error \(e_1 + \dots + e_k\). If every \(|e_i| \le B\), the total error is at most \(kB\), and it decrypts correctly whenever \[k < \frac{p}{4B}. \tag{8.16}\]
Derivation.

The sum is \((\sum_i a_i,\ \sum_i b_i)\). By linearity of the inner product, \(\sum_i b_i - \langle\sum_i a_i, s\rangle = \sum_i e_i + (\sum_i m_i)\frac p2 \bmod p\).
Because \(p\) is even, \(2\cdot\frac p2 = p \equiv 0\), so only the parity of \(\sum_i m_i\) survives: \((\sum_i m_i)\frac p2 \equiv (m_1 \oplus \dots \oplus m_k)\frac p2\).
So the sum is an encryption of the XOR with error \(\sum_i e_i\), and \(|\sum_i e_i| \le kB\) by the triangle inequality. By the correctness statement, \(kB < p/4\) suffices.

In the worked example, the sum is \(a_1 + a_2 = (18, 3, 2)\) and \(b_1 + b_2 = 4999 \equiv 903\). Then \(\langle(18, 3, 2), s\rangle = 9090 \equiv 898\), and \(v = 903 - 898 = 5 = e_1 + e_2\): it decrypts to \(0 = 1 \oplus 1\).
Interpretation: the worst case and the typical case. Equation 8.16 is a worst-case guarantee: it assumes every error is as large as possible and all have the same sign. Independent errors with mean zero mostly cancel. Variances of independent variables add, so the sum of \(k\) errors with standard deviation \(\sigma\) has standard deviation \(\sigma\sqrt k\), not \(kB\). With \(\chi\) uniform on the \(2B + 1\) values \(\{-B, \dots, B\}\), the variance is the average of \(j^2\) over those values, \(2\sum_{j=1}^B j^2/(2B + 1) = 2\cdot\frac{B(B+1)(2B+1)}{6}/(2B+1) = B(B+1)/3\). By the central limit theorem the sum is approximately normal, and decryption fails when the summed error, read round the clock, lands more than \(p/4\) from 0. So the normal approximation predicts \[\Pr[\text{failure after } k \text{ additions}] \approx \Pr\Big[\big|Z \sqrt{kB(B+1)/3}\big| > p/4 \text{ after wrapping mod } p\Big], \quad Z \sim \mathcal N(0, 1). \tag{8.17}\] Figure 8.5 and Table 8.8 compare the two for \(p = 4096\) and \(B = 32\), where Equation 8.16 guarantees correctness for \(k < 32\) (since \(p/(4B) = 4096/128 = 32\)). The simulation adds \(k\) real toy ciphertexts (with \(d = 4\)) of random bits, 20,000 times, and checks the decrypted XOR.



Table 8.8: Decryption failure rate of a sum of \(k\) Regev ciphertexts, \(p = 4096\), errors uniform on \(\{-32, \dots, 32\}\) (seed 0, 20,000 trials).

To see where a row comes from, take \(k = 1024\): the standard deviation of the summed error is \(\sqrt{1024 \times 32 \times 33/3} \approx 600\), and \(p/4 = 1024\) is about 1.7 standard deviations, which a normal variable exceeds in absolute value with probability about 0.088. At \(k = 256\) the standard deviation is about 300 and \(p/4\) is 3.4 standard deviations away, far in the tail.
The worst-case budget is therefore very conservative. Failures only become measurable around \(k = 256\), eight times the guaranteed 32, because the noise grows like \(\sqrt k\) rather than \(k\). But the budget is still finite. Once the noise is comparable to \(p/4\), the decrypted value is spread round the whole clock, decryption becomes a coin flip, and the failure rate tends to \(\frac12\). Larger \(p\) (relative to the noise) buys more additions; that is the parameter trade-off of every LWE-based scheme that computes on ciphertexts.






Figure 8.5: Decryption failure rate of a sum of \(k\) Regev ciphertexts (\(p = 4096\), errors uniform on \(\{-32, \dots, 32\}\)): simulation against the normal approximation. The dashed line is the worst-case guarantee \(k < p/(4B) = 32\).





8.9.6 Ring-LWE, briefly
A Regev ciphertext carries one bit in \(d + 1\) numbers, and the key has \(d\) numbers. Ring-LWE packs much more into the same space by replacing vectors with polynomials. Ring-LWE (Lyubashevsky, Peikert & Regev 2010) replaces vectors in \(\mathbb Z_p^d\) by polynomials in \(R_p = \mathbb Z_p[X]/(X^N + 1)\), that is, polynomials of degree below \(N\) with coefficients mod \(p\), multiplied with the rule \(X^N = -1\), and replaces the inner product by polynomial multiplication. One ring sample \((a, a\cdot s + e)\) stands for \(N\) correlated LWE samples, carries \(N\) message coefficients, and is computed in \(O(N\log N)\) time with the number-theoretic transform, a fast Fourier transform for arithmetic mod \(p\). Its hardness rests on lattice problems restricted to ideal lattices, which have this extra structure. A middle ground, module-LWE, underlies the standardized key-encapsulation mechanism ML-KEM (FIPS 203, 2024).


8.9.7 Check yourself

Why does \(p\) have to be even in the addition argument, and what happens for odd \(p\) with \(\lfloor p/2\rfloor\) as the encoding? (For odd \(p\), \(2\lfloor p/2\rfloor = p - 1 \equiv -1\), so every pair of 1-bits adds an extra error of \(-1\). The error drifts by about \(k/4\) on top of the random part.)
Is the LWE problem with \(\chi\) uniform on \(\{-B, \dots, B\}\) covered by Regev’s theorem? (Not directly. The theorem is for a Gaussian-shaped error; other small distributions need separate arguments. The toy uses a uniform error only because its worst case is easy to state.)

What to take from it. Asymptotic statements need concrete numbers, because a negligible function can be large at the parameter you use: at \(\lambda = 128\), \(2^{-\sqrt\lambda}\) is still \(3.9\times10^{-4}\). The birthday bound is the right order and nearly tight: while it is below 1, the union bound overestimates the collision probability by at most a factor of about 1.6 (that is \(1/(1 - 1/e)\), from the chord argument), and the switching lemma’s best adversary attains the exact collision probability. Hybrid bounds are safe but can be loose: for the biased coin they overstate the advantage by a factor up to \(\sqrt m\), because the hybrid argument pays \(\delta\) per flip while the true advantage grows like \(\delta\sqrt m\). Determinism is fatal, and short nonces leak exactly as the proof predicts. Finally, noise is what makes LWE hard and what limits computing on its ciphertexts. Without it, elimination solves the problem; with it, every addition spends part of a finite budget.

Rules of thumb

Security of \(\kappa\) bits means an attacker with time \(t\) succeeds with probability about \(t/2^\kappa\).
Anything random of \(\kappa\) bits starts colliding after about \(2^{\kappa/2}\) draws: budget identifiers, nonces and block counts accordingly.
Encryption that hides equality must be randomized.
In LWE schemes, noise is a budget: each operation spends some, and decryption fails when it runs out.

Practice. Exercises for this chapter, each with a worked solution, are in the exercise book.

title: Threat models and attacks
text:
Who this part is for
This part teaches you to break models before it teaches you to protect them. Every defence in the rest of the book is measured against an attack: a guarantee is only as meaningful as the strongest adversary it stops, and an evaluation is only as honest as the attack it runs. So you start here, with the adversaries, what they see, what they want, and how well the best of them can do.
You are expected to have read the Prerequisites, or to know their content. This part leans hardest on hypothesis testing (the Neyman–Pearson lemma, trade-off curves, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves read at a low false positive rate), on the total variation distance, and on the link between stability and generalization. Information theory appears in the chapters on attribute inference, memorization and linkage. You should also be comfortable with logistic regression, gradients of a small neural network, and an n-gram language model at the level of writing them in NumPy.
Differential privacy, the defence most of the book is about, is introduced in the next part, and it is designed against exactly the games defined here. The only privacy definitions in this part are the syntactic ones of the last chapter, k-anonymity and its successors, and they appear as targets: the chapter shows what each one promises and the attack that breaks it.

title: Threat models and attacks
text:
The common thread
Every attack in this part is the same object: a game in which a challenger trains or releases something that depends on a hidden secret, and an adversary guesses the secret from what the threat model lets it see. What changes from chapter to chapter is the secret: one bit of membership, a sensitive attribute, a memorized string, the whole dataset, a client’s input, a property of the population behind the data, or a person’s name. Table 1 lists them.



Table 1: The chapters of this part, the question each one answers, and the earlier chapters it uses.

Reconstruction attacks

Two ideas run through all nine chapters.

An attack is a hypothesis test. When the secret is one bit, the best attack is the likelihood-ratio test of the Neyman–Pearson lemma, its advantage (true positive rate (TPR) minus false positive rate (FPR)) is at most the total variation distance between the adversary’s two possible views, and its whole error trade-off is bounded by one curve. Membership inference, attribute inference and property inference are each this statement with a different pair of views. The strongest practical attacks, such as the likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) on membership, are explicit approximations of the optimal test.
The worst case is not the average case. Attacks succeed first on outliers, on duplicated strings, on unique combinations of attributes and on the one example in a batch that a neuron isolates. An average over records can look harmless while a few records are fully exposed. This is why attacks are reported as the TPR at a low FPR rather than as accuracy or area under the curve (AUC), and why the defence of the next part has to hold for every record and every dataset.

A third idea closes the part and frames what comes after it. Reconstruction attacks show that answering too many statistics too accurately destroys privacy no matter how the answers are computed: this is the Fundamental Law of Information Recovery. Some noise is not optional, and the question becomes how little noise is enough.

title: Threat models and attacks
text:
How to read this part
Order. The part opens with chapter 9, which sets up the vocabulary, and then has two halves. Chapters 10 to 14 attack trained models, from the smallest secret to the largest: one bit of membership, a sensitive attribute, a property of the training population, memorized text, and whole inputs recovered from gradients. Chapters 15 to 17 attack released data, from the weakest defence to the strongest: names removed (linkage), records hidden in crowds (syntactic anonymity), and only aggregate statistics published (reconstruction).
Read chapter 9 first. It fixes the vocabulary (challenger, adversary, view, game, advantage, baseline) that the others use without redefining. Then read chapter 10, since membership inference is the reference attack that chapters 11, 12 and 13 extend. Chapters 11 to 14 can then be read in any order. Read chapters 15 to 17 in order: chapter 16 starts from the linkage game of chapter 15 and uses the imputation baseline of chapter 11, and chapter 17 shows that even exact aggregate statistics, with no records released at all, give the data away. Chapters 16 and 17 matter most for what comes next: the attacks of chapter 16 are the requirements the next part’s definition is built to meet, and the results of chapter 17 return as lower bounds there.
Structure of a chapter. Every chapter has the same shape as in the prerequisites: why the topic matters, a toolkit, one section per result with a context, statement, derivation, interpretation, worked example and two check yourself questions, then code, references and a cheat sheet. Exercises with worked solutions are collected in the exercise book, a companion website, with a link at the end of each chapter.
Toy experiments, real pipelines. The attacks in the literature run on image classifiers and large language models trained on GPUs. Here every experiment is a NumPy toy that runs in seconds: logistic regression on synthetic data, Gaussian mean estimation, a small multilayer perceptron written by hand, an n-gram language model with planted canaries. Each toy is chosen so that the optimal attack can be computed exactly and compared with the practical one. Where a chapter’s study-plan exercise needs the full pipeline (such as LiRA with 16 shadow models on CIFAR-10), the chapter describes that pipeline in prose and runs a faithful scaled-down version.
Run the code. From the repository root, for example,
uv run python code/part02-attacks/membership_inference.py
The scripts use fixed seeds, so their output matches the tables in the text.

title: Threat models and attacks
section: What you will be able to do

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.1 Why this matters
A hospital trains a model on patient records and offers it to doctors through a web service. Is the model “private”? The question has no answer until you say against whom. Can the attacker only send inputs and read predicted labels, or does it hold the weights? Does it know the other patients in the training set, or only what the population looks like? Does it follow the rules of the service, or does it also slip crafted records into the training data? And what does it want: to learn that one person was a patient, to learn their diagnosis, or to rebuild the whole table? A threat model answers these questions. Without one, “the model leaks” and “the model is safe” are both untestable claims.
Once the threat model is fixed, an attack can be written down as a game, the way cryptographers write down attacks on encryption. A challenger runs the training pipeline with some hidden secret, such as whether one patient’s record was used. It hands the adversary what the threat model allows it to see, and the adversary guesses the secret. An attack is good if it guesses better than someone who never saw the model.
That is the one idea of this chapter: an attack is a guess about a hidden secret, made from a view that the threat model fixes. When the secret is a single bit, such as “was this patient in the training set?”, the game is a hypothesis test, so everything in Hypothesis testing carries over. The attack’s advantage is its true positive rate (TPR) minus its false positive rate (FPR). No attack can push it above the total variation (TV) distance between what the adversary sees in the two worlds, and one curve bounds the attack’s whole error trade-off.
The chapter builds this up in four steps. It first lists what a threat model has to specify, and proves the one ordering that always holds: more access never makes the adversary weaker. It then writes the attacks of this part as games, each with its own baseline. Next it turns the hypothesis-testing results into ceilings on any attack, and explains why the low false-positive end of the curve is where privacy is really lost. Finally it shows how far apart the average-case and worst-case versions of the same game can be. Every later chapter of this part is an instance of these games: membership inference, attribute inference, dataset properties and reconstruction. Table 9.1 lists the results and where they are used.
What this chapter assumes. The hypothesis-testing vocabulary (type I and II errors, the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the trade-off function \(T(P, Q)\), receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves) is in Hypothesis testing. The total variation distance and the hockey-stick divergence \(E_\gamma\) are in Divergences. Security games and advantage, in their cryptographic form, are in Cryptography basics. No privacy definition is introduced here: this part only attacks. The definition that defends against these games comes in Part 3.
Conventions. \(D\) is a dataset of records drawn from a population \(\pi\). A training algorithm \(\mathcal T\) maps \(D\) to a model \(\theta = \mathcal T(D)\), possibly at random. In a two-world game a hidden bit \(b\) selects the world: \(b = 1\) is the world in which the target’s record is used (“member”, the alternative hypothesis), and \(b = 0\) the world in which it is not (the null). Everything the adversary gets to look at, including what it knew beforehand, is its view \(V\). \(P\) and \(Q\) are the distributions of \(V\) when \(b = 0\) and \(b = 1\). An attack outputs a guess \(b'\), 1 for “member” and 0 for “not a member”. Two numbers describe how it behaves. Its true positive rate is the fraction of members it correctly flags, and its false positive rate is the fraction of non-members it wrongly flags:
\[\mathrm{TPR} = \Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 1], \qquad \mathrm{FPR} = \Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 0]. \tag{9.1}\]

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
section: 9.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses
text:
9.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses

9.2.1 Fact 1 — A game with a hidden bit is a hypothesis test
The challenger flips the hidden bit before anything else happens: \(b = 1\) with probability \(\pi_1\) and \(b = 0\) with probability \(\pi_0 = 1 - \pi_1\). The adversary then sees its view and announces \(b'\). It wins when its guess matches the hidden bit, whichever value the bit has: \(b' = b\) means “\(b' = 1\) and \(b = 1\), or \(b' = 0\) and \(b = 0\)”. So \(\Pr[b' = b]\) is the probability that the guess is correct, taken over the challenger’s coin flip and everything else that is random in the game. It is not the probability that \(b\) is 1, which is just \(\pi_1\). The probability of a correct guess is
\[\Pr[b' = b] = \pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR} + \pi_0\,(1 - \mathrm{FPR}). \tag{9.2}\]
Derivation. The idea is to split the games by which world the challenger chose, count the wins in each world, and add.

Split the win into the two worlds. There are exactly two ways to win: the bit is 1 and the attack says 1, or the bit is 0 and the attack says 0. In a single game the bit has one value, either 1 or 0, so a game can win in one of these ways or the other, never both. Events that cannot happen together are called disjoint, and the probability that one of two disjoint events happens is the sum of their probabilities. Counting games shows why: if you count the games won with \(b = 1\) and the games won with \(b = 0\), every won game is counted exactly once, because no game belongs to both groups. (For events that can overlap you would have to subtract the overlap, which here is empty.) So \[\Pr[b' = b] = \Pr[b = 1 \text{ and } b' = 1] + \Pr[b = 0 \text{ and } b' = 0]. \tag{9.3}\]
Write each joint probability as “prior times conditional”. For any two events, \(\Pr[A \text{ and } B] = \Pr[A]\Pr[B \mid A]\). So \(\Pr[b = 1 \text{ and } b' = 1] = \Pr[b = 1]\Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 1] = \pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}\), by the definition of the TPR.
Do the same in the other world. \(\Pr[b = 0 \text{ and } b' = 0] = \pi_0\Pr[b' = 0 \mid b = 0]\). When the bit is 0 the attack says either 0 or 1, so \(\Pr[b' = 0 \mid b = 0] = 1 - \Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 0] = 1 - \mathrm{FPR}\).
Add the two worlds. This gives Equation 9.2.

A concrete count. Play 1,000 games with an attack whose TPR is 0.6 and FPR is 0.2. Table 9.2 counts the wins for a fair bit, \(\pi_1 = \frac12\), and for a bit that is 1 only one time in ten, \(\pi_1 = 0.1\).



Table 9.2: Expected wins in 1,000 games of an attack with TPR 0.6 and FPR 0.2. The win rate in each world is fixed by the attack; the prior decides how many games are played in each world.

The formula gives the same numbers: \(\frac12(0.6) + \frac12(0.8) = 0.7\) and \(0.1(0.6) + 0.9(0.8) = 0.78\). The second row is a warning. The attack wins more often there, but only because most games are played in the world where saying 0 is easy. Always saying 0, with no attack at all, would win 900 of those games. Accuracy alone cannot tell a good attack from a good guess about the prior, which is why every game below is scored against a baseline.
Most evaluations use a fair bit, \(\pi_1 = \frac12\): half the targets are members and half are not, so that neither answer is right more often by default. In that game an adversary who never looks at its view, and so has nothing to go on, wins exactly half the games, whatever it answers; a coin flip, “always say member” and “always say non-member” all score \(\frac12\). That is the sense of “coin flip” below: not a model of any attack, but the score of knowing nothing in a fair game. With a fair bit, Equation 9.2 becomes \(\frac12\mathrm{TPR} + \frac12(1 - \mathrm{FPR}) = \frac12 + \frac12(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR})\): the know-nothing score, plus half of the difference between the two rates. That difference is the advantage,
\[\mathrm{Adv} = \mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} = 2\Pr[b' = b] - 1, \tag{9.4}\]
and it measures how much better the attack does than an adversary who ignores its view. The second equality is the fair-bit formula solved for \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\): from \(\Pr[b' = b] = \frac12 + \frac12(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR})\), subtract \(\frac12\) and multiply by 2.
Why does this number measure the gain over knowing nothing? Look at what it is: \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\) is how much more often the attack says “member” when the target is a member than when it is not. Three cases show what that means.

An attack that ignores its view scores 0. A coin flip, or “always say member”, does not look at anything that differs between the two worlds, so it says 1 with the same probability in both. Its TPR equals its FPR, its advantage is 0, and by the fair-bit formula it wins with probability exactly \(\frac12\).
A perfect attack scores 1. It says 1 every time the target is a member and never otherwise: \(\mathrm{TPR} = 1\), \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0\), advantage 1, and it wins every game.
Every attack in between is scored by its extra wins. Rearranged, Equation 9.4 says \(\mathrm{Adv} = 2\big(\Pr[b' = b] - \frac12\big)\): the amount by which the attack’s win probability exceeds the know-nothing score \(\frac12\), doubled so that a perfect attack scores 1. An attack can only win more than half the time if its answer depends on which world it is in, and the advantage measures exactly how much it does.

A negative advantage means the attack says “member” more often for non-members; flipping its answers turns it into an attack with the same advantage, positive. In the first row of Table 9.2 the advantage is \(0.6 - 0.2 = 0.4 = 2(0.7) - 1\): the attack wins 0.2 more often than a coin flip, and 0.2 doubled is 0.4. Unlike the win rate, the advantage does not depend on the prior, because TPR and FPR are each measured inside one world. That matters because real targets are rarely half members. With an unequal prior the know-nothing score is no longer \(\frac12\) but the larger of \(\pi_0\) and \(\pi_1\), which is 0.9 in the second row of Table 9.2, where always saying 0 wins 900 games of 1,000. The advantage needs no adjustment: an attack that ignores its view still has \(\mathrm{TPR} = \mathrm{FPR}\) and advantage 0, at any prior. Every two-world game in this part is scored by its advantage, and the best possible guess with an unequal prior (Equation 9.10) starts from Equation 9.2. The same fact, in the language of security games, is Fact 1 of Cryptography basics.


9.2.2 Fact 2 — Processing the view cannot help the adversary
If the adversary throws information away, or adds noise of its own, it cannot do better. Formally, let \(V' = g(V, R)\) for any function \(g\) and any randomness \(R\) independent of \(b\). Then every attack that sees \(V'\) has the same TPR and FPR as some attack that sees \(V\), so the best advantage from \(V'\), and the best TPR at every FPR, are at most those from \(V\).
The reason is that whoever holds \(V\) can always produce \(V'\) themselves. Given an attack \(A'\) on \(V'\), build an attack \(A\) on \(V\) that draws \(R\), computes \(g(V, R)\) and runs \(A'\) on the result. In each world \(A\)’s output has the same distribution as \(A'\)’s, so it has the same TPR and FPR. For instance, if a service returns a confidence score \(s\) and you only look at whether \(s > 0.5\), you can do no better than someone who looks at \(s\) itself, because they could apply the same cut-off.
This is the data processing inequality of Divergences, seen from the attacker’s side. It is what orders the access levels of a threat model.


9.2.3 Fact 3 — Mixing hides, and knowing the mixture index undoes it
This fact compares adversaries who know different amounts, so it needs a number for “the best any attack can do against views \(P\) and \(Q\)”. That number is the total variation distance. For views with probabilities \(p(x)\) and \(q(x)\), it is half the total absolute difference between the two probability tables, \[\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) = \tfrac12\sum_x|p(x) - q(x)|. \tag{9.5}\] It is the best possible advantage for a simple reason. An attack that says “member” on a set \(A\) of views has \(\mathrm{TPR} = Q(A)\) and \(\mathrm{FPR} = P(A)\), so its advantage is \(Q(A) - P(A) = \sum_{x \in A}(q(x) - p(x))\). That sum is largest when \(A\) contains exactly the views where \(q(x) > p(x)\), the views that are more likely in the member world, and its largest value is the total excess of \(q\) over \(p\), which is half the total absolute difference. Section 9.5 returns to this with the full error curve.
Now the fact itself. Often the adversary’s view depends on something it does not know, such as the other records in the dataset. Not knowing it works like extra noise: the adversary sees an average of several possible situations, and averaging two distributions can only blur the difference between them. Knowing it removes that noise, and being allowed to choose it lets the adversary pick the situation where the difference is largest.
In symbols, call the unknown \(\Theta\), with weights \(w_\vartheta\), and let \(P_\vartheta\) and \(Q_\vartheta\) be the views in the two worlds when \(\Theta = \vartheta\). An adversary who does not see \(\Theta\) faces the averages \(\bar P = \sum_\vartheta w_\vartheta P_\vartheta\) and \(\bar Q = \sum_\vartheta w_\vartheta Q_\vartheta\). An adversary who sees it faces the pair \((\Theta, V)\). Their best advantages are ordered, from not knowing, to knowing, to choosing:
\[\mathrm{TV}(\bar P, \bar Q) \;\le\; \sum_\vartheta w_\vartheta\,\mathrm{TV}(P_\vartheta, Q_\vartheta) \;=\; \mathrm{TV}\big((\Theta, V)_{b=0}, (\Theta, V)_{b=1}\big) \;\le\; \max_\vartheta \mathrm{TV}(P_\vartheta, Q_\vartheta). \tag{9.6}\]
Each step has a short proof. The first inequality is the triangle inequality, \(|a + b| \le |a| + |b|\), which says that differences can cancel when they are added up before taking absolute values, but not after: \(\mathrm{TV}(\bar P, \bar Q) = \frac12\sum_x\big|\sum_\vartheta w_\vartheta(p_\vartheta(x) - q_\vartheta(x))\big| \le \frac12\sum_x\sum_\vartheta w_\vartheta|p_\vartheta(x) - q_\vartheta(x)|\), and swapping the sums gives the middle term. The equality holds because the pair \((\Theta, V)\) has probability \(w_\vartheta p_\vartheta(x)\) in world 0 and \(w_\vartheta q_\vartheta(x)\) in world 1, so half the \(L^1\) distance between the two worlds is exactly \(\sum_\vartheta w_\vartheta\mathrm{TV}(P_\vartheta, Q_\vartheta)\). The last inequality says that an average is at most its largest term.
A tiny case shows how much the unknown can hide. Let there be one other record, with a bit \(\vartheta \in \{0, 1\}\) that is 0 or 1 with probability \(\frac12\) each, and let the mechanism release the exact count \(\vartheta + b\). An adversary who knows \(\vartheta\) subtracts it and reads off \(b\), so for each \(\vartheta\) the TV is 1. An adversary who does not know it sees counts 0 or 1 in world 0 and 1 or 2 in world 1, each with probability \(\frac12\). A count of 1 could come from either world, and the TV drops to \(\frac12\) (Exercise 7). This fact is what separates the average-case and worst-case games, and it is how the chapter prices side information.

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.3 Threat models

9.3.1 Context
Papers on privacy attacks report numbers such as “membership advantage 0.2” or “90% of records reconstructed”. Those numbers mean nothing until you know what the attacker was assumed to see, know and do. A threat model fixes these assumptions. This section lists what a threat model has to specify, and proves the one ordering that always holds among the choices: an adversary with more access is never weaker.


9.3.2 Statement
A threat model answers five questions.

Goal: what is the secret? Whether a given record was in the training data (membership), the value of a sensitive field of a known record (attribute), the records themselves (reconstruction), or a statistic of the dataset as a whole (property).
Access: what does the adversary observe? From least to most: only the model’s decisions on inputs it chooses, such as a predicted class or an “anomaly” flag (label-only); the model’s scores on those inputs, such as confidences, losses or log-probabilities (black-box); the parameters \(\theta\) themselves (white-box); or everything the training process exposed along the way, such as intermediate models and per-step gradients (the transcript).
Behaviour: does it follow the rules? An honest-but-curious (semi-honest) adversary follows the protocol and only analyses what it legitimately sees. A malicious (active) adversary may deviate: choose its queries adaptively, insert crafted records into the training data (poisoning), or, if it runs part of the system, send tampered models to the other participants.
Trust: who sees the raw data? In the central model a trusted curator holds the data, and the adversary sees only what is released. In the local model nobody is trusted: each person’s data leave their device already protected, and the adversary may be the collector itself. Distributed settings, where many parties each hold a slice, sit in between.
Side information: what does it know already? The population distribution, a public dataset drawn from it, some or all of the other records, the target’s non-sensitive fields.

Of these, access is the one with a natural order, and the reason is Fact 2. Each level of access lets the adversary compute the level below it: from the weights it can compute any score, and from a score it can compute the label. So whatever an attack does with less access, an attack with more access can do too, and the best attack can only get better as access grows. Write \(\mathrm{Adv}^*(V) = \max_A \mathrm{Adv}(A)\) for the best advantage of any attack whose input is the view \(V\). For the same model and the same side information \(S\),
\[\mathrm{Adv}^*(\text{labels}, S) \le \mathrm{Adv}^*(\text{scores}, S) \le \mathrm{Adv}^*(\theta, S) \le \mathrm{Adv}^*(\text{transcript}, S), \tag{9.7}\]
and the same chain holds for the best TPR at every fixed FPR. In the same way, more side information never lowers the best advantage, \(\mathrm{Adv}^*(V) \le \mathrm{Adv}^*(V, S)\), and neither does allowing malicious behaviour.


9.3.3 Derivation

Each view can be computed from the next one. A label is a function of the scores: the class with the largest score, or “score above a cut-off”. A score on a query \(x\) is a function of \(\theta\) and \(x\), and the adversary chose \(x\) itself. The final \(\theta\) is the last entry of the transcript.
So Fact 2 applies at each link. Each view on the left of Equation 9.7 is \(g(V, R)\) for the view \(V\) to its right. Its achievable \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{TPR})\) pairs are therefore a subset of those to its right, and a maximum over a smaller set is smaller.
Side information works the same way. \(V\) is what you get from \((V, S)\) by forgetting \(S\), so Fact 2 applies again.
Behaviour is a larger set of strategies. An honest-but-curious adversary is a malicious one that chooses not to deviate, and a maximum over more strategies is at least as large.



9.3.4 Interpretation
The chain compares the best attacks at each level, not the attacks people actually run. A particular white-box attack can do worse than a well-designed black-box one, and the example below shows the gap inside a single access level can be larger than the gap between levels.
The access levels map directly onto deployments. Label-only and black-box access describe a model behind an application programming interface (API), such as a cloud prediction service or a chatbot. White-box access describes released weights, and also every participant who receives the global model in federated learning. The transcript describes a federated-learning server that sees each client’s updates, the setting of Gradient inversion. Table 9.3 places four common deployments on all the axes. The same trained model can sit in several rows at once, and its risk is set by the weakest one.

Trust works differently from the other axes: it decides who the adversary is, not how strong it is. In the central model the threat is whoever sees the released model, and the curator is outside the threat model. In the local model the curator is inside it, so protection has to be applied before data leave the user. Part 3 compares the two.
Side information is the hardest axis to bound, because the defender usually does not know what the adversary knows. That is why the strongest assumption, “the adversary knows every record except the target’s”, is the one a guarantee should survive (Section 9.6).


9.3.5 Example: a centroid anomaly detector at four access levels
A security team fits the simplest anomaly detector there is: the mean \(\theta = \frac1n\sum_i x_i\) of \(n = 100\) records \(x_i \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)\) with \(d = 50\) features. A point \(x\) gets the anomaly score \(\|x - \theta\|^2\) and is flagged when the score exceeds \(\tau = d\). The adversary holds a target \(z\) and plays the membership game: if \(b = 1\), \(z\) is one of the \(n\) records; if \(b = 0\), it is a fresh draw from the population. Here is what the adversary can do at each level of access.
With the weights (white-box), the adversary knows \(\theta\). The best thing it can do with \(\theta\) is to ask how much more likely this exact \(\theta\) is in the member world than in the non-member world. That ratio of the two probability densities is the likelihood ratio, and the Neyman–Pearson lemma of Hypothesis testing says that, for any target false positive rate, no attack catches more members than one that says “member” when the likelihood ratio is above a threshold. Intuitively, the views that are most typical of members relative to non-members are the ones to flag first.
Here the two densities are Gaussians. If \(z\) was used, \(\theta = (z + S)/n\), where \(S \sim \mathcal N(0, (n - 1)I_d)\) is the sum of the other records, so \(\theta\) is pulled a little towards \(z\). If it was not, \(\theta \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d/n)\). Expanding the squares in the two Gaussian densities gives the log of the likelihood ratio,
\[\ln\frac{q(\theta \mid z)}{p(\theta \mid z)} = \frac{n}{2(n - 1)}\big(2\langle z, \theta\rangle - \|\theta\|^2\big) - \frac{\|z\|^2}{2(n - 1)} + \text{const}, \tag{9.8}\]
and the best white-box attack thresholds it. The bracket \(2\langle z, \theta\rangle - \|\theta\|^2\) is the part that depends on \(\theta\): it grows when \(\theta\) points towards \(z\), which is exactly what training on \(z\) does.
With only the score (black-box), the adversary gets \(\|z - \theta\|^2 = \|z\|^2 - \big(2\langle z, \theta\rangle - \|\theta\|^2\big)\). It knows \(z\), so the calibrated score \(\|z\|^2 - \|z - \theta\|^2\) gives back exactly the bracket that the white-box likelihood ratio needs, and the remaining term \(-\|z\|^2/(2(n - 1))\) it can compute itself. The calibrated score drops that term, which only shifts the threshold from one target to the next, so it is almost, not exactly, the likelihood-ratio test: in Table 9.4 the two agree to four decimals. In this model the score carries everything about \(\theta\) that matters for the decision (it is a sufficient statistic: the likelihood ratio can be computed from it alone), so white-box access adds nothing. A simpler black-box attack ignores \(\|z\|^2\) and says “member” when the raw score is low. That attack is confused by targets that are simply far from the mean: they have a high score whether or not they were used, so it mixes a target’s typicality with its membership. With only the flag (label-only), the adversary says “member” when \(z\) is not flagged.
The script plays 100,000 games in each world and reports the best advantage over thresholds of each score (Table 9.4).
