The chain Equation 9.7 holds: \(0.0400 \le 0.2789 \le 0.2789\). But the large gap is inside the black-box level, between two attacks on the same view. Calibrating each target against its own typicality multiplies the advantage by about seven. That is the idea behind the per-example attacks of Membership inference. Sablayrolles et al. (2019) prove a general version: if training draws the parameters with a probability that decreases exponentially in the training loss, the Bayes-optimal membership attack depends on the parameters only through the target’s loss, and white-box access then adds little, as here.
Figure 9.1 shows the calibrated scores in the two worlds, and the advantage at each level as the dimension grows. With more parameters per record, a single record moves the model in more directions at once, and the best advantage climbs from 0.0326 at \(d = 1\) to 0.7407 at \(d = 500\) (100,000 games per world).






Figure 9.1: Left: the calibrated black-box score \(\|z\|^2 - \|z - \theta\|^2\) for members and non-members of the centroid detector, \(n = 100\), \(d = 50\). Right: the best advantage at each access level against the dimension \(d\), from 20,000 games per world and point. White-box and calibrated black-box coincide; raw loss and label-only are far below.





9.3.6 Check yourself

A service adds a little random noise to every confidence score it returns. Can that make some attack stronger? (No. The noisy score is \(g(\text{score}, R)\) with \(R\) independent of \(b\), so by Fact 2 every attack on it is matched by an attack on the clean score. Noise can only lower the best advantage, though it may not lower it by much.)
Why can a black-box attack beat a white-box attack in practice, despite Equation 9.7? (The chain compares the best attack at each level. A particular white-box attack can be badly designed, just as the raw-loss attack is far worse than the calibrated one in Table 9.4.)

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.4 Privacy games

9.4.1 Context
The same name, such as “membership inference”, is used for attacks with different assumptions and different ways of scoring success. Salem et al. (“SoK: Let the Privacy Games Begin!”, 2023) collect the attacks in the literature and write each one as a game between a challenger and an adversary. A game pins down three things: how the secret and the data are drawn, what the adversary sees, and how its guess is scored against a baseline. This section defines the games used in the rest of the part, and works out the best possible guess when the secret is a bit.


9.4.2 Statement
Every game in this part has the same four steps. The challenger draws a secret \(s\) from a known distribution, together with a dataset \(D\) whose distribution may depend on \(s\). It trains \(\theta = \mathcal T(D)\) and gives the adversary the view \(V\) that the threat model allows, along with the side information \(S\). The adversary outputs a guess \(s'\) and earns a gain \(g(s, s')\), usually \(\mathbf 1[s' = s]\). Finally, the attack is compared with a baseline: the best expected gain of a guess made from \(S\) alone, without looking at \(V\). Figure 9.2 draws the membership game, and Table 9.5 lists the others.



Table 9.5: The privacy games of this part. The first three are average-case: data come from the population. The distinguishing game is worst-case: the adversary picks the data.

Figure 9.2: The membership game. The challenger trains on a dataset, flips a bit that decides whether the target was in it, and shows the adversary the target and a view of the model. The adversary’s guess is scored by its advantage.



When the secret is a bit that is not equally likely to be 0 or 1, the best possible guess has a closed form, and the idea behind it is simple. Say the bit is 1 only rarely, with prior \(\pi_1 < \frac12\). Then the safe default is to guess 0, which already wins with probability \(\pi_0\). The view should overturn that default only where it is strong enough evidence for 1 to outweigh the prior: where a view is more than \(\gamma = \pi_0/\pi_1\) times as likely when the bit is 1 as when it is 0. With \(\pi_1 = 0.1\) that is 9 times as likely. The best attack’s gain over the default is the probability mass on those strongly convincing views.
The quantity that measures this mass is the hockey-stick divergence. With \(p\) and \(q\) the probabilities of a view when the bit is 0 and 1, \[E_\gamma(Q\|P) = \sum_x\max\big(q(x) - \gamma p(x),\, 0\big), \tag{9.9}\] the total by which \(q\) exceeds \(\gamma\) times \(p\), counted only on the views where it does. At \(\gamma = 1\) it is the total variation distance of Fact 3. The best attack wins with probability
\[\max_A\Pr[b' = b] = \pi_0 + \pi_1\,E_\gamma(Q\|P), \qquad \gamma = \frac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}. \tag{9.10}\]
The first term is the baseline of always guessing 0; the second is everything the view adds.


9.4.3 Derivation
The Bayes-optimal guess (Equation 9.10).

Write an attack as a set. A deterministic attack says 1 on some set \(A\) of views. By Equation 9.2 it wins with probability \(\pi_1Q(A) + \pi_0(1 - P(A))\).
Pull out the baseline. This equals \(\pi_0 + \pi_1\big(Q(A) - \gamma P(A)\big)\) with \(\gamma = \pi_0/\pi_1\).
Choose the best set. \(Q(A) - \gamma P(A) = \sum_{x \in A}\big(q(x) - \gamma p(x)\big)\) is a sum over the views in \(A\). To make it as large as possible, put a view in \(A\) exactly when its term is positive, that is when \(q(x) > \gamma p(x)\). The maximum is then the sum of the positive terms, which is \(E_\gamma(Q\|P)\). In words: say 1 when the likelihood ratio \(q/p\) exceeds the prior odds \(\gamma\) against the bit being 1. A randomized attack says 1 on view \(x\) with some probability \(\phi(x)\) and gets \(\sum_x\phi(x)(q(x) - \gamma p(x))\), which is also largest with \(\phi = 1\) on the positive terms and 0 elsewhere, so randomizing does not help.
Check the fair case. With \(\pi_1 = \frac12\), \(\gamma = 1\) and \(E_1 = \mathrm{TV}\), so the best attack wins with probability \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{TV}\), matching Fact 1 with the best advantage TV of Fact 3.

Reconstruction from one exact count. The secret is \(m\) uniform bits \(x_1, \dots, x_m\), and the release is their sum \(K\).

What the count says about each bit. Given \(K = k\), every arrangement of \(k\) ones among \(m\) places is equally likely, so each bit is 1 with probability \(k/m\).
The best guess for each bit. Guess 1 when \(k/m > \frac12\) and 0 otherwise. Every bit gets the same guess, the majority value, and the expected number right is \(\max(k, m - k)\).
Average over the count. With \(K \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(m, \frac12)\), the expected fraction recovered is \(\mathbb E[\max(K, m - K)]/m = \frac12 + \mathbb E|K - \frac m2|/m\).
How large the gain is. The count is a sum of \(m\) fair bits, each with variance \(\frac14\), so by the central limit theorem \(K - \frac m2\) is approximately normal with mean 0 and variance \(m/4\). The average distance of a normal variable from its mean is its standard deviation times \(\sqrt{2/\pi}\) (integrate \(|x|\) against the normal density), here \(\frac{\sqrt m}{2}\sqrt{2/\pi}\). Dividing by \(m\), the fraction recovered is approximately \(\frac12 + \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi m}}\).



9.4.4 Interpretation
The baseline is part of the game, not an afterthought. A model that lets an attacker guess a rare diagnosis “with 90% accuracy” reveals nothing if 90% of people do not have that diagnosis. Accuracy only means something next to the baseline of Equation 9.10.
Attribute inference needs particular care, because it has two possible baselines that answer different questions. Comparing with a guess from the population asks “does the model help?”. Comparing members with non-members asks “does the model help because this person was in the training data?”. Only the second is a breach of that person’s privacy; the first may be ordinary statistics that any study of the population would reveal. Attribute inference and model inversion develops this.
The games also differ in where the data come from. In the membership, attribute and reconstruction games the data are drawn from the population, so the score is an average over datasets and targets. In the distinguishing game the adversary chooses both datasets, so the score is a worst case. Section 9.6 shows that the first is never larger than the second, and how far apart they can be. Finally, games and threat models combine freely: every row of Table 9.5 can be played at every access level, so “label-only membership” and “white-box reconstruction” are both well defined.


9.4.5 Example: one noisy count, three games
A data team publishes how many people in a dataset have a sensitive condition, with Gaussian noise added: \(Y = \sum_{x \in D}x + \sigma Z\), with bits \(x \in \{0, 1\}\), \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(\sigma = 1\). Suppose the adversary knows every record except the target’s, so the rest of the count is a known number \(c\). The same release can be attacked in three games.
In the membership game, the target has the condition. Without the target, \(Y \sim \mathcal N(c, 1)\); with it, \(Y \sim \mathcal N(c + 1, 1)\): the same bell curve, shifted right by one. The best attack says “member” on the views more likely in the member world, which are the counts to the right of the point where the two curves cross, \(c + \frac12\). Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF), so \(\Phi(t)\) is the probability that a standard normal variable is below \(t\). A member’s count lands above \(c + \frac12\) with probability \(\Phi(\frac12)\), its TPR, and a non-member’s with probability \(1 - \Phi(\frac12)\), its FPR. The advantage is \(2\Phi(\frac12) - 1\), and by Fact 1 the attack wins with probability \(\frac12 + \frac12\big(2\Phi(\frac12) - 1\big) = \Phi(\frac12) = 0.6915\).
In the attribute game with a fair prior, the target is known to be in \(D\) and its bit is the secret. The view has the same two distributions, so the best guess is again right with probability 0.6915 (0.6925 in 200,000 simulated games). Now make the condition rare, with prior \(\pi_1 = 0.1\). Always guessing “no” already wins with probability 0.9, and by Equation 9.10 the release should overturn that only where the count is at least \(\gamma = 9\) times as likely with the condition as without. For two unit-variance normals one apart, the likelihood ratio at \(y\) is \(e^{(y - c) - 1/2}\), which exceeds 9 when \(y > c + \frac12 + \ln 9\). On those counts, \(Q\) puts mass \(\Phi(\frac12 - \ln 9)\) and \(P\) puts mass \(\Phi(-\frac12 - \ln 9)\), so \(E_9 = \Phi(\frac12 - \ln 9) - 9\Phi(-\frac12 - \ln 9) = 0.0134\). The best accuracy is \(0.9 + 0.1 \times 0.0134 = 0.9013\) (simulated: 0.9028). The same release that lifts a fair guess from 0.5 to 0.69 lifts this one by about a tenth of a percentage point, because the likelihood ratio is rarely large enough to overturn 9-to-1 odds.
In the reconstruction game, release the exact count of \(m\) uniform bits instead. The best reconstruction recovers a fraction 0.6230 of the bits for \(m = 10\) (0.6236 in simulation), 0.5398 for \(m = 100\) and 0.5126 for \(m = 1000\). The approximation \(\frac12 + 1/\sqrt{2\pi m}\) gives 0.6262, 0.5399 and 0.5126. One aggregate reveals little about each record, and less as \(m\) grows. Many aggregates are a different matter: Reconstruction attacks shows how a few times as many noisy subset counts as there are bits give away almost every bit.


9.4.6 Check yourself

In the distinguishing game the adversary picks \(D_0\) and \(D_1\). Why does that make its best advantage at least the best advantage in the membership game, for the same mechanism? (It can pick the pair that is hardest to hide, for example the dataset and target on which the mechanism leaks the most. The membership game averages over pairs drawn from the population, and a maximum is at least an average, as Section 9.6 makes precise.)
An attribute attack is right 75% of the time on members and 75% of the time on non-members. Is it a privacy attack on the members? (No. It does equally well on people who were never in the data, so it is inferring the attribute from the population, not from the person’s participation.)

section: 9.5 Advantage, total variation and the trade-off curve
text:
9.5 Advantage, total variation and the trade-off curve

9.5.1 Context
A two-world game is a test of \(H_0: V \sim P\) (“not a member”) against \(H_1: V \sim Q\) (“member”). So everything Hypothesis testing proved about tests becomes a statement about attacks. This section draws out three: a ceiling on the advantage, a ceiling on the whole ROC curve, and a warning about which point of that curve to report.


9.5.2 Statement
Fact 3 already showed that no attack’s advantage exceeds the total variation distance between the two worlds’ views. The first bound restates that. The second goes further: it bounds the attack’s TPR at every false positive rate, not just at the one point where TPR − FPR is largest. The bound comes from the trade-off function \(T(P, Q)\): for each false positive rate \(\alpha\), \(T(P, Q)(\alpha)\) is the smallest fraction of members that any attack with false positive rate \(\alpha\) must miss. An attack can catch at most the rest. For every attack in a two-world game,
\[\mathrm{Adv} = \mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} \le \mathrm{TV}(P, Q), \qquad \Pr[b' = b] \le \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\mathrm{TV}(P, Q), \tag{9.11}\]
\[\mathrm{TPR} \le 1 - T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR}). \tag{9.12}\]
Both bounds are attained by likelihood-ratio attacks, which flag the views that are most typical of members relative to non-members first.
The third quantity answers the question a person who is flagged cares about: given that the attack says “member”, how likely is that to be true? Of all the targets the attack flags, some are members (a fraction \(\pi_1\) of targets are members, and it flags a fraction TPR of them) and some are non-members (a fraction \(\pi_0\), of which it flags FPR). The precision is the members’ share of the flagged:
\[\Pr[b = 1 \mid b' = 1] = \frac{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}}{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR} + \pi_0\,\mathrm{FPR}}. \tag{9.13}\]


9.5.3 Derivation

The attack is a test. It says “member”, rejecting \(H_0\), with probability \(\phi(V)\). Its type I error is the FPR and its type II error is \(1 - \mathrm{TPR}\).
The advantage ceiling (Equation 9.11). The advantage of an attack that says “member” with probability \(\phi(x)\) on view \(x\) is \(\sum_x\phi(x)(q(x) - p(x))\). It is largest when \(\phi = 1\) exactly where \(q > p\), that is, where the likelihood ratio \(q/p\) is above 1, and that largest value is \(\mathrm{TV}(P, Q)\), as in Fact 3. The winning probability follows from Fact 1.
The curve ceiling (Equation 9.12). The fraction of members an attack misses is \(1 - \mathrm{TPR}\). By the definition of the trade-off function, no attack with false positive rate FPR misses fewer than \(T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR})\), so \(1 - \mathrm{TPR} \ge T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR})\). Which attack attains it? The Neyman–Pearson lemma answers: with a budget of false positives to spend, spend it on the views where members are most over-represented, that is, flag views in decreasing order of the likelihood ratio \(q/p\) until the false positive rate reaches the budget. Each view flagged that way buys the most members per false positive.
Precision (Equation 9.13). The precision is a conditional probability, so it is the probability that a target is a member and flagged, divided by the probability that it is flagged. The first is \(\pi_1\mathrm{TPR}\), as in step 2 of Fact 1. A target is flagged either as a member, \(\pi_1\mathrm{TPR}\), or as a non-member, \(\pi_0\mathrm{FPR}\), and these are disjoint, so the second is their sum.



9.5.4 Interpretation
The advantage is only one point of the ROC curve, the plot of an attack’s TPR against its FPR as its threshold varies. Because the advantage is TPR − FPR, it is the height of that curve above the diagonal, and TV is the largest such height, reached at the likelihood-ratio threshold 1, and it says nothing about what happens at the low false-positive end. Yet that end is where privacy breaks. An attack that flags 1% of members with no false alarms has an advantage of only about 0.01, yet it identifies those members with certainty. An attack with advantage 0.1, right on 55% of members and wrong on 45% of non-members, identifies nobody with confidence. Carlini et al. (2022) argue from this that membership attacks should be reported by their TPR at a low FPR, such as \(10^{-3}\), on ROC curves with log axes. The rest of this part does so.
Precision tells the same story from the attacker’s side. If only one target in a hundred is a member, even a good attack produces mostly false alarms (Jayaraman et al. 2021). A low FPR is what keeps precision high when members are rare.
The two ceilings depend only on \(P\) and \(Q\), so they bound every attack, including ones nobody has invented yet. That is what makes them the right target for a defence: a mechanism whose trade-off curve \(T(P, Q)\) stays close to the diagonal for every target defeats every attack at once.


9.5.5 Example: the noisy count, worst case
Take the noisy count of the previous example, \(\sigma = 1\), with the other \(m = 100\) bits known (the script fixes them at 50 ones). Then \(P = \mathcal N(50, 1)\), \(Q = \mathcal N(51, 1)\), and as computed there the best attack says “member” when \(Y > 50.5\), the point where the two curves cross, with advantage \(\mathrm{TV} = 2\Phi(\frac12) - 1 = 0.3829\). Over 200,000 games in each world it scores \(\mathrm{TPR} = 0.6901\) and \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.3092\): advantage 0.3809 and winning probability 0.6905, against the ceilings 0.3829 and 0.6915.
Now hold the false positive rate at \(10^{-3}\). The attack still flags large counts, but it has to move its threshold \(t\) up until only one non-member in a thousand exceeds it: \(\Pr[\mathcal N(50, 1) > t] = 10^{-3}\), so \(t = 50 + \Phi^{-1}(0.999) = 50 + 3.0902 = 53.09\), where \(\Phi^{-1}\) is the inverse of \(\Phi\). A member’s count, centred one higher, exceeds \(t\) with probability \(1 - \Phi(t - 51) = 1 - \Phi(3.0902 - 1) = 0.0183\). That is the TPR, and by the Neyman–Pearson argument above it is the best possible at this FPR (simulated: 0.0184, at an FPR of 0.00109). The attack now catches fewer than 2% of members, but when it fires it is right with precision \(0.0183/(0.0183 + 0.001) = 0.948\) at a fair prior. If only one target in a hundred is a member, the precision drops to 0.156.
The black curve in Figure 9.3 is this ROC curve on log axes. The green one is the same game when the adversary does not know the other records, which is the subject of the next section.






Figure 9.3: Left: the released count in the two worlds when the other 100 records are known (solid) and unknown (dashed). Right: the membership ROC curves of the best attacks on log axes, exact (lines) and from 100,000 simulated games per world (dots). The dotted diagonal is random guessing.





9.5.6 Check yourself

Attack A has TPR 0.5 at FPR 0.3; attack B has TPR 0.02 at FPR \(10^{-4}\). Which has the larger advantage, and which is the bigger privacy threat? (A has advantage 0.2, B about 0.02. B is the bigger threat to the people it flags: its precision at a fair prior is \(0.02/(0.02 + 0.0001) = 0.995\), against \(0.5/0.8 = 0.625\) for A.)
Why can no attack, however clever, beat Equation 9.12? (The bound is a property of the two view distributions. Any attack is a test of \(P\) against \(Q\), and the Neyman–Pearson lemma says no test with that FPR has more power than the likelihood-ratio test.)

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.6 Average case and worst case

9.6.1 Context
A membership game can be scored in two ways. In the average case, the data and the target come from the population, the adversary knows only the population, and the advantage is an average over all of that randomness. In the worst case, the adversary knows, or even picks, the rest of the data and the target, and the advantage is the maximum over those choices. Evaluations of real models usually measure the first; privacy guarantees have to control the second. This section shows how far apart the two can be.


9.6.2 Statement
The comparison is Fact 3 again, with the unknown being the rest of the game. Let \(\vartheta\) collect everything that the average-case game draws at random and that a worst-case adversary is allowed to fix: the other records, and the target. An average-case adversary does not know \(\vartheta\), so it sees an average over its possible values, which blurs the two worlds together. An adversary who knows \(\vartheta\) sees each situation sharply, and one who chooses \(\vartheta\) picks the sharpest. Let \(P_\vartheta, Q_\vartheta\) be the views given \(\vartheta\), and \(\bar P, \bar Q\) their averages. Then, by Fact 3,
\[\underbrace{\mathrm{TV}(\bar P, \bar Q)}_{\text{adversary does not know }\vartheta} \;\le\; \underbrace{\mathbb E_\vartheta\,\mathrm{TV}(P_\vartheta, Q_\vartheta)}_{\text{adversary knows }\vartheta} \;\le\; \underbrace{\max_\vartheta\,\mathrm{TV}(P_\vartheta, Q_\vartheta)}_{\text{adversary chooses }\vartheta}. \tag{9.14}\]
Both gaps can be as large as possible: there are mechanisms for which the left side is close to 0 and the right side is 1.


9.6.3 Derivation

Three adversaries, three views. An adversary that does not know \(\vartheta\) sees \(V\), distributed as the average \(\bar P\) or \(\bar Q\), so its best advantage is \(\mathrm{TV}(\bar P, \bar Q)\) by Equation 9.11. One that knows \(\vartheta\) sees the pair \((\vartheta, V)\), and by Fact 3 its best advantage is \(\mathbb E_\vartheta\mathrm{TV}(P_\vartheta, Q_\vartheta)\). One that chooses \(\vartheta\) picks the most revealing value, which gives the maximum.
The inequalities are the two inequalities of Equation 9.6.
The gaps can be extreme. For the left gap, release the exact count, with the target’s bit 1 and \(m\) other bits the adversary does not know. An adversary who knew the others would read \(b\) off the count, so the middle term is 1. One who does not know them sees the count \(K\) in world 0 and \(K + 1\) in world 1, where \(K \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(m, \frac12)\) is the unknown sum of the others. The two distributions are the same list of binomial weights \(w_k = \Pr[K = k]\), the second shifted one place to the right. Their total variation is the total excess of the shifted list over the original, counted where it is positive. The binomial weights rise up to the middle value \(\lfloor m/2\rfloor\) and fall after it, so the shifted list is the larger one exactly to the right of the middle, and there its excess at \(k\) is \(w_{k-1} - w_k\). Adding these differences from the middle to the end, every weight cancels except the first, so the total is the largest weight, \(\binom{m}{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}2^{-m}\). For large \(m\) the binomial is close to a normal curve with standard deviation \(\sqrt m/2\), whose peak height is \(1/\big(\sqrt{2\pi}\cdot\sqrt m/2\big) = \sqrt{2/(\pi m)}\) (Exercise 2 works this out). It tends to 0 as \(m\) grows. For the right gap, release one record of \(D\) chosen at random, worked out in the example below.



9.6.4 Interpretation
Averaging over datasets hides the target in a crowd, but only from an adversary who does not know the crowd. In the noisy count, the unknown other records act as extra noise with variance \(m/4\). A defence that relies on that noise fails against an adversary who knows the other records, or who planted them, and inserting records the adversary controls is exactly what a malicious adversary of Section 9.3 can do.
Averaging over targets hides the worst-treated person. If a mechanism exposes one person in a thousand completely and everyone else not at all, its average advantage is about 0.001. Privacy is a promise to each person, so the number that matters is the advantage against that one person. Outliers and duplicated records are the usual victims, as Membership inference and Memorization and training-data extraction show.
Average-case numbers are still useful. They measure the risk that a typical record faces from a realistic attacker, and they are what an audit can estimate from data. But they are lower bounds on the worst case, never upper bounds. An audit narrows the gap by playing the adversary that chooses the target: it plants canaries, records built to be as exposed as possible, and measures the attack on those (Memorization and training-data extraction).
This is where the part is heading. A guarantee that holds for every pair of neighbouring datasets bounds the right-hand side of Equation 9.14, and therefore every membership-style game in this part at once, every game whose two worlds differ in one record. A game whose two worlds differ in many records, such as the property games of Property inference, is bounded only through a weaker guarantee for groups of records, which degrades with the size of the group. That is how the definition in Part 3 is designed.


9.6.5 Example: the noisy count and the random-record release
The noisy count. Keep \(\sigma = 1\) and the target’s bit 1, but now let the \(m = 100\) other bits be fresh Bernoulli(\(\frac12\)) draws that the adversary does not see. The count is then \(K + b + Z\) with \(K \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(100, \frac12)\). In the two worlds the count has the same distribution, shifted by 1, and that distribution is log-concave, because a binomial and a normal are both log-concave and so is their sum. A shifted log-concave density has an increasing likelihood ratio, so the best attack is still a threshold, and by symmetry the two densities cross at \(m/2 + \frac12 = 50.5\). Table 9.6 compares the adversaries of Equation 9.14, and adds the case where the target’s own bit is random.



Table 9.6: Membership advantage on a noisy count with 100 other records, for adversaries with different knowledge.

Not knowing the crowd cuts the advantage by a factor of five. A normal approximation explains the number: treating \(K\) as \(\mathcal N(50, 25)\) makes the two worlds Gaussians with shift 1 and standard deviation \(\sqrt{25 + 1}\), which gives \(2\Phi\big(1/(2\sqrt{26})\big) - 1 = 0.0781\). When the target’s own bit is random, the count does not depend on \(b\) for the half of targets whose bit is 0, and the advantage halves to \(0.0779/2 = 0.0390\). At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) the average-case attack has TPR 0.0019 (simulated 0.0016), against 0.0183 for the adversary who knows the rest; these are the green and black curves of Figure 9.3. Figure 9.4 shows the average-case advantage falling as the crowd grows, while the worst case does not move.






Figure 9.4: Best membership advantage on the noisy count against the number \(m\) of other records the adversary does not know, for three noise levels (solid), and the same mechanism against an adversary who knows them (dashed). Dots: the exact count, \(\sigma = 0\), whose worst case is 1.



The random-record release. A mechanism publishes one record of \(D\), chosen uniformly among \(n = 1000\) records that are all different. The attack says “member” if the published record is \(z\). If \(z\) is in \(D\), it is published with probability \(1/n\), so \(\mathrm{TPR} = 0.001\); if not, it is never published, so \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0\). The script measures \(\mathrm{TPR} = 0.00098\) and \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0\) over 200,000 games per world. By the average-case measure, an advantage of \(1/n = 0.001\), the mechanism looks almost perfectly safe. Yet every run exposes one person completely, and when the attack fires its precision is 1. Against the target that is published, the advantage is 1. Only the right side of Equation 9.14, which fixes the dataset and asks about the worst target, reveals the problem.


9.6.6 Check yourself

A team audits its model by running a membership attack on 10,000 random training and held-out examples and reports advantage 0.01. What can you conclude about the worst-case risk? (Only that it is at least 0.01. The audit averages over targets and datasets. A small group of outliers could be exposed far more, and the average would barely show it.)
In the noisy count with unknown others, how could a malicious adversary recover the worst-case advantage? (By controlling the other records, for example by flooding the dataset with records whose bits it knows. Then the rest of the count is known, and the advantage goes back to the 0.3829 of the first row of Table 9.6.)

Rules of thumb

Before reading an attack’s number, read its threat model: access, behaviour, trust, side information, and the game.

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.1 Why this matters
A hospital trains a model to predict a disease and publishes it. You hold one patient’s record. Was that record in the training set? If it was, you have learned that the patient was treated at that hospital for that disease, and the model never output a diagnosis. This is membership inference, the simplest question an attacker can ask about a trained model and the one asked most often. A membership inference attack is also the standard way to measure how much a model leaks: if an attacker cannot even tell whether a record was used, it can do little else with it. The reverse does not hold. A model that leaks membership may leak more, and the later chapters of this part show how.
An attack is scored by two rates. Its true positive rate (TPR) is the fraction of members it flags as members, and its false positive rate (FPR) is the fraction of non-members it wrongly flags. A useful attack flags many members while flagging few non-members. With these two numbers in hand, the chapter answers four questions, each building on the one before.
The first is why a model leaks membership at all. The answer is that it fits its training data better than other data, so its loss on a record it trained on is usually lower than on a fresh one. The simplest attack says “member” when the loss is low, and its advantage, the TPR minus the FPR, turns out to equal the generalization gap: the difference between the model’s average loss on fresh data and on its training data. The second question is how an attacker can learn what members look like when it cannot see the training data. It trains shadow models of its own, on data where it knows who is a member, and watches how they behave. The third is what the best attack is. It is a likelihood-ratio test run separately for each record: the likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) estimates, for each record, how the model’s output on that record is distributed when the record was trained on and when it was not, and asks which of the two the observed output fits better. The fourth is how an attack should be scored and who is at risk. Attacks should be compared by their TPR at a low FPR, because only there does a “member” verdict carry confidence, and the people an attack identifies at that end are almost all outliers.

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.1.1 The one idea: membership inference is a test about one record
Fix a target record \(z\). Train a model on a dataset that contains \(z\), and look at the model’s output on \(z\). Train it again on a dataset that does not, and look again. The two outputs will not repeat exactly if you retrain, because training is random: the rest of the data, the initialization and the order of the examples all change. So each case gives a distribution of outputs, the IN distribution and the OUT distribution of \(z\). The attacker sees one output and must say which distribution it came from.
That is a test between two fully specified hypotheses, and the Neyman–Pearson lemma says how to do it best. Compute the likelihood ratio, the density of the observed output under IN divided by its density under OUT, and say “member” when it is above a threshold. For any allowed FPR, no test flags more members. The reason is a budgeting argument. Each possible output costs its OUT probability in false positives if you call it “member”, and earns its IN probability in true positives. With a fixed false-positive budget, you earn the most by calling “member” on the outputs with the best ratio of earnings to cost first, and that ratio is the likelihood ratio.
The IN and OUT distributions differ from record to record. A typical record is predicted well whether or not it was in the training set, so its two distributions nearly coincide. An atypical record is predicted badly unless the model saw it, so its two distributions are far apart. Every result in this chapter follows from taking that seriously. The loss attack uses one threshold for every record, so it confuses “easy record” with “member”. Shadow models are how the attacker estimates the two distributions, record by record. LiRA fits them per record, and once you account for the record’s identity it is the Neyman–Pearson test for the whole game. And the low-FPR end of the curve is made of the records whose two distributions are far apart, which are the outliers.

10.1.2 The running example
Every number in this chapter comes from one experiment, small enough to run in seconds and rich enough to show every effect. It has a pool of 1,000 labelled points in \(\mathbb R^{100}\), of two kinds, built so that some points are easy to predict and a few are not.
The 950 typical points have features \(x \sim \mathcal N(0, I/100)\): each of the 100 coordinates is normal with variance \(1/100\), so the squared length \(\|x\|^2\) is a sum of 100 terms that average \(1/100\) each, and \(\|x\| \approx 1\). Each gets a label \(y = \pm1\) that follows its first coordinate with some noise: \(\Pr[y = 1 \mid x] = \sigma(30x_1)\), where \(\sigma(t) = 1/(1 + e^{-t})\) is the logistic function, which turns any real number into a probability. The 50 outliers have the same kind of \(x\) scaled by 5, so they are five times longer, and a label drawn by a fair coin. Nothing else in the data predicts an outlier’s label, so a model can only get it right by fitting that point itself.
Each model is \(L_2\)-regularized logistic regression: it chooses the weight vector \(w\) that minimizes the average logistic loss on its training points plus a penalty \(\frac\lambda2\|w\|^2\) that keeps the weights small, with \(\lambda = 10^{-3}\). Each model trains on a random half of the pool (\(n = 500\)). Models come in complementary pairs: one trains on a random half, the next on the other half, so every point is a member of exactly half the models. The attacker targets 128 such models. It also trains 64 shadow models of its own in the same way. The attacker knows the pool and the training recipe but not which half any target model used. Every target model can be asked about all 1,000 pool points, and each (target model, point) pair is one game: 500 of the points are members of that model and 500 are not. Over 128 target models, that is \(128 \times 500 = 64{,}000\) member pairs and 64,000 non-member pairs.
This is the setup of Carlini et al. (2022), scaled down from an image classifier to a linear model. Section 10.8 describes the full-size pipeline.
What this chapter assumes. The membership game, the advantage \(\mathrm{Adv} = \mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\) and its ceiling, and the difference between average-case and worst-case games are in Threat models and privacy games. The Neyman–Pearson lemma, trade-off curves, ROC curves, the Bayesian view and confidence intervals for rates are in Hypothesis testing. The generalization gap and the self-influence of a training example are in Algorithmic stability and generalization. Each is restated below where it is used.
Conventions. As in Threat models and privacy games, \(b = 1\) is the world in which the target is a member (the alternative hypothesis) and \(b = 0\) the world in which it is not (the null). A model is \(\theta\), with weight vector \(w\). A record is \(z = (x, y)\), a feature vector and its label. An attack outputs a score and says “member” when the score exceeds a threshold. Its TPR is the fraction of members it flags and its FPR the fraction of non-members it flags. Logarithms are natural.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses
text:
10.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses

10.2.1 Fact 1 — The membership game and its advantage
Membership inference is scored as a game, so that “the attack works” has a precise meaning. The challenger draws a training set and flips a fair coin to get a hidden bit \(b\). The coin decides the target \(z\): if \(b = 1\), \(z\) is a member of the training set; if \(b = 0\), it is a fresh record from the same population. The challenger trains \(\theta\) and gives the adversary \(z\) and query access to \(\theta\). The adversary guesses \(b'\), 1 for “member” and 0 for “not a member”.
The coin is fair so that neither answer is right more often by default: an adversary that ignores the model and always says “member”, or flips a coin of its own, wins exactly half the games. Any win rate above \(\frac12\) must come from what the model reveals. \(\Pr[b' = b]\) is the probability that the guess is correct, whichever value the bit has; it is not the probability that \(b\) is 1.
To compute it, split the games by the value of the bit. Half the games have \(b = 1\), and the adversary wins those when it says “member”, which it does with probability TPR. The other half have \(b = 0\), and it wins those when it says “not a member”, with probability \(1 - \mathrm{FPR}\). Adding the two halves gives \(\frac12\mathrm{TPR} + \frac12(1 - \mathrm{FPR})\), which rearranges to
\[\Pr[b' = b] = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\mathrm{Adv}, \qquad \mathrm{Adv} = \mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}. \tag{10.1}\]
The advantage is how much more often the attack says “member” to members than to non-members. An attack that ignores the model says “member” equally often in both worlds and scores 0; a perfect attack scores 1. This is Fact 1 of Threat models and privacy games.
In the running example, “pick a target model and a pool point” is this game with the pool as the population: the point is a member of that model’s training set with probability \(\frac12\), because each model trains on half the pool. The loss attack, the shadow attack and the comparison of attacks by advantage all use this fact.


10.2.2 Fact 2 — The best test of two Gaussians, at any FPR
Most of the chapter reduces to one test: an observation \(X\) is a standard normal variable in one world and the same bell curve shifted right by \(s\) in the other. Which world produced it? Write \(H_0: X \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(H_1: X \sim \mathcal N(s, 1)\), with \(s > 0\). The number \(s\) is the separation: the distance between the two means in units of the standard deviation. A large \(s\) means the two bell curves barely overlap.
By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the best test thresholds the likelihood ratio. Here the log of the ratio of the two normal densities is \[\ln\frac{e^{-(X - s)^2/2}}{e^{-X^2/2}} = \frac{X^2 - (X - s)^2}{2} = sX - \frac{s^2}2, \tag{10.2}\] which grows with \(X\). So “the likelihood ratio is large” is the same as “\(X\) is large”, and the best test says “\(H_1\)” when \(X\) exceeds some cut-off.
The cut-off is set by the FPR you allow. Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function: \(\Phi(t)\) is the probability that a standard normal variable is below \(t\), and \(\Phi^{-1}\) is its inverse. To flag a fraction \(\alpha\) of \(H_0\) draws, the cut-off must be the point that a standard normal exceeds with probability \(\alpha\), which is \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha)\). Under \(H_1\), \(X - s\) is standard normal, so \(X\) passes the cut-off with probability \(1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - s\big)\). That is the TPR: \[\mathrm{TPR}(\alpha) = 1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - s\big). \tag{10.3}\] This is the Gaussian trade-off curve of Hypothesis testing, written as TPR against FPR: the most members any test can catch, at each FPR.
To get a feel for it, take \(\alpha = 10^{-3}\), so the cut-off is \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) = 3.0902\): a standard normal exceeds 3.0902 one time in a thousand. With a separation of 0.5, a member’s \(X\) must still clear \(3.0902 - 0.5 = 2.59\) standard deviations above its own mean, so \(\mathrm{TPR} = 1 - \Phi(2.59) = 0.0048\), barely five times the chance rate of 0.001. With a separation of 4, the cut-off sits \(3.0902 - 4 = -0.91\) standard deviations from the member mean, below it, so most members pass: \(1 - \Phi(-0.91) = 0.8185\). LiRA’s Gaussian fits, the two-type example and the exposure of outliers all use this formula.


10.2.3 Fact 3 — For logistic regression, the logit of the confidence is the margin
An attack has to pick some number from the model’s output to look at. Three natural choices are the confidence \(p_y\), the probability the model gives to the true label; the loss \(\ell = -\ln p_y\); and the logit of the confidence, \(\phi = \ln\frac{p_y}{1 - p_y}\), the log of the odds the model gives to the true label. For logistic regression the last one is especially simple. The model gives the true label \(y\) the probability \(p_y = \sigma(y\langle w, x\rangle)\), and the logit undoes the logistic function, \(\ln\frac{\sigma(t)}{1 - \sigma(t)} = \ln\frac{1/(1 + e^{-t})}{e^{-t}/(1 + e^{-t})} = t\). So \(\phi\) is the margin \(y\langle w, x\rangle\), how far the point lies on the correct side of the decision boundary, and the loss is a function of it: \[\phi = \ln\frac{p_y}{1 - p_y} = y\langle w, x\rangle, \qquad \ell = -\ln p_y = \ln\big(1 + e^{-\phi}\big). \tag{10.4}\] The second formula is \(-\ln\sigma(\phi)\) written out, since \(1/\sigma(\phi) = 1 + e^{-\phi}\).
The three numbers behave differently at the confident end. A model that gives the true label probability 0.9 has \(\phi = \ln(0.9/0.1) = \ln 9 = 2.197\) and loss \(\ln(1/0.9) = 0.105\). Probability 0.99 gives \(\phi = 4.595\); 0.999 gives \(6.907\). The probability crowds against 1, while \(\phi\) keeps spreading the values out.
Yet as decision rules they are interchangeable. The confidence and \(\phi\) rise together, and the loss falls as they rise, so each is a monotone function of the others. A threshold on one is a threshold on the others, and all three give the same ROC curve. They differ only when a statistic is combined across records, for example averaged or fitted with a Gaussian, which is where LiRA’s choice of \(\phi\) matters.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.3 The loss attack and the generalization gap
text:
10.3 The loss attack and the generalization gap

10.3.1 Context
A model is fitted to its training data, so it usually has a lower loss on a training point than on a fresh one. Yeom et al. (2018) turned this into an attack: say “member” when the loss is low. The attack needs no shadow models and no knowledge of the population beyond the loss threshold. They also showed that its advantage is exactly the generalization gap: overfitting and membership leakage are, for this attack, the same number.


10.3.2 Statement
The cleanest version of the attack turns the loss directly into a probability of saying “member”: the lower the loss, the more likely the verdict “member”. For that to be a probability, the loss must have a known range, so let it take values in \([0, B]\). The bounded-loss attack says “member” with probability \(1 - \ell(\theta, z)/B\): always at loss 0, never at loss \(B\), and in proportion in between. In the membership game of Fact 1, its advantage is the expected loss on non-members minus the expected loss on members, divided by \(B\). That difference is the generalization gap: the model’s expected loss on fresh data, its risk \(R(\theta_S)\), minus its average loss on its own training set \(S\), its empirical risk \(\hat R_S(\theta_S)\). So \[\mathrm{Adv} = \frac{\mathbb E[\ell(\theta, z) \mid b = 0] - \mathbb E[\ell(\theta, z) \mid b = 1]}{B} = \frac{\mathbb E_S\big[R(\theta_S) - \hat R_S(\theta_S)\big]}{B}, \tag{10.5}\] the expected generalization gap divided by \(B\). For the 0-1 loss (\(B = 1\)), which is 0 on a correct prediction and 1 on a wrong one, the attack is deterministic, “member if and only if the model classifies \(z\) correctly”, and its advantage is the test error minus the training error.


10.3.3 Derivation
The plan is to compute the attack’s TPR and FPR as average losses, subtract them as Fact 1 says, and then recognize the two averages as test loss and training loss.

TPR. Given \(b = 1\), the attack says “member” with probability \(1 - \ell/B\) for whatever loss the target has. Averaging over targets and training runs, \(\mathrm{TPR} = \mathbb E[1 - \ell/B \mid b = 1] = 1 - \mathbb E[\ell \mid b = 1]/B\).
FPR. The same calculation with \(b = 0\) gives \(\mathrm{FPR} = 1 - \mathbb E[\ell \mid b = 0]/B\).
Subtract. By Fact 1 the advantage is \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\). The 1s cancel and \(\mathrm{Adv} = (\mathbb E[\ell \mid b = 0] - \mathbb E[\ell \mid b = 1])/B\).
Identify the two averages. When \(b = 1\), \(z\) is a uniformly chosen training point, so its expected loss is the expected training loss, \(\mathbb E[\ell \mid b = 1] = \mathbb E_S[\hat R_S(\theta_S)]\). When \(b = 0\), \(z\) is a fresh draw independent of \(S\), so its expected loss is the expected test loss, \(\mathbb E[\ell \mid b = 0] = \mathbb E_S[R(\theta_S)]\). Their difference is the expected gap of Algorithmic stability and generalization.
The 0-1 loss. With \(\ell \in \{0, 1\}\) and \(B = 1\), “member with probability \(1 - \ell\)” says “member” with probability 1 when \(\ell = 0\) and 0 when \(\ell = 1\), that is, exactly when \(z\) is classified correctly. The members it flags are the training points the model gets right, so \(\mathrm{TPR} = 1 - \text{train error}\); the non-members it flags are the fresh points it gets right, so \(\mathrm{FPR} = 1 - \text{test error}\); and \(\mathrm{Adv} = \text{test error} - \text{train error}\).



10.3.4 Interpretation
The first lesson is that overfitting implies leakage. Any model with a generalization gap leaks membership through its loss, by at least the gap divided by the loss range. You can read this off from training and test error alone, without running any attack.
The gap also has a finer structure. The stability chapter shows that the expected gap equals the average self-influence of the training examples: how much each example’s own loss rises when it is taken out of training and replaced by a fresh record. The reason is that a training point’s loss and a fresh point’s loss differ exactly by whether the model saw that point. So the loss attack’s advantage is the average, over records, of how much each record is memorized. An average hides who is memorized, and Section 10.7 measures it record by record.
The converse fails: a small gap does not mean a private model. The loss attack is one attack. It is the best attack that sees only the loss and ignores which record it is looking at, but a record-aware attack can beat it by a wide margin, as the rest of this chapter shows. Yeom et al. also construct models that leak membership with no generalization gap at all.
Finally, the randomized rule is convenient for the proof, but an attacker would rather use a plain threshold. Yeom et al. also propose a deterministic version: say “member” when the loss is below the expected training loss \(\tau\). That needs only \(\tau\), which an attacker can estimate from shadow models or a reported training loss.


10.3.5 Example: the running example
Over the 128 target models, the training error is 0.1495 and the test error is 0.2663. “Member if correctly classified” flags the members it gets right, so \(\mathrm{TPR} = 1 - 0.1495 = 0.8505\), and the non-members it gets right, so \(\mathrm{FPR} = 1 - 0.2663 = 0.7337\). Its advantage is \(0.8505 - 0.7337 = 0.1168\), exactly the gap \(0.2663 - 0.1495\).
The logistic loss is unbounded, so the bounded-loss attack needs it clipped: replace any loss above \(B = 2\) by 2. The mean clipped loss is 0.4158 on members and 0.5433 on non-members. Equation 10.5 predicts an advantage of \((0.5433 - 0.4158)/2 = 0.0638\). Drawing the attack’s coins gives 0.0639. With Yeom’s threshold, the mean training loss \(\tau = 0.4159\), the deterministic attack has \(\mathrm{TPR} = 0.5936\), \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.4834\) and advantage 0.1102.
By Fact 1, an advantage between 0.0638 and 0.1168 means winning between \(\frac12 + \frac12(0.0638) = 0.532\) and \(\frac12 + \frac12(0.1168) = 0.558\) of games: the three attacks win between 53% and 56% of games. None identifies anyone with confidence: an FPR near one half means that half of the non-members are flagged too. Figure 10.1 shows why. The two distributions of \(\phi\) (equivalently, of the loss, by Fact 3) are shifted but almost entirely overlap.






Figure 10.1: Distribution of \(\phi\), the logit of the target model’s confidence in the true label, over member pairs and non-member pairs of the 128 target models. The dashed line is Yeom’s threshold: the attack says “member” to its right, where the loss is below the mean training loss.





10.3.6 Check yourself

A model has training accuracy 99% and test accuracy 70%. What advantage does “member if correctly classified” reach? (The test error minus the training error, \(0.30 - 0.01 = 0.29\). It wins the membership game with probability \(\frac12 + \frac12 \times 0.29 = 0.645\).)
Why does the bounded-loss attack need a randomized decision rather than a threshold? (Randomizing with probability \(1 - \ell/B\) makes the probability of saying “member” linear in the loss, so its expectation is the expected loss. A threshold gives an advantage that depends on the whole distribution of the loss, not only its mean.)

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.4 Shadow models

10.4.1 Context
An attacker who wants a better rule than “low loss means member” has to know what members’ outputs look like, and it has no labelled examples: it does not know who is in the target’s training set. Shokri et al. (2017) solved this with shadow models. The attacker trains models of its own that imitate the target: same architecture, same training recipe, data from the same distribution. For its own models it knows who was a member. It collects the shadow models’ outputs on members and non-members, labels them “in” and “out”, and trains an attack model, a classifier from outputs to membership. Shokri et al. train one attack model per class, with the prediction vector as input.


10.4.2 Statement
The claim is that, with enough shadow data, the attack model learns the best rule available from the output alone. Suppose each shadow model is trained exactly as the target is. Let \(o\) be the output the attacker sees (here \(o = (y, \phi)\), the class and the logit of the confidence). Train the attack model \(a(o) \in (0, 1)\), a predicted probability of “in”, by minimizing the cross-entropy, the usual classification loss \(-\ln a\) on “in” pairs and \(-\ln(1 - a)\) on “out” pairs, over the shadow pairs \((o, m)\), with \(m = 1\) for “in”.
As the number of shadow pairs grows, \(a\) tends to the posterior probability of membership, the probability that the record is a member given that the output is \(o\). With a fair prior, the posterior odds equal the likelihood ratio, so the posterior is an increasing function of it: \[a(o) \to \Pr[b = 1 \mid o], \qquad \frac{\Pr[b = 1 \mid o]}{\Pr[b = 0 \mid o]} = \frac{q(o)}{p(o)}, \tag{10.6}\] where \(q\) and \(p\) are the densities of \(o\) for members and for non-members, pooled over all records. So thresholding the attack model is the Neyman–Pearson test for the observation \(o\), and no attack that sees only \(o\) has a higher TPR at any FPR.


10.4.3 Derivation
The argument has four links: the shadow data look like the real game, cross-entropy training recovers the posterior, the posterior is a monotone function of the likelihood ratio, and thresholding the likelihood ratio is optimal.

The shadow pairs have the right distribution. A shadow model is trained like the target, on data from the same population, and each record is in or out with probability \(\frac12\). So a shadow pair \((o, m)\) has the same joint distribution as a pair (target output, membership bit) in the game. Learning from shadow pairs is learning about the real game.
Cross-entropy is minimized by the true posterior. Fix one output \(o\) and let \(\rho = \Pr[m = 1 \mid o]\) be the true fraction of “in” among pairs with that output. If the attack model predicts \(a\) there, its expected loss is \(-\rho\ln a - (1 - \rho)\ln(1 - a)\). Its derivative in \(a\) is \(-\rho/a + (1 - \rho)/(1 - a)\), which is zero at \(a = \rho\), and the function is convex, so that zero is the minimum. Since this holds separately at every \(o\), the minimizer over all functions of \(o\) is \(a(o) = \rho(o)\). With enough shadow data and a flexible enough attack model, training finds it.
Bayes’ rule. Posterior odds equal prior odds times the likelihood ratio (Hypothesis testing): \(\Pr[b = 1 \mid o]/\Pr[b = 0 \mid o] = \frac{\Pr[b = 1]\,q(o)}{\Pr[b = 0]\,p(o)}\), because the joint probability of a world and an output is the prior of the world times the density of the output in that world. With prior odds 1, \(\Pr[b = 1 \mid o]/\Pr[b = 0 \mid o] = q(o)/p(o)\). The posterior \(a\) and the odds \(a/(1 - a)\) rise together, since \(a \mapsto a/(1 - a)\) is increasing.
Neyman–Pearson. So a threshold on \(a(o)\) is a threshold on \(q(o)/p(o)\). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, a likelihood-ratio threshold has the highest TPR at its FPR among all tests that see \(o\).



10.4.4 Interpretation
The attack model is optimal for the wrong question. The densities \(q\) and \(p\) in step 4 are pooled over records: the attack model sees \((y, \phi)\), not which record produced it. So it is the best attack among those that treat all records alike. If \(q(o)/p(o)\) is increasing in \(\phi\) within each class, which is what you expect when members tend to have higher \(\phi\), the attack is a threshold on \(\phi\) per class, which is the loss attack with a class-dependent threshold. It cannot know that \(\phi = 2\) is a high value for one record and a low value for another.
What shadow models really buy, then, is calibration. They let the attacker choose a threshold that gives a target FPR on the real model, without any member of the real training set: the attacker picks the threshold at which the desired fraction of its own shadow non-members pass, and trusts that the real non-members behave the same way. That is the job they keep in LiRA.
The imitation can also be crude. Salem et al. (2019) found that one shadow model is often enough, and that shadow data from a different distribution still works, because what the attack model learns (lower loss means member) transfers across tasks.


10.4.5 Example: the attack model on the running example
For each class, the attack model is a logistic regression of “in” on \((1, \phi)\), trained on the roughly 32,000 shadow pairs of that class (64 shadow models times the pool points with that label). Both slopes are positive (0.238 for \(y = -1\), 0.158 for \(y = +1\)), so within each class the predicted probability of “in” rises with \(\phi\), and a threshold on it is a threshold on \(\phi\). It is a per-class threshold on the loss. Its performance across all thresholds is summarized by the area under the curve (AUC), the area under its ROC curve, which equals the probability that a random member gets a higher score than a random non-member. Its AUC is 0.577, the same as the loss attack’s, and so is its TPR at every FPR to within sampling noise (Table 10.4).
Calibration works. Setting the attack model’s threshold on the shadow models so that their FPR is 1% gives, on the 128 target models it never saw, an FPR of 0.0095 and a TPR of 0.0098. The attacker hits the FPR it aimed for. At that FPR the TPR is no better than chance, since 0.0098 is about the 0.0095 fraction of non-members flagged, because a global threshold on \(\phi\) has nothing to work with at the low end.


10.4.6 Check yourself

The attacker’s shadow data come from a different hospital than the target’s. Which step of the derivation fails, and is the attack useless? (Step 1: the shadow pairs no longer have the target’s joint distribution, so the attack model estimates the wrong posterior. It is not useless. Calibration is off, but “lower loss means member” usually still holds.)
Why does feeding the attack model a richer input, the whole prediction vector instead of \(\phi\), not help in the running example? (For a binary linear model the prediction vector is \((\sigma(\langle w, x\rangle), 1 - \sigma(\langle w, x\rangle))\), and with the label it determines exactly \(\phi\) and \(y\), and \(\phi\) and \(y\) determine it back. Each view can be computed from the other, so by Fact 2 of Threat models and privacy games, which says that processing a view cannot help, they give the same best attack.)

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.5 LiRA: a likelihood-ratio test per example
text:
10.5 LiRA: a likelihood-ratio test per example

10.5.1 Context
The pooled attacks of the last two sections compare a record’s output with everyone else’s. The right comparison is with the same record’s output under models that did and did not train on it. Carlini et al. (2022) built the likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) on that idea. For a target record \(z\), the attacker uses shadow models to estimate two distributions of \(\phi_z\), the logit of the confidence on \(z\): the IN distribution \(\tilde Q_z\) (models trained with \(z\)) and the OUT distribution \(\tilde P_z\) (models trained without \(z\)). It then computes the likelihood ratio of the observed \(\phi_z\) and thresholds it.


10.5.2 Statement
The attacker needs densities to form a likelihood ratio, and it only has a few dozen shadow values of \(\phi_z\) per record. So it summarizes each set by a bell curve: it fits a Gaussian to each distribution, \(\tilde Q_z = \mathcal N(\mu_{\mathrm{in}, z}, \sigma_{\mathrm{in}, z}^2)\) and \(\tilde P_z = \mathcal N(\mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}, \sigma_{\mathrm{out}, z}^2)\), from the shadow models that did and did not train on \(z\). Here \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) are the mean and standard deviation of \(\phi_z\) over those models.
Online LiRA asks how much more likely the target model’s \(\phi_z\) is under the IN fit than under the OUT fit. Its score is the natural log of that ratio, where \(\mathcal N(\phi; \mu, \sigma^2)\) denotes the normal density at \(\phi\): \[\ln\Lambda_z(\phi_z) = \ln\mathcal N\big(\phi_z;\, \mu_{\mathrm{in}, z}, \sigma_{\mathrm{in}, z}^2\big) - \ln\mathcal N\big(\phi_z;\, \mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}, \sigma_{\mathrm{out}, z}^2\big) \tag{10.7}\] It says “member” when \(\ln\Lambda_z\) exceeds a threshold \(c\) that is the same for every record.
Offline LiRA uses only OUT models, which can be trained before the target record is known. It cannot compute an IN density, so it asks only how far above its usual OUT value the observed \(\phi_z\) lies, measured in OUT standard deviations: \[\frac{\phi_z - \mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{out}, z}}, \tag{10.8}\] again with one threshold for all records. When the Gaussian fits are exact, online LiRA is the Neyman–Pearson test for the membership game: no attack that sees \(z\) and \(\phi_z\) has a higher TPR at any FPR.


10.5.3 Derivation
Why one threshold on the per-example ratio is optimal. The adversary does not see \(\phi_z\) alone; it also knows which record it is testing. So the observation is the pair (record, output), and the Neyman–Pearson lemma should be applied to the pair. The point of the steps below is that the record part of the pair carries no evidence and drops out of the ratio, leaving each record’s own ratio.

The view is a pair. In the membership game the adversary sees the target record \(z\) and the output \(\phi_z\). The density of the pair is the probability of drawing that record times the density of the output given the record. Write it as \(g(z)\,q_z(\phi)\) when \(b = 1\) and \(g(z)\,p_z(\phi)\) when \(b = 0\), where \(q_z\) and \(p_z\) are the IN and OUT densities of \(\phi_z\).
The record’s own distribution is the same in both worlds. The challenger picks \(z\) from the same pool whether or not it ends up in the training set, so \(g\) is the same factor in both. (In the running example every point is in the pool and is a member with probability \(\frac12\).)
The likelihood ratio of the pair is \(\frac{g(z)\,q_z(\phi)}{g(z)\,p_z(\phi)} = \frac{q_z(\phi)}{p_z(\phi)} = \Lambda_z(\phi)\). The factor \(g(z)\) cancels.
Neyman–Pearson. The best test of the pair thresholds its likelihood ratio, \(\Lambda_z(\phi)\), at a single value. Different records are compared through their ratios, never through their raw \(\phi\).

This is the mixture argument of Fact 3 in Threat models and privacy games. An attacker that does not know which record it is testing sees an average over records of their IN and OUT distributions, and averaging blurs the differences, as when a large shift for a hard record is diluted among the small shifts of easy ones. An attacker that knows the record can undo that mixing: its best advantage rises from the total variation distance of the pooled distributions (the best advantage of any test between two distributions) to the average of the per-record ones.
Why Gaussian fits on \(\phi\). The fits are only as good as the bell-curve shape they assume, so it matters that \(\phi\), rather than the loss or the confidence, is close to Gaussian.

\(\phi\) is linear in the weights. By Fact 3, \(\phi_z = y\langle w, x\rangle\), a fixed linear function of \(w\) for a fixed record. The regularized logistic-regression estimate \(w\) solves the equation “average gradient over the training points plus \(\lambda w\) equals zero”. Because that is an average of many independent terms, the central limit theorem makes \(w\) approximately Gaussian over the randomness of the training set (statisticians call such an estimate an M-estimator), and any fixed linear function of a Gaussian vector is Gaussian too. For a deep network the same scaling turns the confidence \(p_y\), which piles up against 1, into a quantity whose distribution over retrainings Carlini et al. found close to Gaussian.
Estimate the parameters from shadows. In the running example every point is in exactly 32 of the 64 shadow models, because the shadows come in complementary pairs. The sample means and standard deviations over the 32 IN and the 32 OUT values give \(\mu_{\mathrm{in}, z}, \sigma_{\mathrm{in}, z}, \mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}, \sigma_{\mathrm{out}, z}\).

Offline as a one-sided test. Offline LiRA is a weaker test, and the last two steps say what it tests and when it loses nothing.

Without IN models, the attacker cannot write down \(q_z\). It can still test “\(\phi_z\) is from \(\tilde P_z\)” against “\(\phi_z\) is larger than that”, because training on \(z\) raises \(\phi_z\): the model moves to fit \(z\), which increases its margin on \(z\). The standardized score Equation 10.8 is the natural statistic, and \(1 - \Phi\) of it is a one-sided p-value: the probability that a non-member’s output would lie at least this far above its OUT mean.
When it loses nothing. Suppose the two fits have the same width, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{in}, z} = \sigma_{\mathrm{out}, z} = \sigma_z\). Measure everything in units of \(\sigma_z\) from the OUT mean: the offline score is \(t_z = (\phi_z - \mu_{\mathrm{out}, z})/\sigma_z\), and the IN mean sits at \(s_z = (\mu_{\mathrm{in}, z} - \mu_{\mathrm{out}, z})/\sigma_z\). Then \(t_z\) is standard normal under OUT and normal with mean \(s_z\) under IN, which is exactly the setting of Fact 2, and Equation 10.7 becomes \(\ln\Lambda_z = s_zt_z - s_z^2/2\). For one record, \(s_z\) is a fixed positive number, so both scores rank outputs the same way. Across records, they differ: online LiRA multiplies \(t_z\) by \(s_z\), so it turns a given \(t_z\) into strong evidence when \(s_z\) is large and weak evidence when \(s_z\) is small; offline LiRA treats every \(t_z\) the same.



10.5.4 Example: two kinds of record, in closed form
A population with two kinds of record shows how much the per-record comparison matters, with numbers you can check by hand. Take unit variances everywhere (Table 10.2). A typical record is predicted confidently whether or not the model trained on it, so its OUT and IN means are both high and close together. An atypical record has a negative \(\phi\) (it is misclassified) unless the model trained on it.

The separations are the gaps between the means, \(3.5 - 3 = 0.5\) and \(2 - (-2) = 4\), and the last column is the Fact 2 calculation done above for exactly these two separations. Now run three attacks, each set to a pooled FPR of \(10^{-3}\): over all non-members together, one in a thousand is flagged.
One threshold on \(\phi\) is the loss attack. The OUT values of typical records are high, and they make up 95% of non-members, so the threshold must sit high to let through only 0.1% of non-members: at \(\phi = 6.075\), typical non-members pass with probability \(1 - \Phi(6.075 - 3) = 1 - \Phi(3.075)\), about 0.00105, and times their share of 0.95 that is the whole budget of \(10^{-3}\). Atypical non-members, centred at \(-2\), essentially never pass. An atypical member scores around 2 and almost never passes. Only typical members, whose IN mean is 3.5, occasionally do, and the pooled TPR is 0.0048.
One threshold on the z-score is offline LiRA. Each record is standardized against its own OUT distribution, so every record gets FPR \(10^{-3}\), at \(t_z \ge 3.0902\). Each kind then gets its own best TPR from the table, and the pooled TPR is their weighted average, \(0.95 \times 0.0048 + 0.05 \times 0.8185 = 0.0455\).
One threshold on \(\ln\Lambda\) is online LiRA. The threshold is \(\ln\Lambda \ge 1.497\). With equal variances \(\ln\Lambda = st - s^2/2\) (step 8), so for typical records the threshold is \(t \ge (1.497 + 0.125)/0.5 = 3.244\), which lets through an FPR of only \(5.90\times10^{-4}\); for atypical records it is \(t \ge (1.497 + 8)/4 = 2.374\), which lets through FPR 0.0088. The pooled FPR is \(0.95 \times 5.90\times10^{-4} + 0.05 \times 0.0088 = 10^{-3}\). The pooled TPR is 0.0503, the best possible at that FPR by the derivation above.
The global threshold is ten times worse than either per-example test. The likelihood ratio does better still than the z-score because it moves FPR budget from records where it buys little to records where it buys a lot. A typical record’s extra false positives buy almost no true positives, since its two curves overlap; an atypical record’s buy many, since its IN curve lies far to the right. The likelihood ratio makes that trade automatically.
Figure 10.2 shows the IN and OUT distributions for two real points of the running example: a typical point and an outlier.






Figure 10.2: The logit \(\phi\) of one point over the 64 shadow models, split into the 32 that trained on it (IN) and the 32 that did not (OUT), with the fitted Gaussians. Left: a typical point, whose two distributions overlap. Right: an outlier, which the models predict wrongly unless they trained on it.





10.5.5 Interpretation
Online against offline. Online LiRA needs models trained with each target record, so to attack a new record you must train new shadow models. Offline LiRA’s OUT models can be trained once, before the targets are known, and reused for every query. That is why it matters in practice, at some cost in power.
Per-example or global variance. Each per-example variance is estimated from half the shadow models, and with few shadow models those estimates are noisy. Noise in the variance is most harmful exactly where it counts. A record whose spread happens to be underestimated has its OUT curve drawn too narrow, so an ordinary output looks far out in the tail, its likelihood ratio is inflated, and it becomes a false positive at the strict thresholds that define the low-FPR end. Carlini et al. recommend one global variance, shared by all records, when shadow models are few: it averages over every record, so it is estimated from far more values and is stable. Figure 10.3 shows the effect on the running example.
More queries. For image models, Carlini et al. query each target on several augmented copies (flips, shifts) and fit a multivariate Gaussian. More observations of the same record give more evidence.






Figure 10.3: TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\) of four LiRA variants on the 128 target models, as the attacker uses the first 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64 of its shadow models. With a global variance the attack is strong even with few shadow models; with per-example variances it needs many. The dotted line is the loss attack, which needs no shadow models.





10.5.6 Check yourself

The IN and OUT distributions of a record are identical. What is its likelihood ratio, and can LiRA ever flag it? (The ratio is 1, \(\ln\Lambda = 0\), for every output. With a positive threshold it is never flagged, which is right: no test can tell member from non-member for that record.)
Why does the derivation need the target record to be drawn the same way in both worlds (step 2)? (Otherwise the factor \(g(z)\) does not cancel, and the record’s identity is itself evidence. If, say, members were drawn from one hospital and non-members from another, the record alone would reveal \(b\).)

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.6 Evaluating attacks: TPR at a low FPR
text:
10.6 Evaluating attacks: TPR at a low FPR

10.6.1 Context
Two numbers dominate older papers on membership inference: the attack’s accuracy (equivalently its advantage, by Fact 1) and its AUC, the probability that a random member scores higher than a random non-member. Both average over all members and non-members. A privacy breach is not an average. It happens when an attacker can say with confidence that a particular person was in the data. That means a low FPR, because at a low FPR almost every “member” verdict is right. Carlini et al. (2022) argued that attacks should be reported by their TPR at a fixed low FPR, such as \(10^{-3}\), and by the full ROC curve on log axes. The ROC curve plots TPR against FPR as the threshold sweeps from strict to lenient.


10.6.2 Statement
Two attacks can have the same AUC and nearly the same accuracy, yet TPRs at FPR \(10^{-3}\) that differ by a factor of 38. The two attacks below are built to show how. Both concern a population of members and non-members; \(q\) is a fraction of members, and \(\alpha\) is the FPR at which a TPR is read off.
Attack A exposes a few members completely and learns nothing about anyone else. It recognizes a fraction \(q\) of members with certainty and gives every other record, member or not, the same random score. Its AUC is \(\frac12 + \frac q2\), its best advantage is \(q\), and \(\mathrm{TPR}(\alpha) = q + (1 - q)\alpha\).
Attack B learns a little about everyone. It gives members a score \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) and non-members \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\), with the shift \(\mu\) chosen so that its AUC is the same as A’s: \(\Phi(\mu/\sqrt2) = \frac12 + \frac q2\). Its best advantage is \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\) and its TPR is Equation 10.3 with \(s = \mu\).


10.6.3 Derivation

AUC of A. The AUC is the probability that a random member outscores a random non-member, with ties counted as one half (Hypothesis testing). Split on whether the member is one of the recognized ones. With probability \(q\) it is, and it wins. Otherwise both scores have the same distribution, so neither is more likely to be higher and the member wins with probability \(\frac12\). Total: \(q + (1 - q)\frac12 = \frac12 + \frac q2\).
TPR of A. At any threshold with FPR \(\alpha\), the recognized members always pass, and the others have the same score distribution as non-members, so they pass with the same probability \(\alpha\). So \(\mathrm{TPR} = q + (1 - q)\alpha\), and \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} = q + (1 - q)\alpha - \alpha = q(1 - \alpha)\), at most \(q\).
AUC of B. A member outscores a non-member when the difference of their scores is positive. That difference is a member’s \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) minus an independent \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\), so it is normal with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(1 + 1 = 2\). It is positive with probability \(\Phi(\mu/\sqrt2)\), the chance that a normal variable lies less than \(\mu/\sqrt2\) of its standard deviations below its mean.
Advantage of B. The best advantage of a test between two distributions is their total variation distance: the most that the probability of any set of scores can differ between the two, reached by the set where one density exceeds the other. For two unit-variance Gaussians at distance \(\mu\) the densities cross halfway, at \(\mu/2\), so the best test says “member” above \(\mu/2\). Its TPR is \(\Pr[\mathcal N(\mu, 1) > \mu/2] = \Phi(\mu/2)\), its FPR is \(\Pr[\mathcal N(0, 1) > \mu/2] = 1 - \Phi(\mu/2)\), and its advantage is the difference, \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\) (both facts are in Hypothesis testing).

With \(q = 0.05\) (Table 10.3), both AUCs are \(\frac12 + \frac{0.05}2 = 0.5250\), and solving \(\Phi(\mu/\sqrt2) = 0.5250\) gives \(\mu = 0.0887\). A’s best advantage is \(q = 0.0500\) and B’s is \(2\Phi(0.0887/2) - 1 = 0.0354\). At FPR \(10^{-3}\), A has TPR \(0.05 + 0.95 \times 10^{-3} = 0.05095\), while B has \(1 - \Phi(3.0902 - 0.0887) = 0.00134\), a factor of 38.

10.6.4 Interpretation
Who is exposed matters more than how many. Attack A is a severe breach for one person in twenty, and B is a negligible one for everyone. AUC cannot tell them apart, and their best advantages differ by only \(0.0500 - 0.0354\), about 0.015. Only the low-FPR end of the ROC curve shows the difference.
Log axes are how you see that end. On linear axes, everything below FPR 0.01 is squeezed into one pixel column (Figure 10.4). On log axes, chance is the diagonal \(\mathrm{TPR} = \mathrm{FPR}\) at every scale, and an attack that is useful at low FPR stands out as a curve that flattens above it.
Measuring a low FPR takes many non-members. An FPR is estimated by counting false positives, and a count of \(k\) events has a relative error of about \(1/\sqrt k\), so the estimate is only as good as the number of false positives behind it (Hypothesis testing). To see \(k\) false positives at FPR \(\alpha\) you need about \(k/\alpha\) non-members. That is why the running example evaluates many target models: 64,000 non-member pairs give about \(64{,}000 \times 10^{-3} = 64\) false positives at \(10^{-3}\).
Precision is the fraction of “member” verdicts that are right. At a fair prior, members and non-members are equally many, so the right verdicts are proportional to TPR and the wrong ones to FPR, and the precision is \(\mathrm{TPR}/(\mathrm{TPR} + \mathrm{FPR})\). At TPR 0.05 and FPR \(10^{-3}\) that is \(0.05/0.051 = 0.98\). Real targets are rarely members with probability one half. Threat models and privacy games shows how the prior changes this.


10.6.5 Example: the five attacks on the running example
Table 10.4 scores every attack on the 128 target models, and Figure 10.5 draws their ROC curves on log axes. “Best advantage” is the largest TPR − FPR over all thresholds.



Table 10.4: Every attack on the running example: 128 target models, 64 shadow models, 64,000 member and 64,000 non-member pairs.
