title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.7 The hypothesis-testing interpretation

18.7.1 Context
A membership attacker is a test. It sees the output and decides between “the data were \(D\)” and “the data were \(D'\)”. Part 1 described any test by its two error rates, and the best achievable pairs by the trade-off function: for each false positive rate \(\alpha\), the smallest false negative rate any test can reach. Differential privacy turns out to be exactly a lower bound on the trade-off function, uniform over all neighbours (Wasserman & Zhou, 2010; Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath, 2015). This is the most operational reading of the definition: it says what an attacker’s receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, its true positive rate plotted against its false positive rate, can look like.


18.7.2 Statement
Let a test say “\(D'\)” (reject the null hypothesis \(H_0\) that the data are \(D\)) on the event \(S\), possibly randomized. Write \(\alpha\) for its false positive rate (FPR), \(\Pr[M(D) \in S]\), and \(\beta\) for its false negative rate (FNR), \(\Pr[M(D') \notin S]\). By Fact 3, both are probabilities of the event \(S\) or its complement, so the definition, which bounds the probability of every event, bounds them. Applied to the complement of \(S\), it says a test cannot have a small FPR without paying in FNR; applied with the roles of \(D\) and \(D'\) swapped, it says the same the other way round. Precisely, \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP if and only if every test, for every pair of neighbours, satisfies \[\alpha + e^\varepsilon\beta \ge 1 - \delta \qquad\text{and}\qquad e^\varepsilon\alpha + \beta \ge 1 - \delta. \tag{18.11}\] Each inequality is a line in the plane of \((\alpha, \beta)\), and no test can lie below either line. So the smallest FNR at a given FPR, which is the trade-off function, is at least the higher of the two lines (or 0, since an error rate cannot be negative). Equivalently, the trade-off function of every pair of neighbours lies above \[f_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\alpha) = \max\big\{0,\ 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon\alpha,\ e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \alpha)\big\}. \tag{18.12}\] In terms of the true positive rate (TPR) \(1 - \beta\), the fraction of the time the test correctly says “\(D'\)”, the second inequality reads: at every false positive rate \(\alpha\), \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\alpha + \delta\).


18.7.3 Derivation

The first inequality. Apply Equation 18.7 to the pair \((D, D')\) and the complement event \(S^c\), the outputs on which the test says “\(D\)”: \(\Pr[M(D) \notin S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \notin S] + \delta\). The left side is \(1 - \alpha\) and the probability on the right is \(\beta\), so \(1 - \alpha \le e^\varepsilon\beta + \delta\), which rearranges to the first inequality.
The second inequality. Apply Equation 18.7 to the swapped pair \((D', D)\) and the event \(S\): \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D) \in S] + \delta\). The left side is \(1 - \beta\) and the probability on the right is \(\alpha\), so \(1 - \beta \le e^\varepsilon\alpha + \delta\).
Randomized tests. A test \(\phi(y) \in [0, 1]\) is not an event, so the definition does not apply to it directly. But Fact 2 showed that a randomized choice \(\phi\) can make \(\mathbb E_{M(D)}[\phi] - e^\varepsilon\mathbb E_{M(D')}[\phi]\) no larger than the best event can, which is \(E_{e^\varepsilon} \le \delta\). So the definition holds for \(\phi\) as well, and steps 1 and 2 go through with \(\phi\) and \(1 - \phi\) in place of the events.
The converse. Every event \(S\) is a test. If Equation 18.11 holds for all tests, steps 1 and 2 read backwards give Equation 18.7 for every event and both orders of the pair.
The trade-off form. Rearranged for \(\beta\), the two inequalities say \(\beta \ge 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon\alpha\) and \(\beta \ge e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \alpha)\), and \(\beta \ge 0\) always. So the smallest \(\beta\) any test can reach at level \(\alpha\) is at least the largest of the three, which is Equation 18.12.



18.7.4 Interpretation
The result draws a forbidden region. In the plane of (FPR, FNR), every attack against an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism lies on or above the two lines of Equation 18.11 (Figure 18.4, left). The two lines are mirror images of each other across the diagonal \(\alpha = \beta\), so they cross on it: setting \(\alpha = \beta\) in \(\alpha + e^\varepsilon\beta = 1 - \delta\) gives \(\alpha = \beta = (1 - \delta)/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\).
Low FPR is where DP bites. Part 2 evaluated membership attacks by their TPR at a low FPR, because an attack that flags someone while almost never flagging non-members is one that confidently identifies people. DP caps that TPR at \(e^\varepsilon\alpha + \delta\). At \(\alpha = 10^{-3}\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), no attack has TPR above \(e \times 10^{-3} + 10^{-5} = 0.002728\). The ratio TPR/FPR is at most \(e^\varepsilon + \delta/\alpha\), and as \(\alpha \to 0\) the \(\delta/\alpha\) term dominates (Figure 18.4, right): at very low FPR, the guarantee rests almost entirely on \(\delta\).
Auditing runs this in reverse. Measure an attack’s FPR and TPR on a trained model, and Equation 18.11 gives a lower bound on the \(\varepsilon\) the training algorithm can have: solving \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\) for \(\varepsilon\) gives the smallest value consistent with what you measured. The neighbouring pair is a training set with and without a planted canary, a record inserted on purpose to be detected. The canary is chosen to be as easy to detect as possible (a mislabeled or out-of-distribution example), because the definition bounds the worst record and an ordinary one gives a loose lower bound (memorization and extraction introduced canaries). Later parts use this to check the privacy claims of trained models.
The bound is tight for randomized response. Its test “say \(D'\) on report 0” (for neighbours \(x = 1\) and \(x' = 0\)) has \(\alpha = \beta = 1/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), which is exactly the crossing point, the corner of the region. Most mechanisms sit strictly inside. The trade-off curve of the Gaussian count is smooth and curved, so it touches each of the two straight lines of \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta(\varepsilon)}\) at one point and lies above them elsewhere. Keeping the whole curve, instead of one \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\), is the idea of f-DP in Gaussian differential privacy.






Figure 18.4: Left: in the plane of false positive rate and false negative rate, the lower boundary \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) for \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) and \(\delta = 0\) (shaded below: no test can be there), and for \(\varepsilon = 1\) with \(\delta = 0\) and \(\delta = 0.05\). The randomized response test at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) sits exactly at the corner. Right: the same bound as a curve of the largest TPR against FPR on log axes, for \(\varepsilon = 1\) with and without \(\delta\), and the exact best TPR against a count with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 2, which is \((1, 0.0068)\)-DP.





18.7.5 Example: randomized response and the Gaussian count, as tests
Randomized response at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\). The neighbours are a person’s bit being 1 (\(D\)) or 0 (\(D'\)). The best test says “\(D'\)” (bit 0) when the report is 0. Its FPR is \(\Pr[\text{report } 0 \mid 1] = 0.25\) and its FNR is \(\Pr[\text{report } 1 \mid 0] = 0.25\). Then \(\alpha + 3\beta = 0.25 + 0.75 = 1\): the first inequality of Equation 18.11 holds with equality. At FPR 0.25 the bound allows TPR at most \(3 \times 0.25 = 0.75\), and the test achieves exactly \(1 - 0.25 = 0.75\).
The Gaussian count with \(\sigma = 2\) is \((1, 0.00683)\)-DP by Table 18.4. At FPR \(10^{-3}\) the bound allows TPR up to \(e \times 10^{-3} + 0.00683 = 0.0095\). To compare, you need the best TPR any test can actually reach. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the best test thresholds the likelihood ratio, and for two Gaussians with the same spread that ratio grows steadily with \(y\), so the best test thresholds \(y\) itself. In units of the noise, \(y\) is standard normal under \(D\), so an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) needs the threshold \(\Phi^{-1}(0.999) \approx 3.09\), the point with 0.1% of the standard normal mass above it (\(\Phi^{-1}\) is the inverse of \(\Phi\)). Under \(D'\) the output is shifted by \(\mu = 0.5\), so the TPR is the probability that a normal with mean 0.5 exceeds that threshold. This is the Gaussian trade-off curve of Part 1: the exact best TPR is \(1 - \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(0.999) - 0.5) = 0.0048\). The bound holds, with a factor 2 of room, because at this FPR the \(\delta\) term is generous: \(0.00683\) alone is larger than the true TPR.


18.7.6 Check yourself

Under \(\varepsilon\)-DP with \(\delta = 0\), can any test have FPR 0 and TPR above 0? (No. \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon \times 0 + 0 = 0\). Certain identification with no false alarm is ruled out entirely; only \(\delta > 0\) allows it.)
An attack reports TPR 0.05 at FPR 0.001 against a model trained with a claimed \(\varepsilon = 2\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). What do you conclude? (The claim is false, or the attack’s rates are mis-measured: the bound allows TPR at most \(e^2 \times 0.001 + 10^{-5} \approx 0.0074\).)

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.8 Bound on the membership advantage

18.8.1 Context
Part 2 measured a membership attacker by its advantage. In the membership game, the challenger flips a fair coin to pick \(D\) or \(D'\), runs \(M\) on it, and the adversary guesses which dataset was used. A guesser who ignores the output is right half the time, so the useful quantity is how much better than half the adversary does, doubled so that a perfect adversary scores 1: the advantage is \(2\Pr[\text{correct}] - 1\). With a fair coin, \(\Pr[\text{correct}] = \frac12\mathrm{TPR} + \frac12(1 - \mathrm{FPR})\), so the advantage equals \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} = 1 - \alpha - \beta\). Its best value over all adversaries is the total variation (TV) distance between \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\), the largest difference \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] - \Pr[M(D) \in S]\) over events (Threat models and privacy games). The testing form of the previous section bounds the sum of errors \(\alpha + \beta\) from below, and so gives the largest advantage any DP mechanism can allow.


18.8.2 Statement
The adversary wants both error rates small at once, so it wants the smallest possible sum \(\alpha + \beta\). The two lines of Equation 18.11 keep it away from the origin, and the closest it can get is the point where the lines cross, \(\alpha = \beta = (1 - \delta)/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\). Plugging that point into \(1 - \alpha - \beta\) gives the bound: if \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, every adversary in the game between any two neighbours has \[\mathrm{Adv} = \mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} \le \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1 + 2\delta}{e^\varepsilon + 1}, \qquad \Pr[\text{correct}] \le \frac{e^\varepsilon + \delta}{e^\varepsilon + 1}. \tag{18.13}\] For \(\delta = 0\) the bound is \((e^\varepsilon - 1)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\). Multiplying top and bottom by \(e^{-\varepsilon/2}\) gives \((e^{\varepsilon/2} - e^{-\varepsilon/2})/(e^{\varepsilon/2} + e^{-\varepsilon/2})\), which is the hyperbolic tangent \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), about \(\varepsilon/2\) for small \(\varepsilon\). Randomized response attains it.


18.8.3 Derivation

Turn the advantage into a sum of errors. The advantage is \(1 - (\alpha + \beta)\), so the largest advantage comes from the smallest \(\alpha + \beta\) allowed by Equation 18.11, together with \(\alpha, \beta \ge 0\).
Draw the feasible region. The allowed \((\alpha, \beta)\) pairs are the points on or above both lines of Equation 18.11 with both coordinates non-negative. This region’s lower boundary is a polygon with corners \((0, 1 - \delta)\) (where the first line meets the \(\beta\) axis), \((1 - \delta, 0)\) (where the second meets the \(\alpha\) axis) and the crossing point \(\alpha = \beta = (1 - \delta)/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\).
Check the corners. A linear function such as \(\alpha + \beta\) is smallest over such a region at one of its corners, because moving along a straight edge changes it at a constant rate, so it keeps decreasing until a corner. At the first two corners \(\alpha + \beta = 1 - \delta\). At the crossing point it is \(2(1 - \delta)/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), which is smaller since \(e^\varepsilon \ge 1\) makes \(2/(1 + e^\varepsilon) \le 1\).
Compute the advantage. \(1 - 2(1 - \delta)/(1 + e^\varepsilon) = (e^\varepsilon - 1 + 2\delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\). With a fair coin the success probability is \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{Adv} = (e^\varepsilon + \delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\).
Show tightness. Randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) has \(\alpha = \beta = 1/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), the crossing point with \(\delta = 0\), so its advantage is \((e^\varepsilon - 1)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\), exactly the bound.
Extend to random datasets. Part 2’s game draws the dataset from a distribution before the coin flip. The bound holds for each fixed pair of neighbours, so it holds for the average over pairs, since an average of numbers below a bound is below the bound.



18.8.4 Interpretation
Small \(\varepsilon\) is strong. At \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) the bound is \(\tanh(0.05) \approx 0.05\), so the best attacker guesses right with probability at most \((1 + 0.05)/2 = 0.525\).
Large \(\varepsilon\) promises little. At \(\varepsilon = 5\) the bound is 0.9866: the definition allows an attacker who is right \((1 + 0.9866)/2 = 99.3\)% of the time. A model trained with \(\varepsilon = 8\) may be far safer than that in practice, but the guarantee itself does not say so.
There is an older, looser bound. Yeom et al. (2018) showed \(\mathrm{Adv} \le e^\varepsilon - 1\) for \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Since \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2) \approx \varepsilon/2\) and \(e^\varepsilon - 1 \approx \varepsilon\), the two have the same order at small \(\varepsilon\), but the older bound is about twice as large there, and it exceeds 1, so says nothing, once \(e^\varepsilon \ge 2\), that is, from \(\varepsilon = \ln 2\) on.
Most mechanisms do not reach the bound. The bound is for the worst mechanism with this \(\varepsilon\). A count with Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) has best advantage \(\mathrm{TV} = 1 - e^{-\varepsilon/2}\): the TV distance is the hockey-stick divergence at \(\gamma = 1\), and the Laplace calculation of Section 18.6, redone for centres \(s\) apart and scale \(b\), gives \(1 - e^{-s/(2b)}\), which is \(1 - e^{-\varepsilon/2}\) for \(s = 1\) and \(b = 1/\varepsilon\) (Part 1). It is below \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\) at every \(\varepsilon\) (Figure 18.5).






Figure 18.5: The largest membership advantage against an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism (black), the looser bound \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) (dotted), and the exact best advantage against a count with Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) (orange). Markers are advantages measured in 100,000 simulated membership games with the likelihood-ratio adversary; randomized response sits on the bound.

Why is the advantage bound reached at \(\alpha = \beta\)? (The two constraints are mirror images, so the region is symmetric about \(\alpha = \beta\), and the corner that minimizes \(\alpha + \beta\) is on that line.)
The advantage bound at \(\varepsilon = 2\) is 0.76. Does this mean 76% of members are identified? (No. Advantage is TPR − FPR averaged over the coin flip, a single-pair worst case. It says nothing direct about the TPR at a low FPR, which Equation 18.11 bounds separately and much more tightly.)

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.9 The Bayesian interpretation

18.9.1 Context
People often ask a different question: “after seeing the output, how sure can someone be about me?” That is a question about posterior probabilities, the adversary’s beliefs after seeing the output. Fact 4 says the posterior odds are the prior odds times \(e^L\), so a bound on the privacy loss \(L\) turns directly into a bound on how far any posterior can move, whatever the prior. This is the reading that explains \(\varepsilon\) to someone who thinks in probabilities of a secret (Kasiviswanathan & Smith, 2014).


18.9.2 Statement
Consider an adversary who knows that the data are \(D\) or \(D'\), two neighbours, and believes beforehand that they are \(D\) with prior probability \(\pi = \Pr[D]\). Its prior odds are \(\pi/(1 - \pi)\). Each output multiplies these odds by \(e^{L}\), and pure DP keeps \(L\) between \(-\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon\), so the odds can be multiplied by at most \(e^\varepsilon\) and divided by at most \(e^\varepsilon\). If \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, then after any output \(y\), \[e^{-\varepsilon}\frac{\pi}{1 - \pi} \le \frac{\Pr[D \mid y]}{\Pr[D' \mid y]} \le e^\varepsilon\frac{\pi}{1 - \pi}, \qquad \Pr[D \mid y] \le \frac{e^\varepsilon\pi}{e^\varepsilon\pi + 1 - \pi}. \tag{18.14}\]
Under approximate DP the privacy loss is not bounded everywhere, so this cannot hold for every output. What does hold is that outputs with a loss well above \(\varepsilon\) are rare. Pick a larger level \(\varepsilon' > \varepsilon\). Each output whose loss exceeds \(\varepsilon'\) is at least \(e^{\varepsilon'}\) times as likely under \(D\) as under \(D'\), so it contributes at least a fraction \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'}\) of its probability to the excess mass that \(\delta\) bounds. So such outputs can have total probability at most \(\delta\) divided by that fraction. If \(M\) is only \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, the upper bounds hold with \(\varepsilon'\) in place of \(\varepsilon\) for every output except those in a set \(B\) with \[\Pr_{y \sim M(D)}[y \in B] \le \frac{\delta}{1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'}}, \qquad \varepsilon' > \varepsilon. \tag{18.15}\]


18.9.3 Derivation
Pure DP.

By Fact 4, the posterior odds are the prior odds times \(e^{L_{D,D'}(y)}\).
Pure DP gives \(|L_{D,D'}(y)| \le \varepsilon\) for every \(y\) (the pointwise form of Section 18.4), so \(e^{L}\) lies between \(e^{-\varepsilon}\) and \(e^\varepsilon\). Multiplying the prior odds by these two extremes gives the odds bound.
To get a bound on the probability itself, convert odds \(o\) to a probability, \(o/(1 + o)\). This is increasing in \(o\), so the largest odds give the largest probability. With \(o = e^\varepsilon\pi/(1 - \pi)\), multiplying top and bottom by \(1 - \pi\) gives the bound on \(\Pr[D \mid y]\).

Approximate DP. Let \(B = \{y : L_{D,D'}(y) > \varepsilon'\}\), the outputs whose privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon'\). The goal is to show \(B\) has small probability under \(P = M(D)\).

Apply Equation 18.7 to the event \(B\): \(P(B) - e^\varepsilon Q(B) \le \delta\), with \(Q = M(D')\).
On \(B\), the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon'\), which means \(p > e^{\varepsilon'}q\), or \(q < e^{-\varepsilon'}p\). Summing over \(B\) gives \(Q(B) < e^{-\varepsilon'}P(B)\).
Substitute this into step 1. Replacing \(Q(B)\) by the larger \(e^{-\varepsilon'}P(B)\) makes the left side smaller, so \(P(B)\big(1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'}\big) < \delta\). Since \(\varepsilon' > \varepsilon\), the factor in brackets is positive, and dividing by it gives Equation 18.15.
Outside \(B\), the loss is at most \(\varepsilon'\), and steps 1–3 of the pure case, with \(\varepsilon'\) in place of \(\varepsilon\), give the upper bounds.



18.9.4 Interpretation
DP bounds the change in belief, not the belief. It is relative, not absolute. An adversary who is already 99% sure stays about that sure; DP only promises that the output does not make it much surer.
The adversary in this statement is as strong as can be. It knows every record except the one in question, since it knows the data are \(D\) or \(D'\). Against weaker adversaries, who are unsure about other records too, the same bound holds in a slightly different form: for the posterior about one person’s record, compared with the posterior computed from the data without that record (Kasiviswanathan & Smith, 2014).
With \(\delta\), the guarantee holds for most outputs only. Taking \(\varepsilon' = 2\varepsilon\) in Equation 18.15, the pure-DP reading holds at level \(2\varepsilon\) except on outputs of probability at most \(\delta/(1 - e^{-\varepsilon})\). A tiny \(\delta\) keeps that exception tiny; a large one does not.






Figure 18.6: The largest (solid) and smallest (dashed) posterior probability of \(D\) after one output of an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism, against the prior, for four values of \(\varepsilon\). The dotted diagonal is no change. Small priors stay small: even at \(\varepsilon = 3\) a prior of 0.01 can rise only to 0.169.





18.9.5 Example: how sure can the interviewer be?
Back to Warner’s survey at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\). The interviewer knows everyone’s answer except Alice’s and thinks there is a 50% chance that her true answer is “yes”. She reports “yes”. The prior odds are \(0.5/0.5 = 1\), and a “yes” report is 3 times as likely from a true “yes”, so the posterior odds are \(1 \times 3\), and the interviewer is now at most \(3/(3 + 1) = 75\)% sure. If the prior was 1%, the posterior is at most \(3 \times 0.01/(3 \times 0.01 + 0.99) = 0.0294\). Table 18.6 gives the bound for other values.

For approximate DP, take the Gaussian count with \(\sigma = 2\), which is \((1, 0.0068)\)-DP. Equation 18.15 with \(\varepsilon' = 2\) bounds the probability of an output with privacy loss above 2 by \(0.0068/(1 - e^{-1}) = 0.0108\). The exact probability is \(\Pr[L > 2] = 8.842\times10^{-5}\), from Table 18.4. The bound holds by a wide margin, because it uses only \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), not the shape of the Gaussian tail.


18.9.6 Check yourself

An adversary is certain (\(\pi = 1\)) that Alice is in the data. Can an \(\varepsilon\)-DP output change that? (No. Prior odds are infinite, and multiplying by a factor in \([e^{-\varepsilon}, e^\varepsilon]\) keeps them infinite. DP limits what the output adds, not what the adversary already knows.)
Why does Equation 18.14 not need the adversary’s prior to be “correct”? (Fact 4 holds for any prior. The bound is on the likelihood ratio, which does not depend on the prior.)

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
section: 18.10 Why \(\delta\) must be much smaller than \(1/n\)
text:
18.10 Why \(\delta\) must be much smaller than \(1/n\)

18.10.1 Context
Equation 18.7 lets \(\delta\) be anything in \([0, 1]\), and the advantage bound barely notices a small \(\delta\). So how small must it be? A deliberately terrible mechanism answers the question. It satisfies approximate DP with \(\varepsilon = 0\), the strongest possible \(\varepsilon\), and yet it publishes people’s records verbatim.


18.10.2 Statement
The mechanism “release each record with probability \(\delta\)” goes through the dataset and publishes each record, in full, independently with probability \(\delta\). It is DP because any one person is published only with probability \(\delta\), and otherwise the output does not depend on them at all: under add/remove it is \((0, \delta)\)-DP. But over a whole dataset of \(n\) records it publishes \(n\delta\) records on average. Each record escapes with probability \(1 - \delta\), independently, so all of them escape with probability \((1 - \delta)^n\), and at least one is published with probability \[1 - (1 - \delta)^n \approx 1 - e^{-n\delta}. \tag{18.16}\] So \(\delta = 1/n\) exposes someone with probability about \(1 - e^{-1} = 0.632\). A meaningful \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee needs \(\delta \ll 1/n\).


18.10.3 Derivation

Couple the two runs. To compare the outputs on \(D\) and on \(D' = D \cup \{x\}\), run both with the same coins. Run the mechanism on \(D'\) by first running it on \(D\), then tossing one more coin for \(x\). The output on \(D'\) equals the output on \(D\) unless that last coin publishes \(x\), which happens with probability \(\delta\).
Bound one direction. For any event \(S\), the output on \(D'\) can land in \(S\) either because the output on \(D\) did, or because the extra coin changed it. So \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] \le \Pr[M(D) \in S] + \Pr[x\text{ published}] = \Pr[M(D) \in S] + \delta\).
Bound the other direction. With probability \(1 - \delta\) the extra coin does nothing and the outputs are equal, so \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] \ge (1 - \delta)\Pr[M(D) \in S] \ge \Pr[M(D) \in S] - \delta\), where the last step uses \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le 1\).
Read off the parameters. Both directions match Equation 18.7 with factor \(1 = e^0\) and slack \(\delta\), so the mechanism is \((0, \delta)\)-DP.
Count the exposure. Each of the \(n\) records is published independently with probability \(\delta\), so the number published is \(\mathrm{Binomial}(n, \delta)\), with mean \(n\delta\) and \(\Pr[\text{none}] = (1 - \delta)^n\). For small \(\delta\), \(\ln(1 - \delta) \approx -\delta\) (the first term of its Taylor series), so \((1 - \delta)^n = e^{n\ln(1 - \delta)} \approx e^{-n\delta}\).



18.10.4 Interpretation
\(\delta\) is a per-person budget for catastrophe. The definition allows each person to be exposed with probability up to about \(\delta\). Over \(n\) people, that is \(n\delta\) catastrophes on average. Only \(n\delta \ll 1\) makes the expected number of fully exposed people small.
Approximate DP allows certain identification. In the testing picture of Section 18.7, the test “is \(x\) in the output?” never fires when \(x\) is absent, so its FPR is 0, and it fires with probability \(\delta\) when \(x\) is present, so its TPR is \(\delta\). All of the \(\delta\) is spent at FPR 0, where pure DP allows nothing.
In practice, pick \(\delta\) well below \(1/n\); \(\delta = 1/n^{1.5}\) or a fixed small value such as \(10^{-5}\) for 60,000 training examples (Abadi et al., 2016) are common. This is less costly than it sounds. Reasonable mechanisms, like the Gaussian count, spread their \(\delta\) over many outputs with a moderately large loss, not over a few with infinite loss, so in practice a small \(\delta\) costs little \(\varepsilon\): in Table 18.4, going from \(\varepsilon = 1\) to \(\varepsilon = 3\) cuts \(\delta\) from \(6.830\times10^{-3}\) to \(3.401\times10^{-10}\).
If one person has many records, the relevant \(n\) is the number of people, not records, and the group-privacy cost of Post-processing, group privacy and composition also multiplies \(\delta\).






Figure 18.7: The probability that the mechanism “release each record with probability \(\delta\)” publishes at least one of \(n = 10{,}000\) records (red), against \(n\delta\), on log axes. Below \(n\delta \approx 0.1\) the probability is essentially \(n\delta\); at \(\delta = 1/n\) it is already 0.63.





18.10.5 Example: ten thousand records
On a tiny dataset the script checks the claim directly. With \(n = 3\) and \(\delta = 0.1\), it enumerates the \(2^4\) possible outputs on \(D\) and on \(D \cup \{x\}\) (each of the at most four records is published or not) and finds \(\max_S|\Pr[M(D) \in S] - \Pr[M(D') \in S]| = 0.1000\), the hockey-stick divergence at \(\varepsilon = 0\). So the mechanism is \((0, 0.1)\)-DP and no better.
Now take \(n = 10{,}000\) records (Table 18.7).

In 100,000 simulated runs at \(\delta = 1/n\), the mechanism published 1.0077 records on average and at least one record in a fraction 0.6351 of the runs, against 1 and 0.6321 from the formulas. A guarantee of \((0, 1/n)\)-DP is compatible with publishing a random person’s full record in most releases.


18.10.6 Check yourself

Why doesn’t the advantage bound Equation 18.13 warn about this mechanism? (At \(\varepsilon = 0\) it gives advantage at most \(\delta\), which is small. The harm is concentrated: a few people are exposed completely while most are untouched. An average over the coin flip hides that.)
Is \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) appropriate for a dataset of 10 million users? (No. \(n\delta = 100\), so the definition allows about 100 people to be fully exposed. It needs \(\delta\) well below \(10^{-7}\).)

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
section: 18.11 What differential privacy does not protect
text:
18.11 What differential privacy does not protect

18.11.1 Context
The definition compares two worlds that differ in one record. It does not compare the world before and after the release, and it does not say anything about records that are not independent of each other. Those are exactly the cases where people’s intuitions about “privacy” go beyond what DP promises. Kifer & Machanavajjhala (2011) made this precise: no definition can protect against every inference without assumptions on how the data were generated.


18.11.2 Statement
DP bounds \(\Pr[M(D) \in S]\) against \(\Pr[M(D') \in S]\) for neighbours. It does not bound three kinds of inference:

What the output reveals about the population. If the data show that smokers get cancer at a high rate, everyone now believes a smoker is at higher risk, including smokers who were not in the data.
What it reveals about correlated records. If \(k\) records move together (a household, a user’s duplicates, a contact network), changing all of them is a group change of size \(k\), and for \(\varepsilon\)-DP with record-level neighbours the privacy loss of the group can be as large as \(k\varepsilon\).
Anything outside the mathematical mechanism. Floating-point implementations that leak through low-order bits (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms), timing side channels, the raw data stored on a server, or releases of the same data through other channels.



18.11.3 Derivation
Population inference is not a privacy loss. The point is that DP compares Alice in against Alice out, not before against after. Suppose the cancer rate \(\theta\) among smokers is either 0.1 or 0.3, each with prior probability \(\frac12\). Your belief that Alice, a smoker, will get cancer is the average, \(\frac12(0.1) + \frac12(0.3) = 0.2\). A study that excludes Alice reveals \(\theta = 0.3\). Your belief about Alice rises to 0.3. The mechanism did not take Alice’s record as input, so it is \(0\)-DP with respect to her, yet your belief about her changed by half. In both worlds that DP compares, with and without Alice, the study shows \(\theta = 0.3\), so DP correctly says nothing happened to Alice because she took part. Preventing this kind of inference would mean preventing the study from learning anything, which is the No-Free-Lunch result of Kifer & Machanavajjhala.
Correlated records. Take a count released with Laplace noise of scale \(b = 1/\varepsilon\), which is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for one record. A household of \(k\) people who always answer alike moves the count by \(k\). The log ratio of two Laplace densities whose centres are \(k\) apart is at most \(k/b = k\varepsilon\), by the triangle-inequality argument of Section 18.3 (the Laplace pair of Part 1), and it reaches that value for outputs beyond both centres. Record-level DP treats each household member as hiding behind the others, but the others carry the same information.


18.11.4 Interpretation
DP protects the individual’s contribution, not the individual’s secrets. If a secret can be inferred from other people’s data, DP does not hide it. That is the price of letting anyone learn anything from data at all.
The unit of privacy must therefore match the unit of correlation. User-level DP, or group privacy with \(k\) set to the size of the correlated unit, is how you handle correlations you know about. Correlations you do not know about are outside the guarantee.
Finally, DP is a guarantee about an algorithm: a property of \(M\) as a mathematical object. Its implementation, its inputs and everything around it need separate care.


18.11.5 Example: a household of five
At \(\varepsilon = 1\), a household of \(k = 5\) correlated records faces a largest privacy loss of 5.0000 (found by the script on a grid), as the \(k\varepsilon\) argument predicts. The household is therefore protected only as if by a 5-DP mechanism. The advantage bound Equation 18.13 at \(\varepsilon = 5\) is 0.9866, and the exact best advantage against this Laplace count is \(1 - e^{-5/2} = 0.9179\), the Laplace TV formula \(1 - e^{-s/(2b)}\) with shift \(s = 5\) and scale \(b = 1\). An attacker who wants to know whether the household took part is right with probability up to \(\frac12(1 + 0.9179) = 0.959\), although each record is “protected at \(\varepsilon = 1\)”.


18.11.6 Check yourself

A model trained with DP predicts that people in a given postcode are likely to default on loans. Has it violated the privacy of those people? (Not in the DP sense. The prediction would be the same with or without any one person’s record; it reflects the population. Whether such inferences are acceptable is a question DP does not answer.)
A dataset contains one record per message, and users write up to 50 messages. Example-level \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) is claimed. What is the user-level guarantee for a heavy user, with the group bound? (Up to \(50 \times 0.5 = 25\), which promises essentially nothing.)

18.12 Code: check every number by enumeration and simulation
The script code/definition.py computes every number in this chapter and draws every figure. Each mechanism is a small typed function returning its output distribution. The definition is checked by brute force over all events where the outcome set is small, and the closed forms are checked against simulated surveys, membership games and Monte Carlo averages. What to take from it. First, one formula replaces all events: the brute force over 256 events and the max-divergence and hockey-stick formulas agree exactly, and that agreement is what makes DP checkable for continuous outputs, where brute force is impossible. Second, \(\delta\) depends on \(\varepsilon\): every mechanism has a curve \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), and the simple tail bound \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon]\) overstates it by a factor of 4 to 13 for the Gaussian count, because it ignores the discount on outputs just past \(\varepsilon\). Third, the bounds are tight, but not for every mechanism: randomized response meets the testing and advantage bounds exactly, while the Laplace count stays below them. Finally, a small \(\delta\) is not automatically safe: \((0, 1/n)\)-DP published at least one full record in 64% of runs.

text:
18.13 References

Dwork, McSherry, Nissim & Smith, “Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis” (TCC 2006; journal version in the Journal of Privacy and Confidentiality, 2016). The original definition of pure DP, with sensitivity and the Laplace mechanism.
Dwork, Kenthapadi, McSherry, Mironov & Naor, “Our Data, Ourselves: Privacy via Distributed Noise Generation” (EUROCRYPT 2006). Introduces approximate \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.
Dwork & Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (2014), ch. 2: the definition, randomized response, what DP promises and does not (§2.3), and the “release a random record” argument for small \(\delta\). The standard reference for this whole chapter.
Warner, “Randomized Response: A Survey Technique for Eliminating Evasive Answer Bias” (Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1965). The original two-coin protocol and its estimator.
Wasserman & Zhou, “A Statistical Framework for Differential Privacy” (Journal of the American Statistical Association, 2010). DP as a bound on the power of tests.
Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath, “The Composition Theorem for Differential Privacy” (ICML 2015). The hypothesis-testing characterization Equation 18.11 and its use for optimal composition (Advanced and optimal composition).
Dong, Roth & Su, “Gaussian Differential Privacy” (JRSS Series B, 2022). Trade-off functions as the privacy definition itself (f-DP); Equation 18.12 is their \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\).
Kasiviswanathan & Smith, “On the ‘Semantics’ of Differential Privacy: A Bayesian Formulation” (Journal of Privacy and Confidentiality, 2014). The posterior reading for arbitrary priors, and the bad-set argument for approximate DP.
Yeom, Giacomelli, Fredrikson & Jha, “Privacy Risk in Machine Learning: Analyzing the Connection to Overfitting” (CSF 2018). Membership advantage and the bound \(e^\varepsilon - 1\).
Kifer & Machanavajjhala, “No Free Lunch in Data Privacy” (SIGMOD 2011). Why DP cannot protect correlated data without assumptions on how it was generated.
Desfontaines & Pejó, “SoK: Differential Privacies” (PETS 2020). A map of the many variants of the definition, including the choice of neighbouring relation.
Abadi et al., “Deep Learning with Differential Privacy” (CCS 2016). Example-level DP for training neural networks, with \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for 60,000 examples.

Table 18.9: Every result of this chapter.









Result
Statement




\((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP
\(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta\) for all \(D \simeq D'\) and all \(S\)


Pure DP
\(\delta = 0\); equivalently \(\lvert L_{D,D'}\rvert \le \varepsilon\) everywhere; \(D_\infty(P\Vert Q) \le \varepsilon\)


Approximate DP
\(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\Vert Q) = \mathbb E_P[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+] \le \delta\); sufficient: \(\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] \le \delta\)


Add/remove vs replace
\(\varepsilon\) under add/remove \(\Rightarrow\) \(2\varepsilon\) under replace; \((\varepsilon, \delta) \Rightarrow (2\varepsilon, (1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta)\)


Randomized response
Truth with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\); \(\varepsilon\)-DP; estimate error \(e^{\varepsilon/2}/((e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt n)\)


Testing form
\(\mathrm{FPR} + e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FNR} \ge 1 - \delta\) and \(e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \mathrm{FNR} \ge 1 - \delta\); \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\)


Trade-off form
\(T(P, Q) \ge f_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\alpha) = \max\{0, 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon\alpha, e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \alpha)\}\)


Membership advantage
\(\le (e^\varepsilon - 1 + 2\delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\); \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\) for pure DP; tight for randomized response


Bayesian form
Posterior odds within \(e^{\pm\varepsilon}\) of prior odds; with \(\delta\), except on outputs of probability \(\le \delta/(1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'})\)


Release each record w.p. \(\delta\)
\((0, \delta)\)-DP; exposes someone with probability \(1 - (1 - \delta)^n\)






Rules of thumb

State the neighbouring relation and the unit of privacy with every \(\varepsilon\).
\(\varepsilon\) below 1 is strong, a few is moderate, and around 10 the worst-case guarantee says little.
Pick \(\delta \ll 1/n\), with \(n\) the number of people, not records.
Low-FPR attack success is capped at \(e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\): that is the number to compare with a measured membership attack.
A bounded privacy loss gives pure DP; an unbounded one gives a whole curve \(\delta(\varepsilon)\).
DP protects your contribution, not secrets that others’ data reveal about you.

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.1 Why this matters
You have proved that one mechanism is differentially private. Now you use it. You round its output, plot it, or train a model on it. The dataset you protect has families in it, or users who each contributed fifty records. And you never run just one mechanism: an analyst asks a hundred queries, and a training run takes thousands of noisy gradient steps. Three questions come up at once:
The answers are the three properties that make differential privacy (DP) usable as an engineering tool. Post-processing is free: nothing you compute from the output without touching the data can weaken the guarantee. Group privacy costs a factor \(k\) in \(\varepsilon\), and more than that in \(\delta\). Composition adds: running mechanisms with budgets \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\) costs at most \((\sum\varepsilon_i, \sum\delta_i)\). Without these three properties, every pipeline would need its own privacy proof. With them, you prove each building block once and add up the costs.
crumbs: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
After processing, is the result still private, and do you need to prove anything new?
For a group of \(k\) records, such as one user’s records or one household, what does a guarantee about one record give?
For many mechanisms run on the same data, what is the guarantee of all their outputs together?



19.1.1 The one idea: privacy losses add, processing only averages them
A mechanism \(M\) is a randomized algorithm that takes a dataset and returns an output. Two datasets are neighbouring, written \(D \simeq D'\), when they differ in one person’s record. Differential privacy asks that \(M\) behave almost the same on every neighbouring pair, so that its output reveals little about any one record. The way to measure “almost the same” at a single output \(y\) is to ask how much more likely \(y\) is when the data are \(D\) than when they are \(D'\). If \(y\) is three times as likely under \(D\), seeing \(y\) is evidence for \(D\); if it is equally likely under both, seeing it tells you nothing. The logarithm of that ratio is the privacy loss of \(y\), from The definition of differential privacy. Writing \(p_{M(D)}(y)\) for the probability (or density) that \(M\) outputs \(y\) on data \(D\), \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \ln\frac{p_{M(D)}(y)}{p_{M(D')}(y)}. \tag{19.1}\] It is positive when \(y\) favours \(D\), negative when it favours \(D'\), and zero when \(y\) carries no evidence either way. Pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP says that no output carries much evidence: \(|L_{D,D'}(y)| \le \varepsilon\) for every output and every neighbouring pair \(D \simeq D'\). Equivalently, the likelihood ratio \(e^{L}\) always lies in the band \([e^{-\varepsilon}, e^\varepsilon]\). All three properties of this chapter are statements about how \(L\) behaves.
Post-processing replaces \(y\) by \(z = f(y)\). Several outputs \(y\) can lead to the same \(z\), and the probability of \(z\) is the sum of their probabilities. So the likelihood ratio of \(z\) is a weighted average of the likelihood ratios of those \(y\), which is the content of the data processing inequality (DPI) of Divergences: processing pools evidence, and pooling can only dilute it. An average of numbers that all lie in \([e^{-\varepsilon}, e^\varepsilon]\) stays in \([e^{-\varepsilon}, e^\varepsilon]\), so the processed output is just as private.
Group privacy compares \(D\) with a dataset \(D''\) that differs in \(k\) records. You can walk from \(D\) to \(D''\) one record at a time, through \(k\) neighbouring pairs. The likelihood ratio between the two ends is the product of the \(k\) ratios along the way, so the privacy loss between the ends, its logarithm, is the sum of the \(k\) step losses, each at most \(\varepsilon\).
Composition releases \(y = (y_1, \dots, y_k)\) from \(k\) mechanisms that use independent coins. The probability of independent outcomes is the product of their probabilities, so the log-ratio of the whole release, its privacy loss, is the sum of the individual losses.
So the rule is: along a path of datasets or across a sequence of mechanisms, privacy losses add; under processing, they only average. Table 19.1 lists the results and where each is used.



Table 19.1: The results of this chapter and where each is used.





Result
Where it is used




Post-processing
Publishing anything computed from a private output: rounded counts, plots, models trained on private statistics, synthetic data; every attack of Part 2 is a post-processing


Group privacy, pure and approximate
Turning a per-record guarantee into a per-user or per-household one; why correlated records weaken DP


Basic sequential composition, non-adaptive and adaptive
Budgeting an analysis of many queries; the starting point for every accountant in Advanced and optimal composition and later


Parallel composition
Histograms, per-group statistics, local randomized response: disjoint data cost the maximum, not the sum


What composes and what doesn’t
Fresh noise, matching neighbouring relations, not touching the data again






How to read this chapter. Each section follows the same arc: context, statement, derivation, interpretation, example, check yourself. Read the post-processing and composition sections first; they are used everywhere. The approximate-DP derivations (Fact 2 in the toolkit, the two-step lemma in the composition section) are short but abstract; walk through the concrete tables next to them. Basic composition is tight in the worst case but loose for most purposes. How much better you can do is the subject of Advanced and optimal composition; here you only see why there is room.
Conventions. \(M\) is a randomized mechanism, \(D \simeq D'\) neighbouring datasets, and \(P = M(D)\), \(Q = M(D')\) its two output distributions with mass functions or densities \(p\) and \(q\). Sums over outputs \(\sum_y\) are integrals for continuous outputs. Logarithms are natural. The running mechanism is randomized response with \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\): a person reports their true bit with probability \(\frac34\) and the other bit with probability \(\frac14\). Comparing a person whose bit is 1 with one whose bit is 0, the report 1 has probability \(\frac34\) against \(\frac14\), a ratio of 3, and the report 0 has the ratio \(\frac13\). So \(L = \pm\ln 3\) on every output.

section: 19.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses
text:
19.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses

19.2.1 Fact 1 — Three forms of the definition
The definition of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP can be written in three ways, and each derivation below uses whichever makes its step shortest. The first form talks about events: whatever set \(S\) of outputs an observer cares about, its probability under \(D\) is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times its probability under \(D'\), plus a small slack \(\delta\). The second form packs all events into one number, the hockey-stick divergence: scale \(q\) up by the factor \(e^\varepsilon\) and add up the probability mass of \(p\) that still sticks out above it. Here \((x)_+ = \max(x, 0)\) keeps only the parts that stick out. The third form, for \(\delta = 0\), is the bound on the privacy loss you already met. From The definition of differential privacy, these are equivalent for a pair \(P = M(D)\), \(Q = M(D')\):

Events: \(P(S) \le e^\varepsilon Q(S) + \delta\) for every set of outputs \(S\).
Hockey-stick: \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = \sum_y\big(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\big)_+ \le \delta\).
Pure case (\(\delta = 0\)): \(|L_{D,D'}(y)| \le \varepsilon\) for every \(y\) (on the common support).

\(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP when this holds for every ordered neighbouring pair.
Forms 1 and 2 are equivalent because the worst event is easy to find. The gap \(P(S) - e^\varepsilon Q(S) = \sum_{y \in S}\big(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\big)\) is a sum of one term per output in \(S\). It is largest when \(S\) contains exactly the outputs whose term is positive, those with \(p(y) > e^\varepsilon q(y)\), and its largest value is then the sum of the positive parts, which is \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q)\). This is Fact 3 of Divergences. So “every event satisfies the bound” and “the worst event satisfies it” say the same thing. Form 3 follows from form 1 with \(\delta = 0\) by taking single outputs, \(S = \{y\}\): this gives \(p(y) \le e^\varepsilon q(y)\), and the reversed pair gives \(q(y) \le e^\varepsilon p(y)\), which together say \(|L(y)| \le \varepsilon\). Conversely, summing \(p(y) \le e^\varepsilon q(y)\) over the outputs \(y \in S\) gives the event form back.
Since \(\delta\) is the hockey-stick divergence at the scale \(e^\varepsilon\), you can ask for every \(\varepsilon\) at once how much slack is needed. The function \(\varepsilon \mapsto \delta(\varepsilon) = \max\{E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q), E_{e^\varepsilon}(Q\|P)\}\), maximized over neighbouring pairs, is the privacy profile of \(M\). \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when \(\delta(\varepsilon) \le \delta\). The script computes it exactly for every mechanism in this chapter.


19.2.2 Fact 2 — Tests instead of events
An event is an all-or-nothing rule: an output is in \(S\) or it is not. Later steps of a pipeline are often softer than that. A randomized test rejects with some probability that depends on the output, and a later stage of an algorithm does something with a probability that depends on what it was given. Such a rule is a function \(g\) from outputs to \([0, 1]\). It is a mixture of events, so it should obey the same bound, and it does. If \(P(S) \le e^\varepsilon Q(S) + \delta\) for every event \(S\), then for every function \(g\) of the output with values in \([0, 1]\), \[\mathbb E_P[g(Y)] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E_Q[g(Y)] + \delta. \tag{19.2}\]
The proof reuses the worst-event argument of Fact 1. The gap \(\mathbb E_P[g] - e^\varepsilon\mathbb E_Q[g] = \sum_y g(y)\big(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\big)\) is a sum in which each value \(g(y)\) multiplies a fixed bracket. To make it as large as possible, you set \(g(y) = 1\) where the bracket is positive and \(g(y) = 0\) where it is negative; any value in between only gives up part of a positive term or adds part of a negative one. That choice of \(g\) is the indicator of the worst event, and the maximum is \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) \le \delta\). This is the randomized version of Fact 3 in Divergences.
A small case shows what the fact says. Take randomized response with \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\), \(\delta = 0\), and a later step that acts with probability \(g(1) = 0.6\) on the report 1 and \(g(0) = 0.2\) on the report 0. Under bit 1 the report is 1 with probability \(\frac34\), so \(\mathbb E[g] = \frac34(0.6) + \frac14(0.2) = 0.5\); under bit 0, \(\frac14(0.6) + \frac34(0.2) = 0.3\). Indeed \(0.5 \le 3 \times 0.3 = 0.9\). You will use this fact for post-processing, and in every approximate-DP proof where a later stage depends on an earlier output.


19.2.3 Fact 3 — Privacy losses of independent outputs add
When two outputs come from independent coins, the probability of seeing both is the product of their probabilities. The logarithm turns that product into a sum, so the evidence carried by the pair is the evidence of the first plus the evidence of the second. In symbols, if \(Y = (Y_1, Y_2)\) where \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) use independent coins, then \(p(y_1, y_2) = p_1(y_1)p_2(y_2)\) and the same for \(q\), so \[L(y_1, y_2) = \ln\frac{p_1(y_1)p_2(y_2)}{q_1(y_1)q_2(y_2)} = L_1(y_1) + L_2(y_2). \tag{19.3}\]
Take two randomized-response answers from a person whose bit is 1 (\(D\)) or 0 (\(D'\)). The answers \((1, 1)\) have probability \(\frac34 \cdot \frac34 = \frac9{16}\) under \(D\) and \(\frac14 \cdot \frac14 = \frac1{16}\) under \(D'\), so \(L = \ln 9 = \ln 3 + \ln 3\): two pieces of evidence pointing the same way. The answers \((1, 0)\) have \(\frac34 \cdot \frac14 = \frac3{16}\) under both, so \(L = 0 = \ln 3 - \ln 3\): the two pieces of evidence cancel.
The fact survives when the second mechanism depends on the first output (the adaptive case). The chain rule of probability writes any joint probability as “first, times second given first”, \(p(y_1, y_2) = p_1(y_1)\,p_2(y_2 \mid y_1)\), so the same sum holds with \(p_2(y_2 \mid y_1)\) in place of \(p_2(y_2)\). This is what composition and parallel composition use.

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.3 Post-processing

19.3.1 Context
A private output is rarely published as is. You round a noisy count to an integer, clip it at zero, threshold it, fit a model to a table of noisy marginals, or let an analyst look at it and decide what to do next. Each of these is a function of the output, possibly randomized with its own coins, that does not look at the data again. The question is whether such processing can undo the protection. It cannot: the data processing inequality of Part 1 says that processing averages likelihood ratios together, and averaging cannot push a ratio outside the band \([e^{-\varepsilon}, e^\varepsilon]\).


19.3.2 Statement
To state the result for randomized processing too, describe the processing as a channel \(K\): \(K(z \mid y)\) is the probability that the processing outputs \(z\) when its input is \(y\). A deterministic \(f\) is the case \(K(z \mid y) = \mathbf 1[z = f(y)]\), which is 1 when \(z = f(y)\) and 0 otherwise. The processed output on data \(D\) then has the distribution \(PK(z) = \sum_y p(y)K(z \mid y)\): sum over every \(y\) the mechanism could give, weighted by how likely it is to become \(z\). Write \(L^f_{D,D'}(z)\) for the privacy loss of the processed output \(z\).
The claim is that processing can never make the two worlds easier to tell apart. Let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP and let \(f\) be any randomized function whose coins are independent of the data and of \(M\)’s coins. Then \(f \circ M\), the mechanism \(D \mapsto f(M(D))\), is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. Equivalently, for every channel \(K\) and every neighbouring pair, the hockey-stick divergence and the largest privacy loss can only go down: \[E_{e^\varepsilon}\big(PK\,\|\,QK\big) \le E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q), \qquad \max_z\big|L^{f}_{D,D'}(z)\big| \le \max_y\big|L_{D,D'}(y)\big|, \tag{19.4}\] where \(PK(z) = \sum_y p(y)K(z \mid y)\) is the distribution of \(f(M(D))\). In words: the privacy profile of \(f \circ M\) lies on or below that of \(M\) at every \(\varepsilon\).


19.3.3 Derivation
The plan is to turn any event about the processed output into a soft test on the original output, then apply Fact 2. Recall that \(K(z \mid y)\) is the probability that \(f\) outputs \(z\) on input \(y\).

Fix an event \(S\) of processed outputs. Let \(g(y) = K(S \mid y) = \sum_{z \in S}K(z \mid y)\), the probability that processing \(y\) lands in \(S\). It is a probability, so it takes values in \([0, 1]\). It does not depend on the data, because \(f\) does not look at the data: the same \(g\) serves for \(D\) and for \(D'\).
Average over \(Y\). To land in \(S\), the mechanism first produces some \(y\), and then processing sends it into \(S\) with probability \(g(y)\). Summing over \(y\), \(\Pr[f(M(D)) \in S] = \sum_y p(y)g(y) = \mathbb E_P[g(Y)]\), and the same with \(q\) for \(D'\).
Apply Fact 2 to \(g\): \(\mathbb E_P[g] \le e^\varepsilon\mathbb E_Q[g] + \delta\), that is \(\Pr[f(M(D)) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[f(M(D')) \in S] + \delta\). This holds for every \(S\) and every ordered neighbouring pair, which is the event form of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for \(f \circ M\) (Fact 1). The hockey-stick inequality of Equation 19.4 is the same statement for the worst event \(S\).
The privacy-loss form. This is step 1 of the DPI derivation in Divergences. The likelihood ratio of \(z\) is \(PK(z)/QK(z)\). In the numerator, write each \(p(y)\) as \(q(y)\) times its likelihood ratio \(e^{L(y)} = p(y)/q(y)\). That turns the ratio into a weighted average of the likelihood ratios of the \(y\) that can produce \(z\): \[e^{L^f(z)} = \frac{PK(z)}{QK(z)} = \sum_y\frac{q(y)K(z \mid y)}{QK(z)}\,e^{L(y)}. \tag{19.5}\] The weight of each \(y\) is the share of the \(D'\)-probability of \(z\) that comes through \(y\). The weights are non-negative and sum to 1, because \(\sum_y q(y)K(z \mid y) = QK(z)\). So \(e^{L^f(z)}\) lies between the smallest and the largest \(e^{L(y)}\), which is the second inequality in Equation 19.4.

Concretely, randomized response followed by a second coin. You collect answers with \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) (truth with probability \(\frac34\)), then, before publishing, flip each answer with probability \(f = \frac14\) using a fresh coin. (Here \(f\) is a number, the flip probability.) The published answer \(z = 1\) can be reached in two ways: the first answer was 1 and was kept, or it was 0 and was flipped. Each path’s probability is the product of its two steps. Table 19.2 follows the published answer \(z = 1\).

The likelihood ratio of \(z = 1\) is \(0.625/0.375 = \frac53\). Step 4 predicts it as the average of \(3\) and \(\frac13\), weighted by each path’s share of the \(D'\) column: each path contributes \(\frac3{16}\) of the total \(\frac6{16}\), a weight \(\frac{3/16}{6/16} = \frac12\) each, so \(\frac12(3 + \frac13) = \frac53\). The published \(z = 0\) gets the remaining probability, \(\frac6{16}\) under \(D\) and \(\frac{10}{16}\) under \(D'\), a ratio of \(\frac35\). So the published answers are \(\ln\frac53 = 0.5108\)-DP, less than \(\ln 3 = 1.0986\). The right panel of Figure 19.1 shows \(\varepsilon\) for every flip probability: it falls to 0 at \(f = \frac12\), where the published bit is a fair coin whatever the first answer was.


19.3.4 Interpretation
The first consequence is that nothing downstream needs a new proof. A model trained on DP statistics, synthetic data sampled from a DP model, a plot, a dashboard: all are functions of the private output that never read the data again, so all inherit the guarantee. This is why DP systems privatize at one narrow point (noisy counts, noisy gradients) and treat everything after it as public.
The same argument covers attackers. A membership-inference attacker of Part 2, who tries to tell whether a given record was in the data, sees \(y\) and outputs a guess \(A(y)\), possibly using auxiliary knowledge and its own randomness. That guess is a channel applied to \(y\), so it is a post-processing. So the bounds of The definition of differential privacy on an attack’s true and false positive rates hold for every attack, including attacks invented after the release. In hypothesis-testing terms: the trade-off curve of Hypothesis testing gives, for each false positive rate, the smallest false negative rate any test can reach. Under processing it can only rise, because any test on \(z\) is also a test on \(y\): compute \(z\) from \(y\), then apply it.
How much does processing lose? Deterministic, invertible processing (relabelling, a change of units) keeps the privacy loss exactly, since each \(z\) comes from a single \(y\) and nothing is averaged. Processing that merges outputs with different privacy losses lowers it, as the coin flip does when it mixes a ratio of 3 with a ratio of \(\frac13\). Most processing you do for utility (rounding, clipping) merges only a little, so do not count on it: the guarantee you report is the one of \(M\).
The one condition is that \(f\) must not touch the data, because step 1 of the derivation needed the same \(g\) under \(D\) and \(D'\). “Compute the noisy count, then look up the exact count of the winning category” is not post-processing. The second step reads the data, so it is a second mechanism, and a non-private one (Section 19.7).


19.3.5 Example: rounding and thresholding a noisy count
Add Laplace noise of scale \(b = 1\) to a count. Neighbouring datasets have counts 0 and 1, so the outputs are \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) and \(\mathrm{Lap}(1, 1)\), with densities \(\frac12e^{-|y|}\) and \(\frac12e^{-|y - 1|}\). Their privacy loss at \(y\) is \(|y - 1| - |y|\). Two points 1 apart cannot differ in their distance to \(y\) by more than 1 (the triangle inequality: \(|y - 1| \le |y| + 1\) and \(|y| \le |y - 1| + 1\)), so this loss is never more than 1 in size, and it equals \((1 - y) - (-y) = 1\) for every \(y \le 0\). The largest log-ratio, the max-divergence of Divergences, is therefore 1: the noisy count is 1-DP. (The Laplace mechanism in general is in The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms.) Now post-process it in two ways: round it to the nearest integer, or publish only whether it exceeds \(\frac12\). Table 19.3 gives the exact privacy profiles from the script, and Figure 19.1 draws them.

Three things can be read from the table and the figure, and each follows from the averaging picture of step 4.
Rounding keeps the pure \(\varepsilon\). Every output \(j \le -1\) of the rounded count collects the cell \([j - \frac12, j + \frac12]\), which lies entirely left of 0. There the two Laplace densities have the constant ratio \(e\), so rounding merges outputs with the same loss, and an average of equal ratios is that ratio: nothing is averaged away.
Rounding still lowers \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) for smaller \(\varepsilon\), because of the cell around 0. That cell, \([-\frac12, \frac12]\), mixes outputs whose losses run from \(-1\) to \(1\). Its probability is \(1 - e^{-1/2} = 0.3935\) when the count is 0 and \(\frac12(e^{-1/2} - e^{-3/2}) = 0.1917\) when it is 1, so its loss is \(\ln(0.3935/0.1917) = 0.7191\). For \(\varepsilon\) below that value, the worst event of the rounded output is “the rounded count is at most 0”. That is the same as “\(c + Z < \frac12\)”, exactly the threshold event, so the rounded and thresholded curves coincide there.
The one-bit summary is the most private. Its “yes” event, \(c + Z > \frac12\), needs \(Z > \frac12\) when the count is 0, which has probability \(\frac12e^{-1/2} = 0.3033\) under the Laplace tail, and \(Z > -\frac12\) when the count is 1, which has probability \(1 - 0.3033 = 0.6967\). Its privacy loss is \(\ln(0.6967/0.3033) = 0.8318\), and the “no” event gives the same loss with the opposite sign.


19.3.6 Check yourself

A data scientist reads a DP histogram, notices that one bin looks odd, and decides to publish a second histogram with finer bins. Is the second histogram covered by post-processing? (No. Choosing to publish is post-processing, but computing a finer histogram reads the data again. It is a second mechanism, and its cost adds by composition.)
Can post-processing turn a \((1, 10^{-6})\)-DP mechanism into a \((0.5, 10^{-6})\)-DP one? (It can, as the coin flip shows, but only by destroying information. It can never do the reverse.)

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.4 Group privacy

19.4.1 Context
The definition protects one record: datasets that differ in one row. But people are not rows. A user of a messaging app contributes hundreds of messages, a household shares an address and an income, and a disease runs in a family. If the neighbouring relation is example-level and you want to know what an adversary learns about all \(k\) records of one user at once, you need a guarantee for datasets that differ in \(k\) records. Group privacy gives it from the one-record guarantee, at a price.


19.4.2 Statement
Say \(D\) and \(D''\) are at distance \(k\) if a path \(D = D_0 \simeq D_1 \simeq \dots \simeq D_k = D''\) joins them, changing one record per step. The idea is to apply the one-record guarantee once per step and chain the results. Each step multiplies the probability bound by \(e^\varepsilon\) and adds a slack \(\delta\), so after \(k\) steps the factor is \(e^{k\varepsilon}\). The slacks pile up in a geometric sum, because a \(\delta\) added early is multiplied by \(e^\varepsilon\) again at every later step. If \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, then for every such pair and every event \(S\), \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{k\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D'') \in S] + \delta_k, \qquad \delta_k = \delta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e^{j\varepsilon} = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1} \le k\,e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\delta. \tag{19.6}\] In particular, pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP gives pure \(k\varepsilon\)-DP for groups of size \(k\). For \(\delta > 0\) the bound \(\delta_k\) grows exponentially in \(k\), and it is attained by some mechanisms.


19.4.3 Derivation
Pure DP, through the privacy loss. The likelihood ratio between the two ends of the path factors into the ratios of the steps, so the losses add, and each one is at most \(\varepsilon\).

Telescope the likelihood ratio along the path. Multiply and divide by the densities at the intermediate datasets \(D_1, \dots, D_{k-1}\); each one appears once in a numerator and once in a denominator, so they cancel and only the two ends remain: \[\frac{p_{M(D_0)}(y)}{p_{M(D_k)}(y)} = \prod_{i=1}^k\frac{p_{M(D_{i-1})}(y)}{p_{M(D_i)}(y)}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad L_{D_0,D_k}(y) = \sum_{i=1}^k L_{D_{i-1},D_i}(y). \tag{19.7}\]
Bound each term by Fact 1, form 3: each pair \(D_{i-1} \simeq D_i\) is neighbouring, so \(|L_{D_{i-1},D_i}(y)| \le \varepsilon\).
Add: a sum of \(k\) terms, each between \(-\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon\), lies between \(-k\varepsilon\) and \(k\varepsilon\), so \(|L_{D_0,D_k}(y)| \le k\varepsilon\) for every \(y\).

Concretely, a noisy count. Take a count with \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) noise and the path of counts \(0, 1, 2, 3\) (\(k = 3\)). The noisy count has density \(\frac12e^{-|y - c|}\) when the true count is \(c\). The ratio of the densities at counts \(c\) and \(c + 1\) is \(e^{|y - c - 1| - |y - c|}\), so the privacy loss between counts \(c\) and \(c + 1\) at output \(y\) is \(L_{c,c+1}(y) = |y - c - 1| - |y - c|\) (the ratio of two Laplace densities): how much farther \(y\) is from \(c + 1\) than from \(c\). Table 19.4 adds the steps at three outputs.

At \(y = -2\) the output lies left of every count on the path, so every step points the same way and the sum reaches \(3\varepsilon\). At \(y = 1.5\), in the middle of the path, the steps point in different directions and cancel. The script confirms that the rounded noisy count has pure \(\varepsilon\) exactly \(k\) for counts that differ by \(k = 1, 2, 3, 5\): for a count, group privacy is tight.
Approximate DP, through events. With \(\delta > 0\) the privacy loss is no longer bounded, so there is nothing to add up. Instead, chain the event form of the definition: bound the probability under \(D_0\) by the one under \(D_1\), that one by the one under \(D_2\), and so on.

One step. For every event \(S\), \(\Pr[M(D_{i-1}) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D_i) \in S] + \delta\) (Fact 1, form 1).
Substitute the next step into the right side. Writing \(P_i = \Pr[M(D_i) \in S]\), the bound on \(P_1\) goes in place of \(P_1\): \[P_0 \le e^\varepsilon P_1 + \delta \le e^\varepsilon\big(e^\varepsilon P_2 + \delta\big) + \delta = e^{2\varepsilon}P_2 + \delta(1 + e^\varepsilon). \tag{19.8}\]
Repeat \(k\) times (induction): \(P_0 \le e^{k\varepsilon}P_k + \delta(1 + e^\varepsilon + \dots + e^{(k-1)\varepsilon})\). Each new \(\delta\) enters before \(k - 1, k - 2, \dots, 0\) more multiplications by \(e^\varepsilon\), which is where the geometric sum comes from.
Simplify: the geometric sum is \(\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}\) (multiply it by \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) and all terms but the first and last cancel). Each of its \(k\) terms is at most the largest one, \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\), giving the simpler but looser \(k\,e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\delta\).

The bound is attained. To show that no better bound holds for all \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanisms, build one for which every inequality in the chain is an equality. That needs an event on which each one-step bound is met exactly, so that step 2 loses nothing. Here is a mechanism on counts for which Equation 19.6 holds with equality. Fix a size \(K\) and let \(M\) output “alarm” with probability \(a_c = \delta\sum_{j=0}^{K-c-1}e^{j\varepsilon}\) when the count is \(c \le K\) (and \(a_c = 0\) above \(K\)), and “quiet” otherwise. Pulling the first term out of the sum and \(e^\varepsilon\) out of the rest shows that the \(a_c\) satisfy \(a_c = e^\varepsilon a_{c+1} + \delta\), so each neighbouring pair meets the event form with equality on “alarm”, and the script checks that the other events are also within \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). For counts \(0\) and \(k\) the telescoping of step 3 runs with equality: \(a_0 - e^{k\varepsilon}a_k = \delta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e^{j\varepsilon} = \delta_k\).


19.4.4 Interpretation
Pure DP degrades linearly. A \(0.1\)-DP guarantee per record is a \(1\)-DP guarantee for a user with 10 records and a \(10\)-DP guarantee, almost nothing, for a user with 100: a likelihood ratio of up to \(e^{10} \approx 22{,}000\) lets an adversary be nearly certain. This is the formal version of the “correlated records” caveat of The definition of differential privacy: if one person’s data appear in \(k\) rows, protecting one row does not protect the person.
Approximate DP degrades exponentially in \(\delta\). With \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(k = 10\), the geometric sum gives \(\delta_k = \frac{e^{10} - 1}{e - 1}\,\delta = 12818.3\,\delta\). And \(\delta\) must already be much smaller than \(1/n\) for a dataset of \(n\) records, because \(\delta\) is a probability of failing outright: a mechanism that publishes each record in full with probability \(\delta\) is \((0, \delta)\)-DP and still leaks \(n\delta\) records on average (The definition of differential privacy). Multiply such a \(\delta\) by thousands and group privacy for large groups is often vacuous.
The bound is generic; a specific mechanism can do much better. For a count with Gaussian noise, a group of \(k\) records just shifts the count by \(k\) instead of 1, so its exact group profile is that of a Gaussian pair with a larger shift, as the Gaussian column of Table 19.5 shows. The tool that tracks this exactly for the Gaussian is in Part 4.
In practice, the better fix is to change the neighbouring relation. If you care about users, define neighbours as datasets that differ in one user’s records, bound each user’s contribution (clip it), and prove DP directly at that level. Group privacy is the fallback when you cannot.


19.4.5 Example: from records to users
Each record is protected at \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (0.5, 10^{-5})\). Table 19.5 compares the bound with two exact answers. The first is the alarm mechanism, built to attain the bound. The second is a count with Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\), calibrated so that \(\delta(0.5) = 10^{-5}\) exactly at shift 1. For two normal distributions with standard deviation \(\sigma\) whose means differ by \(s\), the privacy loss is a straight line in the output, so the event “loss above \(\varepsilon\)” is a half-line and the hockey-stick divergence is a difference of two normal tail probabilities. With \(\mu = s/\sigma\) and \(\Phi\) the standard normal cumulative distribution function, it is \(\Phi(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu) - e^\varepsilon\Phi(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu)\), the closed form from Divergences. The script finds \(\sigma = 7.0318\) by bisection on it, and for a group of \(k\) records it evaluates the same formula with the shift \(s = k\). 19.4.6 Check yourself

A dataset has one row per hospital visit, and a mechanism is \(0.2\)-DP at the visit level. A patient made 7 visits. What guarantee does the patient get? (\(7 \times 0.2 = 1.4\)-DP, by group privacy, assuming nothing else about the mechanism.)
Why does the derivation for \(\delta > 0\) not just add \(k\) copies of \(\delta\)? (Each step multiplies everything before it, including the \(\delta\)s already accumulated, by \(e^\varepsilon\). A \(\delta\) that entered early is inflated by the later steps.)

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.5 Basic sequential composition

19.5.1 Context
An analyst asks \(k\) queries of the same dataset, each answered by a DP mechanism with fresh noise. A training run takes \(k\) noisy gradient steps. A survey asks the same question twice. Each output alone is private, but an adversary sees all of them. The question is what guarantee holds for the whole transcript \((y_1, \dots, y_k)\), including when each mechanism is chosen after seeing the previous outputs. Fact 3 already gives the answer for pure DP: outputs with independent coins have probabilities that multiply, so their privacy losses add, and so do the budgets.


19.5.2 Statement
Let \(M_1, \dots, M_k\) run on the same dataset with independent coins. Each \(M_i\) may also take the previous outputs \(y_1, \dots, y_{i-1}\) as input, the way an analyst picks the next query after reading the last answer; this is adaptive composition, and non-adaptive composition is the special case where \(M_i\) ignores them. The condition is that each step is private however the earlier outputs turned out. If, for every fixed value of the previous outputs, \(D \mapsto M_i(D; y_1, \dots, y_{i-1})\) is \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\)-DP, then the mechanism that releases \((y_1, \dots, y_k)\) is \[\Big(\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i\Big)\text{-DP}. \tag{19.9}\] For pure DP the bound \(\sum\varepsilon_i\) is the exact worst-case privacy loss whenever each \(M_i\) attains its own worst case at outputs that can occur together, as \(k\) randomized-response answers about the same bit do.


19.5.3 Derivation
Pure DP, through the privacy loss. Write the probability of a transcript as a product of one factor per step, take logs, and bound each term.

Factor the probability of a transcript by the chain rule: the probability of \((y_1, \dots, y_k)\) is the probability of \(y_1\), times that of \(y_2\) given \(y_1\), and so on. Under \(D\), \[p_D(y_1, \dots, y_k) = \prod_{i=1}^k p_{M_i(D;\,y_{<i})}(y_i), \tag{19.10}\] where \(y_{<i} = (y_1, \dots, y_{i-1})\) and each factor uses fresh coins. The same holds under \(D'\), with the same previous outputs plugged in.
Take the log-ratio (Fact 3, adaptive version): the log of a ratio of products is a sum of log-ratios, \(L_{D,D'}(y_1, \dots, y_k) = \sum_{i=1}^k L^{(i)}_{D,D'}(y_i;\,y_{<i})\), where \(L^{(i)}\) is the privacy loss of \(M_i\) with its previous outputs fixed.
Bound each term. For the fixed \(y_{<i}\), \(M_i\) is \(\varepsilon_i\)-DP by assumption, so \(|L^{(i)}| \le \varepsilon_i\).
Add: \(|L_{D,D'}| \le \sum_i\varepsilon_i\) at every transcript, which is pure \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\)-DP (Fact 1, form 3).

Concretely, an adaptive survey. Ask a person for a randomized-response answer with \(\varepsilon_1 = \ln 3\). If the answer is 1, ask again with \(\ln 3\); if it is 0, ask again with \(0.5\), which means telling the truth with probability \(e^{0.5}/(1 + e^{0.5}) = 0.6225\) (randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) tells the truth with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), so that truth and lie have ratio \(e^\varepsilon\)). The second mechanism depends on the first output, but for each value of \(y_1\) it is at most \(\ln 3\)-DP. Table 19.6 lists the four transcripts, from the script. Each probability is the product of the two steps; for example \((0, 1)\) under bit 1 is a lie at the first step and the truth at the second, \(\frac14 \times 0.6225 = 0.1556\).

The worst loss is \(2.1972 = \ln 3 + \ln 3\), exactly the bound with \(\varepsilon_2 = \max(\ln 3, 0.5)\), the largest budget the second step can have.
Approximate DP, through a two-step lemma. With \(\delta > 0\) the losses are no longer bounded, so work with events and Fact 2. The plan is to split an event over the first output, use the second mechanism’s guarantee for each value of that output, and then use the first mechanism’s guarantee on what is left, which is a soft test of the first output. Take \(k = 2\); induction on \(k\) does the rest, since the first \(k - 1\) steps form one mechanism.

Split an event over the first output. For a set \(S\) of transcripts, let \(S_{y_1} = \{y_2 : (y_1, y_2) \in S\}\), the second outputs that complete \(y_1\) into \(S\). The transcript lands in \(S\) when the first output is some \(y_1\) and the second lands in \(S_{y_1}\), so \[\Pr_D[(Y_1, Y_2) \in S] = \sum_{y_1}p_1(y_1)\,P_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}), \tag{19.11}\] where \(p_1\) is the distribution of \(M_1(D)\) and \(P_2^{y_1}\) that of \(M_2(D; y_1)\). Write \(q_1\) and \(Q_2^{y_1}\) for \(D'\).
Apply the second mechanism’s guarantee inside the sum. For each \(y_1\), \(P_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}) \le e^{\varepsilon_2}Q_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}) + \delta_2\), and also \(P_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}) \le 1\) because it is a probability. So \(P_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}) \le g(y_1) + \delta_2\) with \[g(y_1) = \min\big(1,\ e^{\varepsilon_2}Q_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1})\big) \in [0, 1]. \tag{19.12}\]
Sum over \(y_1\): the weights \(p_1(y_1)\) add up to 1, so \(\delta_2\) comes out once, \(\Pr_D[S] \le \sum_{y_1}p_1(y_1)g(y_1) + \delta_2 = \mathbb E_{p_1}[g] + \delta_2\).
Apply the first mechanism’s guarantee to \(g\) (Fact 2, which needs values in \([0, 1]\); that is why \(g\) was capped at 1): \(\mathbb E_{p_1}[g] \le e^{\varepsilon_1}\mathbb E_{q_1}[g] + \delta_1\).
Undo the cap: \(g(y_1) \le e^{\varepsilon_2}Q_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1})\), so \(\mathbb E_{q_1}[g] \le e^{\varepsilon_2}\sum_{y_1}q_1(y_1)Q_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}) = e^{\varepsilon_2}\Pr_{D'}[S]\), by step 1 under \(D'\).
Combine: \(\Pr_D[S] \le e^{\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2}\Pr_{D'}[S] + \delta_1 + \delta_2\). Nothing used that \(M_2\) ignores \(y_1\), so this covers adaptive composition.



19.5.4 Interpretation
Basic composition is exact for the worst case. For \(k\) randomized-response answers about the same bit, the transcript “all answers equal the true bit” has loss exactly \(k\ln 3\), since each answer contributes \(+\ln 3\). No smaller pure \(\varepsilon\) holds.
But the worst case is rare. That transcript has probability \((\frac34)^k\) under \(D\). Typical transcripts mix truthful answers with lies, and their losses cancel in part. Each answer contributes \(+\varepsilon_0\) with probability \(t = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\) (it told the truth) and \(-\varepsilon_0\) otherwise, so its mean is \(\varepsilon_0(2t - 1) = \varepsilon_0\frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1} = \varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\). For \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) this is \(\varepsilon_0\cdot\frac{3 - 1}{3 + 1} = \frac{\varepsilon_0}2\). The privacy loss of \(k\) answers is a sum of \(k\) independent terms of \(\pm\varepsilon_0\), so it concentrates around its mean \(k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\) (half of \(k\ln 3\) for \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\)) with spread of order \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt k\). That is the behaviour of any sum of bounded independent terms (Concentration): its standard deviation grows like \(\sqrt k\), and deviations much larger than that are exponentially unlikely. Allowing a small \(\delta\) lets you ignore that unlikely tail, and the \(\varepsilon\) you need grows like \(\sqrt k\) rather than \(k\). That is advanced composition, derived in Advanced and optimal composition; Exercise 6 previews it.
The \(\delta\)s add without inflation. Unlike group privacy, composition adds \(\delta\)s plainly: there is no chain of multiplications, because each mechanism compares the same pair \(D, D'\). In group privacy each step moved to a new dataset, and the bound for the next step had to be multiplied through; here step 3 of the lemma just averages the second slack over the first output.
Adaptivity is free here, but only with fixed budgets. The theorem allows \(M_i\) to depend on previous outputs, but its budget \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\) must be fixed in advance. Choosing the budgets themselves from the outputs (“stop when the answer is good enough”) needs privacy filters, also in Advanced and optimal composition.


19.5.5 Example: asking the same question \(k\) times
A survey asks the same yes/no question \(k\) times, each time with fresh randomized response at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\). Only the number \(j\) of answers equal to 1 matters for the privacy loss, which is \((2j - k)\ln 3\): \(j\) answers with loss \(+\ln 3\) and \(k - j\) with \(-\ln 3\). When the true bit is 1, \(j\) follows a binomial distribution with \(k\) trials and success probability \(\frac34\); when it is 0, success probability \(\frac14\). Figure 19.3 shows the distribution of the privacy loss for \(k = 10\), and Table 19.7 gives the exact numbers from the script. “Exact \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\)” is the smallest \(\varepsilon\) with \(\delta(\varepsilon) \le 10^{-6}\) for the \(k\) answers, computed from the binomial distribution of the number of truthful answers.
