title: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.5 Report-noisy-max

22.5.1 Context
Here is the obvious way to select privately. Add independent noise to every score, and report the index of the largest noisy score. Release only the index. If you released the noisy scores as well, you would be releasing a vector, and its \(\ell_1\) sensitivity, the total change over all coordinates, would set the noise. For \(k\) counting queries that one record can all change (for example “how many records have feature \(j\)”, for \(k\) features), that sensitivity is \(k\), and the Laplace mechanism would need noise of scale \(k/\varepsilon\). Releasing only the argmax needs noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\), for any \(k\), because of the bar argument sketched at the start of this chapter.


22.5.2 Statement
Report-noisy-max adds an independent Laplace noise of scale \(b\) to every score and outputs the candidate with the largest noisy score: \[M_N(D) = \arg\max_{r \in \mathcal R}\big(u(D, r) + Z_r\big), \qquad Z_r \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b) \text{ independent}. \tag{22.7}\] Ties have probability zero, because the noise is continuous.

General scores. With \(b = 2\Delta/\varepsilon\), \(M_N\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
Monotone scores (Dwork & Roth, Claim 3.9, stated there for counting queries with \(\Delta = 1\)). With \(b = \Delta/\varepsilon\), \(M_N\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
Accuracy. With probability at least \(1 - \beta\), \(\mathrm{OPT}(D) - u(D, M_N(D)) \le 2b\ln(k/\beta)\).



22.5.3 Derivation
The proof below covers both privacy claims. It is the argument of Dwork & Roth’s Claim 3.9, written so that the general and the monotone case differ in one step. It uses all four facts of the toolkit in order: look at one output (Fact 1), freeze the other candidates’ noise (Fact 2), see that the output happens when one Laplace noise clears a bar, bound the bar’s movement (Fact 4), and pay for it (Fact 3).

Fix everything but one noise. Fix neighbours \(D \simeq D'\), a candidate \(i\), and the noise \(z_{-i}\) of all other candidates. The noises are drawn the same way whatever the data, so by Fact 2 it is enough to bound \(\Pr[M_N(D) = i \mid z_{-i}]\) against the same probability on \(D'\).
Candidate \(i\) wins when its noise clears a bar. With the others’ noise fixed, their noisy scores are fixed numbers, and \(i\) wins on \(D\) exactly when its own noisy score beats the best of them, \(u(D, i) + Z_i > \max_{j \ne i}(u(D, j) + z_j)\). Moving \(u(D, i)\) to the right-hand side, that is \(Z_i > t(D)\) with the bar \[t(D) = \max_{j \ne i}\big(u(D, j) + z_j\big) - u(D, i). \tag{22.8}\] So \(\Pr[M_N(D) = i \mid z_{-i}] = \Pr[Z_i > t(D)]\), and likewise for \(D'\).
The bar moves by at most \(2\Delta\). The first term of \(t\) is a maximum of numbers \(u(\cdot, j) + z_j\), and each moves by at most \(\Delta\) between \(D\) and \(D'\) because the \(z_j\) are fixed. By Fact 4 the maximum moves by at most \(\Delta\), however many terms it has. The second term, \(u(\cdot, i)\), moves by at most \(\Delta\) too. So \(|t(D) - t(D')| \le 2\Delta\).
With monotone scores, by at most \(\Delta\). If every score goes up by an amount in \([0, \Delta]\), the maximum goes up by an amount in \([0, \Delta]\) (Fact 4, the same-direction case) and so does \(u(\cdot, i)\). Their difference, the bar, changes by an amount in \([-\Delta, \Delta]\), because subtracting two numbers in \([0, \Delta]\) gives a number in \([-\Delta, \Delta]\). The same holds if every score goes down.
Shift the threshold. By Fact 3 with \(s = t(D) - t(D')\), \(\Pr[Z_i > t(D)] \le e^{|t(D) - t(D')|/b}\Pr[Z_i > t(D')]\). In the general case that factor is at most \(e^{2\Delta/b} = e^\varepsilon\) with \(b = 2\Delta/\varepsilon\), and in the monotone case at most \(e^{\Delta/b} = e^\varepsilon\) with \(b = \Delta/\varepsilon\).
Average and collect. Fact 2 removes the conditioning on \(z_{-i}\), and Fact 1 turns the bound for each \(i\) into \(\varepsilon\)-DP.

Figure 22.3 draws steps 2 to 5 for \(b = 1\), \(t(D) = 0.7\) and a bar lowered by \(s = 1\) on \(D'\): the winning probability rises from \(\Pr[Z_i > 0.7] = \frac12e^{-0.7} = 0.2483\) to \(\Pr[Z_i > -0.3] = 1 - \frac12e^{-0.3} = 0.6296\), a ratio of 2.5357, below \(e = 2.7183\). The ratio falls short of \(e\) because the lowered bar has crossed 0, out of the exponential tail where Fact 3 is exact.






Figure 22.3: The proof of report-noisy-max in one picture. With the other candidates’ noise fixed, candidate \(i\) wins when its own noise \(Z_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(1)\) exceeds a bar \(t\). Moving to a neighbouring dataset moves the bar by at most \(s\), and the winning probability changes by at most a factor \(e^{s/b}\).



Accuracy. The idea is that if no noise is large, the noise cannot reorder candidates whose scores are far apart. A single Laplace noise exceeds \(x\) in absolute value with probability \(e^{-x/b}\). By the union bound, the probability that at least one of \(k\) events happens is at most the sum of their probabilities, so some \(|Z_r|\) reaches \(x\) with probability at most \(k\,e^{-x/b}\). Setting this to \(\beta\) gives \(x = b\ln(k/\beta)\): every \(|Z_r| < b\ln(k/\beta)\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\). This is the maximum-of-Laplace rule of Concentration inequalities. On that event the winner \(i\) beat a best candidate \(r^*\) despite noise of at most \(b\ln(k/\beta)\) on each side, so \(u(D, i) + b\ln(k/\beta) > u(D, i) + Z_i \ge u(D, r^*) + Z_{r^*} > \mathrm{OPT} - b\ln(k/\beta)\), and the gap is less than \(2b\ln(k/\beta)\). This is Exercise 5 of that chapter.


22.5.4 Interpretation
The privacy cost is not \(k\varepsilon\) because of step 3. That is where the losers would cost something, and they don’t: they enter only through one maximum, which moves by at most \(\Delta\) however many of them there are (Fact 4).
The noise must be \(2\Delta/\varepsilon\) in general because the bar has two parts that can move in opposite directions: the competitors can rise while candidate \(i\) falls, and then the bar rises by both amounts. Monotone scores cannot do that, which halves the noise. This is the same factor of 2 as in the exponential mechanism, for the same reason.
Should you use Laplace report-noisy-max or the exponential mechanism? They are different mechanisms with the same privacy, and neither dominates. On the 50 models at \(\varepsilon = 1\), Laplace report-noisy-max with \(b = 2\) picks the best model with probability 0.4241 against 0.3935 and has expected gap 1.40 against 1.54. With two candidates the exponential mechanism is slightly better (Exercise 6). Adding one-sided exponential noise instead of Laplace noise gives a third mechanism, which equals the “permute-and-flip” mechanism of McKenna & Sheldon (2020); its expected score is never below the exponential mechanism’s.
Finally, release only the index. Releasing the winning noisy score as well breaks the proof: the bar argument conditions on everything but \(Z_i\) and averages over \(Z_i\), and \(Z_i\) itself would then be published. To release the winner’s score, spend extra budget on a fresh Laplace answer for that one query.


22.5.5 Example: the vote and the 50 models
On the vote of Table 22.3, counts are monotone, so \(b = 1/\varepsilon = 1\) is allowed. The script integrates the winning probabilities exactly: on \(D\) they are \((0.6551, 0.2380, 0.0794, 0.0275)\), on \(D'\) \((0.4639, 0.4639, 0.0534, 0.0189)\), and the largest privacy loss over the four outputs, the largest \(|\ln|\) of a ratio of matching entries, is 0.6674, below \(\varepsilon = 1\). With the general scale \(b = 2\) it is 0.3626.
On the 50 models at \(\varepsilon = 1\), the general mechanism (\(b = 2\)) has expected gap 1.40 (1.39 in 200,000 simulated runs), and the monotone one (\(b = 1\)) has 0.54 and picks the best model with probability 0.6463. The accuracy bound at \(\beta = 0.05\) is \(2b\ln(50/0.05) = 2b\ln 1000\), which is 27.63 for \(b = 2\) and 13.82 for \(b = 1\). Like the exponential mechanism’s bound, it is loose for spread-out scores.


22.5.6 Check yourself

Where does the proof use that the noises are independent? (In step 1: conditioning on \(z_{-i}\) must leave \(Z_i\) with its Laplace distribution, so that Fact 3 applies.)
If the scores are a histogram under replace neighbours (one count goes down by 1, another goes up by 1), can you use \(b = 1/\varepsilon\)? (No. The scores move in opposite directions, so they are not monotone; use \(b = 2/\varepsilon\).)

text:
22.6 Gumbel noise: report-noisy-max is the exponential mechanism

22.6.1 Context
Report-noisy-max with Laplace noise is close to the exponential mechanism but not equal to it (Figure 22.4). Is there a noise distribution for which “add noise and take the argmax” gives exactly the softmax probabilities of Equation 22.3? There is: the Gumbel distribution. This is the Gumbel-max trick, used throughout machine learning to sample from a softmax. For privacy it gives a second proof that the exponential mechanism is private, a numerically stable way to sample it, and a fast way to select the top \(c\) candidates.


22.6.2 Statement
The Gumbel distribution arises as the limit of the maximum of many independent variables with exponential tails, after shifting; what matters here is only its formula. \(G \sim \mathrm{Gumbel}(\beta)\), with scale \(\beta\), has cumulative distribution function (CDF) \(\Pr[G \le g] = \exp(-e^{-g/\beta})\); NumPy’s rng.gumbel(0, beta) samples it. The claim is that adding independent Gumbel noise to each score and taking the argmax picks candidate \(i\) with exactly its softmax probability. For independent \(G_r \sim \mathrm{Gumbel}(\beta)\), \[\Pr\Big[\arg\max_r\big(u_r + G_r\big) = i\Big] = \frac{e^{u_i/\beta}}{\sum_r e^{u_r/\beta}}. \tag{22.9}\] With \(\beta = 2\Delta/\varepsilon\) this is the exponential mechanism.


22.6.3 Derivation
Rescaling all scores and noises by \(1/\beta\) does not change which one is largest, so take \(\beta = 1\). The Gumbel CDF is then \(F(g) = \exp(-e^{-g})\), and its derivative, the density, is \(f(g) = e^{-g}\exp(-e^{-g})\).
Two candidates first. Candidate 1 wins when \(G_2 - G_1 < u_1 - u_2\), so you need the distribution of the difference of two independent Gumbels. It is the logistic distribution, with CDF \(\Pr[G_1 - G_2 \le x] = 1/(1 + e^{-x})\), and \(G_2 - G_1\) has the same distribution, because swapping the names of two identically distributed independent noises changes nothing. (To get it, integrate \(F(g + x)\) against \(f(g)\); it is the general calculation below with \(k = 2\).) So \[\Pr[u_1 + G_1 > u_2 + G_2] = \Pr[G_2 - G_1 < u_1 - u_2] = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(u_1 - u_2)}} = \frac{e^{u_1}}{e^{u_1} + e^{u_2}}, \tag{22.10}\] where the last step multiplies top and bottom by \(e^{u_1}\). That is the softmax of two scores.
In general. The plan is to condition on the value of the winner’s noise, use independence to multiply the probabilities that each other candidate falls short, and notice that the resulting integral can be done exactly.

Condition on the winner’s noise. If candidate \(i\)’s noise is \(G_i = g\), it wins when every other candidate’s noisy score is below \(u_i + g\), that is, when every other \(G_j < g + u_i - u_j\). Each of these has probability \(F(g + u_i - u_j)\), and the noises are independent, so the probabilities multiply. Averaging over \(g\) with density \(f\), \[\Pr[i \text{ wins}] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(g)\prod_{j \ne i}F(g + u_i - u_j)\,dg. \tag{22.11}\]
Collect the exponentials. The density can be written \(f(g) = e^{-g}F(g)\), and \(F(g)\) is \(F(g + u_i - u_j)\) for \(j = i\). Each factor is \(F(g + u_i - u_j) = \exp(-e^{-g}e^{u_j - u_i})\), and a product of exponentials is the exponential of the sum, so the product of all the \(F\) factors, including the one inside \(f\), is \(\exp\big(-e^{-g}\sum_je^{u_j - u_i}\big) = \exp(-e^{-g}A)\) with \(A = e^{-u_i}\sum_je^{u_j}\). The integrand is \(e^{-g}\exp(-e^{-g}A)\).
Substitute \(w = e^{-g}\), so \(dw = -e^{-g}\,dg\), and \(g\) from \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\) is \(w\) from \(\infty\) to 0; the minus sign flips the limits back: \[\Pr[i \text{ wins}] = \int_0^\infty e^{-wA}\,dw = \frac1A = \frac{e^{u_i}}{\sum_je^{u_j}}. \tag{22.12}\]



22.6.4 Interpretation
The exponential mechanism now has two proofs. It can be analysed by its weights (Section 22.3) or as a noisy max. The bar argument of Section 22.5 also works with Gumbel noise of scale \(2\Delta/\varepsilon\), because the Gumbel tail also satisfies \(\Pr[G > t - s] \le e^{s/\beta}\Pr[G > t]\) for \(s \ge 0\) (for \(s < 0\) the probability only falls). To see why, write the tail as \(1 - e^{-y}\) with \(y = e^{-t/\beta}\). Lowering \(t\) by \(s\) multiplies \(y\) by \(e^{s/\beta} \ge 1\), and because \(1 - e^{-y}\) is zero at \(y = 0\) and concave, multiplying \(y\) by a factor of at least 1 multiplies \(1 - e^{-y}\) by at most that factor.
The noisy-max form also gives stable sampling. Computing \(e^{\varepsilon u/(2\Delta)}\) for scores in the thousands overflows. The noisy max works in score units directly. (Subtracting the largest score before exponentiating, as the script does, is the other fix; it is allowed because adding a constant to every score does not change the mechanism.)
It also gives top-\(c\) selection in one shot. Taking the \(c\) largest of \(u_r + G_r\) gives the same distribution as running the exponential mechanism \(c\) times, removing each winner (Durfee & Rogers 2019). Its privacy is that of \(c\) exponential mechanisms, \(c\varepsilon\) by basic composition.
Laplace noise is close, not equal. Laplace and Gumbel noise of the same scale have similar bodies but different tails, so the selection probabilities differ by a few percent.






Figure 22.4: Selection probabilities for five candidates with scores \((4, 3, 3, 1, 0)\) and noise scale \(2\Delta/\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon = 1\): the exponential mechanism’s exact probabilities, the frequencies of the Gumbel noisy max in 200,000 runs, and the exact probabilities of the Laplace noisy max.





22.6.5 Example: five candidates, a million draws
For scores \((4, 3, 3, 1, 0)\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\Delta = 1\), the noise scale is \(2\Delta/\varepsilon = 2\). Table 22.5 compares the three mechanisms.

The Gumbel frequencies are within 0.0008 of the exponential mechanism. That is about the sampling error of a million draws: a frequency estimated from \(n\) draws has standard deviation \(\sqrt{p(1 - p)/n}\), here \(\sqrt{0.39\times0.61/10^6} \approx 0.0005\). The Laplace noisy max is further away. Measured by the total variation distance, half the sum of the absolute differences between the two rows, which is the largest difference in probability the two can assign to any set of candidates, it is at distance 0.0216 from the exponential mechanism. Here that is exactly the extra \(0.4105 - 0.3889 = 0.0216\) it puts on the top candidate: it favours the top candidate more and the bottom ones less.


22.6.6 Check yourself

How do you sample from the exponential mechanism over \(10^7\) candidates without computing a normalizer? (Draw one Gumbel per candidate, add it to \(\varepsilon u/(2\Delta)\), and take the argmax. It is one pass over the scores.)
Does adding Gumbel noise and releasing the top 3 cost \(\varepsilon\) or \(3\varepsilon\)? (\(3\varepsilon\) under basic composition: it has the distribution of three exponential mechanisms run one after the other.)

text:
22.7 The sparse vector technique

22.7.1 Context
Now the candidates arrive one at a time and you only care about the first one that is good enough. You monitor a thousand statistics and want to know which one first crosses an alarm level. You try hyperparameter settings until one reaches a target validation accuracy. Most queries in such a stream are uninteresting: their answer is “below”. Answering each one with the Laplace mechanism costs \(\varepsilon\) per query, so a thousand queries would cost \(1000\varepsilon\) under basic composition. The sparse vector technique (Dwork, Naor, Reingold, Rothblum & Vadhan 2009) compares each query with a single noisy threshold and pays only for the one that is above. Its basic form, AboveThreshold, is in Dwork & Roth (2014), Algorithm 1.


22.7.2 Statement
AboveThreshold adds noise to the threshold once, adds fresh noise to each query, and stops at the first noisy query that reaches the noisy threshold. It writes \(\bot\) (“below”) for each query that does not and \(\top\) (“above”) for the one that does.
AboveThreshold. Input: a dataset \(D\), a stream of queries \(f_1, f_2, \dots\), each with sensitivity \(\Delta\) (they may be chosen adaptively), a threshold \(T\), and budgets \(\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2 > 0\).

Draw the threshold noise \(\rho \sim \mathrm{Lap}(\Delta/\varepsilon_1)\) once.
For each query \(i = 1, 2, \dots\): draw fresh noise \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2\Delta/\varepsilon_2)\). If \(f_i(D) + \nu_i \ge T + \rho\), output \(\top\) and halt. Otherwise output \(\bot\) and continue.

The output is the sequence \(\bot^{k-1}\top\) (\(k - 1\) answers “below”, then one “above”), or \(\bot^m\) if all \(m\) queries are below; equivalently, the index \(k\) of the first \(\top\).

Privacy (Dwork & Roth Thm 3.23 for \(\varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon/2\); Lyu, Su & Li 2017, Algorithm 1 with \(c = 1\), for a general split). AboveThreshold is \((\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)\)-DP, for any number of queries.
Monotone queries (Lyu, Su & Li 2017). If the queries are monotone, as counts under add/remove are, \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(\Delta/\varepsilon_2)\) suffices.
Accuracy (Dwork & Roth Thm 3.24). With \(\varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon/2\), that is \(\rho \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2\Delta/\varepsilon)\) and \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(4\Delta/\varepsilon)\), consider a run that stops at query \(k\) (or answers all \(k\)). The noisy comparisons can be wrong only for queries close to the threshold, and the margin \(\alpha\) of “close” is the size the noises stay below with high probability. With probability at least \(1 - \beta\), every \(\bot\) query has \(f_i(D) < T + \alpha\), and the \(\top\) query has \(f_k(D) \ge T - \alpha\), where \[\alpha = \frac{8\Delta\big(\ln k + \ln(2/\beta)\big)}{\varepsilon}. \tag{22.13}\]
\(c\) answers above. To find the first \(c\) queries above the threshold, restart AboveThreshold with fresh threshold noise after each \(\top\), with budget \(\varepsilon/c\) per run. By basic composition this is \(\varepsilon\)-DP (Dwork & Roth’s algorithm Sparse).



22.7.3 Derivation
Privacy. The output “stop at query \(k\)” says two things: the noisy threshold sits above every earlier noisy answer, and it sits at or below the \(k\)-th noisy answer. Moving from \(D\) to \(D'\) moves those noisy answers. The proof undoes that move by sliding the two noises that matter. It slides the threshold noise \(\rho\) by however much the largest earlier answer moved, so that the threshold keeps its place relative to all the earlier answers at once; by Fact 4 that is at most \(\Delta\), however many earlier queries there are. Then it slides the \(k\)-th query’s noise \(\nu_k\) so that query \(k\) keeps its place relative to the slid threshold, which takes at most \(2\Delta\). Each slide is paid for by the Laplace density, as in Fact 3.
Fix neighbours \(D \simeq D'\). Write \(\nu = \nu_i\) for the noise of a single query and \(g(D) = \max_{i < k}\big(f_i(D) + \nu_i\big)\) for the largest noisy answer before query \(k\).

Fix the noise of the earlier queries. Consider the output “stop at query \(k\)”. Fix \(\nu_1, \dots, \nu_{k-1}\). By Fact 2 it is enough to bound the conditional probability, because these noises do not depend on the data. (With adaptive queries, the queries \(f_1, \dots, f_k\) are fixed too: they can depend only on earlier answers, which on this output are all \(\bot\).)
Write the output as two conditions on \((\rho, \nu_k)\). All earlier queries say \(\bot\) exactly when even the largest of them is below the noisy threshold, \(g(D) < T + \rho\). Query \(k\) says \(\top\) when \(f_k(D) + \nu_k \ge T + \rho\). The probability of the output is the probability that both hold, which is the integral of the two noise densities \(p_\rho\) and \(p_\nu\) over the region where both indicators are 1: \[\Pr[\text{stop at } k \mid D] = \iint p_\rho(r)\,p_\nu(v)\,\mathbf 1\big[g(D) < T + r\big]\,\mathbf 1\big[f_k(D) + v \ge T + r\big]\,dr\,dv. \tag{22.14}\]
Shift both noises. Substitute \(r = r' + g(D) - g(D')\) and \(v = v' + \big(g(D) - g(D')\big) - \big(f_k(D) - f_k(D')\big)\). Then \(g(D) < T + r\) becomes \(g(D') < T + r'\), and \(f_k(D) + v \ge T + r\) becomes \(f_k(D') + v' \ge T + r'\) (substitute and cancel the terms that appear on both sides). The two indicators are exactly those for \(D'\) in the variables \((r', v')\). The substitution is a translation, so \(dr\,dv = dr'\,dv'\). What has changed is only the densities, which are now evaluated at shifted points: \(p_\rho(r' + g(D) - g(D'))\) and \(p_\nu(v' + \text{shift of } v)\).
Size of the shifts. \(g\) is a maximum of numbers \(f_i + \nu_i\) that each move by at most \(\Delta\) (the \(\nu_i\) are fixed), so \(|g(D) - g(D')| \le \Delta\) by Fact 4, whatever \(k\) is. The shift of \(v\) is a difference of two terms of size at most \(\Delta\), so at most \(2\Delta\).
Pay for the shifts. The Laplace density satisfies \(p(x) \le e^{|x - x'|/b}p(x')\), as shown in the proof of Fact 3. The threshold noise has \(b = \Delta/\varepsilon_1\) and shift at most \(\Delta\): a factor \(e^{\varepsilon_1}\). The query noise has \(b = 2\Delta/\varepsilon_2\) and shift at most \(2\Delta\): a factor \(e^{\varepsilon_2}\). Pulling both factors out of the integral leaves exactly the integral for \(D'\), so \(\Pr[\text{stop at } k \mid D, \nu_{<k}] \le e^{\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2}\Pr[\text{stop at } k \mid D', \nu_{<k}]\).
The output “all below”. Only the first indicator is present, with the maximum over all \(m\) queries. Shifting \(\rho\) alone costs \(e^{\varepsilon_1}\).
Collect. Fact 2 removes the conditioning, and Fact 1 gives \((\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)\)-DP.

Monotone queries. If all \(f_i\) move the same way by at most \(\Delta\), then \(g\) and \(f_k\) move the same way, each by an amount in \([0, \Delta]\) or each in \([-\Delta, 0]\) (Fact 4). The shift of \(v\) in step 3 is their difference, which is then at most \(\Delta\) in size. A query noise with \(b = \Delta/\varepsilon_2\) then costs \(e^{\varepsilon_2}\).
Accuracy. A comparison of noisy numbers gives the same answer as the comparison of true numbers whenever the noises are smaller than the distance between the true numbers. So the proof finds a margin that all the noises stay below with probability \(1 - \beta\), splitting the failure probability \(\beta\) equally between the threshold noise and the query noises. Let \(\varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon/2\).

Threshold noise. The Laplace tail \(\Pr[|\rho| \ge x] = e^{-x/b}\) with \(b = 2\Delta/\varepsilon\) and \(x = \alpha/2\) gives \(\Pr[|\rho| \ge \alpha/2] = e^{-(\alpha/2)/(2\Delta/\varepsilon)} = e^{-\alpha\varepsilon/(4\Delta)}\).
Query noise. Each \(\nu_i\) has scale \(4\Delta/\varepsilon\), so \(\Pr[|\nu_i| \ge \alpha/2] = e^{-\alpha\varepsilon/(8\Delta)}\). By the union bound over \(k\) queries, the probability that any of them is that large is \(\Pr[\max_i|\nu_i| \ge \alpha/2] \le k\,e^{-\alpha\varepsilon/(8\Delta)}\).
Both small. Setting each to at most \(\beta/2\) needs \(\alpha \ge 8\Delta\ln(2k/\beta)/\varepsilon\) for the second (the first then holds too, since its exponent is twice as large and it has no factor \(k\)), which is Equation 22.13 because \(\ln(2k/\beta) = \ln k + \ln(2/\beta)\).
Read off the answers. If \(|\rho| < \alpha/2\) and every \(|\nu_i| < \alpha/2\), the noises together can move a comparison by less than \(\alpha\). A \(\bot\) means \(f_i + \nu_i < T + \rho\), so \(f_i < T + \rho - \nu_i < T + \alpha\); the \(\top\) means \(f_k + \nu_k \ge T + \rho\), so \(f_k > T - \alpha\).



22.7.4 Interpretation
The \(\bot\) answers are free because the derivation pays for all of them at once, in step 4, through one maximum \(g\) and one shift of the threshold noise. Fact 4 makes that shift at most \(\Delta\) whether there are 3 or 3 million queries below the threshold. The single \(\top\) is paid for separately, by its own noise.
The run must halt because that payment covers only one \(\top\). After the first \(\top\), the remaining answers would still compare against the same \(\rho\). The proof’s shift of \(\rho\) was chosen to keep the \(\bot\)s consistent; each further \(\top\) would need another shift of size up to \(2\Delta\) in its own noise, and so another factor \(e^{\varepsilon_2}\). With \(c\) answers above, Lyu, Su & Li’s Algorithm 1 keeps one threshold noise and uses \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2c\Delta/\varepsilon_2)\), so that the \(c\) shifts together cost \(e^{\varepsilon_2}\); without any limit on \(c\) the cost is unbounded (Section 22.8).
AboveThreshold answers a yes/no question. It outputs positions, not values. To also release the value of the query that fired, spend extra budget on a fresh Laplace answer to that query.
The split between \(\varepsilon_1\) and \(\varepsilon_2\) matters for accuracy, not privacy. Any \(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The equal split is simple but not optimal: Exercise 4 finds the split that minimizes \(\alpha\), and Lyu, Su & Li recommend \(\varepsilon_1 : \varepsilon_2 = 1 : (2c)^{2/3}\) to maximize the probability of correct answers.
The proof is tight. On the neighbouring pair of the next section, the output “stop at query \(m + 1\)” has privacy loss exactly \(\varepsilon\) for \(m = 20\) (Table 22.7): both shifts in step 4 reach their maximum.
Figure 22.5 shows one run.






Figure 22.5: One run of AboveThreshold with \(\varepsilon = 1\) on 30 queries whose true answers rise from 8 to 22.5, with threshold \(T = 20\). Each query’s noisy answer is compared with the same noisy threshold. The first one above it is reported and the run halts; later queries are never looked at.





22.7.5 Example: an alarm among 1,000 statistics
You monitor \(k = 1000\) counting queries (\(\Delta = 1\)) with threshold \(T = 500\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\). With \(\beta = 0.05\), Equation 22.13 gives \(\alpha = 8(\ln 1000 + \ln 40) = 84.77\), since \(2/\beta = 40\). So with probability at least 0.95, no query below \(500 - 84.77 = 415.23\) fires (a \(\top\) needs \(f_k \ge T - \alpha\)) and no query above \(500 + 84.77 = 584.77\) is skipped (a \(\bot\) needs \(f_i < T + \alpha\)). In the script’s stream, every query has count 400 except query 700, which has 600. The counts of 400 are below 415.23 and cannot fire, and the count of 600 is above 584.77 and cannot be skipped, so the guarantee says the output is query 700 with probability at least 0.95; in 10,000 simulated runs it was query 700 every time.
The union bound behind \(\alpha\) is nearly tight. The margin that the noises actually needed is \(2\max(|\rho|, \max_i|\nu_i|)\), the smallest \(\alpha\) for which every noise is below \(\alpha/2\). Its 95% quantile over 10,000 simulated runs is 78.59, against 84.77. The alternative, answering all 1,000 queries with the Laplace mechanism at \(\varepsilon/1000\) each, adds noise of scale 1,000 to counts of a few hundred.


22.7.6 Check yourself

AboveThreshold answers 999 queries with \(\bot\) and halts at the 1000th. How much of its budget did the 999 \(\bot\) answers use? (All of them together used \(\varepsilon_1\), through the threshold noise; the \(\top\) used \(\varepsilon_2\). With 9 or 999,999 \(\bot\) answers the cost would be the same.)
Why does the accuracy bound depend on \(k\), while the privacy does not? (Accuracy needs every query noise to be small at once, which costs a union bound over \(k\) queries. Privacy needs only the maximum of the noisy answers to move by at most \(\Delta\), which holds for any \(k\).)

text:
22.8 When the sparse vector technique goes wrong

22.8.1 Context
The sparse vector technique is easy to state and easy to break. Lyu, Su & Li (2017) surveyed published variants and found that several were not differentially private at all, although each looked like a harmless optimization of AboveThreshold. Each bug removes one ingredient that a step of the proof above relies on. Seeing which step fails is the fastest way to review an implementation.


22.8.2 Statement
Table 22.6 lists the variants analysed by Lyu, Su & Li (2017) and what each changes.



Table 22.6: Variants of the sparse vector technique and their actual privacy, from Lyu, Su & Li (2017).










Variant (as numbered by Lyu, Su & Li)
What it changes
Privacy shown by Lyu, Su & Li




Algorithm 1 (theirs); Algorithm 2 (Dwork & Roth)
Correct, with \(c\) answers above
\(\varepsilon\)


Algorithm 3 (Roth’s 2011 lecture notes)
Outputs the noisy value \(f_i + \nu_i\) for each \(\top\)
\(\infty\)


Algorithm 4 (Lee & Clifton 2014)
Query noise does not grow with \(c\)
\(\frac{1 + 6c}{4}\varepsilon\)


Algorithm 5 (Stoddard et al. 2014)
No noise on the queries
\(\infty\)


Algorithm 6 (Chen et al. 2015)
Never halts
\(\infty\)






This section proves the last row for the no-halt variant of AboveThreshold: the same noise (\(\rho \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2\Delta/\varepsilon)\), \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(4\Delta/\varepsilon)\)), but every query is answered and the run never stops. To show a mechanism is not private, it is enough to find one pair of neighbours and one output whose probability ratio is too large. The pair below is built so that every answer of the output \(\bot^m\top^m\) (\(m\) answers “below”, then \(m\) answers “above”) is a little more likely under \(D\): on \(D\) the first \(m\) queries are low, which makes their \(\bot\) easier, and the last \(m\) are high, which makes their \(\top\) easier. Each of the \(2m\) answers contributes a small factor, and without a halt nothing stops the factors from multiplying. Take \(\Delta = 1\), \(2m\) queries, and neighbours with \[f(D) = (\underbrace{0, \dots, 0}_m, \underbrace{1, \dots, 1}_m), \qquad f(D') = (\underbrace{1, \dots, 1}_m, \underbrace{0, \dots, 0}_m). \tag{22.15}\] Each query changes by 1 between the two, so each has sensitivity 1. For the output \(\bot^m\top^m\), the privacy loss grows at least linearly in \(m\): \[\ln\frac{\Pr[\bot^m\top^m \mid D]}{\Pr[\bot^m\top^m \mid D']} \ge \frac{m\varepsilon}{4}. \tag{22.16}\] The privacy loss grows without bound in \(m\), so the variant is not \(\varepsilon'\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon'\).


22.8.3 Derivation
The answers are not independent, because they all compare against the same noisy threshold. But once the threshold is fixed they are, since each then depends only on its own fresh noise. So the proof fixes the threshold, multiplies the per-query probabilities, shows that the ratio is at least \(e^{1/b}\) per pair of queries for every threshold, and averages over the threshold at the end. Let \(b = 4/\varepsilon\), the query-noise scale with \(\Delta = 1\), and let \(F\) and \(S = 1 - F\) be the CDF and the survival function of \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\): \(F(x) = \Pr[\nu \le x]\) and \(S(x) = \Pr[\nu > x]\).

Fix the threshold. Condition on \(T + \rho = t\). The query noises are independent, so the answers are independent. A query with value \(f\) says \(\bot\) when \(f + \nu < t\), that is \(\nu < t - f\), with probability \(F(t - f)\), and \(\top\) with probability \(S(t - f)\).
The two conditional probabilities. Under \(D\) the output needs \(m\) queries of value 0 to say \(\bot\) and \(m\) of value 1 to say \(\top\); under \(D'\) it needs \(m\) of value 1 to say \(\bot\) and \(m\) of value 0 to say \(\top\). Multiplying, \[a_D(t) = F(t)^m\,S(t - 1)^m, \qquad a_{D'}(t) = F(t - 1)^m\,S(t)^m. \tag{22.17}\]
Their ratio is a power. \(a_D(t)/a_{D'}(t) = h(t)^m\) with \(h(t) = \frac{F(t)}{F(t - 1)}\cdot\frac{S(t - 1)}{S(t)}\). Both factors are at least 1, because \(F\) increases and \(S\) decreases: a query of value 0 is more likely to say \(\bot\) than one of value 1, and a query of value 1 is more likely to say \(\top\).
\(h(t) \ge e^{1/b}\) for every \(t\). The Laplace CDF is \(F(x) = \frac12e^{x/b}\) for \(x \le 0\) and the survival function is \(S(x) = \frac12e^{-x/b}\) for \(x \ge 0\); on each of those half-lines, moving \(x\) by 1 changes the value by exactly the factor \(e^{1/b}\). There are three cases, according to where \(t\) sits. If \(t \le 0\), both \(t\) and \(t - 1\) are on the half-line where \(F\) is exponential, so \(F(t)/F(t - 1) = e^{1/b}\), and the second factor is at least 1. If \(t \ge 1\), both \(t - 1\) and \(t\) are on the half-line where \(S\) is exponential, so \(S(t - 1)/S(t) = e^{1/b}\), and the first factor is at least 1. If \(0 < t < 1\), the two points straddle 0, and each factor gets part of the shift: \(F(t) \ge \frac12\) and \(F(t - 1) = \frac12e^{(t - 1)/b}\), so the first factor is at least \(e^{(1 - t)/b}\); likewise \(S(t - 1) \ge \frac12\) and \(S(t) = \frac12e^{-t/b}\), so the second is at least \(e^{t/b}\). The product is at least \(e^{(1 - t)/b + t/b} = e^{1/b}\).
Average over the threshold. The threshold noise has the same distribution under \(D\) and \(D'\), so \(\Pr[\bot^m\top^m \mid D] = \mathbb E[a_D(T + \rho)] \ge e^{m/b}\,\mathbb E[a_{D'}(T + \rho)] = e^{m\varepsilon/4}\Pr[\bot^m\top^m \mid D']\), using \(h^m \ge e^{m/b}\) at every threshold and \(m/b = m\varepsilon/4\).

Why AboveThreshold’s proof does not apply. Every \(\top\) in the second half is a new comparison with the same threshold. Step 3 of the AboveThreshold proof can shift \(\rho\) once to fix all the \(\bot\) answers, but each \(\top\) needs its own noise shifted by up to \(2\Delta\), at a cost of \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\) each with this noise scale. The halt is what limits the number of \(\top\) answers to one.
No query noise (Algorithm 5). Without \(\nu_i\) even the halting version fails, with two queries: \(f(D) = (0, 1)\) and \(f(D') = (1, 0)\). Without query noise, a query with value \(f\) says \(\top\) exactly when \(f \ge T + \rho\), a deterministic comparison with the noisy threshold. The output \(\bot\top\) needs \(0 < T + \rho \le 1\) on \(D\), which has positive probability, and \(1 < T + \rho \le 0\) on \(D'\), which is impossible. A probability ratio of \(\infty\) cannot be bounded by any \(e^{\varepsilon}\). Exercise 5 computes the first probability.


22.8.4 Interpretation
Each ingredient of AboveThreshold protects one step of its proof. The fresh noise \(\nu_k\) pays for the \(\top\) (step 5 of the AboveThreshold proof): remove it and the \(\top\) reveals a deterministic comparison, as in Algorithm 5. The halt limits the \(\top\)s to one: remove it and the cost per \(\top\) accumulates, as in the no-halt variant. Publishing \(f_k + \nu_k\) releases the very noise that the proof integrates over, as in Algorithm 3.
The bug is in the accounting, not in the noise. The no-halt variant adds exactly as much noise per query as AboveThreshold. A reviewer who checks only noise scales will not find it.
Empirical audits catch it, and you do not need the exact probabilities to run one. If a mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, then every event, including “the test says \(D\)”, is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times as likely under \(D\) as under \(D'\). So any test whose probability of firing under \(D\) is more than \(e^\varepsilon\) times its probability under \(D'\) proves the mechanism is not \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and the log of that ratio is a lower bound on the true \(\varepsilon\). This is the hypothesis-testing form of DP in The definition of differential privacy. A simple test, “are there more \(\top\) answers in the second half than in the first?”, already exceeds what \(\varepsilon = 1\) allows once \(m\) is a few dozen (Figure 22.6, right).






Figure 22.6: Left: privacy loss on the neighbouring pair \(f(D) = (0^m, 1^m)\), \(f(D') = (1^m, 0^m)\) with \(\varepsilon = 1\), computed exactly by integrating over the threshold noise. For the no-halt variant, the loss of the output \(\bot^m\top^m\) grows linearly in \(m\), above the lower bound \(m\varepsilon/4\). For AboveThreshold, the largest loss over all outputs levels off at \(\varepsilon\). Right: the no-halt variant under a simple test, the probability that the second half has more \(\top\) answers than the first. Once the probability under \(D\) exceeds \(e^\varepsilon\) times the probability under \(D'\) (dotted), no \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism could produce it.





22.8.5 Example: the loss, computed and simulated
Table 22.7 gives the script’s exact values for \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(T = 0\). For AboveThreshold the table takes the largest privacy loss over all its possible outputs on this pair; for the no-halt variant it takes the loss of the one output \(\bot^m\top^m\).

At \(m = 1\) the two mechanisms coincide, because \(\bot\top\) is a complete AboveThreshold output: AboveThreshold halts after the \(\top\) anyway. From then on the no-halt loss grows by about \(18.1246/40 = 0.45\) nats (units of natural logarithm) for each pair of queries added, while AboveThreshold never exceeds \(\varepsilon\). The lower bound is loose by a factor of a little under 2 (18.1246 against 10.00 at \(m = 40\)), because step 4 of the derivation used a lower bound on \(h(t)\) that holds at every threshold, and at every threshold \(h\) is in fact larger.
The integrals are checked by simulation at \(m = 2\): the exact probability of \(\bot\bot\top\top\) under \(D\) is 0.0669, and 400,000 runs give 0.0671. From \(m = 40\) on, the log-ratio is above 1, so this test alone proves that the variant is not 1-DP.


22.8.6 Check yourself

A colleague’s implementation of AboveThreshold reuses a single noise draw \(\nu\) for all queries to “save randomness”. Which step of the proof fails? (Step 1: fixing \(\nu_1, \dots, \nu_{k-1}\) would also fix \(\nu_k\), so the \(\top\) could not be paid for by shifting its own noise. With one shared \(\nu\), every answer compares \(f_i\) with the same random level \(T + \rho - \nu\), which is Algorithm 5’s bug.)
Is releasing the index of the first \(\top\) different from releasing the whole sequence \(\bot^{k-1}\top\)? (No. Each determines the other. The bug in the no-halt variant is answering after the \(\top\), not the output format.)

Four things stand out. First, the privacy proofs are right, and some are tight: on every neighbouring pair the script tries, the largest privacy loss stays below \(\varepsilon\), and AboveThreshold reaches it exactly. Second, the utility bounds are right but often loose. The exponential mechanism’s tail bound is tight only when all runners-up are tied; for spread-out scores it overestimates the probability of a large gap by orders of magnitude, because it treats every bad candidate as if it were barely bad. Third, Gumbel noise is the exponential mechanism, and Laplace noise is a close relative; neither of the two private argmaxes dominates the other. Fourth, one missing line breaks the sparse vector technique. Without the halt, the privacy loss grows linearly in the number of queries, and a two-line test detects it.

Proof pattern. Fix every noise except one (Fact 2). The output happens when that noise clears a bar. The bar is built from a maximum, which moves by at most \(\Delta\) however many terms it has (Fact 4). Shifting a Laplace variable by \(s\) costs \(e^{s/b}\) (Fact 3).
Rules of thumb

Release positions, not values. Every released noisy value needs its own budget.
The number of candidates costs \(\ln k\) in accuracy and nothing in privacy.
Use \(2\Delta\) unless you have checked that the scores are monotone under your neighbouring relation; counts are monotone under add/remove, a histogram under replace is not.
To sample the exponential mechanism, add Gumbel noise and take the argmax.
An implementation of the sparse vector technique must draw fresh noise for every query, keep one threshold noise per run, halt after the allowed number of \(\top\) answers, and never publish the noisy values it compared.

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.1 Why this matters
The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms answer a numeric query \(f\) by adding random noise to the true answer, and they set the size of that noise by the global sensitivity: the most that changing one record can move \(f\), looking at every pair of neighbouring datasets that could exist, not just at yours. In symbols, \(\Delta f = \max_{D \simeq D'}|f(D) - f(D')|\), where \(D \simeq D'\) means the two datasets are neighbours. For counts and bounded sums this is the right scale: one person changes a count by at most 1, whatever the data. For many other statistics it is hopeless, for three different reasons.
The first is that the worst case can be absurd. The median of ages in \([0, 100]\) has global sensitivity 100. To see it, take a dataset in which half the people are 0 and half are 100, with one more person at 0 so that the median is 0. Replacing that one person by a 100-year-old moves the median from one end to the other. So the Laplace mechanism must add noise of scale \(100/\varepsilon\), which swamps any real answer, even though no realistic dataset of ages looks like this. The second is that the worst case can be infinite. The mean of unbounded data (incomes, session lengths, gradient norms) can be moved arbitrarily far by one record, because that record can be arbitrarily large, so no amount of Laplace noise makes it private. The third is that the worst case can be unknown. For a statistic you can only compute, such as an estimator fitted by an algorithm, nobody knows how to bound how far one record moves it.
Yet on the dataset you actually hold, the median of 1,001 ages typically moves by a tenth of a year when one person changes, because with that many people the ages near the middle are packed tightly together. That is the local sensitivity, and it is hundreds of times smaller than the global one. This chapter asks: can you add noise on the scale of the data you have, rather than the worst dataset there could be, and still satisfy differential privacy (DP)?
Recall what DP asks for. A randomized mechanism \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP if, for every pair of neighbouring datasets \(D \simeq D'\) and every set \(S\) of outputs, \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta\): one record can change the probability of any outcome by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), up to a small slack \(\delta\). With \(\delta = 0\) this is pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The answer to the question is yes, with one idea that organizes the whole chapter:
If you calibrate noise to the local sensitivity of your dataset, the size of the noise reveals something about the dataset: an observer who sees a release with very wide noise learns that the data were of the kind that has a large local sensitivity. That is enough to break the guarantee. Each technique of this chapter repairs this in a different way:
Table 23.1 lists where each result is used.
Throughout, datasets have a fixed size \(n\) and \(D \simeq D'\) means that \(D'\) is obtained from \(D\) by replacing one record (the bounded relation of The definition of differential privacy). The Hamming distance \(d(D, D')\) counts the records in which two datasets differ, so neighbours are datasets at distance 1, and \(d(D, D'') = k\) means you can walk from \(D\) to \(D''\) by changing one record at a time in \(k\) steps. Every proof below compares the output densities \(p_{M(D)}\) and \(p_{M(D')}\) of a mechanism on two neighbours, point by point. The natural quantity for that is the log of their ratio at an output \(y\), the privacy loss: it says how much more likely \(y\) is under \(D\) than under \(D'\), and pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP holds when it never exceeds \(\varepsilon\). In symbols, \(L_{D,D'}(y) = \ln\frac{p_{M(D)}(y)}{p_{M(D')}(y)}\).

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
The noise scale is itself a function of the data, so it must be private too.



Smooth sensitivity replaces the local sensitivity by an upper bound that changes slowly between neighbours, so that the noise scale leaks little.
Propose-test-release proposes a noise scale, and privately tests whether the dataset is far from any dataset where that scale would be too small.
Subsample-and-aggregate makes the sensitivity small by construction: run the statistic on disjoint blocks and privately combine the block answers, each of which one record can affect only once.
Clipping forces bounded sensitivity on unbounded data, at the price of a bias that you trade against the noise.

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
section: 23.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
23.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

23.2.1 Fact 1 — The Laplace mechanism with global sensitivity
If one record never moves \(f\) by more than \(\Delta\), then adding Laplace noise of scale \(\Delta/\varepsilon\) is enough. Formally, if \(|f(D) - f(D')| \le \Delta\) for all \(D \simeq D'\), then \(f(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(\Delta/\varepsilon)\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. This is the Laplace mechanism, and the reason is short. The Laplace density with centre \(\mu\) and scale \(b\) is \(\frac1{2b}e^{-|y - \mu|/b}\), so with \(b = \Delta/\varepsilon\) the normalizing constants cancel in the ratio of the two densities, and the privacy loss is \(\big(|y - f(D')| - |y - f(D)|\big)\varepsilon/\Delta\). The triangle inequality says \(|y - f(D')| \le |y - f(D)| + |f(D) - f(D')|\), so the bracket is at most \(|f(D) - f(D')| \le \Delta\), and the loss is at most \(\varepsilon\) at every \(y\). A density that is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times another at every point has at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times its probability on every set (integrate over the set), which is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Every technique in this chapter ends by applying this fact, or a cousin of it, to something whose sensitivity is bounded.


23.2.2 Fact 2 — A tail bound on the privacy loss gives \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)
Some mechanisms in this chapter have a privacy loss that is at most \(\varepsilon\) for almost every output, but not for all of them. This fact says that is enough for \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, with \(\delta\) the probability of the rare outputs where the loss is too large. For every set \(S\) of outputs, \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon \Pr[M(D') \in S] + \Pr_{y \sim M(D)}\big[L_{D,D'}(y) > \varepsilon\big]. \tag{23.1}\]
The proof splits \(S\) into the outputs where the loss is small and those where it is large: \(S_1 = S \cap \{L \le \varepsilon\}\) and \(S_2 = S \cap \{L > \varepsilon\}\). On \(S_1\) the loss is at most \(\varepsilon\), which says exactly that the densities satisfy \(p_{M(D)} \le e^\varepsilon p_{M(D')}\) there, so integrating over \(S_1\) gives \(\Pr[M(D) \in S_1] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S_1] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S]\). On \(S_2\) you give up comparing and just bound the probability: \(\Pr[M(D) \in S_2]\) is at most the probability that the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\) at all, \(\Pr_{M(D)}[L > \varepsilon]\). Adding the two pieces gives Equation 23.1.
So if the privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\) only with probability \(\delta\), the mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. This “bad event” argument is behind every \(\delta\) in this chapter.


23.2.3 Fact 3 — Distances to a set have sensitivity 1
A question of the form “how many records would have to change before something bad happens?” has an answer that one record can change by at most 1. Formally, for any set \(\mathcal B\) of datasets (the “bad” ones), let \(\operatorname{dist}(D, \mathcal B) = \min_{D'' \in \mathcal B} d(D, D'')\) be the number of changes needed to reach the nearest of them. Then \(|\operatorname{dist}(D, \mathcal B) - \operatorname{dist}(D', \mathcal B)| \le 1\) for \(D \simeq D'\).
The reason is that a path from \(D'\) to a bad dataset can always go through \(D\) first, at the cost of one extra step. In terms of the Hamming distance, which satisfies the triangle inequality, \(d(D', D'') \le d(D', D) + d(D, D'') = 1 + d(D, D'')\) for every \(D''\). Minimizing both sides over \(D'' \in \mathcal B\) gives \(\operatorname{dist}(D', \mathcal B) \le 1 + \operatorname{dist}(D, \mathcal B)\), and the same argument with \(D\) and \(D'\) exchanged gives the other direction. So such a count can be released with \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) noise by Fact 1. Propose-test-release is built on it.


23.2.4 Fact 4 — Changing \(k\) records moves each order statistic by at most \(k\) places
If you change \(k\) records, the \(j\)-th smallest value can move, but only as far as the \((j-k)\)-th or \((j+k)\)-th smallest value of the original data. To state it, sort the values of \(D\) as \(x_1 \le \dots \le x_n\) (the order statistics), all in \([0, \Lambda]\). Ranks \(j - k\) or \(j + k\) can fall outside \(1, \dots, n\), so pad with \(x_i = 0\) for \(i \le 0\) and \(x_i = \Lambda\) for \(i > n\): “below the smallest” means “possibly as low as 0”, and “above the largest” means “possibly as high as \(\Lambda\)”. If \(D''\) differs from \(D\) in at most \(k\) records and has sorted values \(y_1 \le \dots \le y_n\), then \[x_{j-k} \le y_j \le x_{j+k} \quad\text{for every } j. \tag{23.2}\]
For the upper bound, count the values below \(x_{j+k}\). At least \(j + k\) values of \(D\) are \(\le x_{j+k}\) (when \(j + k > n\) the padding sets \(x_{j+k} = \Lambda\), which bounds every value, so the claim is trivially true). Changing \(k\) records removes at most \(k\) of them, so at least \(j\) values of \(D''\) are still \(\le x_{j+k}\), and that says the \(j\)-th smallest value of \(D''\) is at most \(x_{j+k}\): \(y_j \le x_{j+k}\). The lower bound is the same argument counting values above \(x_{j-k}\). This fact pins down how far the median of a modified dataset can travel.

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
section: 23.3 Local sensitivity, and why it leaks
text:
23.3 Local sensitivity, and why it leaks

23.3.1 Context
Global sensitivity takes a maximum over all pairs of neighbours, including pathological ones that look nothing like your data. The natural fix is to take the maximum only over the neighbours of the dataset you hold. That gives a much smaller number. But adding noise proportional to it is not private, and seeing exactly why is the key to everything else in this chapter.


23.3.2 Statement
The local sensitivity of \(f\) at \(D\) is the most that one record can move \(f\) starting from \(D\) itself, rather than from the worst dataset: \[\mathrm{LS}_f(D) = \max_{D':\ d(D, D') = 1}|f(D) - f(D')|, \tag{23.3}\] and the global sensitivity is its worst case over all datasets, \(\Delta f = \max_D \mathrm{LS}_f(D)\).
For the median, one change can push the median at most one place up or down the sorted list, so its local sensitivity is the larger of the two gaps next to it. Take \(n\) values in \([0, \Lambda]\), with \(n\) odd and \(m = (n+1)/2\) the rank of the median, so that the median is \(x_m\). Then \[\mathrm{LS}_{\mathrm{med}}(D) = \max\big(x_m - x_{m-1},\ x_{m+1} - x_m\big), \qquad \Delta\,\mathrm{med} = \Lambda. \tag{23.4}\]


23.3.3 Derivation

The median of a neighbour lies between \(x_{m-1}\) and \(x_{m+1}\). This is Fact 4 with \(k = 1\) change and rank \(j = m\). So the median moves from \(x_m\) by at most the larger of the gaps to its two sorted neighbours: \(|\mathrm{med}(D') - x_m| \le \max(x_m - x_{m-1}, x_{m+1} - x_m)\).
Both ends are reached. To show the bound is attained, move the median value itself to an extreme. Replace \(x_m\) by \(\Lambda\): the sorted values become \(x_1, \dots, x_{m-1}, x_{m+1}, \dots, x_n, \Lambda\), and the \(m\)-th of them is \(x_{m+1}\). Replace \(x_m\) by 0 instead, and everything above it keeps its rank while the new 0 goes first, so the \(m\)-th value becomes \(x_{m-1}\). So the bound of step 1 is attained, which is Equation 23.4.
The global sensitivity is \(\Lambda\). Take \(m\) values equal to 0 and \(m - 1\) equal to \(\Lambda\). Then \(x_m = 0\) and \(x_{m+1} = \Lambda\), so Equation 23.4 gives \(\Lambda\), and no dataset can do worse because every value lies in \([0, \Lambda]\), so no gap exceeds \(\Lambda\).



23.3.4 Interpretation: the noise scale is a statistic
Consider the mechanism that adds Laplace noise scaled to the local sensitivity of the data it is given, \(M_{\mathrm{LS}}(D) = f(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(\mathrm{LS}_f(D)/\varepsilon)\). Its noise scale is the function \(\mathrm{LS}_f\) of the data, and \(\mathrm{LS}_f\) itself can have large sensitivity: one record can change the local sensitivity of the median from 0 to \(\Lambda\). The mechanism then releases \(f(D)\) with no noise on one dataset and with enormous noise on its neighbour, and the noise level alone tells the two apart, even when \(f\) is the same on both.
The degenerate case makes this stark (Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith 2007, Example 1). With \(n = 5\) and \(\Lambda = 100\), the dataset \(D = (0, 0, 0, 0, 100)\) has median 0, and both gaps next to the median are 0, so \(\mathrm{LS} = 0\) and \(M_{\mathrm{LS}}(D) = 0\) exactly. Its neighbour \(D' = (0, 0, 0, 100, 100)\) also has median 0, but the gap above the median is now 100, so \(\mathrm{LS} = 100\) and \(M_{\mathrm{LS}}(D')\) has a continuous distribution, which equals 0 with probability 0. The event “the output is exactly 0” has probability 1 under \(D\) and 0 under \(D'\). No finite \(\varepsilon\) and no \(\delta < 1\) cover that, because the DP inequality would need \(1 \le e^\varepsilon \cdot 0 + \delta\).


23.3.5 Example: two neighbours with the same median
The leak does not need a degenerate dataset. Take \(\Lambda = 100\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), and the two datasets of Table 23.2, which differ in one record and have the same median, but whose local sensitivities differ by a factor of six.



Table 23.2: Two neighbouring datasets with the same median and very different local sensitivities.

The two releases are \(30 + \mathrm{Lap}(10)\) and \(30 + \mathrm{Lap}(60)\). They have the same centre, so the privacy loss depends only on the distance \(u = |y - 30|\) from it. Far from the centre the wide density is much larger than the narrow one, because the narrow one decays six times faster, so the loss should grow with \(u\). Writing the two Laplace densities \(\frac1{2b}e^{-u/b}\) with \(b = 60\) and \(b = 10\) and taking the log of their ratio: \[L_{D',D}(y) = \ln\frac{e^{-u/60}/120}{e^{-u/10}/20} = -\ln 6 + u\Big(\frac1{10} - \frac1{60}\Big) = -1.792 + \frac{u}{12}. \tag{23.5}\] The constant is \(\ln(20/120) = -\ln 6 = -1.792\), and the slope is \(\frac{6 - 1}{60} = \frac1{12}\). The loss grows without bound in \(u\) (Figure 23.1), so no pure \(\varepsilon\) can hold. It exceeds \(\varepsilon = 1\) once \(-\ln 6 + u/12 > 1\), that is once \(u > 12(1 + \ln 6) = 33.50\). A Laplace variable of scale \(b\) lands more than \(u\) from its centre with probability \(e^{-u/b}\), so this happens with probability \(e^{-33.5/60} = 0.572\) under \(D'\) and \(e^{-33.5/10} = 0.0351\) under \(D\).
How large must \(\delta\) be for this pair? The smallest \(\delta\) for which the pair satisfies the \((1, \delta)\) inequality is the hockey-stick divergence of Divergences: the largest gap \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] - e^{1}\Pr[M(D) \in S]\) over all sets \(S\), which is attained by taking \(S\) to be exactly the outputs where the loss exceeds 1. The script computes it as \(0.477\) in the direction \(D'\) against \(D\) (and \(0.215\) in the other direction). An adversary who sees a value more than 34 away from 30 can bet on \(D'\) and be right far more often than any reasonable \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) allows. This is the distinguishing game of Threat models and privacy games, in which an adversary who knows both candidate datasets sees one release and guesses which dataset produced it. Here it wins by looking at the spread of the noise, not its centre.






Figure 23.1: Left: the densities of the median of \(D\) and of \(D'\) released with Laplace noise scaled to their own local sensitivities, 10 and 60. Right: the privacy loss \(L_{D',D}(y)\) grows linearly in \(|y - 30|\) and crosses \(\varepsilon = 1\) at distance 33.5.





23.3.6 Check yourself

Is \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D) \le \Delta f\) always, and when are they equal? (Always, since the global sensitivity is the maximum of the local one over all datasets. They are equal at the datasets where that maximum is attained, such as half zeros and half \(\Lambda\) for the median.)
Why doesn’t the Laplace proof of Fact 1 go through for \(M_{\mathrm{LS}}\)? (It needs the same scale \(\Delta\) on both sides. With scales \(b \ne b'\) the loss contains \(|y - f(D')|/b' - |y - f(D)|/b\), whose slopes no longer cancel, so it is unbounded in \(y\).)

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.4 Smooth sensitivity

23.4.1 Context
The leak came from the noise scale jumping between neighbours. So use a noise scale that cannot jump: an upper bound on the local sensitivity whose logarithm changes by at most \(\beta\) between neighbours, so that the scale itself changes by at most a factor \(e^\beta\). A change by a bounded factor is the right kind of control, because a privacy loss is a log-ratio: rescaling the noise by \(e^\beta\) shifts log-densities by about \(\beta\). Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith (2007) call such a bound smooth, find the smallest one, and show which noise distributions can be scaled by it. Two questions need answers: how to compute the bound, and which noise makes the result private.


23.4.2 Statement
A function \(S\) is a \(\beta\)-smooth upper bound on \(\mathrm{LS}_f\) if it is never below the local sensitivity and changes by at most a factor \(e^\beta\) between neighbours: \[S(D) \ge \mathrm{LS}_f(D) \quad\text{and}\quad S(D) \le e^\beta S(D') \quad\text{for all } D \simeq D'. \tag{23.6}\] The smallest such bound has an explicit form. If some dataset \(D''\) at distance \(k\) has a large local sensitivity, a smooth bound cannot be small at \(D\), because it can only decrease by a factor \(e^{-\beta}\) per step on the way from \(D''\) to \(D\). So the bound at \(D\) must be at least \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D'')e^{-\beta k}\) for every \(D''\), and the \(\beta\)-smooth sensitivity takes exactly the largest of these: \[S^*_{f,\beta}(D) = \max_{D''}\ \mathrm{LS}_f(D'')\,e^{-\beta\,d(D, D'')} \tag{23.7}\] It is a \(\beta\)-smooth upper bound, and it is the smallest one: \(S^*_{f,\beta}(D) \le S(D)\) for every \(\beta\)-smooth upper bound \(S\).
The mechanism adds noise from a fixed shape, stretched by \(S(D)\): \[M(D) = f(D) + \frac{S(D)}{\alpha}\,Z, \tag{23.8}\] where \(Z\) is drawn from a fixed density \(h\) and \(\alpha > 0\) is a constant that sets how many noise scales one record’s shift is worth. Which \(h\) work is the content of the next two results. They differ in how heavy the tail of \(h\) is, and the derivation will show why that matters: the noise scale differs between neighbours, and a light-tailed density compared with a stretched copy of itself has a log-ratio that grows without bound in the tail, as in the example of Table 23.2.
Pure DP with Cauchy-like noise. Let \(h_\gamma(z) \propto 1/(1 + |z|^\gamma)\) with \(\gamma > 1\), a density whose tails decay like the power \(|z|^{-\gamma}\) (\(\gamma = 2\) is the standard Cauchy). If \(S\) is a \(\beta\)-smooth upper bound and the sources of privacy loss together fit within the budget (the shift of the centre is worth \(\gamma\alpha\), and the change of scale is worth \(\beta\) through the density’s normalizing factor plus \(\gamma\beta\) through the stretch of its shape), \[\gamma\alpha + (\gamma + 1)\beta \le \varepsilon, \tag{23.9}\] then Equation 23.8 is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith (2007, Lemma 2.7) use \(\alpha = \beta = \varepsilon/(2(\gamma + 1))\), which satisfies Equation 23.9 with room to spare. For the Cauchy, \(\gamma = 2\) gives \(\alpha = \beta = \varepsilon/6\), the often-quoted release \(f(D) + \frac{6}{\varepsilon}S^*_{f,\varepsilon/6}(D)\cdot Z\).
Approximate DP with Laplace noise. Let \(Z \sim \mathrm{Lap}(1)\), the Laplace density \(\frac12e^{-|z|}\). Its tail is too light for pure DP, so the condition gains a term that charges for the rare draws of size above \(\ln(1/\delta)\). If \(S\) is a \(\beta\)-smooth upper bound and \[\beta + e^\beta\alpha + (e^\beta - 1)\ln(1/\delta) \le \varepsilon, \tag{23.10}\] then Equation 23.8 is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith (2007, Lemma 2.9) prove a version with a slightly different split of the budget, \(\alpha = \varepsilon/2\) and \(\beta = \varepsilon/(2\ln(2/\delta))\). Because the third term is roughly \(\beta\ln(1/\delta)\) for small \(\beta\), here \(\beta\) must shrink like \(1/\ln(1/\delta)\), and no \(\beta > 0\) gives pure DP with Laplace noise.


23.4.3 Derivation
\(S^*\) is a smooth upper bound, and the smallest one.

Upper bound. One of the datasets in the maximum of Equation 23.7 is \(D'' = D\) itself, at distance 0, which contributes \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D)e^0 = \mathrm{LS}_f(D)\). A maximum is at least each of its terms, so \(S^*_{f,\beta}(D) \ge \mathrm{LS}_f(D)\).
Smooth. Moving from \(D\) to a neighbour \(D'\) makes every dataset at most one step further away: \(d(D', D'') \le d(D, D'') + 1\), by the triangle inequality of Fact 3. So each term \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D'')e^{-\beta d(D', D'')}\) of \(S^*(D')\) is at least \(e^{-\beta}\) times the term for the same \(D''\) in \(S^*(D)\). Taking the maximum over \(D''\) on both sides, \(S^*(D') \ge e^{-\beta}S^*(D)\). Nothing in this argument depended on which of the two neighbours was called \(D\), so running it with \(D\) and \(D'\) exchanged gives \(S^*(D) \ge e^{-\beta}S^*(D')\), the smoothness condition.
Smallest. This is the argument that motivated the definition. Let \(S\) be any \(\beta\)-smooth upper bound and \(D''\) any dataset at distance \(k\) from \(D\). Walk from \(D''\) to \(D\) through \(k\) neighbours; smoothness lets \(S\) drop by at most a factor \(e^{-\beta}\) per step, so \(S(D) \ge e^{-\beta k}S(D'')\), and \(S(D'') \ge \mathrm{LS}_f(D'')\) because \(S\) is an upper bound. So \(S(D) \ge e^{-\beta k}\mathrm{LS}_f(D'')\) for every \(D''\); maximize over \(D''\).

Pure DP for Cauchy-like noise. The plan is to write the privacy loss at an output \(y\) as a sum of three pieces, one for each way the two output distributions differ (their scales differ, their centres differ, and the noise draw that explains \(y\) is stretched), and to bound each piece by smoothness or by the upper-bound property.

Write out the privacy loss. Stretching \(Z\) by \(S(D)/\alpha\) divides its density by that factor, so the density of \(M(D)\) at \(y\) is \(\frac{\alpha}{S(D)}h\big(z\big)\), where \(z = \alpha\frac{y - f(D)}{S(D)}\) is the noise draw that would produce \(y\) from \(D\). Likewise that of \(M(D')\) is \(\frac{\alpha}{S(D')}h(z')\) with \(z' = \alpha\frac{y - f(D')}{S(D')}\). To compare the two draws, substitute \(y = f(D) + S(D)z/\alpha\) into \(z'\): \(z' = \frac{S(D)}{S(D')}\big(z + \alpha\frac{f(D) - f(D')}{S(D)}\big)\). That is, \(z'\) is \(z\) shifted and then stretched: \[z' = e^{\lambda}(z + \Delta), \qquad e^\lambda = \frac{S(D)}{S(D')},\quad \Delta = \alpha\,\frac{f(D) - f(D')}{S(D)}. \tag{23.11}\] (Here \(\Delta\) is this shift, not the global sensitivity.) The log of the ratio of the two densities splits into the ratio of the prefactors and the ratio of \(h\) at \(z\) and at \(z'\), and inserting \(h(z + \Delta)\) in the middle splits the second part into the shift and the stretch: \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \underbrace{\ln\frac{S(D')}{S(D)}}_{\text{scale}} + \underbrace{\ln\frac{h(z)}{h(z + \Delta)}}_{\text{sliding}} + \underbrace{\ln\frac{h(z + \Delta)}{h(e^\lambda(z + \Delta))}}_{\text{dilation}}. \tag{23.12}\]
Size of the shift and the stretch. Smoothness says \(S(D)/S(D')\) lies between \(e^{-\beta}\) and \(e^\beta\), so \(|\lambda| \le \beta\). And one record moves \(f\) by at most the local sensitivity, which is at most \(S(D)\): \(|f(D) - f(D')| \le \mathrm{LS}_f(D) \le S(D)\), so \(|\Delta| \le \alpha\). This is the only place where “\(S\) is an upper bound on the local sensitivity” enters.
Scale term: at most \(\beta\), by smoothness again.
Sliding term. The question is how fast \(-\ln h\) can change when its argument shifts by \(|\Delta|\). Write \(\varphi(u) = \ln(1 + u^\gamma)\) for \(u \ge 0\), so \(-\ln h_\gamma(z) = \varphi(|z|) + \text{const}\). Its slope is \(\varphi'(u) = \gamma u^{\gamma-1}/(1 + u^\gamma) \le \gamma\), because \(u^{\gamma-1} \le 1 + u^\gamma\) (if \(u \le 1\) the left side is at most 1; if \(u > 1\) it is below \(u^\gamma\)). The mean value theorem says a function whose slope is at most \(\gamma\) in size changes by at most \(\gamma\) times the change in its argument. The argument changes from \(|z|\) to \(|z + \Delta|\), and these differ by at most \(|\Delta|\) (the reverse triangle inequality). So \(|\varphi(|z + \Delta|) - \varphi(|z|)| \le \gamma\big||z + \Delta| - |z|\big| \le \gamma|\Delta| \le \gamma\alpha\).
Dilation term. Here the question is how much \(h\) changes when its argument is stretched by \(e^\lambda\). With \(w = |z + \Delta|\) and \(\lambda \ge 0\), \(\frac{h(w)}{h(e^\lambda w)} = \frac{1 + e^{\lambda\gamma}w^\gamma}{1 + w^\gamma} \le e^{\lambda\gamma}\), since \((1 + ca)/(1 + a) \le c\) for \(c \ge 1\) (multiply out: \(1 + ca \le c + ca\)). This bound holds for every \(w\), however far in the tail, and that is what the power-law tail buys. For \(\lambda < 0\) the stretch moves the argument towards 0, where \(h\) is larger, so the ratio is at most 1. Either way the term is at most \(\gamma|\lambda| \le \gamma\beta\).
Add up: \(L_{D,D'}(y) \le \beta + \gamma\alpha + \gamma\beta\) for every \(y\). That is \(\gamma\alpha + (\gamma + 1)\beta\), so under Equation 23.9 it is at most \(\varepsilon\), which is pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP. With \(\alpha = \beta = \varepsilon/6\) and \(\gamma = 2\) the bound is \(\gamma\alpha + (\gamma + 1)\beta = \frac{2}{6} + \frac{3}{6} = 0.8333\,\varepsilon\).

Approximate DP for Laplace noise. Steps 1–3 are unchanged. For \(h(z) = \frac12e^{-|z|}\) the log of a ratio of \(h\) values is just a difference of absolute values, so the sliding and dilation terms combine into one. Using \(|e^\lambda(z + \Delta)| \le e^\lambda(|z| + |\Delta|)\), then \(e^\lambda \le e^\beta\) and \(|\Delta| \le \alpha\) from step 2: \[\ln\frac{h(z)}{h(z')} = |e^\lambda(z + \Delta)| - |z| \le e^\lambda(|z| + |\Delta|) - |z| \le (e^\beta - 1)|z| + e^\beta\alpha. \tag{23.13}\] Adding the scale term, \(L_{D,D'}(y) \le \beta + e^\beta\alpha + (e^\beta - 1)|z|\), where \(z\) is the noise actually drawn, \(Z \sim \mathrm{Lap}(1)\). This is not bounded: the stretch makes the Laplace log-density change by an amount proportional to \(|z|\), so far in the tail the dilation term wins. But large draws are rare. A \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\) variable exceeds \(t\) in absolute value with probability \(e^{-t}\) (integrate the two tails of \(\frac12e^{-|z|}\); see Concentration inequalities), so \(\Pr[|Z| > \ln(1/\delta)] = \delta\). Outside that event of probability \(\delta\), \(|z| \le \ln(1/\delta)\) and the loss is at most the left side of Equation 23.10, hence at most \(\varepsilon\). Fact 2 turns that into \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.


23.4.4 Interpretation: why heavy tails, and what admissibility means
Pure DP forces polynomial tails. The dilation step needed \(h(w)/h(e^\lambda w)\) to be bounded for all \(w\), however large. Write \(h(w) \approx e^{-g(w)}\); the condition says \(g(e^\beta w) - g(w)\) stays below some constant \(c\). Applying it \(k\) times from \(w = 1\) gives \(g(e^{k\beta}) \le g(1) + kc\), so \(g\) can grow at most like \(\frac{c}{\beta}\ln w\), and \(h\) can decay at most like a power of \(w\): Cauchy-like. Laplace noise has \(g(w) = w\), for which \(g(e^\beta w) - g(w) = (e^\beta - 1)w\) grows without bound, and the Gaussian is worse. That is why both fail for pure DP and pay with \(\delta\).
The two conditions are what Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith call admissibility. They call \(h\) \((\alpha, \beta)\)-admissible when shifting it by at most \(\alpha\) (sliding) and rescaling it by at most a factor \(e^{\pm\beta}\) (dilation) each change probabilities by at most a factor \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\) plus \(\delta/2\). The derivation above bounds the two together, which gives slightly different constants.
The price of heavy tails shows up in the error. The Cauchy has no mean, so its error is reported through the median. For a standard Cauchy, \(\Pr[|Z| \le t] = \frac2\pi\arctan t\), which is \(\frac12\) at \(t = 1\) because \(\arctan 1 = \pi/4\). So \(|Z|\) has median 1, and the typical error is the noise scale \(S/\alpha\). But the tail is heavy: \(\Pr[|Z| > 10] = 1 - \frac2\pi\arctan 10 = 0.0635\), so about one release in 16 is off by more than ten times the typical error. With Laplace noise the same probability is \(e^{-10} \approx 4.5\times10^{-5}\).
Finally, \(\beta\) is a lever. A small \(\beta\) makes \(S^*\) larger, because the factor \(e^{-\beta k}\) discounts distant datasets less and so lets more of them raise the maximum. In exchange it costs less privacy per unit of noise. Laplace noise needs \(\beta \approx \varepsilon/(2\ln(1/\delta))\), much smaller than the Cauchy’s \(\varepsilon/6\), because in Equation 23.10 the change of scale is charged once for every unit of \(\ln(1/\delta)\).


23.4.5 Computing \(S^*\) for the median
Equation 23.7 is a maximum over all datasets, which is not something you can enumerate. The way out is to group the datasets by their distance \(k\) from \(D\): all datasets at distance \(k\) get the same discount \(e^{-k\beta}\), so within a group you only need the largest local sensitivity, \(A^{(k)}(D)\), and then the best discounted group: \[S^*_{\beta}(D) = \max_{k = 0, \dots, n} e^{-k\beta}A^{(k)}(D), \qquad A^{(k)}(D) = \max_{D'':\ d(D, D'') \le k}\mathrm{LS}(D''). \tag{23.14}\] (Using “\(\le k\)” instead of “\(= k\)” changes nothing: a dataset at distance \(j < k\) is counted again with the smaller weight \(e^{-k\beta}\), which never beats its own weight \(e^{-j\beta}\).)
For the median, \(A^{(k)}\) asks: by changing \(k\) records, how wide a gap can you open next to the median? A gap is opened by moving the values that lie inside an interval of the sorted data out of it, to 0 or to \(\Lambda\). With \(k\) changes you can empty out the \(k\) values between two order statistics \(k + 1\) ranks apart, and you can choose how many to move down and how many up so that the emptied interval ends up next to the median. So the answer is the widest such window that sits close enough to rank \(m\). With the padding of Fact 4, Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith (2007, Proposition 3.4) show \[A^{(k)}(D) = \max_{0 \le t \le k+1}\big(x_{m+t} - x_{m+t-k-1}\big). \tag{23.15}\] Each window runs from rank \(m + t - k - 1\) to rank \(m + t\), and \(t\) slides it across the median. Each \(A^{(k)}\) costs \(O(k)\) to evaluate, one subtraction per window, and \(k\) never needs to exceed \(n\): at \(k = n\) the window with \(t = m\) spans \(x_0 = 0\) to \(x_{n+1} = \Lambda\), so \(A^{(n)} = \Lambda\), the largest possible value, and larger \(k\) only lowers the weight. So the exact \(S^*_\beta\) takes \(O(n^2)\) time. (An \(O(n\log n)\) algorithm exists; the script uses the plain formula.)
Derivation of Equation 23.15. Steps 1–4 show that no dataset within distance \(k\) has a gap next to its median wider than the widest window, and step 5 shows that every window is achieved.

What the gap looks like. Let \(D''\) be within distance \(k\) of \(D\), with sorted values \(y_i\). By Equation 23.4 its local sensitivity is one of its two gaps next to the median. Take the upper one, \((y_m, y_{m+1})\). The lower one needs no separate argument: reflecting every value, \(x \mapsto \Lambda - x\), turns lower gaps into upper gaps and maps the set of windows in Equation 23.15 to itself.
The gap contains at most \(k\) original values. Assume the gap is positive (otherwise there is nothing to bound), so exactly \(m\) values of \(D''\) are \(\le y_m\). No value of \(D''\) lies strictly inside \((y_m, y_{m+1})\), so every value of \(D\) strictly inside it must have been one of the \(k\) changed records. Call the values of \(D\) inside the gap \(x_{a+1}, \dots, x_{a+j}\) with \(j \le k\). Then \(x_a \le y_m\) and \(x_{a+j+1} \ge y_{m+1}\), so the gap is at most \(x_{a+j+1} - x_a\), a window of the original data.
The gap sits near rank \(m\). Now pin down \(a\) by counting values of \(D''\) at or below \(y_m\), of which there are exactly \(m\). Each is either an unchanged value of \(D\), and those are among \(x_1, \dots, x_a\) (everything above \(x_a\) is inside the gap or beyond it), or one of at most \(k\) new values. So \(m \le a + k\), that is \(a \ge m - k\). In the other direction, at least \(a - (k - j)\) of \(x_1, \dots, x_a\) are unchanged (the \(j\) values inside the gap used up \(j\) of the \(k\) changes), and all of them are \(\le y_m\), so \(a - (k - j) \le m\), that is \(a \le m + k - j\).
Fit it in a window. Let \(i = \min(a, m)\), the lower end of the window to use. If \(a \le m\), the window \([x_a, x_{a+k+1}]\) has \(i = a \ge m - k\), so it is one of the windows of Equation 23.15 (\(t = a + k + 1 - m \in [0, k+1]\)), and it contains \([x_a, x_{a+j+1}]\) because \(j \le k\). If \(a > m\), the window \([x_m, x_{m+k+1}]\) (\(t = k + 1\)) starts below \(x_a\) and contains \([x_a, x_{a+j+1}]\) because \(a + j + 1 \le m + k + 1\) by step 3. Either way the gap is at most the right side of Equation 23.15.
Every window is reached. For a window \([x_\ell, x_u]\) with \(\ell = m + t - k - 1\) and \(u = m + t\), there are exactly \(u - \ell - 1 = k\) values strictly between its ends. Change them: move \(k + 1 - t\) of them to 0 and the rest to \(\Lambda\) (for \(t = 0\), move all \(k\) to 0). Each value moved to 0 now sits below \(x_\ell\) and raises its rank by one. So \(x_\ell\) has rank \(\ell + (k + 1 - t) = m\) and \(x_u\) rank \(m + 1\) for \(t \ge 1\) (for \(t = 0\), ranks \(m - 1\) and \(m\)). Either way the median sits at one end of an empty interval of length \(x_u - x_\ell\), which is then one of its two gaps.

A walkthrough. Take \(n = 5\) values on \([0, 10]\), \(D = (1, 3, 4, 6, 9)\), so \(m = 3\) and the median is 4, and pad with \(x_i = 0\) for \(i \le 0\) and \(x_i = 10\) for \(i \ge 6\). Table 23.3 evaluates Equation 23.15 window by window, with \(\beta = 0.5\), and checks it against brute force: the script enumerates all \(11^5 = 161{,}051\) datasets with values in \(\{0, \dots, 10\}\), computes the local sensitivity of each and its distance from \(D\), and takes the maximum for each \(k\).

But one change, moving the 6 up to 10, opens a gap of \(9 - 4 = 5\) next to the median, and even after the discount \(e^{-0.5} = 0.6065\) for one step, \(e^{-0.5}\times 5 = 3.03\) beats 2.
