23.4.6 Example: the median age
The script draws \(n = 1001\) ages from a normal distribution with mean 38 and standard deviation 14, clipped to \([0, 100]\), and releases the median (36.96) with \(\varepsilon = 1\). Each option is compared by its median absolute error. For noise \(bZ\) that is \(b\) times the median of \(|Z|\): 1 for the Cauchy, as shown above, and \(\ln 2\) for the Laplace, because \(\Pr[|Z| > t] = e^{-t}\) equals \(\frac12\) at \(t = \ln 2\).
With global sensitivity, Laplace noise has scale \(\Lambda/\varepsilon = 100\) and median absolute value \(100\ln 2 = 69.31\) years: useless. The local sensitivity is 0.1386 years, but releasing with it is not private, as Section 23.3 showed.
Smooth sensitivity with Cauchy noise uses \(\alpha = \beta = 1/6\). Then \(S^*_{1/6} = 0.1632\), attained at \(k = 7\): only slightly above the local sensitivity, because with this many people even seven changes cannot open a wide gap near the middle. The noise scale \(6S^*/\varepsilon = 6 \times 0.1632 = 0.979\) is also the median absolute error (simulation: 0.980).
Smooth sensitivity with Laplace noise uses \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) and \(\alpha = 1/2\). The largest \(\beta\) allowed by Equation 23.10 is then \(0.0322\) (close to the \(0.0345\) of Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith). The smaller \(\beta\) lets more distant datasets count, so \(S^*_{0.0322} = 0.5144\), attained at \(k = 21\). The noise scale is \(S^*/\alpha = 2S^*/\varepsilon = 1.029\) and the median absolute error \(1.029\ln 2 = 0.713\).
Both smooth releases are 70 to 100 times more accurate than the global one (\(69.31/0.979\) and \(69.31/0.713\)). Figure 23.3 shows the gain grows with \(n\): the smooth noise falls roughly like \(1/n\), the spacing of the data near the median, while the global noise stays put. For \(n \lesssim 20\) the smooth noise is worse than the global one, because with few points a handful of changes can open a gap of nearly the whole range, so \(S^*\) can be close to \(\Lambda\), and then the factor \(1/\alpha\) multiplies it.


23.4.7 Check yourself

Why does \(S^*_\beta(D) > 0\) even when \(\mathrm{LS}(D) = 0\)? (Some dataset at finite distance \(k\) has positive local sensitivity, and it contributes \(e^{-k\beta}\) times that. For the median, \(A^{(n)} = \Lambda\) gives \(S^* \ge e^{-n\beta}\Lambda > 0\), which also means the scale in Equation 23.8 is never zero.)
In the Cauchy derivation, where is “upper bound” used and where is “smooth” used? (Upper bound bounds the shift: \(|\Delta| \le \alpha\). Smoothness bounds the scale term and the stretch \(|\lambda| \le \beta\).)

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.5 Propose-test-release

23.5.1 Context
Smooth sensitivity needs a formula like Equation 23.15, and those are known for only a few functions. Dwork & Lei (2009) take a cruder route that needs much less. Guess a bound \(b\) on the local sensitivity, check privately that the data are not near any dataset where the guess fails, and only then release with noise of scale \(b/\varepsilon\). If the check fails, refuse to answer. The check is private because it is a “how many changes until something bad” count, which has sensitivity 1 by Fact 3.


23.5.2 Statement
Fix a proposed bound \(b > 0\), a privacy parameter \(\varepsilon > 0\) and a failure probability \(\delta \in (0, 1)\). The quantity to test is the number of records you must change before the local sensitivity can exceed \(b\), that is, how far \(D\) is from the nearest dataset where the proposal would be too small: \[\operatorname{dist}_b(D) = \min\big\{d(D, D''):\ \mathrm{LS}_f(D'') > b\big\}. \tag{23.16}\] Propose-test-release adds Laplace noise to this distance and compares it with a threshold \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), chosen so that the noise alone pushes a distance of 0 over it only with probability \(\delta/2\). It outputs one of two things:

\(\bot\) (“no answer”) if \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon) \le \ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\);
\(f(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(b/\varepsilon)\) otherwise.

It is \((2\varepsilon, \delta/2)\)-DP, so in particular \((2\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. For the median, \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D) = \min\{k : A^{(k)}(D) > b\}\), directly from Equation 23.15: \(A^{(k)}\) is the largest local sensitivity within \(k\) changes, so the first \(k\) where it exceeds \(b\) is the distance to the first dataset where \(b\) fails.


23.5.3 Derivation
The idea is to split neighbouring pairs into two cases. If the proposal \(b\) is right for this pair, the release is an ordinary Laplace mechanism. If it is wrong, both datasets sit right at an unstable point, the distance is 0, and the test almost always refuses.

The test is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. \(\operatorname{dist}_b\) is a distance to the set of datasets whose local sensitivity exceeds \(b\), so it has sensitivity 1 (Fact 3), and adding \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) is the Laplace mechanism (Fact 1). Whether the test passes is a post-processing of that noisy value: a function of it that does not look at the data again, which cannot increase the privacy loss.
Case 1: \(|f(D) - f(D')| \le b\). Then the release step is also \(\varepsilon\)-DP (Fact 1 with \(\Delta = b\)). The output is a function of two independent \(\varepsilon\)-DP outputs, the noisy distance and the noisy value. Basic composition says that running two mechanisms with independent noise costs the sum of their \(\varepsilon\)s, because the privacy loss of the pair is the sum of the two losses; post-processing says the function of them costs nothing more (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). So the mechanism is \(2\varepsilon\)-DP on this pair.
Case 2: \(|f(D) - f(D')| > b\). Then both \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D) > b\) and \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D') > b\), because each local sensitivity is the largest change over that dataset’s neighbours, and each of \(D\), \(D'\) is a neighbour of the other. So \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D) = 0\), and the test passes only if \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon) > \ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\). A \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) variable exceeds \(t\) with probability \(\frac12e^{-\varepsilon t}\) (one tail of the density), so this has probability \(\frac12e^{-\ln(1/\delta)} = \delta/2\).
Bound case 2. For any set \(S\) of outputs, \(M(D)\) lands in \(S\) either by refusing (if \(\bot \in S\)) or by releasing, and the release happens with probability at most \(\delta/2\) by step 3. So \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le \Pr[M(D) = \bot]\,\mathbf 1[\bot \in S] + \delta/2\), where \(\mathbf 1[\bot \in S]\) is 1 if \(\bot\) is in \(S\) and 0 otherwise. The refusal is a post-processing of the \(\varepsilon\)-DP test of step 1, so the first term is at most \(e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') = \bot]\,\mathbf 1[\bot\in S] \le e^{2\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D') \in S]\).
Combine: in both cases \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{2\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta/2\).

The “release the median for free” failure of the previous section is now confined to step 3: a dataset whose local sensitivity exceeds the proposal leaks only when a Laplace draw lands \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) above zero.


23.5.4 Interpretation
Propose-test-release is all or nothing. When the data are stable, you get noise of scale \(b/\varepsilon\), set by your proposal rather than by the data, so the noise scale reveals nothing. When they are not, you get \(\bot\), and \(\bot\) itself is a private answer: it says only that the data were probably near an unstable dataset.
The threshold the distance must clear is large. The test passes with probability \(\frac12\) when the distance equals the threshold, because the Laplace noise is positive half the time. With \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) that threshold is \(\ln(10^6) = 13.82\), so the test needs \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D) \gtrsim 13.82\) to pass with probability \(\frac12\). The data must be stable against more than a dozen changes, not just one.
The proposal \(b\) must not depend on the data. It is a proposal made before looking. Choosing \(b\) as, say, twice the observed local sensitivity makes the noise scale of the release a function of the data again, and reintroduces the leak of the previous section through the back door.
Compared with smooth sensitivity, propose-test-release needs only the distance to instability, which is often easier to compute or bound than \(S^*\). It pays \(2\varepsilon\) instead of \(\varepsilon\), and it can refuse.


23.5.5 Example: the median age
On the 1,001 ages, propose \(b = 1\) year. The first \(k\) with \(A^{(k)} > 1\) is \(k = 21\), so \(\operatorname{dist}_1(D) = 21\), comfortably above the threshold \(13.82\). The test fails only if the noise drops the distance by more than \(21 - 13.82\), which a \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\) draw does with probability \(\frac12e^{-(21 - 13.82)}\). So the pass probability is \(1 - \frac12e^{-(21 - 13.82)} = 0.999621\), and the release has noise \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\), with median absolute error \(\ln 2 = 0.693\) years at a total budget of \(2\varepsilon = 2\). On a sample of 101 ages, \(\operatorname{dist}_1 = 1\), and the test passes only if the noise adds more than \(13.82 - 1\), which has probability \(\frac12e^{-(13.82 - 1)} = 1.36\times10^{-6}\): there, one year is far too optimistic a proposal. Figure 23.3 (right) shows the pass probability switching from 0 to 1 between \(n = 500\) and \(n = 1000\).






Figure 23.3: Left: median absolute noise when releasing the median age with \(\varepsilon = 1\), by global sensitivity, smooth sensitivity with Cauchy noise and with Laplace noise (\(\delta = 10^{-6}\)), and propose-test-release with \(b = 1\) when it passes, averaged over 10 synthetic datasets per \(n\). The dotted line is the non-private local sensitivity. Right: the probability that propose-test-release with \(b = 1\) answers.





23.5.6 Check yourself

Why does step 3 need both local sensitivities to exceed \(b\), and why is that automatic? (If either were at most \(b\), the pair would fall into case 1. It is automatic because \(|f(D) - f(D')|\) is one of the terms in the maximum defining each local sensitivity.)
Why does propose-test-release cost \(2\varepsilon\) while smooth sensitivity costs \(\varepsilon\)? (It runs two Laplace mechanisms, one for the test and one for the release, and composes them. Smooth sensitivity folds the cost of a data-dependent scale into the single noise draw.)

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.6 Subsample-and-aggregate

23.6.1 Context
Sometimes you cannot analyse \(f\) at all: it is an estimator fitted by an optimizer, a trained model, or a pipeline you did not write. Subsample-and-aggregate (Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith 2007; Smith 2011) treats \(f\) as a black box. It runs \(f\) on disjoint pieces of the data and privately combines the answers. One record lives in one piece, so it can change only one answer, and the aggregator needs to be private only with respect to changing one of its inputs.


23.6.2 Statement
Split the \(n\) records into \(B\) disjoint blocks of \(n/B\) records, by a partition fixed in advance (for example by position, or by a hash of a record identifier). Compute the block answers \(z_j = f(\text{block } j)\), clip each to a range \([0, R]\) (replace values below 0 by 0 and above \(R\) by \(R\)), and release their average plus Laplace noise. One record can move one clipped answer by at most \(R\), so it moves the average by at most \(R/B\), and that sets the noise: \[M(D) = \frac1B\sum_{j=1}^B \operatorname{clip}_{[0,R]}(z_j) + \mathrm{Lap}\Big(\frac{R}{B\varepsilon}\Big). \tag{23.17}\] This is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any \(f\).
How accurate is it, as an estimate of a target \(\theta\)? Three things go wrong, and they add up in the mean squared error. Each block sees only \(n/B\) records, so \(f\) on a block can be biased in a way that \(f\) on the whole dataset is not; averaging the blocks keeps some random sampling error; and the Laplace noise has variance \(2(R/(B\varepsilon))^2\). Writing \(z\) for the output of \(f\) on one block, \[\underbrace{\big(\mathbb E[z] - \theta\big)^2}_{\text{bias of } f \text{ on } n/B \text{ records}} + \underbrace{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(z)}{B}}_{\text{sampling}} + \underbrace{2\Big(\frac{R}{B\varepsilon}\Big)^2}_{\text{noise}}, \tag{23.18}\] when the clipping is inactive and the blocks are independent samples.


23.6.3 Derivation

One record touches one block. Replacing record \(i\) changes only the block that contains it, because the partition does not depend on the values. So the vector \((z_1, \dots, z_B)\) changes in at most one coordinate.
The aggregate has sensitivity \(R/B\). After clipping, that coordinate moves by at most \(R\), the width of the clip range, and dividing by \(B\) in the average divides that by \(B\).
Privacy: Fact 1 with \(\Delta = R/B\).
Error. The released value minus \(\theta\) is the sum of three pieces: \(\mathbb E[z] - \theta\) (a constant, the bias), \(\frac1B\sum_j(z_j - \mathbb E z)\) (mean zero; it is an average of \(B\) independent terms, each with variance \(\operatorname{Var}(z)\), so its variance is \(\operatorname{Var}(z)/B\)) and the Laplace noise (mean zero, variance \(2(R/(B\varepsilon))^2\), since a \(\mathrm{Lap}(s)\) variable has variance \(2s^2\)). Squaring the sum gives the three squares plus cross terms. Each cross term is a product involving at least one mean-zero piece that is independent of the other factor, so it averages to zero. That leaves Equation 23.18.



23.6.4 Interpretation
The number of blocks sets the trade-off: more blocks means less noise but more bias. The noise falls like \(1/B\), because one record’s influence on the average is diluted over more blocks. The sampling term hardly moves: for estimators whose variance scales like one over the sample size, a block estimate has variance about \(B\) times that of \(f\) on all \(n\) records, and averaging \(B\) of them divides it by \(B\) again, so the term stays near \(\operatorname{Var}(f \text{ on } n \text{ records})\). The bias of \(f\) on small blocks grows with \(B\), because the blocks get smaller. The best \(B\) balances the first and the last.
The privacy proof never looks inside \(f\). This is what makes the method useful for trained models: an ensemble of “teacher” models, each trained on a disjoint shard and combined by a noisy vote (private aggregation of teacher ensembles, Papernot et al. 2017), is subsample-and-aggregate with a vote as the aggregator.
The range \(R\) is still a global bound, on the output of \(f\) rather than on the data, and a loose \(R\) means large noise. Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith replace the clipped average by a “center of attention” aggregator with smooth sensitivity, which adapts to how tightly the \(z_j\) cluster. Smith (2011) shows that for asymptotically normal estimators a version of this method loses nothing in the leading-order error.


23.6.5 Example: estimating a rate
You observe \(n = 10{,}000\) inter-arrival times, independent \(\mathrm{Exponential}\) with rate \(\theta = 1\), and want to estimate \(\theta\) privately with \(\varepsilon = 1\). The maximum-likelihood estimate is one over the sample mean, \(1/\bar x\), whose global sensitivity is infinite: a dataset of tiny times has a huge \(1/\bar x\), and one record changes it by an arbitrary amount.
To fill in Equation 23.18 you need the mean and variance of \(1/\bar x\) on a block of \(n_b = n/B\) records. The block sum \(n_b\bar x\) is a sum of \(n_b\) independent exponentials with rate \(\theta\), which has the gamma distribution with shape \(n_b\) and rate \(\theta\): \(n_b\bar x \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(n_b, \theta)\). The inverse moments of a gamma variable \(G\) with shape \(k\) are \(\mathbb E[1/G] = \theta/(k - 1)\) and \(\mathbb E[1/G^2] = \theta^2/((k - 1)(k - 2))\): integrate \(g^{-1}\) or \(g^{-2}\) against the gamma density \(\theta^kg^{k-1}e^{-\theta g}/\Gamma(k)\), recognize what is left as a gamma density with shape \(k - 1\) or \(k - 2\), and use \(\Gamma(k) = (k - 1)\Gamma(k - 1)\). Since \(z = 1/\bar x = n_b/G\), multiplying by \(n_b\) and \(n_b^2\) gives \[\mathbb E[z] = \frac{n_b\theta}{n_b - 1}, \qquad \text{bias } \frac{\theta}{n_b - 1}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(z) = \frac{n_b^2\theta^2}{(n_b - 1)^2(n_b - 2)}. \tag{23.19}\] The variance is \(\mathbb E[z^2] - \mathbb E[z]^2 = n_b^2\theta^2\big(\frac1{(n_b-1)(n_b-2)} - \frac1{(n_b-1)^2}\big)\), which simplifies to the form shown. With clip range \(R = 5\), Table 23.4 and Figure 23.4 show the trade-off. For example, with \(B = 10\) blocks the noise standard deviation is \(\sqrt2\,R/(B\varepsilon) = \sqrt2 \times 0.5 = 0.7071\), and the bias on blocks of 1,000 is \(1/999 = 0.0010\).

23.6.6 Check yourself

Why must the partition into blocks not depend on the data values? (Otherwise replacing one record could reshuffle many records between blocks and change many \(z_j\), breaking step 1.)
Why does the sampling term in Table 23.4 barely move with \(B\)? (The average of \(B\) block estimates, each with variance about \(\theta^2 B/n\), has variance about \(\theta^2/n\) whatever \(B\) is. Only the higher-order terms of the inverse-gamma variance depend on the block size.)

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.7 Clipping

23.7.1 Context
The mean is the most common statistic of all, and on unbounded data its global sensitivity is infinite. Clipping forces a bound: replace each value \(x\) by \(\min(x, C)\) before averaging. The sensitivity becomes \(C/n\), and Laplace noise of scale \(C/(n\varepsilon)\) makes the mean private. Nothing is free, though. Clipping changes the quantity you estimate, and the choice of \(C\) trades that bias against the noise. The same move, applied to per-example gradients rather than to values, is the heart of private model training in later parts.


23.7.2 Statement
Take non-negative data \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) drawn independently from a distribution with mean \(\mu\). The clipped mean averages the clipped values and adds noise for sensitivity \(C/n\): \[M(D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\min(x_i, C) + \mathrm{Lap}\Big(\frac{C}{n\varepsilon}\Big) \tag{23.20}\] It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Its error has the same three parts as in subsample-and-aggregate. Clipping cuts off the part of each value above \(C\), written \((x - C)_+ = \max(x - C, 0)\), and its average is the bias. The clipped values still vary from sample to sample, and the noise adds its own variance. So the mean squared error is \[\operatorname{err}(C)^2 = \underbrace{\mathbb E[(X - C)_+]^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\min(X, C))}{n}}_{\text{sampling}} + \underbrace{\frac{2C^2}{n^2\varepsilon^2}}_{\text{noise}}. \tag{23.21}\] Raising \(C\) shrinks the bias and grows the noise, so the best \(C\) is where the two rates of change balance, which is where the derivative of Equation 23.21 in \(C\) is zero. Here \(\Pr[X > C]\) is the fraction of values that clipping touches. The best \(C\) solves \[\Pr[X > C]\Big(\mathbb E[(X - C)_+] - \frac{C - \mathbb E[\min(X, C)]}{n}\Big) = \frac{2C}{n^2\varepsilon^2}. \tag{23.22}\]


23.7.3 Derivation

Sensitivity. Each clipped value lies in \([0, C]\), so replacing one record changes the sum by at most \(C\) and the mean by at most \(C/n\). Fact 1 gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
The bias. Clipping removes exactly the excess above \(C\): \(x - \min(x, C) = (x - C)_+\). Taking expectations, \(\mu - \mathbb E[\min(X, C)] = \mathbb E[(X - C)_+]\): the mass that clipping cuts off.
Error decomposition. As in the subsample-and-aggregate derivation, the error is a constant (minus the bias), a mean-zero sampling term with variance \(\operatorname{Var}(\min(X, C))/n\), and independent Laplace noise with variance \(2(C/(n\varepsilon))^2\). Squaring and averaging kills the cross terms, since each contains a mean-zero factor independent of the other: Equation 23.21.
Derivatives in \(C\). Raising \(C\) by a small amount \(h\) raises \(\min(X, C)\) by \(h\) exactly when \(X > C\) and leaves it alone otherwise, so \(\frac{d}{dC}\mathbb E[\min(X, C)] = \Pr[X > C]\). By the same reasoning \(\frac{d}{dC}\mathbb E[\min(X, C)^2] = 2C\Pr[X > C]\). The bias is \(\mathbb E[(X - C)_+] = \mu - \mathbb E[\min(X, C)]\), whose derivative is \(-\Pr[X > C]\), so by the chain rule the bias term has derivative \(-2\,\mathbb E[(X - C)_+]\Pr[X > C]\). The variance is \(\mathbb E[\min(X, C)^2] - \mathbb E[\min(X, C)]^2\), so the sampling term has derivative \(\frac1n\big(2C\Pr[X > C] - 2\,\mathbb E[\min(X, C)]\Pr[X > C]\big) = \frac2n\Pr[X > C]\big(C - \mathbb E[\min(X, C)]\big)\). The noise term has derivative \(\frac{4C}{n^2\varepsilon^2}\).
Set the sum to zero and divide by 2: Equation 23.22.



23.7.4 Interpretation
The bias does not shrink with \(n\), but the noise does. So the best \(C\) grows with \(n\): with more data you can afford to clip less. For large \(n\) the sampling part of Equation 23.22, which has an extra \(1/n\), drops out, and the condition reads \(\Pr[X > C]\,\mathbb E[(X - C)_+] \approx 2C/(n\varepsilon)^2\). The right side shrinks as \(n\varepsilon\) grows, so the left side must shrink too, which pushes \(C\) out into the tail.
The bias has a sign. Clipping only from above always lowers values, so it always underestimates. For data on both sides of zero, clipping to \([-C, C]\) cuts off mass on both sides, and the two cuts cancel only for distributions symmetric about 0, so only those are estimated without bias.
Choosing \(C\) is itself a data-dependent decision. Setting \(C\) to the observed maximum, or to the empirical 99th percentile, makes the noise scale a function of the data, and the leak of Section 23.3 returns. Choose \(C\) from domain knowledge, or spend part of the budget on a private quantile: the exponential mechanism, or the smooth-sensitivity and propose-test-release methods above applied to an order statistic.
Clipping is the honest version of “bounded data”. Every “assume \(x \in [0, \Lambda]\)” in earlier chapters is a clip in disguise, and its bias is the price of that assumption.


23.7.5 Example: mean income
Incomes (in thousands) follow a log-normal distribution with \(\ln X \sim \mathcal N(\ln 40, 0.8^2)\): the log of an income is normal. The median is \(e^{\ln 40} = 40\), because the exponential preserves the median. The mean is larger, \(e^{\ln 40 + 0.32} = 55.085\), because a log-normal with \(\ln X \sim \mathcal N(\eta, s^2)\) has mean \(e^{\eta + s^2/2}\) and here \(s^2/2 = 0.64/2 = 0.32\); the gap reflects a heavy right tail.
Every term of Equation 23.21 needs averages of \(X\) and \(X^2\) over the values below \(C\). For a log-normal these partial moments have a closed form, \(\mathbb E[X^j\mathbf 1\{X \le c\}] = e^{j\eta + j^2s^2/2}\,\Phi\big((\ln c - \eta - js^2)/s\big)\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function and \(\mathbf 1\{X \le c\}\) is 1 when \(X \le c\) and 0 otherwise. To get it, write \(X = e^Y\) with \(Y\) normal, so the integral is \(\int_{-\infty}^{\ln c}e^{jy}\varphi(y)\,dy\) with \(\varphi\) the normal density of \(Y\); completing the square in the exponent turns \(e^{jy}\varphi(y)\) into \(e^{j\eta + j^2s^2/2}\) times a normal density with mean shifted to \(\eta + js^2\), whose integral up to \(\ln c\) is the \(\Phi\) term (as in Probability distributions). Under the add/remove relation, why is a clipped sum easier to release than a clipped mean? (Adding or removing one record changes the sum by at most \(C\), but it also changes \(n\), so the mean’s denominator is not public. One releases a noisy sum and a noisy count and divides.)
If you double \(n\), roughly how does the noise term change, and which way does \(C^*\) move? (The noise standard deviation halves at fixed \(C\), so the balance in Equation 23.22 shifts toward a larger \(C^*\) with less bias.)

What to take from it. The first lesson is that a data-dependent noise scale can leak more than the answer: in the leak example both datasets have the same median, so the whole \(\delta = 0.477\) comes from the spread of the noise. The repair for the median rests on an exact formula, and the \(O(n^2)\) formula for \(A^{(k)}\) matches brute force at every distance \(k\), so the smooth sensitivities it produces can be trusted. With it, smooth sensitivity and propose-test-release buy about two orders of magnitude over global sensitivity for the median of a thousand points, though they lose to it on tiny datasets, where a few changes can open a gap across the whole range. Finally, every method ends in a bias–noise trade-off you can compute: the number of blocks and the clip bound both have optima you can find in closed form before touching the data.

Rules of thumb

If the noise scale depends on the data, ask what the noise scale reveals. If you cannot answer, use one of the four repairs.
Pure DP with a data-dependent scale needs polynomial tails; light tails need \(\delta\) and a much smaller \(\beta \approx \varepsilon/(2\ln(1/\delta))\).
Smooth sensitivity pays off once the data are dense around the statistic: for the median, once \(n\) is in the hundreds.
Choose clip bounds and block counts before looking at the data, by the error formula, or with a separate slice of the privacy budget.

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
24.1 Why this matters
Every privacy proof so far was a statement about real numbers. The Laplace mechanism adds a real-valued \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) draw to a real-valued \(f(D)\), and the proof compares two densities on the real line. A computer has neither. It has floating-point numbers, a finite set with uneven gaps, and a source of random bits. The program that “samples \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\)” outputs a distribution on that finite set, and nothing in the proof says anything about it.
The gap is not a rounding nuisance. Mironov (2012) showed that the textbook Laplace sampler, run in double precision, leaks \(f(D)\) through the low-order bits of its output. Some outputs can be produced from \(D\) and not from \(D'\), and an observer who sees one knows which dataset was used. No \(\varepsilon\) covers that.
The organizing idea of this chapter is that differential privacy (DP) is a property of the output distribution the code actually produces, so the code must produce exactly the distribution the proof is about. There are two ways to get there. You can keep floating point and repair the output: round it to a coarse grid and clamp it, so that every reachable output is reachable from every input. Or you can leave floating point behind: work with integer-valued queries and sample integer noise exactly, using only integer and rational arithmetic and uniform random integers. The second route gives the discrete Laplace and the discrete Gaussian mechanisms. Their privacy proofs are as clean as the continuous ones, and their samplers produce exactly the distribution in the proof. Table 24.1 lists the results.
What this chapter assumes, restated. \(M\) is a mechanism: a randomized program that takes a dataset and returns an output. \(D \simeq D'\) are neighbouring datasets, which differ in one person’s record. A query \(f\) has \(\ell_1\) sensitivity \(\Delta_1 f\) and \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2 f\): the largest change in \(f\), measured as a sum of absolute coordinate changes or as a Euclidean length, when one record changes. \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP if, for every pair of neighbours and every set \(S\) of outputs, \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta\): no event becomes more than \(e^\varepsilon\) times more likely when one record changes, except for an additive slack \(\delta\). With \(\delta = 0\) this is pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The privacy loss of an output \(y\) is the log of the ratio of its probabilities under the two neighbours, \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \ln\frac{p_{M(D)}(y)}{p_{M(D')}(y)}, \tag{24.1}\] which measures how much evidence \(y\) gives for \(D\) over \(D'\). For a discrete output, \(p_{M(D)}\) is a probability mass function (PMF), the probability of each single output. Pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP is the statement \(|L_{D,D'}(y)| \le \varepsilon\) for every \(y\), because the probability of a set is the sum of its outputs’ probabilities, and if each term grows by at most \(e^\varepsilon\) so does the sum. The full treatment is in The definition of differential privacy, the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms are in The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, and the Laplace and geometric distributions are in Probability distributions.

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
section: 24.2 Toolkit: exact randomness from uniform integers
text:
24.2 Toolkit: exact randomness from uniform integers
The exact samplers below need only one primitive: a uniform integer in \(\{0, 1, \dots, d - 1\}\) for any \(d \ge 1\). Python’s random.Random.randrange(d) provides it exactly: it draws \(\lceil\log_2 d\rceil\) random bits and redraws when the result is \(d\) or more, so every integer below \(d\) comes out with probability exactly \(1/d\). A deployment draws the bits from the operating system with secrets.SystemRandom(), which has the same interface. Three facts turn this primitive into everything else: how to make a coin with a fraction as its bias, how to reshape one distribution into another by throwing some draws away, and how counting coin flips gives a geometric variable.

24.2.1 Fact 1: an exact coin with rational bias
To make a coin that comes up 1 with probability \(n/d\), draw a uniform integer below \(d\) and call it a success when it is one of the first \(n\) values. For integers \(0 \le n \le d\), let \(U\) be uniform on \(\{0, \dots, d - 1\}\). Then \[\Pr[U < n] = \frac{n}{d}, \tag{24.2}\] because there are \(n\) favourable values out of \(d\) equally likely ones. So \(\mathbf 1[U < n]\), the indicator that is 1 when \(U < n\) and 0 otherwise, is an exact \(\mathrm{Bernoulli}(n/d)\) draw, with no rounding anywhere. A coin with an irrational bias such as \(e^{-1}\) can’t be made this way, because no fraction \(n/d\) equals it, which is why Algorithm 1 below exists.


24.2.2 Fact 2: rejection sampling
Suppose you can sample from a PMF \(q\), the proposal, but you want samples from a different PMF \(p\). If \(p(x)\) is proportional to \(q(x)a(x)\) for some acceptance probability \(0 \le a(x) \le 1\), you can draw from \(q\) and keep each draw \(x\) only with probability \(a(x)\): values that \(p\) favours less than \(q\) get thrown away more often. Precisely, let \(p(x) = q(x)a(x)/A\), where \(A = \sum_x q(x)a(x)\) is the normalizer. Repeat: draw \(Y \sim q\), then accept it with probability \(a(Y)\); output the first accepted \(Y\). Three steps show that this is exact and what it costs.

Look at one round. A round outputs \(x\) when it proposes \(x\) (probability \(q(x)\)) and accepts it (probability \(a(x)\)), so with probability \(q(x)a(x)\). Adding over \(x\), a round outputs something with probability \(A\) and nothing with probability \(1 - A\).
Add up the rounds. The rounds are independent and identical, so the output is \(x\) when the first \(j\) rounds output nothing and round \(j + 1\) outputs \(x\), for some \(j \ge 0\). That has probability \(\sum_{j \ge 0}(1 - A)^jq(x)a(x)\), a geometric series with ratio \(1 - A < 1\), which sums to \(q(x)a(x)/A = p(x)\).
Count the cost. Each round succeeds with probability \(A\) independently, so the number of rounds is geometric with success probability \(A\), and its mean is \(1/A\).

The output is exact as long as each acceptance is an exact coin. What matters is that proposal times acceptance is proportional to the target. You never need to compute the normalizer \(A\); it only sets how many rounds you wait.


24.2.3 Fact 3: counting successes gives a geometric variable
Flip independent coins with success probability \(r\) and let \(V\) be the number of successes before the first failure. The event \(V = v\) means exactly \(v\) successes followed by one failure, and independent flips multiply, so \[\Pr[V = v] = r^v(1 - r), \qquad v = 0, 1, 2, \dots \tag{24.3}\] This is the geometric distribution of Probability distributions, counted from 0. Its tail is \(\Pr[V \ge v] = r^v\), since \(V \ge v\) just says the first \(v\) flips were successes.

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
24.3 Floating-point Laplace breaks differential privacy

24.3.1 Context
The textbook way to sample \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) is inverse cumulative distribution function (CDF) sampling: turn a uniform number into a draw with the right tail by solving for where the tail probability equals it. Draw \(U\) uniform on \((0, 1)\) and a fair sign \(\xi \in \{-1, +1\}\), and output \(\xi\cdot b\ln(1/U)\). The magnitude \(b\ln(1/U)\) is exponential with mean \(b\), written \(\mathrm{Exp}(b)\), because \(b\ln(1/U) > t\) exactly when \(U < e^{-t/b}\), so \(\Pr[b\ln(1/U) > t] = \Pr[U < e^{-t/b}] = e^{-t/b}\). A fair sign turns it into \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\), whose density \(\frac1{2b}e^{-|z|/b}\) is the exponential mirrored around 0. The Laplace mechanism then outputs \(y = f(D) + \xi\cdot b\ln(1/U)\). Run in floating point, \(U\), the logarithm and the sum are each rounded. The question is whether the rounded mechanism is still DP.


24.3.2 Statement
The test is simple: if some outputs can only come from \(D\), seeing one of them reveals \(D\) with certainty, and no multiplicative factor \(e^\varepsilon\) can account for that, so all of their probability has to be paid for by \(\delta\). Write \(\mathcal Y_D\) for the set of outputs \(M(D)\) can produce and let \(S = \mathcal Y_D \setminus \mathcal Y_{D'}\) be the outputs reachable from \(D\) but not from \(D'\). If \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, then for every \(\varepsilon\) \[\delta \;\ge\; \Pr[M(D) \in S].  \tag{24.4}\] In particular, if \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] > 0\), then \(M\) is not \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any finite \(\varepsilon\). The floating-point Laplace sampler has such outputs. In a toy model with a 12-bit significand that can be enumerated exactly, \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] = 0.4791\) for \(f(D) = 0\), \(f(D') = 1\) and \(b = 1\).


24.3.3 Derivation

Apply the definition to the event \(S\). \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP says \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta\) for every event. Here \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] = 0\) by the choice of \(S\), so the multiplicative term is \(e^\varepsilon \cdot 0 = 0\) however large \(e^\varepsilon\) is, and what remains is \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le \delta\). That is Equation 24.4.
Read it as an attack. Use the convention of The definition of differential privacy: a test decides between “the data were \(D\)” and “the data were \(D'\)”, its false positive rate \(\alpha\) is the chance of saying “\(D'\)” when the data were \(D\), and its false negative rate \(\beta\) is the chance of saying “\(D\)” when the data were \(D'\). Consider the test “say \(D\) when \(y \in S\), and \(D'\) otherwise”. Under \(D'\) the output never lands in \(S\), so the test never says “\(D\)” and \(\beta = 0\). Under \(D\) it says “\(D'\)” whenever \(y\) misses \(S\), so \(\alpha = 1 - \Pr[M(D) \in S]\). The hypothesis-testing form of DP in that chapter says that every test has \(\alpha + e^\varepsilon\beta \ge 1 - \delta\); this is the definition applied to the event on which the test says “\(D\)”. With \(\beta = 0\) the factor \(e^\varepsilon\) multiplies nothing, and the inequality reads \(1 - \Pr[M(D) \in S] \ge 1 - \delta\), which is again \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le \delta\). And whenever this test says “\(D\)”, it is right.
Floating-point outputs form a finite set that depends on \(f(D)\). A float with a \(p\)-bit significand (IEEE 754 doubles have \(p = 53\)) is \(m\cdot2^e\) with an integer \(m < 2^p\) and an integer exponent \(e\). Between \(2^e\) and \(2^{e+1}\) the floats are spaced \(2^{e - p + 1}\) apart, so they are dense near 0 and sparse far from it. The sampler computes \(\mathrm{round}(f(D) + \xi\cdot\mathrm{round}(b\ln(1/U)))\). Its outputs are the rounded sums of \(f(D)\) with a fixed, finite set of noise values. Shifting by \(f(D') \ne f(D)\) before rounding lands on a different set of floats.
Why the two sets differ. Near 0 the noise values are fine-grained: the floats there are spaced far more closely than near 1. \(M(D)\) with \(f(D) = 0\) outputs those noise values as they are. \(M(D')\) with \(f(D') = 1\) must produce an output near 0 as \(1 - (\text{noise near } 1)\), which is a multiple of the coarser spacing of the noise near 1. So most of the fine-grained outputs of \(M(D)\) near 0 are impossible under \(M(D')\). Away from the inputs the two grids interleave and coincide only in part. Figure 24.1 (left) shows a narrow window: 3 of the 9 outputs of \(M(D)\) there can’t come from \(M(D')\), and 4 of the 10 outputs of \(M(D')\) can’t come from \(M(D)\).

Concretely, in a toy model. Doubles have too many values to enumerate, so the script uses \(p\)-bit floats with \(p\) from 6 to 14. \(U\) is an ideal uniform \(p\)-bit float: a real uniform rounded down to a \(p\)-bit float, so each float in \([2^{-40}, 1)\) has probability equal to its gap to the next one. The logarithm is computed and rounded to \(p\) bits, then the sum is rounded to \(p\) bits. Every output and its probability is computed exactly. Table 24.2 lists the results.



Table 24.2: The toy floating-point Laplace sampler with \(b = 1\), \(f(D) = 0\) and \(f(D') = 1\). \(S\) is the set of outputs of \(M(D)\) that \(M(D')\) can’t produce, and \(S'\) the reverse.












Significand bits \(p\)
Outputs of \(M(D)\)

Left: every output that \(f(D) = 0\) (top) and \(f(D') = 1\) (bottom) can produce in a narrow window, coloured by whether the other input can produce it too. Right: the probability that \(M(D)\) produces an output \(M(D')\) cannot, as a function of the significand length \(p\), for the textbook sampler and for the snapped one of Section 24.4.





24.3.4 Interpretation
More precision does not help. The right panel of Figure 24.1 is flat: from 6 to 14 bits, about 48% of the mass of \(M(D)\) is on outputs \(M(D')\) can’t produce. Adding bits refines both grids together, so the mismatch stays. Mironov (2012) found the same effect at \(p = 53\) in the samplers of several DP libraries of the time, and showed how to recover \(f(D)\) from single outputs.
The leak sits in the low-order bits. It is not in where the output lands on the real line but in which float it is. Printing the output to a few decimals would hide it, and that is the intuition behind snapping in the next section.
There is a second, smaller leak: the tails are cut off. A 53-bit uniform \(U = k\cdot2^{-53}\), with \(k\) a positive integer, is never below \(2^{-53}\), so the noise magnitude \(b\ln(1/U)\) never exceeds \(b\ln(2^{53}) = b\cdot53\ln2 \approx 36.74\,b\). Outputs between \(f(D) + 36.74b\) and \(f(D') + 36.74b\) are then reachable from only one input. Their probability is about \(2^{-53}\), but by Equation 24.4 it is still a floor on \(\delta\), and it rules out pure DP.
Finally, the model is a toy, but the effect is not. Real libraries differ from the toy in how they draw \(U\) and round the logarithm. Those details change the numbers, not the conclusion. Jin et al. (2022) found floating-point and timing leaks in DP libraries released after Mironov’s paper.


24.3.5 Example: a count released with \(\varepsilon = 1\)
A hospital releases the number of patients with a rare diagnosis, a count with \(\Delta_1 f = 1\), using the textbook sampler with \(b = 1\), so that the exact mechanism would have \(\varepsilon = \Delta_1 f/b = 1\). An analyst who knows that the count is either 0 or 1 (say, whether one particular patient is in the data) checks whether the released float can be produced from 1. In the 12-bit toy, the check identifies the count 0 with certainty 47.91% of the time: that is \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] = 0.4791\) from Table 24.2. The proof of the Laplace mechanism promised that one output could move the analyst’s odds by at most a factor \(e\); the code delivers certainty almost half the time.


24.3.6 Check yourself

Why doesn’t the support argument need \(\varepsilon\) to be small? (Because \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] = 0\), the term \(e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S]\) vanishes for every \(\varepsilon\), however large.)
Would the problem go away if \(f(D)\) and \(f(D')\) were both integers and \(b\) were a power of 2? (No. The noise values \(b\ln(1/U)\) are still rounded differently once added to different integers, because the spacing of floats depends on the magnitude of the sum. The toy uses \(b = 1\) and integer \(f\).)

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
24.4 The snapping mechanism

24.4.1 Context
If the output must be a float, the low-order bits have to go. The snapping mechanism of Mironov (2012) removes them by rounding the noisy answer to a coarse grid, and clamps both the input and the output to a bounded range so that floating-point rounding errors stay small relative to the grid. This section gives the mechanism and its guarantee in outline.


24.4.2 Statement
In words: clamp the true answer into \([-B, B]\), add Laplace noise computed in floating point, round the result to the nearest multiple of a power of 2 at least as large as the noise scale, and clamp again. Let \(f\) have sensitivity 1, let \(\lambda\) be the noise scale, let \(\Lambda\) be the smallest power of 2 with \(\Lambda \ge \lambda\), and let \(B\) be a clamping bound. The snapping mechanism outputs \[M(D) = \mathrm{clamp}_B\Big(\big\lfloor \mathrm{clamp}_B(f(D)) \oplus \xi\otimes\lambda\otimes\mathrm{LN}(U^*)\big\rceil_\Lambda\Big), \tag{24.5}\] where \(\oplus\), \(\otimes\) and \(\mathrm{LN}\) are floating-point addition, multiplication and logarithm, \(\xi\) is a fair sign, \(U^*\) is an ideal uniform double, \(\lfloor\cdot\rceil_\Lambda\) rounds to the nearest multiple of \(\Lambda\), and \(\mathrm{clamp}_B\) maps to \([-B, B]\). (\(\mathrm{LN}(U^*)\) is negative, and the fair sign \(\xi\) makes the sign of the noise irrelevant.)
Its guarantee is the exact Laplace mechanism’s \(\varepsilon = 1/\lambda\) plus two small terms that pay for floating-point error. The error of one floating-point operation is at most a fraction \(\eta = 2^{-53}\) of the number it produces, and clamping keeps every number below \(B\) in size, so the terms grow with \(B\eta\). Mironov (2012, Theorem 1) proves that for \(\lambda < B < 2^{46}\lambda\) the mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP with \[\varepsilon = \frac{1 + 12B\eta}{\lambda} + \frac{2^{-49}B}{\lambda}, \qquad \eta = 2^{-53}. \tag{24.6}\]


24.4.3 Derivation (outline)

Clamping the input bounds \(|f(D)| \le B\), so every sum is computed at magnitudes where the float spacing is at most about \(B\eta\).
Rounding to a multiple of \(\Lambda \ge \lambda\) discards every bit finer than \(\Lambda\). The output is one of the multiples of \(\Lambda\) in \([-B, B]\), the same finite set for every input, so the support argument of Section 24.3 has nothing to bite on: no output is reachable from one input only.
Each grid point collects an interval of noise values of width \(\Lambda\): all noise values that round to that point. In exact arithmetic, its probability under \(D\) and under \(D'\) is the probability that a Laplace variable lands in one of two intervals shifted by \(|f(D) - f(D')| \le 1\). The Laplace density changes by at most a factor \(e^{1/\lambda}\) under a shift of 1, because \(e^{-|z|/\lambda}\) and \(e^{-|z - 1|/\lambda}\) differ in the exponent by at most \(1/\lambda\), so the ratio of the two interval probabilities is at most \(e^{1/\lambda}\). In other words, rounding exact Laplace noise is post-processing of the exact Laplace mechanism, and post-processing never increases the privacy loss.
Floating-point error moves each interval’s endpoints by a relative amount of order \(\eta\), measured against magnitudes up to \(B\). Bounding the effect of those moves on the interval probabilities gives the extra terms proportional to \(B\eta/\lambda\). Mironov (2012, §5) does this bookkeeping.



24.4.4 Interpretation
The price is accuracy: rounding to \(\Lambda\) adds up to \(\Lambda/2 \le \lambda\) of error (since \(\Lambda\) is the smallest power of 2 at or above \(\lambda\), it is below \(2\lambda\)), and clamping biases answers near \(\pm B\). The extra terms in \(\varepsilon\) are tiny for doubles. With \(\lambda = 1\) and \(B = 10\), the first term exceeds \(1/\lambda\) by \(12B\eta = 120\cdot2^{-53}\) and the second is \(10\cdot2^{-49}\), so the excess is \(120\cdot2^{-53} + 10\cdot2^{-49} \approx 3.1\times10^{-14}\). The guarantee also assumes a correctly behaved logarithm and an ideal uniform \(U^*\), which a library has to supply.


24.4.5 Example: the toy, snapped
Snap the toy sampler to integers (\(\Lambda = 1\) for \(b = 1\)) and clamp to \([-10, 10]\). Both inputs now reach the same 21 outputs, the integers from \(-10\) to 10, so \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] = 0\) at every precision (Figure 24.1, right). The largest privacy loss over those outputs, the largest log-ratio of an output’s probabilities under the two inputs, is \(\max_y|L_{D,D'}(y)| = 1.0010\) at \(p = 12\) and 1.0002 at \(p = 14\), against \(\varepsilon = 1\) for the exact mechanism. The excess shrinks with precision, as the \(\eta\) terms predict.


24.4.6 Check yourself

Why must the grid be at least as coarse as \(\lambda\)? (Finer grids keep bits whose pattern still depends on \(f(D)\). The proof needs each grid cell to collect a whole interval of noise values, wide enough that floating-point errors at its edges move only a tiny fraction of its probability.)
Is snapping post-processing of the floating-point Laplace mechanism? (It is post-processing, but post-processing of a mechanism that isn’t DP proves nothing. The proof compares the snapped output with snapped exact Laplace noise and bounds the difference.)

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
24.5 Exact \(\mathrm{Bernoulli}(e^{-\gamma})\)

24.5.1 Context
Both exact samplers below need a coin that comes up 1 with probability \(e^{-\gamma}\) for a rational \(\gamma \ge 0\). The obvious code, random() < exp(-gamma), is inexact twice over: exp rounds, and random() has only 53 bits. Algorithm 1 of Canonne, Kamath and Steinke (2020), based on a method of von Neumann (1951), makes the coin from rational coins alone.


24.5.2 Statement
The idea is to build \(e^{-\gamma}\) from its power series \(e^{-\gamma} = 1 - \gamma + \frac{\gamma^2}{2!} - \frac{\gamma^3}{3!} + \cdots\), whose terms are probabilities you can produce with rational coins. Flip coins whose success probabilities shrink as \(\gamma, \gamma/2, \gamma/3, \dots\) until one fails. The chance of surviving \(k\) flips is then \(\gamma \cdot \frac\gamma2 \cdots \frac\gamma k = \gamma^k/k!\), the \(k\)-th term of the series. The series alternates in sign, and the parity of the stopping time produces exactly that alternation.
For \(0 \le \gamma \le 1\): draw \(A_k \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\gamma/k)\) for \(k = 1, 2, \dots\), and stop at the first \(A_K = 0\), so \(K\) is the index of the first failure. Output 1 if \(K\) is odd and 0 if \(K\) is even. Then the survival probability, the output probability and the mean number of flips are \[\Pr[K > k] = \frac{\gamma^k}{k!}, \qquad \Pr[K\ \text{odd}] = e^{-\gamma}, \qquad \mathbb E[K] = e^\gamma. \tag{24.7}\] For \(\gamma > 1\) the first coin would need a probability above 1, so split \(\gamma\) into its integer part \(\lfloor\gamma\rfloor\) and a remainder below 1: draw \(\lfloor\gamma\rfloor\) coins with probability \(e^{-1}\), stopping at the first 0, and then one coin with probability \(e^{-(\gamma - \lfloor\gamma\rfloor)}\). Output 1 only if all of them are 1.


24.5.3 Derivation

The survival probabilities. \(K > k\) means the first \(k\) coins all came up 1. They are independent with probabilities \(\gamma/1, \gamma/2, \dots, \gamma/k\), so \(\Pr[K > k]\) is their product, \(\gamma^k/k!\). For \(\gamma = n/d\), each \(\gamma/j = n/(dj)\) is a ratio of integers, at most 1 since \(\gamma \le 1\), so each coin is exact by Fact 1.
The point probabilities. \(K = k\) means the coins survived \(k - 1\) flips but not \(k\), so \(\Pr[K = k] = \Pr[K > k - 1] - \Pr[K > k] = \frac{\gamma^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} - \frac{\gamma^k}{k!}\).
Add over odd \(k\). With \(k = 1, 3, 5, \dots\) the terms are \((1 - \gamma) + (\frac{\gamma^2}{2!} - \frac{\gamma^3}{3!}) + (\frac{\gamma^4}{4!} - \frac{\gamma^5}{5!}) + \cdots\). Every power \(\gamma^j\) appears exactly once: with a plus sign when \(j = k - 1\) is even and a minus sign when \(j = k\) is odd. So the sum is the series \(\sum_{j \ge 0}(-\gamma)^j/j! = e^{-\gamma}\).
The mean. A variable \(K\) on \(\{1, 2, \dots\}\) can be written as a count, \(K = \sum_{k \ge 0}\mathbf 1[K > k]\), since exactly \(K\) of the indicators \(\mathbf 1[K > 0], \mathbf 1[K > 1], \dots\) are 1. Taking expectations, \(\mathbb E[K] = \sum_{k \ge 0}\Pr[K > k] = \sum_k\gamma^k/k! = e^\gamma\). Each round uses one uniform integer, so a coin costs \(e^\gamma \le e\) uniform draws on average.
Large \(\gamma\). \(e^{-\gamma} = (e^{-1})^{\lfloor\gamma\rfloor}\,e^{-(\gamma - \lfloor\gamma\rfloor)}\), and a product of probabilities is the probability that independent coins all come up 1. Each coin has an exponent of at most 1, so steps 1–3 cover it. Stopping at the first 0 doesn’t change the output, which is 0 as soon as one coin is 0.

Concretely, for \(\gamma = 0.7\) (Table 24.3). The odd rows add up to \(0.3000 + 0.1878 + 0.0086 + \cdots = 0.4966 = e^{-0.7}\).

24.5.4 Interpretation
The coin is exact: no step rounds, and the only randomness is uniform integers. The cost is small and bounded: at most \(e\) draws for \(\gamma \le 1\), and below \(\frac{e}{1 - e^{-1}} + 1 \approx 5.3\) for any \(\gamma\) (Exercise 1). The cost curve in Figure 24.2 jumps at each integer. At \(\gamma = 1\) the algorithm runs one full \(e^{-1}\) coin and then a coin for the fractional part 0, which costs one extra draw when the first coin comes up 1 (probability \(e^{-1}\)), so the cost goes from \(e = 2.7183\) just below 1 to \(e + e^{-1} = 3.0862\) at 1. Splitting \(\gamma\) differently would smooth this out; it doesn’t matter for exactness.


24.5.5 Example: one coin per proposal
Algorithm 3 below accepts a proposal \(y\) with probability \(e^{-\gamma}\) for a rational \(\gamma = (|y| - \sigma^2/t)^2/(2\sigma^2)\), where \(\sigma^2\) is the target variance and \(t\) an integer scale. With \(\sigma^2 = 4\), \(t = 3\) and \(y = 4\), that is \(\gamma = (4 - 4/3)^2/8 = (8/3)^2/8 = 8/9\), so the coin is 1 with probability \(e^{-8/9} = 0.4111\) and costs \(e^{8/9} \approx 2.43\) draws on average. Everything stays a fraction: \(\gamma\) is computed with fractions.Fraction, and each \(\gamma/k\) is a ratio of integers.


24.5.6 Check yourself

Why does the algorithm use \(\gamma/k\) rather than a fixed probability \(\gamma\) at every step? (The decreasing probabilities make \(\Pr[K > k] = \gamma^k/k!\), the terms of the exponential series. A fixed \(\gamma\) would give \(\gamma^k\), a geometric series, and the alternating sum would be \(1/(1 + \gamma)\).)
What does the algorithm output for \(\gamma = 0\)? (The first coin is \(\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0)\), so \(K = 1\), which is odd, and the output is 1 = \(e^0\).)

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
24.6 The discrete Laplace mechanism

24.6.1 Context
Most queries in DP are counts or histograms: integer-valued, with sensitivity 1. For them the natural noise is integer-valued too. Then the output is an integer, there are no low-order bits to leak, and the noise can be sampled exactly. The discrete Laplace distribution is the integer analogue of the Laplace, and adding it is the geometric mechanism of Ghosh, Roughgarden and Sundararajan (2009).


24.6.2 Statement
Take the Laplace density \(e^{-|z|/b}\), keep only its values at the integers, and divide by their sum so they add up to 1. Each step away from 0 multiplies the probability by the same factor \(r = e^{-1/b}\), just as the continuous density drops by \(e^{-1/b}\) per unit. The discrete Laplace distribution with scale \(b > 0\), written \(\mathrm{Lap}_{\mathbb Z}(b)\), has PMF \[\Pr[Z = z] = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r}\,r^{|z|}, \qquad z \in \mathbb Z, \qquad r = e^{-1/b}. \tag{24.8}\] Its variance is \(2r/(1 - r)^2\), slightly below the \(2b^2\) of \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\). Because shifting the input by one unit changes each output’s probability by at most the factor \(r^{-1} = e^{1/b}\), as for the continuous Laplace, the privacy guarantee is the same. For an integer-valued \(f\) with sensitivity \(\Delta_1 f\), the mechanism \(M(D) = f(D) + Z\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP with \[\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta_1 f}{b}. \tag{24.9}\] For rational \(b = t/s\), Algorithm 2 of Canonne, Kamath and Steinke (2020) samples \(\mathrm{Lap}_{\mathbb Z}(b)\) exactly.


24.6.3 Derivation
The PMF and variance. Both come from sums of geometric series.

Normalize. The weights \(r^{|z|}\) are 1 at \(z = 0\) and appear twice, at \(\pm z\), for each \(z \ge 1\). So \(\sum_{z \in \mathbb Z}r^{|z|} = 1 + 2\sum_{z \ge 1}r^z = 1 + \frac{2r}{1 - r} = \frac{1 + r}{1 - r}\), and dividing by it gives the constant in Equation 24.8.
Variance. The PMF gives \(z\) and \(-z\) the same probability, so their contributions \(z\Pr[Z = z]\) and \(-z\Pr[Z = -z]\) cancel and the mean is 0. The variance is then \(\mathbb E Z^2\). Differentiating \(\sum_{z \ge 0}r^z = \frac1{1 - r}\) and multiplying by \(r\) gives \(\sum_{z \ge 1}zr^z = \frac{r}{(1 - r)^2}\); doing it once more gives \(\sum_{z \ge 1}z^2r^z = \frac{r(1 + r)}{(1 - r)^3}\). Counting \(\pm z\) twice, \(\mathbb E Z^2 = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r}\cdot2\cdot\frac{r(1 + r)}{(1 - r)^3} = \frac{2r}{(1 - r)^2}\).

Privacy. The plan is to compute the privacy loss of each output and bound it by \(\varepsilon\), which is pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP.

The privacy loss. For neighbours with \(f(D) = a\) and \(f(D') = a'\), an output \(y\) requires noise \(y - a\) under \(D\) and \(y - a'\) under \(D'\). The normalizing constant is the same for both, so it cancels in the ratio: \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \ln\frac{r^{|y - a|}}{r^{|y - a'|}} = \frac{|y - a'| - |y - a|}{b}, \tag{24.10}\] using \(\ln r = -1/b\).
Bound it. The triangle inequality says that two numbers’ distances to \(y\) differ by at most their distance to each other: \(|y - a'| - |y - a| \le |a - a'| \le \Delta_1 f\). So \(|L_{D,D'}(y)| \le \Delta_1 f/b\) for every integer \(y\), which is pure DP with Equation 24.9. The bound is reached for every \(y \ge \max(a, a')\), so it is tight.
Vectors. For \(f \in \mathbb Z^d\) with independent noise per coordinate, the probability of an output vector is a product over coordinates, so its log, the privacy loss, is a sum of per-coordinate losses. Each is at most \(|a_i - a'_i|/b\), and \(\sum_i|a_i - a'_i| \le \Delta_1 f\) gives the same \(\varepsilon\) with the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity.

Step 1 is where integers matter. The constant cancels because \(\sum_z r^{|z - a|}\) is the same for every integer \(a\): shifting by an integer only relabels the terms. Shifting by a non-integer would move the noise off the lattice, and the mechanism would have different supports for different inputs: the floating-point failure again.
The exact sampler (Algorithm 2). The plan is to build a one-sided geometric variable with ratio \(e^{-1/b}\) out of exact pieces, then attach a random sign. A geometric with ratio \(e^{-1/t}\) is assembled from a remainder \(U\) below \(t\) and a quotient \(V\), the way an integer \(x\) is \(u + tv\); dividing by \(s\) then turns ratio \(e^{-1/t}\) into \(e^{-s/t} = e^{-1/b}\). Input integers \(s, t \ge 1\), so \(b = t/s\). Repeat until a value is returned:

Draw \(U\) uniform on \(\{0, \dots, t - 1\}\) and accept it with probability \(e^{-U/t}\) (Algorithm 1); on rejection, start over.
Count the successes \(V\) of independent \(e^{-1}\) coins before the first failure (Algorithm 1 with \(\gamma = 1\)).
Set \(X = U + tV\) and \(Y = \lfloor X/s\rfloor\).
Draw a fair sign bit \(B\). If \(B = 1\) and \(Y = 0\), start over. Otherwise return \((1 - 2B)Y\).

Five steps show that the output is exactly \(\mathrm{Lap}_{\mathbb Z}(b)\), following the algorithm’s own order.

\(U\) given acceptance has \(\Pr[U = u] \propto e^{-u/t}\) on \(\{0, \dots, t - 1\}\), by Fact 2 with a uniform proposal and acceptance \(e^{-u/t}\).
\(V\) is geometric with \(\Pr[V = v] = (1 - e^{-1})e^{-v}\), by Fact 3 with \(r = e^{-1}\).
\(X = U + tV\) is geometric with ratio \(e^{-1/t}\). Each \(x \ge 0\) is \(u + tv\) for exactly one pair (\(u = x \bmod t\), \(v = \lfloor x/t\rfloor\)), and the independent weights multiply to \(e^{-u/t}e^{-v} = e^{-(u + tv)/t} = e^{-x/t}\). So \(\Pr[X = x] \propto e^{-x/t}\).
\(Y = \lfloor X/s\rfloor\) is geometric with ratio \(e^{-s/t} = e^{-1/b}\). \(Y = y\) collects \(x = sy, \dots, sy + s - 1\), with total weight \(e^{-sy/t}(1 + e^{-1/t} + \dots + e^{-(s-1)/t})\). The bracket does not depend on \(y\), so the weight is \(\propto e^{-sy/t} = r^y\).
The sign. \(\pm Y\) with a fair sign gives \(\pm y\) with probability \(\frac12\Pr[Y = y]\) each, but 0 would get both halves, since \(+0\) and \(-0\) are the same output. Rejecting \((B = 1, Y = 0)\) leaves \(\frac12\Pr[Y = y]\) for every \(z = \pm y\), including 0. After renormalizing (Fact 2), \(\Pr[Z = z] \propto r^{|z|}\).

24.6.4 Interpretation
The discrete Laplace gives the same guarantee with less noise. It has the same \(\varepsilon\) as the continuous one at the same scale and a slightly smaller variance: 1.8413 against 2 at \(b = 1\). Exercise 3 shows the gap tends to \(1/6\) as \(b\) grows. Rounding \(f(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(b)\) to the nearest integer would also be \(\varepsilon\)-DP in exact arithmetic, as post-processing, but it is not the same distribution, and it needs a floating-point sampler.
It is also the best possible mechanism for one count. Ghosh, Roughgarden and Sundararajan (2009) show that for a single count, the geometric mechanism is universally utility-maximizing: every user, whatever their loss function and prior, can post-process its output to do as well as with any other \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism.
The cost follows from Fact 2. A pass of Algorithm 2 survives step 1 with probability \(A_U = \frac1t\sum_{u < t}e^{-u/t}\), the average acceptance over the \(t\) uniform values. It then survives step 4 unless \(B = 1\) and \(Y = 0\); since \(Y\) is geometric with ratio \(e^{-s/t}\), \(\Pr[Y = 0] = 1 - e^{-s/t}\), so that happens with probability \(\frac12(1 - e^{-s/t})\). The mean number of passes is one over the product of the two survival probabilities, \(1/\big(A_U(1 - \frac12(1 - e^{-s/t}))\big)\). That is 1.462 passes at \(b = 1\), and about 10 to 12 uniform draws per sample over the scales in Table 24.7.


24.6.5 Example: a count with \(\varepsilon = 1\)
Release a count with sensitivity 1 at \(\varepsilon = 1\), so \(b = \Delta_1 f/\varepsilon = 1\) and \(r = e^{-1} = 0.3679\). The exact count is released when the noise is 0, which happens with probability \(\Pr[Z = 0] = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r} = \frac{0.6321}{1.3679} = 0.4621\). The noise has variance \(\frac{2r}{(1 - r)^2} = 1.8413\), so its standard deviation is \(\sqrt{1.8413} = 1.357\). The output is an integer, sampled exactly, so the analysis in this section is the analysis of the code.


24.6.6 Check yourself

Why is the bound in step 2 of the privacy proof reached for \(y \ge \max(a, a')\)? (There both \(|y - a|\) and \(|y - a'|\) are \(y\) minus the input, so their difference is exactly \(|a - a'|\).)
In Algorithm 2, why can’t you skip the rejection of \((B = 1, Y = 0)\)? (Then \(\Pr[Z = 0] = \Pr[Y = 0]\) while \(\Pr[Z = \pm y] = \frac12\Pr[Y = y]\): zero would get double weight, and the PMF would not be Equation 24.8.)

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
24.7 The discrete Gaussian mechanism

24.7.1 Context
The Gaussian mechanism is the workhorse of private machine learning, because its noise grows with the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity rather than the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity, and because sums of Gaussians stay Gaussian. Canonne, Kamath and Steinke (2020) define its integer analogue and show that it keeps the privacy of the continuous Gaussian. The US Census Bureau used it for the 2020 Census redistricting data (Abowd et al., 2022), and it is the noise of choice when clients add noise before secure aggregation, which works with integers modulo a fixed number (Kairouz, Liu & Steinke, 2021).


24.7.2 Statement
As with the discrete Laplace, take the Gaussian bell curve, keep its values at the integers and normalize. The discrete Gaussian with parameter \(\sigma > 0\) and integer location \(\mu\), written \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), has PMF \[\Pr[X = x] = \frac{e^{-(x - \mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}}{\sum_{y \in \mathbb Z}e^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)}}, \qquad x \in \mathbb Z. \tag{24.11}\] The parameter \(\sigma^2\) is the variance of the continuous bell curve, not quite the variance of \(X\), as the last claim below shows. For an integer-valued \(f\), consider \(M(D) = f(D) + X\) with \(X \sim \mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, \sigma^2)\), and neighbours with \(f(D) - f(D') = \Delta\). Four claims describe how it compares with the continuous Gaussian mechanism.
First, the privacy loss is the continuous Gaussian’s, evaluated at integers. The reason is that the normalizer is the same for every integer location, so the log-ratio of two PMFs is the log-ratio of the two bell curves: \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \frac{(y - f(D'))^2 - (y - f(D))^2}{2\sigma^2}, \qquad y \in \mathbb Z. \tag{24.12}\]
Second, the smallest \(\delta\) at each \(\varepsilon\) has the same formula as for the continuous Gaussian. That smallest \(\delta\) is the probability mass by which \(M(D)\) exceeds \(e^\varepsilon\) times \(M(D')\), summed over outputs, and since the privacy loss is linear in \(y\) the outputs that contribute form a tail. The exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) (Canonne, Kamath & Steinke 2020, Theorem 7) is \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Pr\Big[X > \frac{\varepsilon\sigma^2}{\Delta} - \frac\Delta2\Big] - e^\varepsilon\Pr\Big[X > \frac{\varepsilon\sigma^2}{\Delta} + \frac\Delta2\Big], \qquad X \sim \mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, \sigma^2), \tag{24.13}\] the same expression as the continuous Gaussian’s analytic curve with \(X \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), only with the tails of the discrete distribution in place of the continuous ones.
Third, the discrete Gaussian is never worse than the continuous one in Rényi divergence. The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha > 1\), \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\sum_xp(x)^\alpha q(x)^{1 - \alpha}\), is a way of averaging the privacy loss that weights large losses more as \(\alpha\) grows; for continuous Gaussians with means \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) it equals \(\alpha(\mu - \nu)^2/(2\sigma^2)\). For every \(\alpha > 1\), \[D_\alpha\big(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(\mu, \sigma^2)\,\|\,\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(\nu, \sigma^2)\big) \le \frac{\alpha(\mu - \nu)^2}{2\sigma^2}, \tag{24.14}\] with equality for integer \(\alpha\).
Fourth, the variance is below \(\sigma^2\). Restricting the bell curve to integers pulls a little mass towards 0, by an amount that the Poisson summation lemma in the derivation computes exactly: \[\operatorname{Var}X = \sigma^2 - \frac{\sum_{k \ne 0}4\pi^2\sigma^4k^2e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2k^2}}{1 + \sum_{k \ne 0}e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2k^2}} < \sigma^2. \tag{24.15}\]


24.7.3 Derivation
Privacy loss and \(\delta(\varepsilon)\). Take \(f(D) = 0\) and \(f(D') = \Delta\); the general case shifts everything by an integer, which changes nothing.

The normalizer cancels. Under \(D\) the output \(y\) has probability \(e^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)}/Z\), and under \(D'\) it has \(e^{-(y - \Delta)^2/(2\sigma^2)}/Z\), with the same \(Z = \sum_ye^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), because shifting the sum by the integer \(\Delta\) only relabels its terms. So the ratio is the ratio of the two exponentials, and \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \frac{(y - \Delta)^2 - y^2}{2\sigma^2} = \frac{\Delta^2 - 2\Delta y}{2\sigma^2}, \tag{24.16}\] the formula of the continuous Gaussian, now only at integers \(y\).
\(\delta\) as an excess. \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP asks \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] - e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] \le \delta\) for every set \(S\). The left side is a sum of \(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\) over \(y \in S\), where \(p\) is the PMF under \(D\) and \(q\) under \(D'\), so it is largest when \(S\) holds exactly the outputs with a positive term. The smallest valid \(\delta\) is therefore \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \sum_y\big(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\big)_+\), where \((\cdot)_+\) keeps positive values and replaces negative ones by 0. This is the hockey-stick divergence of Divergences. The summand is positive exactly when \(p(y)/q(y) > e^\varepsilon\), that is when \(L_{D,D'}(y) > \varepsilon\), which by step 1 means \(\Delta^2 - 2\Delta y > 2\sigma^2\varepsilon\), or \(y < \frac\Delta2 - \frac{\varepsilon\sigma^2}{\Delta}\).
The first sum. \(\sum_{y < \Delta/2 - \varepsilon\sigma^2/\Delta}p(y) = \Pr[X < \frac\Delta2 - \frac{\varepsilon\sigma^2}{\Delta}]\). The PMF of \(X\) gives \(x\) and \(-x\) the same probability, so \(X\) and \(-X\) have the same distribution, and \(\Pr[X < c] = \Pr[-X < c] = \Pr[X > -c]\). With \(c = \frac\Delta2 - \frac{\varepsilon\sigma^2}{\Delta}\) this is \(\Pr[X > \frac{\varepsilon\sigma^2}{\Delta} - \frac\Delta2]\).
The second sum. Under \(D'\) the output is \(X + \Delta\), so \(q(y) = p(y - \Delta)\) and \(\sum_{y < \Delta/2 - \varepsilon\sigma^2/\Delta}q(y) = \Pr[X + \Delta < \frac\Delta2 - \frac{\varepsilon\sigma^2}{\Delta}] = \Pr[X < -\frac\Delta2 - \frac{\varepsilon\sigma^2}{\Delta}] = \Pr[X > \frac{\varepsilon\sigma^2}{\Delta} + \frac\Delta2]\), by the same symmetry. Subtracting \(e^\varepsilon\) times step 4 from step 3 gives Equation 24.13.

A lemma from Poisson summation. The remaining two claims rest on one question: if you sum a Gaussian bump over the integers, how does the sum depend on where the bump is centred? The answer is that it is largest when the centre is an integer. The tool is the Poisson summation formula, which turns a sum of a function over the integers into a sum of its Fourier transform over the integers: \(\sum_{x \in \mathbb Z}g(x) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb Z}\hat g(k)\) for a smooth, fast-decaying \(g\) with Fourier transform \(\hat g(k) = \int g(x)e^{-2\pi ikx}dx\) (Stein & Shakarchi 2003, ch. 5). The Fourier transform of a Gaussian is again a Gaussian, and shifting \(g\) by \(c\) multiplies the transform by the phase \(e^{-2\pi ikc}\): for \(g(x) = e^{-(x - c)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), \(\hat g(k) = \sqrt{2\pi}\sigma e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2k^2}e^{-2\pi ikc}\). Pairing \(k\) with \(-k\) adds \(e^{-2\pi ikc} + e^{2\pi ikc} = 2\cos(2\pi kc)\), which gives \[\sum_{x \in \mathbb Z}e^{-(x - c)^2/(2\sigma^2)} = \sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma\sum_{k \in \mathbb Z}e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2k^2}\cos(2\pi kc). \tag{24.17}\] Every coefficient is positive and \(\cos \le 1\), with \(\cos(2\pi kc) = 1\) for all \(k\) exactly when \(c\) is an integer. So the left side is largest at integer \(c\): shifting the lattice off the integers can only lower the sum. At \(\sigma = 0.5\) the script finds 1.271342 at \(c = 0\) and 1.235287 at \(c = 0.5\). At \(\sigma = 1\) both are 2.506628, which is \(\sqrt{2\pi}\) to six decimals: the \(k \ne 0\) terms are below \(10^{-8}\).
Rényi divergences. The idea is that the sum defining \(D_\alpha\) is, after completing a square, a Gaussian bump summed over the integers with centre \(c\), and the lemma says that sum is at most its value at an integer centre. Write \(p_\mu(x) = e^{-(x - \mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}/Z\), with \(Z\) the same for every integer \(\mu\).

Write out the summand. \(D_\alpha = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\sum_xp_\mu(x)^\alpha p_\nu(x)^{1 - \alpha}\). The powers of \(Z\) combine to \(Z^{-\alpha}Z^{\alpha - 1} = 1/Z\), and the exponent is \(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\big(\alpha(x - \mu)^2 + (1 - \alpha)(x - \nu)^2\big)\).
Complete the square. \(\alpha(x - \mu)^2 + (1 - \alpha)(x - \nu)^2 = (x - c)^2 - \alpha(\alpha - 1)(\mu - \nu)^2\) with \(c = \alpha\mu + (1 - \alpha)\nu\). (Expand: the \(x^2\) and \(x\) terms match by the choice of \(c\), and the constant is what is left.)
So \(\sum_xp_\mu^\alpha p_\nu^{1 - \alpha} = e^{\alpha(\alpha - 1)(\mu - \nu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\cdot\frac1Z\sum_xe^{-(x - c)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\).
Apply the lemma. \(Z\) is the same sum centred at 0, so the last factor is the sum centred at \(c\) divided by the sum centred at an integer. By the lemma it is at most 1, with equality when \(c\) is an integer, which it is for integer \(\alpha\) because \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are integers. Taking \(\frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\) gives Equation 24.14. The continuous Gaussian has exactly \(\alpha(\mu - \nu)^2/(2\sigma^2)\) (Divergences), so the discrete Gaussian is never worse in Rényi divergence. In the language of Privacy accounting, where zero-concentrated DP is the guarantee that every Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) is at most a constant times \(\alpha\), this is the statement that the discrete Gaussian satisfies the same zero-concentrated DP as the continuous one (Canonne, Kamath & Steinke 2020, Theorem 4).

Variance. The idea is that the normalizer, seen as a function of \(1/(2\sigma^2)\), encodes the variance in its derivative, and the lemma gives the normalizer in closed form. Let \(\tau = 1/(2\sigma^2)\) and \(Z(\tau) = \sum_xe^{-\tau x^2}\).

Variance from the normalizer. The mean is 0 because \(x\) and \(-x\) have the same probability, so \(\operatorname{Var}X = \mathbb E X^2 = \sum_xx^2e^{-\tau x^2}/Z\). Differentiating \(e^{-\tau x^2}\) in \(\tau\) brings down a factor \(-x^2\), so \(\frac{d}{d\tau}Z = -\sum_xx^2e^{-\tau x^2}\), and \(\mathbb E X^2 = -\frac{Z'(\tau)}{Z(\tau)} = -\frac{d}{d\tau}\ln Z(\tau)\).
Poisson summation at \(c = 0\). Equation 24.17, with \(\sigma = 1/\sqrt{2\tau}\), gives \(Z(\tau) = \sqrt{\pi/\tau}\,(1 + \theta(\tau))\) with \(\theta(\tau) = \sum_{k \ne 0}e^{-\pi^2k^2/\tau}\).
Differentiate. The log splits into \(\frac12\ln\pi - \frac12\ln\tau + \ln(1 + \theta(\tau))\), so \(-\frac{d}{d\tau}\ln Z = \frac{1}{2\tau} - \frac{\theta'(\tau)}{1 + \theta(\tau)}\), where \(\theta'(\tau) = \sum_{k \ne 0}\frac{\pi^2k^2}{\tau^2}e^{-\pi^2k^2/\tau} > 0\).
Substitute \(\tau = 1/(2\sigma^2)\): \(\frac{1}{2\tau} = \sigma^2\), \(\frac{\pi^2k^2}{\tau} = 2\pi^2\sigma^2k^2\) and \(\frac{\pi^2k^2}{\tau^2} = 4\pi^2\sigma^4k^2\). This is Equation 24.15. The correction is positive, so \(\operatorname{Var}X < \sigma^2\), and its leading term, from \(k = \pm1\) with the denominator close to 1, is \(8\pi^2\sigma^4e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2}\).



24.7.4 Interpretation
The privacy proof is the continuous one. The privacy loss is the same linear function, so every statement about it carries over, restricted to integer points. The only new ingredient is that integer shifts don’t change the normalizer. That is why the query must be integer-valued. To use the discrete Gaussian for a real-valued query, scale it by \(1/\gamma\) for a small step \(\gamma\) and round it to an integer first. Randomized rounding, which rounds up with probability equal to the fractional part, keeps it unbiased. Then account for the sensitivity of the rounded query, which can be slightly larger than the scaled original.
\(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is close to the continuous curve, not equal to it. The privacy loss takes only the values \((\Delta^2 - 2\Delta y)/(2\sigma^2)\) for integer \(y\); moving \(y\) by one changes the loss by \(2\Delta/(2\sigma^2) = \Delta/\sigma^2\), so these values form a lattice with spacing \(\Delta/\sigma^2\) (\(1/\sigma^2\) for \(\Delta = 1\)). As \(\varepsilon\) crosses one of these values, a whole output enters or leaves the sum for \(\delta\), so \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) has a kink at each lattice value and oscillates around the continuous curve (Figure 24.4). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\Delta = 1\) the script finds \(\delta = 0.6032\) against 0.5099 at \(\sigma = 0.5\), 0.1414 against 0.1269 at \(\sigma = 1\), and 0.0072 against 0.0068 at \(\sigma = 2\). At other \(\varepsilon\), such as just past a kink, the discrete curve is below. Neither dominates, and the gap closes as \(\sigma\) grows. In Rényi divergence, by contrast, the discrete Gaussian is never worse: at \(\sigma = 0.5\), \(D_{2.5} = 4.9808\) against 5.
The variance deficit is invisible in practice. Its relative size \(1 - \operatorname{Var}X/\sigma^2\) has leading term \(8\pi^2\sigma^2e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2}\), the leading term of Equation 24.15 divided by \(\sigma^2\). At \(\sigma = 1\) that is \(8\pi^2e^{-2\pi^2} = 78.96 \times 2.67\times10^{-9}\), so \(1 - \operatorname{Var}X/\sigma^2 = 2.11\times10^{-7}\); at \(\sigma = 2\) it is at the level of rounding error. Only below \(\sigma \approx 0.6\) does the discrete Gaussian concentrate visibly more than \(\sigma^2\) suggests: at \(\sigma = 0.5\), \(\operatorname{Var}X = 0.8601\,\sigma^2\), and at \(\sigma = 0.25\) almost all the mass is at 0 (Figure 24.5).
Sums are not discrete Gaussians. Unlike the continuous case, the sum of two independent discrete Gaussians is not exactly a discrete Gaussian. For \(\sigma \ge 1\) it is very close (Exercise 6), which is what distributed noise addition, where each client adds its own share of the noise, relies on.






Figure 24.4: Discrete against continuous Gaussian for sensitivity 1: \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) from Equation 24.13 (solid) and the analytic curve of the continuous Gaussian (dashed), for \(\sigma = 0.5\), 1 and 2. The discrete curve has a kink at each value of the lattice-valued privacy loss.









Figure 24.5: Left: \(\operatorname{Var}X/\sigma^2\) for \(X \sim \mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, \sigma^2)\), by direct summation and from Equation 24.15, against 1 for the continuous Gaussian. Right: the relative deficit \(1 - \operatorname{Var}X/\sigma^2\) on a log scale, with its leading term \(8\pi^2\sigma^2e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2}\).





24.7.5 Example: the Rényi divergence, computed
The script sums the PMFs directly to get \(D_\alpha(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, \sigma^2)\|\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(1, \sigma^2))\) (Table 24.5). Integer orders match \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) exactly, because then the centre \(c\) of the completed square is an integer and the lemma holds with equality. The order 2.5 at \(\sigma = 0.5\) has \(c = 2.5 \cdot 0 + (1 - 2.5) \cdot 1 = -1.5\), half-way between integers, and falls below the continuous value. At \(\sigma = 1\) the lemma’s slack is too small to show.

Where does the proof of Equation 24.14 use that \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are integers? (In writing both PMFs with the same normalizer \(Z\). For non-integer locations, the normalizers differ by the lemma, and the clean formula breaks.)

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
24.8 Sampling the discrete Gaussian exactly

24.8.1 Context
The privacy analysis is only as good as the sampler. Inverse-CDF sampling of \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, \sigma^2)\) needs the normalizer, which is irrational, and a floating-point uniform, which brings back the problems of Section 24.3. Algorithm 3 of Canonne, Kamath and Steinke (2020) instead proposes from the discrete Laplace and thins with an exact \(e^{-\gamma}\) coin.


24.8.2 Statement
The discrete Laplace has heavier tails than the discrete Gaussian, so it can serve as the proposal of rejection sampling (Fact 2): draw from it, and throw draws away with a probability chosen so that proposal times acceptance is proportional to \(e^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)}\). The acceptance probability is a Gaussian factor in \(|y|\), shifted so that it cancels the Laplace factor exactly.
Input a rational \(\sigma^2 > 0\). Let \(t = \lfloor\sigma\rfloor + 1\). Repeat: draw \(Y \sim \mathrm{Lap}_{\mathbb Z}(t)\) with Algorithm 2 (\(s = 1\)), and accept it with probability \[\exp\Big(-\frac{(|Y| - \sigma^2/t)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big) \tag{24.18}\] using Algorithm 1. Output the first accepted \(Y\). The output is exactly \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, \sigma^2)\). The acceptance probability per proposal is the proposal’s normalizing constant times the constant left over from the cancellation times the discrete Gaussian’s unnormalized total mass: \[A = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r}\,e^{-\sigma^2/(2t^2)}\sum_{y \in \mathbb Z}e^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)}, \qquad r = e^{-1/t}, \tag{24.19}\] which tends to \(\sqrt{\pi/2}\,e^{-1/2} = 0.7602\) as \(\sigma\) grows.


24.8.3 Derivation

Proposal times acceptance. By Fact 2, the output is the target if proposal times acceptance is proportional to \(e^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)}\). The proposal has \(\Pr[Y = y] \propto e^{-|y|/t}\). Multiply by the acceptance probability, add the exponents and expand the square: \[-\frac{|y|}{t} - \frac{(|y| - \sigma^2/t)^2}{2\sigma^2} = -\frac{|y|}{t} - \frac{y^2}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{|y|}{t} - \frac{\sigma^2}{2t^2} = -\frac{y^2}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{\sigma^2}{2t^2}. \tag{24.20}\] The \(|y|/t\) terms cancel, and what is left is \(e^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)}\) times a constant. By Fact 2 the output is \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, \sigma^2)\).
The acceptance probability is valid. The exponent \(-(|y| - \sigma^2/t)^2/(2\sigma^2)\) is at most 0, so its exponential is at most 1 and is a probability.
Everything is rational. \(t\) is an integer, computed as \(\lfloor\sqrt{\lfloor\sigma^2\rfloor}\rfloor + 1\) with integer square roots (an integer \(n\) has \(n^2 \le \sigma^2\) exactly when \(n^2 \le \lfloor\sigma^2\rfloor\), so this equals \(\lfloor\sigma\rfloor + 1\) without computing \(\sigma\)). So \(\gamma = (|y| - \sigma^2/t)^2/(2\sigma^2)\) is a ratio of integers, and Algorithm 1 applies.
The acceptance rate. \(A = \sum_y\Pr[Y = y]\,e^{-(|y| - \sigma^2/t)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), the average acceptance over proposals. With \(\Pr[Y = y] = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r}r^{|y|}\), step 1 turns each term into \(\frac{1 - r}{1 + r}e^{-\sigma^2/(2t^2)}e^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), and summing over \(y\) gives Equation 24.19. Exercise 5 derives the limit.

Concretely, for \(\sigma^2 = 4\) (\(t = \lfloor 2\rfloor + 1 = 3\), \(r = e^{-1/3}\), \(\frac{1 - r}{1 + r} = 0.1651\)). Table 24.6 computes a few rows by hand.
