ORDERS = [1 + x / 10 for x in range(1, 100)] + list(range(12, 64)) + [128, 256, 512]

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.2 Toolkit: four facts from Part 1
Every derivation below reuses four facts about the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha > 1\). They are proved in Divergences and Concentration; each is restated here with the short reason it holds. Throughout, \(r = p/q\) is the likelihood ratio, how many times more likely an output is under \(P\) than under \(Q\), and \(L = \ln r\) is the privacy loss.

27.2.1 Fact 1 — A moment of the likelihood ratio
The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) is defined as \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\int p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\,dy. \tag{27.1}\] The integral inside is an average of a power of the likelihood ratio, and you can take that average under either distribution. Multiply both sides of the definition by \(\alpha - 1\) and exponentiate: \[e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} = \int p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\,dy = \mathbb E_Q\big[r^\alpha\big] = \mathbb E_P\big[r^{\alpha - 1}\big] = \mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big]. \tag{27.2}\] The first equality after the integral holds because \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha} = q\,(p/q)^\alpha\), and integrating \(q\) times something is averaging that something under \(Q\). The next one is the change of measure \(\mathbb E_P[g] = \mathbb E_Q[r g]\), which holds because \(\int p\,g = \int q\,(p/q)\,g\): an average under \(P\) is an average under \(Q\) with each output reweighted by its likelihood ratio. Applied with \(g = r^{\alpha - 1}\), it turns \(\mathbb E_Q[r \cdot r^{\alpha-1}]\) into \(\mathbb E_P[r^{\alpha-1}]\). The last form uses \(r^{\alpha - 1} = e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\). It says that \((\alpha - 1)D_\alpha\) is the logarithm of the moment generating function (MGF) of \(L\) under \(P\), the function \(\lambda \mapsto \mathbb E_P[e^{\lambda L}]\), evaluated at \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\) (Equation 3.12). That is why a Rényi divergence is a statement about the exponential moments of the privacy loss.


27.2.2 Fact 2 — Limits and monotonicity
\(D_\alpha\) is non-decreasing in \(\alpha\). As \(\alpha \to 1\) it tends to the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence \(\mathbb E_P[L]\), the average privacy loss, and as \(\alpha \to \infty\) it tends to the max-divergence \(D_\infty = \sup_y L(y)\), the largest privacy loss of any output.
The reason is a picture. Write \(\psi(\lambda) = \ln\mathbb E_P[e^{\lambda L}]\), the log-MGF of Fact 1. It passes through the origin, since \(\psi(0) = \ln 1 = 0\), and it is convex, as every log-MGF is. By Fact 1, \(D_\alpha = \psi(\alpha - 1)/(\alpha - 1)\), the slope of the chord of \(\psi\) from the origin to the point at \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\). Chords of a convex function from a fixed point get steeper as their far end moves right, so \(D_\alpha\) grows with \(\alpha\). As \(\alpha \to 1\) the chord shrinks to the tangent at 0, whose slope is \(\psi'(0) = \mathbb E_P[L]\), the KL divergence. As \(\alpha \to \infty\), \(D_\alpha\) is the log of \(\big(\mathbb E_P[r^{\alpha - 1}]\big)^{1/(\alpha-1)}\), a power mean of \(r\) with a growing exponent, and such a mean is pulled toward the largest value of \(r\); its logarithm tends to \(\sup_y L(y)\).


27.2.3 Fact 3 — Data processing
Processing the output cannot make two distributions easier to tell apart. For any channel \(K\), a randomized map applied to the output that does not depend on which distribution produced it, \(D_\alpha(PK\|QK) \le D_\alpha(P\|Q)\), for every \(\alpha\) including \(\infty\) (Section 3.10). Here \(PK\) is the distribution of the processed output when the input is drawn from \(P\). The idea is that the likelihood ratio of a processed output is an average of the ratios of the original outputs that could have produced it, and averaging pulls ratios toward each other. Since \(x \mapsto x^\alpha\) is convex for \(\alpha > 1\), Jensen’s inequality (the power of an average is at most the average of the powers) says that averaging can only lower the moment \(\mathbb E_Q[r^\alpha]\), and with it \(D_\alpha\).


27.2.4 Fact 4 — Markov on an exponential (the Chernoff method)
For any random variable \(X\), any \(c\) and any \(\lambda > 0\), \[\Pr[X \ge c] \le e^{-\lambda c}\,\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda X}\big]. \tag{27.3}\] The reason is one line. On the event \(X \ge c\) the non-negative quantity \(e^{\lambda X}\) is at least \(e^{\lambda c}\), so its average is at least \(e^{\lambda c}\Pr[X \ge c]\); divide by \(e^{\lambda c}\). This is how an exponential moment, which is what a Rényi divergence controls, becomes a bound on a tail probability.

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.3 Rényi differential privacy

27.3.1 Context
\(\varepsilon\)-DP bounds the privacy loss \(L(y)\) at every output. That is a statement about the maximum of \(L\), which is the max-divergence. \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP allows the bound to be exceeded on outputs carrying a small amount of probability mass, measured by \(\delta\). Both summarize the distribution of the privacy loss by one point of its upper tail. The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) summarizes it differently, by an exponential moment \(\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}]\) (Fact 1). An exponential moment weights large losses more heavily than small ones, and the larger the order, the more heavily. So small orders look at the typical loss and large orders at the worst case (Fact 2). Requiring a bound at every order describes the whole upper tail of the loss, not one point of it.


27.3.2 Statement
The definition asks for the same bound on the Rényi divergence for every pair of neighbours. A mechanism \(M\) is \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP, for an order \(\alpha > 1\), if for all neighbouring datasets \(D \simeq D'\) \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big) \le \varepsilon. \tag{27.4}\] The RDP curve of \(M\) records, at each order, the smallest \(\varepsilon\) that works, which is the divergence of the worst pair of neighbours: \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) = \sup_{D \simeq D'} D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big). \tag{27.5}\] The curve has three properties, which tie its two ends to familiar quantities.

\(\alpha = \infty\) is pure DP. \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP if and only if \(\varepsilon_M(\infty) \le \varepsilon\).
Monotone. \(\varepsilon_M(\alpha)\) is non-decreasing in \(\alpha\). So an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism is \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP at every order.
\(\alpha \to 1\) is KL. As \(\alpha \to 1\), \(\varepsilon_M(\alpha)\) tends to a limit at least the largest KL divergence between neighbours, with equality for every mechanism in this chapter.



27.3.3 Derivation

Pure DP is the max-divergence. \(\varepsilon\)-DP says \(P(S) \le e^\varepsilon Q(S)\) for every event \(S\), that is, \(\ln\frac{P(S)}{Q(S)} \le \varepsilon\). The largest value of that log ratio over events equals the largest privacy loss of a single output, which is the event form of the max-divergence (Section 3.4). The reason: \(\frac{P(S)}{Q(S)} = \frac{\int_S q\,r}{\int_S q}\) is an average of the likelihood ratio \(r\) over the outputs in \(S\), weighted by \(q\), so it can never exceed the largest \(r\), and an event concentrated on the outputs where \(r\) is largest comes as close to it as you like. So \(\sup_S \ln\frac{P(S)}{Q(S)} = D_\infty(P\|Q)\), and \(\varepsilon\)-DP holds exactly when \(D_\infty(M(D)\|M(D')) \le \varepsilon\) for all neighbours, that is, when \(\varepsilon_M(\infty) \le \varepsilon\).
Monotonicity passes through the supremum. For each pair, \(D_\alpha\) is non-decreasing in \(\alpha\) (Fact 2). A supremum of non-decreasing functions is non-decreasing, because if every function in the family is larger at \(\alpha'\) than at \(\alpha\), so is the largest of them. Combined with step 1, \(\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \varepsilon_M(\infty) \le \varepsilon\) for an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism.
The KL limit. For each pair, \(D_\alpha \ge \mathrm{KL}\) and \(D_\alpha \to \mathrm{KL}\) as \(\alpha \to 1\) (Fact 2). So \(\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \ge \sup_{D \simeq D'}\mathrm{KL}\) at every order, and the limit is at least the largest KL. Equality would need the limit and the supremum to commute, which can fail in general: each pair’s divergence could approach its KL at a different speed. For the mechanisms below the curves are explicit, and you can check the limit directly.



27.3.4 Interpretation
An RDP guarantee is a curve, not a number. “Randomized response with \(p = 0.75\) is \((2, 0.8473)\)-RDP” (from the example below) is one point of it. What accountants store is the curve on a grid of orders. Each point is a valid guarantee, and different orders serve different purposes: composition works at every order at once, and the conversion to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) picks the best order at the end.
The curve sits between the average case and the worst case. As \(\alpha \to 1\) it sees only the average loss, the KL divergence. A mechanism whose loss is usually small but occasionally large has a small KL divergence, because the rare large losses barely move the average, but large high-order divergences, because a high exponential moment is dominated by those rare large losses. So it is caught at large orders. Pure DP, at \(\alpha = \infty\), is the most demanding point of the curve.
Why only \(\alpha > 1\)? Orders below 1 exist as divergences, but they are not used for privacy. The conversion to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) applies the Chernoff method to the loss, which needs an exponential moment \(\mathbb E_P[e^{\lambda L}]\) with \(\lambda = \alpha - 1 > 0\), and only orders above 1 provide one (Section 27.8).


27.3.5 Example: randomized response, outcome by outcome
Randomized response reports one person’s bit truthfully with probability \(p > \frac12\), the keep-probability, and flips it otherwise. The two neighbouring inputs are the two values of the bit. Take \(p = 0.75\). The likelihood ratio of any output is \(0.75/0.25 = 3\) or its inverse, so the mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP with \(\varepsilon = \ln\frac{p}{1-p} = \ln 3\). The curve rises from the KL value to the pure DP level (Figure 27.1). The KL value is the average loss under \(P\): the loss is \(\ln 3\) with probability 0.75 and \(-\ln 3\) with probability 0.25, so \(\mathbb E_P[L] = (0.75 - 0.25)\ln 3 = 0.5\ln 3 = 0.5493\). The pure DP level is the largest loss, \(\ln 3 = 1.0986\). The script also evaluates the formula at \(\alpha = 1.0001\) (0.5494) and \(\alpha = 1000\) (1.0983), approaching both ends. Randomized response is already a pure DP mechanism, so here the curve says little that \(\ln 3\) did not. The curve matters most for mechanisms whose \(D_\infty\) is large or infinite.






Figure 27.1: The RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) of randomized response with \(p = 0.75\), on a log scale in \(\alpha\). It starts at the KL divergence 0.549 as \(\alpha \to 1\) and rises to the pure DP level \(\ln 3 = 1.099\) as \(\alpha \to \infty\).





27.3.6 Check yourself

A mechanism is \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP. Is it \((\alpha', \varepsilon)\)-RDP for \(\alpha' < \alpha\)? For \(\alpha' > \alpha\)? (For \(\alpha' < \alpha\) yes, by monotonicity: the curve at \(\alpha'\) is at most the curve at \(\alpha\). For \(\alpha' > \alpha\) not in general: the curve can keep rising, as the Gaussian’s does.)
Why is \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) for randomized response the same in both directions of the pair? (Swapping the bit swaps \(p(y)\) and \(q(y)\) between the two outputs, and the sum \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\) over both outputs is unchanged.)

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
section: 27.4 RDP curves of the basic mechanisms
text:
27.4 RDP curves of the basic mechanisms

27.4.1 Context
To account for a mechanism you need its curve. For a mechanism that adds noise to a query’s answer, the two outputs on neighbours are the same noise distribution centred at two different answers. So the curve comes from the Rényi divergence between the noise distribution and a shifted copy of itself, which Part 1 computed for the normal and the Laplace distributions. The only new step is the supremum over neighbours: you need to know which pair of neighbouring inputs is the worst, and for these mechanisms it is the pair whose answers are furthest apart.


27.4.2 Statement
With sensitivity 1, the three curves are as follows. The Gaussian mechanism adds normal noise with standard deviation \(\sigma\) (the noise multiplier). The Laplace mechanism adds noise from the Laplace distribution with scale \(b\), whose density \(\frac{1}{2b}e^{-|y|/b}\) falls off exponentially on both sides. Randomized response has keep-probability \(p\). The Gaussian curve is a straight line in \(\alpha\), the Laplace curve is the Part 1 formula for a shift of one scale unit \(1/b\), and the randomized response curve is the sum over two outputs from the previous section: \[\text{Gaussian:}\quad \varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}, \tag{27.7}\] \[\text{Laplace:}\quad \varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\left(\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}e^{(\alpha - 1)/b} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\alpha/b}\right), \tag{27.8}\] \[\text{randomized response:}\quad \varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\Big(p^\alpha(1-p)^{1-\alpha} + (1-p)^\alpha p^{1-\alpha}\Big). \tag{27.9}\] These are Corollaries 3 and 2 and the randomized response entry of Table 2 in Mironov (2017). The Laplace formula is for a real-valued query.


27.4.3 Derivation
Gaussian. The plan is to reduce any pair of neighbours to two one-dimensional normals a distance \(s\) apart, use the Part 1 formula, and then take the largest \(s\).

One pair. With \(\Delta_2 = 1\) the noise is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I)\). On neighbours with answers \(f(D)\) and \(f(D')\), the outputs are \(\mathcal N(f(D), \sigma^2 I)\) and \(\mathcal N(f(D'), \sigma^2 I)\).
Divergence of the pair. Translating and rotating the output space is a bijection, a relabelling of the outputs that can be undone, so it changes no divergence (apply Fact 3 in both directions). So you can move \(f(D)\) to 0 and \(f(D') - f(D)\) onto the first axis. The noise is the same in every direction, so after the rotation the two distributions differ only in the first coordinate; the other coordinates are identical, independent normals under both. Rényi divergence is additive over independent coordinates (Section 3.4), because the moment of Fact 1 factorizes into a product over coordinates, and identical coordinates contribute 0. What remains is the one-dimensional divergence \(D_\alpha(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\|\mathcal N(s, \sigma^2)) = \alpha s^2/(2\sigma^2)\) (Equation 3.15), with \(s = \|f(D) - f(D')\|_2\). Part 1 derives it by noting that the privacy loss of a normal pair is itself normal, with mean \(s^2/(2\sigma^2)\) and variance \(s^2/\sigma^2\), and a normal variable’s log-MGF is known in closed form.
Supremum. The divergence grows with \(s\), and \(s \le \Delta_2 = 1\) for neighbours. So the worst pair has \(s = 1\) and gives Equation 27.7. The script also integrates \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\) numerically and gets 1.0000 at \(\alpha = 2\) and 5.0000 at \(\alpha = 10\) for \(\sigma = 1\), matching \(2/2\) and \(10/2\).

Laplace. The plan is the same: reduce to a shift, use Part 1’s closed form, and show the worst shift is the largest.

One pair. The outputs are \(\mathrm{Lap}(f(D), b)\) and \(\mathrm{Lap}(f(D'), b)\). After a translation, this is \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, b)\) against \(\mathrm{Lap}(s, b)\) with \(s = |f(D) - f(D')| \le 1\).
Divergence of the pair. Part 1 computes it by splitting the integral \(\int p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\) at the two kinks of the densities, 0 and \(s\), where the absolute values change sign; on each of the three pieces the integrand is a plain exponential (Equation 3.19). With \(t = s/b\), the shift in units of the scale, the result is the formula above with \(1/b\) replaced by \(t\).
Supremum. You need the divergence to grow with the shift, so that the largest shift is the worst. Write the argument of the logarithm as \(g(t) = \frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}e^{(\alpha - 1)t} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\alpha t}\). Its derivative is \(g'(t) = \frac{\alpha(\alpha - 1)}{2\alpha - 1}\big(e^{(\alpha - 1)t} - e^{-\alpha t}\big)\), which is positive for \(t > 0\) because the first exponent is positive and the second negative. So \(\ln g(t)/(\alpha - 1)\) increases with \(t\). The reverse direction, \(\mathrm{Lap}(s, b)\) against \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, b)\), gives the same value, because the reflection \(y \mapsto s - y\) swaps the two distributions and changes no divergence. So the worst pair has \(s = 1\), \(t = 1/b\), and gives Equation 27.8.
Numerical check. The script integrates \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\) on a grid of step \(10^{-4}\), with both kinks as grid points. For \(b \in \{0.5, 1, 4\}\) and \(\alpha \in \{1.5, 2, 10, 64\}\), the largest difference from Equation 27.8 is \(1.3 \times 10^{-8}\).

Randomized response. There is only one pair of inputs, the two values of the bit, so no supremum is needed, and Table 27.2 is its distribution. Fact 1 sums \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\) over the two outputs, as in the previous section.


27.4.4 Interpretation
Figure 27.2 draws the three curves. Two shapes appear, and which one you get depends on whether the privacy loss is bounded.
When the privacy loss is bounded, the curve levels off. For randomized response the loss is \(\pm\ln 3\). For Laplace the loss at \(y\) is \((|y - 1| - |y|)/b\), and by the triangle inequality \(\big||y - 1| - |y|\big| \le 1\), so \(|L| \le 1/b\). Since every \(D_\alpha\) is at most \(D_\infty\), the largest loss (Fact 2), the curves rise towards \(1/b\) and \(\ln 3\) and stay below them. For large \(\alpha\) you can see the approach. The first term of Equation 27.8 dominates, because \(e^{(\alpha - 1)/b}\) grows while \(e^{-\alpha/b}\) shrinks. Keeping only it, the logarithm splits as \(\ln\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{b}\), and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) gives \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \approx \frac1b + \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}\). As \(\alpha\) grows, \(\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}\) tends to \(\frac12\), so \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \approx \frac1b - \frac{\ln 2}{\alpha - 1}\): the curve approaches \(1/b\) from below at rate \(1/(\alpha - 1)\). At \(\alpha = 512\) and \(b = 1\), both the formula and this approximation give 0.9986.
When the privacy loss is unbounded, the curve grows linearly. The Gaussian privacy loss is a straight line in the output \(y\) (the squares in the two exponents cancel, leaving a linear term), so it has no maximum, and the curve \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) grows without bound. The Gaussian mechanism is therefore not \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon\). It is still \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP at every finite order, and that is all composition and conversion need.
The straight-line shape of the Gaussian curve has a meaning of its own. For a single pair, a curve of the form \(\rho\alpha\) means the privacy loss is exactly normal, \(\mathcal N(\rho, 2\rho)\). The reason is Fact 1: \((\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is the log-MGF of the loss at \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\), and with \(\varepsilon = \rho\alpha = \rho(\lambda + 1)\) it is \(\rho\lambda + \rho\lambda^2\). The log-MGF of a normal variable with mean \(m\) and variance \(v\) is \(m\lambda + v\lambda^2/2\), so this one has \(m = \rho\) and \(v = 2\rho\). Concentrated DP builds a definition on it.






Figure 27.2: RDP curves of the Gaussian mechanism (\(\sigma = 1\)), the Laplace mechanism (\(b = 1\)) and randomized response (\(p = 0.75\)), all with sensitivity 1, on a log scale in \(\alpha\) (so the straight line \(\alpha/2\) looks curved). The Laplace and randomized response curves level off at their pure DP levels \(1/b\) and \(\ln 3\) (dotted). The Gaussian curve \(\alpha/2\) grows linearly.

Table 27.4 gives the curves at four orders, from the script.

The Gaussian row is \(\alpha/2\), read off at each order. You can check the Laplace row by hand at order 2: the coefficients in Equation 27.8 are \(\frac{2}{3}\) and \(\frac13\), the prefactor \(1/(\alpha - 1)\) is 1, and with \(b = 1\) the curve is \(\ln\big(\frac23e + \frac13e^{-2}\big) = 0.6191\), the same number as in Part 1’s Laplace example. As \(\alpha \to 1\) the Laplace curve tends to the KL divergence \(1/b + e^{-1/b} - 1 = 0.3679\). You can see this from Equation 27.8: at \(\alpha = 1\) the argument of the logarithm is \(1\), and its derivative in \(\alpha\) there is \(\frac1b - 1 + e^{-1/b}\), so for \(\alpha\) near 1 the logarithm is about \((\alpha - 1)\) times that derivative, and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) leaves the derivative. At \(b = 1\) it is \(1 + e^{-1} - 1 = e^{-1} = 0.3679\).


27.4.6 Check yourself

What is the RDP curve of the Gaussian mechanism with \(\sigma = 2\) and sensitivity 1, and at which order is it 1? (\(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/(2 \cdot 2^2) = \alpha/8\), which equals 1 at \(\alpha = 8\).)
For the Gaussian mechanism on a vector query, why does only the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity matter, and not the \(\ell_1\)? (The divergence between two isotropic normals depends only on the Euclidean distance between their means, by rotation invariance.)

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.5 Composition adds curves

27.5.1 Context
Training a model runs thousands of mechanisms, each chosen after seeing the outputs of the earlier ones. You need the curve of the whole run. For a product of independent distributions, Part 1 showed that Rényi divergences add: the moment of Fact 1 is an integral of a product, which splits into a product of integrals, and the logarithm turns the product into a sum. Adaptive composition is not a product of independent distributions, because the second mechanism depends on the first output. The chain rule below shows that the curves still add, as long as each step’s curve is bounded whatever the earlier outputs were.


27.5.2 Statement
Let \(M_1\) have RDP curve \(\varepsilon_1\). Let \(M_2(\cdot\,; y_1)\) be a mechanism chosen using the first output \(y_1\), whose RDP curve is at most \(\varepsilon_2\) for every \(y_1\). The adaptive composition releases both outputs, \(M(D) = (y_1, y_2)\), with \(y_1 \sim M_1(D)\) and \(y_2 \sim M_2(D; y_1)\). Its curve is at most the sum of the two curves: \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \varepsilon_1(\alpha) + \varepsilon_2(\alpha) \qquad\text{for every } \alpha > 1. \tag{27.10}\] By induction, treating the first \(k - 1\) steps as one mechanism, \(k\) adaptively chosen mechanisms have curve at most \(\sum_{i=1}^k \varepsilon_i(\alpha)\). This is Mironov (2017), Proposition 1.


27.5.3 Derivation
The idea is to write the order-\(\alpha\) moment of the pair of outputs as a double integral, bound the inner integral (over \(y_2\)) by the worst case of the second step, and recognise what is left as the moment of the first step. Fix neighbours \(D \simeq D'\) and an order \(\alpha > 1\). Write \(p_1, q_1\) for the densities of \(y_1\) under \(D\) and \(D'\), and \(p_2(\cdot \mid y_1), q_2(\cdot \mid y_1)\) for those of \(y_2\) given \(y_1\).

Factor the joint densities. By the definition of the adaptive composition, \(y_1\) is drawn first and \(y_2\) is drawn given \(y_1\), so \(p(y_1, y_2) = p_1(y_1)\,p_2(y_2 \mid y_1)\), and the same for \(q\).
Write the order-\(\alpha\) moment as a double integral (Fact 1): \[e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} = \int\!\!\int p_1^\alpha q_1^{1-\alpha}\;p_2(y_2\mid y_1)^\alpha q_2(y_2\mid y_1)^{1-\alpha}\,dy_2\,dy_1. \tag{27.11}\] The integrand splits into a factor for \(y_1\) and a factor for \(y_2\) given \(y_1\), because a power of a product is the product of the powers.
Do the inner integral first, with \(y_1\) fixed. It is \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P_2(\cdot\mid y_1)\|Q_2(\cdot\mid y_1))}\), by Fact 1 again. For fixed \(y_1\), \(P_2(\cdot\mid y_1)\) and \(Q_2(\cdot\mid y_1)\) are the outputs of the mechanism \(M_2(\cdot\,; y_1)\) on \(D\) and \(D'\), so the divergence is at most \(\varepsilon_2(\alpha)\). Since \(\alpha - 1 > 0\), the exponential is increasing, and the inner integral is at most \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_2(\alpha)}\), whatever \(y_1\) is.
The outer integral. Pull that constant out. What is left is \(\int p_1^\alpha q_1^{1-\alpha}\,dy_1\), which by Fact 1 is \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P_1\|Q_1)} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_1(\alpha)}\). So the double integral is at most \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_2(\alpha)}e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_1(\alpha)}\).
Take logarithms and divide by \(\alpha - 1\). This gives \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \varepsilon_1(\alpha) + \varepsilon_2(\alpha)\) for this pair. The right side does not depend on the pair, so the supremum over neighbours satisfies the same bound.

To see the steps on numbers, take an adaptive pair of randomized responses. The first step reports the bit with keep-probability 0.75. The second reports it again, with keep-probability 0.75 if the first output was 1 and 0.6 if it was 0. Table 27.5 lists the four joint outcomes when the true bit is 1 (\(P\)) and 0 (\(Q\)). Each joint probability is the first step’s probability times the second’s, as in step 1.

The terms sum to 5.3472, so \(D_2 = \ln 5.3472 = 1.6766\). The bound adds the first step’s curve to the worst curve the second step can have. At order 2 the second step’s curve is \(\varepsilon_{0.75}(2) = 0.8473\) on the branch \(y_1 = 1\) and \(\varepsilon_{0.6}(2) = 0.1542\) on the branch \(y_1 = 0\), writing \(\varepsilon_p\) for the curve of randomized response with keep-probability \(p\). So the bound is \(\varepsilon_1(2) + \max\big(\varepsilon_{0.75}(2), \varepsilon_{0.6}(2)\big) = 0.8473 + \max(0.8473, 0.1542) = 1.6946\). The bound holds, and it is not tight here, because step 3 replaced the inner divergence by its worst case, 0.8473, on the branch \(y_1 = 0\) where it is really 0.1542. When the second step does not adapt (keep-probability 0.75 on both branches), the joint distribution is a product and \(D_2 = 1.6946\) exactly.


27.5.4 Interpretation
The bound is tight for products and exact for the Gaussian. When the mechanisms are independent, the inner divergence in step 3 is the same for every \(y_1\), so replacing it by its worst case loses nothing and the curves add exactly (additivity, Section 3.4). A sum of independent Gaussian steps is again Gaussian, so for Gaussian steps the composed curve is exactly the curve of a single mechanism.
This is why composition works for RDP and not for \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) directly. The order-\(\alpha\) moment is an integral of a product, so it factorizes over the steps, as step 2 used. The smallest \(\delta\) that works for a given \(\varepsilon\) is the hockey-stick divergence \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \int(p - e^\varepsilon q)_+\), the total probability by which \(P\) exceeds \(e^\varepsilon\) times \(Q\), where \((x)_+ = \max(x, 0)\). A positive part of a difference does not factorize over the steps. That is why composing \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) points needs a separate theorem with its own slack.
One condition remains. The mechanisms can be chosen adaptively, but each step’s curve bound \(\varepsilon_i\) must be fixed in advance; it must not depend on the data. When the budget itself is chosen on the fly, you need the filters and odometers of Adaptive composition.


27.5.5 Example: \(k\) Gaussian steps
With \(\sigma = 20\), each step has \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/(2 \cdot 20^2) = \alpha/800\). After \(k\) steps, the curve is \(k\alpha/800\). Setting \(k\alpha/800 = \alpha/(2\sigma'^2)\) shows that this is the curve of one Gaussian step with noise multiplier \(\sigma' = 20/\sqrt k\):

\(k = 10\): \(0.0125\,\alpha\), the curve of one Gaussian with \(\sigma = 6.3246\);
\(k = 100\): \(0.1250\,\alpha\), one Gaussian with \(\sigma = 2.0000\);
\(k = 1000\): \(1.2500\,\alpha\), one Gaussian with \(\sigma = 0.6325\).

In general, \(k\) Gaussian steps with noise multiplier \(\sigma\) have the curve of one Gaussian with noise multiplier \(\sigma/\sqrt k\). The function compose_rdp adds 1000 copies of the curve on the grid of orders and returns 2.5000 at \(\alpha = 2\), which is \(1000 \times 2/800\).
Different mechanisms compose just as easily, because their curves are added order by order. A Laplace step with \(b = 1\) followed by a Gaussian step with \(\sigma = 1\) has \(\varepsilon(2) = 0.6191 + 1 = 1.6191\) and \(\varepsilon(10) = 0.9287 + 5 = 5.9287\), reading both terms from Table 27.4.
Full-batch DP-SGD. The part’s running example runs 10,000 steps of DP-SGD with \(\sigma = 1\). If each step used the whole dataset, each would have the curve \(\alpha/2\), and the composed curve would be \(10{,}000\,\alpha/2 = 5000\,\alpha\). The converted guarantee at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) would be \(\varepsilon = 5425.5\) even when computed exactly. That is no guarantee at all. With the conversion of Section 27.8, which adds a tail term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) with \(\ln(1/\delta) = 11.5129\), RDP on ORDERS gives \(5000 \times 1.1 + 11.5129/0.1 = 5615.1\) at \(\alpha = 1.1\), the lowest order of the grid. The continuous optimum (Equation 27.18 with the composed noise multiplier \(1/\sqrt{10{,}000} = 0.01\)) is \(\alpha^* = 1 + 0.01 \times 4.7985 = 1.048\), with \(5000 + 4.7985/0.01 = 5479.9\). A curve this steep needs orders just above 1. DP-SGD is private only because each step touches a random 1% of the data. Amplification by subsampling computes the curve of a subsampled step.


27.5.6 Check yourself

Two mechanisms with curves \(\alpha/8\) and \(\alpha/2\) are composed. Which single Gaussian mechanism has the same curve? (The sum is \(5\alpha/8 = \alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma^2 = 0.8\), so \(\sigma = 0.8944\).)
In Table 27.5, where does the derivation lose \(1.6946 - 1.6766 = 0.0180\) nats? (In step 3, which bounds the inner divergence on the branch \(y_1 = 0\) by the worst case 0.8473, while the keep-probability 0.6 gives only 0.1542.)

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.6 Post-processing and group privacy

27.6.1 Context
Two properties of DP carry over to RDP. Post-processing matters because a released model or its predictions must not leak more than the training procedure that produced them. Group privacy matters because records are correlated: a family shares a household, and a user contributes many rows. For \(\varepsilon\)-DP, a group of \(k\) records gets \(k\varepsilon\) (Properties of DP), because the likelihood ratios along a chain of \(k\) neighbours multiply. For RDP the answer is weaker: the Rényi divergence does not satisfy a plain triangle inequality, so going through an intermediate dataset costs a higher order, and the order of the group guarantee must shrink as the group grows.


27.6.2 Statement
Post-processing. Applying any randomized map \(g\) that does not look at the data to the output cannot raise the curve: \(\varepsilon_{g\circ M}(\alpha) \le \varepsilon_M(\alpha)\) for every \(\alpha\).
Weak triangle inequality (Mironov 2017, Proposition 11). To bound the divergence from \(P\) to \(Q\) through an intermediate distribution \(R\), you pay with higher orders on the two legs, and the exponents \(u\) and \(v\) choose how the cost is split between them. For distributions \(P, R, Q\), an order \(\alpha > 1\) and exponents \(u, v > 1\) with \(\frac1u + \frac1v = 1\), \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \frac{\alpha - 1/u}{\alpha - 1}D_{u\alpha}(P\|R) + D_{v(\alpha - 1) + 1}(R\|Q). \tag{27.12}\] The even split \(u = v = 2\) (Corollary 4 there) doubles the order on the first leg and nearly doubles it on the second: \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \frac{\alpha - 1/2}{\alpha - 1}D_{2\alpha}(P\|R) + D_{2\alpha - 1}(R\|Q). \tag{27.13}\]
Group privacy (Mironov 2017, Proposition 2). If \(M\) is \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP and \(\alpha \ge 2^{c+1}\), then on inputs that differ in \(2^c\) records \(M\) satisfies the RDP bound of order \(\alpha/2^c\) with \(\varepsilon\) replaced by \(3^c\varepsilon\).


27.6.3 Derivation
Post-processing. \(g \circ M(D)\) is \(M(D)\) passed through the channel \(g\), the same channel whichever dataset was used, so \(D_\alpha\) can only decrease (Fact 3). Take the supremum over neighbours. For a concrete case, pass the output of randomized response (\(p = 0.75\)) through a channel that flips it with probability 0.2. When the bit is 1, the final output is 1 if the first output was 1 and was kept, or was 0 and was flipped: \(0.75 \times 0.8 + 0.25 \times 0.2 = 0.65\). When the bit is 0, it is \(0.25 \times 0.8 + 0.75 \times 0.2 = 0.35\). The two outputs are now closer in probability, and \(D_2\) drops from 0.8473 to \(\ln\big(0.65^2/0.35 + 0.35^2/0.65\big) = 0.3333\), while \(D_\infty\) drops from 1.0986 to \(\ln(0.65/0.35) = 0.6190\).
Weak triangle inequality. The idea is to write the moment for \(P\) against \(Q\) as an average under \(R\) of a product of two likelihood ratios, \(p/r\) and \(r/q\), and then separate the two factors with Hölder’s inequality. Write \(p, r, q\) for the densities of \(P, R, Q\).

Insert the middle distribution. Multiply and divide by powers of \(r\): since \((p/r)^\alpha (r/q)^{\alpha-1} r = p^\alpha r^{-\alpha + \alpha - 1 + 1} q^{1-\alpha} = p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\), Fact 1 gives \[e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} = \int p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha} = \mathbb E_R\Big[\Big(\frac pr\Big)^\alpha\Big(\frac rq\Big)^{\alpha - 1}\Big]. \tag{27.14}\]
Separate the two ratios with Hölder’s inequality. Hölder’s inequality bounds the average of a product of two non-negative quantities by a product of their higher moments: for \(u, v > 1\) with \(\frac1u + \frac1v = 1\), \(\mathbb E_R[XY] \le \big(\mathbb E_R X^u\big)^{1/u}\big(\mathbb E_R Y^v\big)^{1/v}\). (With \(u = v = 2\) it is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.) Apply it with \(X = (p/r)^\alpha\) and \(Y = (r/q)^{\alpha-1}\).
The first factor is \(\mathbb E_R[(p/r)^{u\alpha}]\), the moment of the ratio \(p/r\) at order \(u\alpha\) under \(R\). By Fact 1 at order \(u\alpha\), it equals \(e^{(u\alpha - 1)D_{u\alpha}(P\|R)}\).
The second factor is \(\mathbb E_R[(r/q)^{v(\alpha-1)}]\). By the change of measure (\(\mathbb E_R[g] = \mathbb E_Q[(r/q)g]\)) it equals \(\mathbb E_Q[(r/q)^{v(\alpha - 1) + 1}]\), and by Fact 1 at order \(v(\alpha - 1) + 1\) that is \(e^{v(\alpha - 1)D_{v(\alpha-1)+1}(R\|Q)}\).
Combine. Raise the two factors to the powers \(1/u\) and \(1/v\) and take logarithms: \((\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \frac{u\alpha - 1}{u}D_{u\alpha}(P\|R) + (\alpha - 1)D_{v(\alpha-1)+1}(R\|Q)\). Divide by \(\alpha - 1\) to get Equation 27.12, since \(\frac{u\alpha - 1}{u} = \alpha - \frac1u\). With \(u = v = 2\), \(v(\alpha - 1) + 1 = 2\alpha - 1\), which gives Equation 27.13.

Group privacy, two records (\(c = 1\)). The idea is to walk from \(D\) to \(D'\) through a dataset that differs from each in one record, and apply the weak triangle inequality to the two neighbouring steps. Let \(D\) and \(D'\) differ in two records, and let \(D_1\) be the dataset in between, a neighbour of both. Put \(P = M(D)\), \(R = M(D_1)\), \(Q = M(D')\) and let \(\beta = \alpha/2 \ge 2\) be the order of the group guarantee.

Apply Equation 27.13 at order \(\beta\). Its orders become \(2\beta = \alpha\) and \(2\beta - 1 = \alpha - 1\): \(D_\beta(P\|Q) \le \frac{\beta - 1/2}{\beta - 1}D_{\alpha}(P\|R) + D_{\alpha - 1}(R\|Q)\).
Both pairs are neighbours, so \(D_\alpha(P\|R) \le \varepsilon\), and \(D_{\alpha-1}(R\|Q) \le D_\alpha(R\|Q) \le \varepsilon\) by monotonicity (Fact 2).
Bound the factor. The factor \(\frac{\beta - 1/2}{\beta - 1} = 1 + \frac{1/2}{\beta - 1}\) decreases in \(\beta\) and equals \(\frac{1.5}{1} = \frac32\) at \(\beta = 2\), so it is at most \(\frac32\) for \(\beta \ge 2\). So \(D_\beta(P\|Q) \le \frac32\varepsilon + \varepsilon = \frac52\varepsilon \le 3\varepsilon\). Mironov states the bound with the constant 3; the argument gives \(\frac52\).

For \(c > 1\), repeat: a group of \(2^c\) records is two groups of \(2^{c-1}\), so each round halves the order and multiplies \(\varepsilon\) by 3. After \(c\) rounds the order is \(\alpha/2^c\) and the bound is \(3^c\varepsilon\); the condition \(\alpha \ge 2^{c+1}\) keeps the order of the last round at least 2.


27.6.4 Interpretation
Each doubling of the group costs half the order as well as a factor in \(\varepsilon\). The reason is step 2 of the Hölder argument: the divergence across two steps involves the product of two likelihood ratios, and to control the average of a product you need higher moments of each factor. A bound at order \(\alpha\) for one record therefore buys a bound at only about order \(\alpha/2\) for two.
How loose is this? Test it on the Gaussian, where the exact answer is known. A group of \(2^c\) records shifts a Gaussian query of sensitivity 1 by up to \(2^c\), so the exact group curve is Equation 27.7 with the shift \(2^c\) in place of 1, \(\alpha(2^c)^2/(2\sigma^2)\). Table 27.6 compares it with the bounds at \(\sigma = 1\). For two records, the weak triangle inequality loses little once \(\beta \ge 4\), and Proposition 2’s constant 3 costs a factor 1.5, because the exact value is \(2\varepsilon(2\beta)\) (\(4\beta/2 = 2 \cdot 2\beta/2\)) and Proposition 2 gives \(3\varepsilon(2\beta)\). The loss compounds with \(c\): \(3^c\) against \(2^c\) gives a factor \(1.5^c\).
So use the mechanism when you can. For the Gaussian, the exact group curve is just the curve with sensitivity \(2^c\). The generic bound matters for mechanisms whose curve on far-apart inputs you cannot compute.

27.6.5 Example: two records under Gaussian and Laplace noise
Figure 27.3 draws the two-record case for the Gaussian with \(\sigma = 1\). The weak-triangle bound hugs the exact line \(2\beta\) for \(\beta \ge 3\) and blows up near \(\beta = 1\), where its factor \(\frac{\beta - 1/2}{\beta - 1}\) does. Proposition 2 applies only from \(\beta = 2\), and its line has slope 3 instead of 2.
For the Laplace mechanism with \(b = 1\) at order 2, two records apart, the exact value is the Laplace curve with shift 2, that is Equation 27.8 with \(1/b\) replaced by 2: 1.5958. The weak triangle gives 1.9674 and Proposition 2 gives 2.4411. The pure DP group bound, \(2/b = 2\), is better than Proposition 2 here. Because the Laplace mechanism is \(1/b\)-DP, a group of two is \(2/b\)-DP, and by monotonicity that bound holds at every order. In general, for a mechanism that is already \(\varepsilon\)-DP, the group bound \(k\varepsilon\) of pure DP holds at every order, and it can beat the RDP route.

Dotted: Proposition 2’s bound \(3\varepsilon(2\beta)\), drawn from \(\beta = 2\), where its condition \(\alpha = 2\beta \ge 4\) starts to hold.

Why does post-processing need \(g\) to ignore the data? (If \(g\) reads the data, \(g \circ M\) is not a channel applied to \(M\)’s output, and Fact 3 does not apply: \(g\) could simply print a record.)

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
section: 27.7 The moments accountant is RDP in disguise
text:
27.7 The moments accountant is RDP in disguise

27.7.1 Context
Abadi et al. (2016) introduced the moments accountant to train neural networks with DP. For each \(\lambda > 0\) (in practice, the integers up to 32), it tracks the logarithm of the moment generating function (MGF) of the privacy loss, \(\ln\mathbb E[e^{\lambda L}]\). It adds these numbers over the training steps and converts the total to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) with a tail bound. Their paper predates RDP and is written in different notation. But Fact 1 already says that the log-MGF of the privacy loss at \(\lambda\) is \((\alpha - 1)D_\alpha\) at \(\alpha = \lambda + 1\). This section makes that precise: the moments accountant tracks the same object as the RDP curve, so everything in this chapter applies to it.


27.7.2 Statement
Abadi et al. define the log-moment \(\alpha_M(\lambda) = \sup_{D \simeq D'}\ln\mathbb E_{Y \sim M(D)}\big[e^{\lambda L(Y)}\big]\), the log-MGF of the privacy loss for the worst pair of neighbours. Their letter \(\alpha\) clashes with our order, so write it \(K_M(\lambda)\). It is the RDP curve one order up, multiplied by \(\lambda\): \[K_M(\lambda) = \lambda\,\varepsilon_M(\lambda + 1), \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \varepsilon_M(\alpha) = \frac{K_M(\alpha - 1)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{27.15}\] The two parts of their Theorem 2 (Abadi et al. 2016) then become the two results of this chapter that RDP needs.

Composability: \(K_M(\lambda) \le \sum_i K_{M_i}(\lambda)\). This is Equation 27.10 at order \(\lambda + 1\), multiplied by \(\lambda\).
Tail bound: \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\delta = \min_\lambda\exp\big(K_M(\lambda) - \lambda\varepsilon\big)\). This is the conversion of Section 27.8, read in the other direction: it fixes \(\varepsilon\) and solves for \(\delta\) instead of fixing \(\delta\) and solving for \(\varepsilon\) (Exercise 3).



27.7.3 Derivation
The identity is Fact 1 written out, with one change of measure.

Write the moment as a sum over outputs (for densities, an integral). Since \(e^{\lambda L} = (p/q)^\lambda\), \(\mathbb E_P\big[e^{\lambda L}\big] = \sum_y p(y)\Big(\frac{p(y)}{q(y)}\Big)^\lambda\).
Change of measure. Move one factor of \(p/q\) onto the weight: \(p\,(p/q)^\lambda = q\,(p/q)^{\lambda + 1}\). So the sum is an average under \(Q\), \(\mathbb E_Q\big[r^{\lambda + 1}\big]\).
Fact 1 at order \(\alpha = \lambda + 1\): \(\mathbb E_Q[r^{\alpha}] = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} = e^{\lambda D_{\lambda+1}(P\|Q)}\).
Take logarithms and the supremum over neighbours. The factor \(\lambda > 0\) does not change which pair is worst, so \(K_M(\lambda) = \lambda\,\varepsilon_M(\lambda + 1)\).

As a concrete check, take randomized response with \(p = 0.75\) at \(\lambda = 1\), using Table 27.2. The output 1 has \(p(1) = 0.75\) and \(e^{L} = 3\), the output 0 has \(p(0) = 0.25\) and \(e^{L} = 1/3\). So \(\mathbb E_P[e^L] = 0.75 \times 3 + 0.25 \times \frac13 = 2.2500 + 0.0833 = 2.3333\), the same two terms as in the order-2 column of Table 27.2. Its logarithm, 0.8473, is \(1 \cdot \varepsilon(2)\). At \(\lambda = 2\), the direct sum and \(2\varepsilon(3)\) both give 1.9136.


27.7.4 Interpretation
The two accountants give the same numbers with different bookkeeping. The moments accountant stores \((\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)\) where RDP stores \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), and both add over steps. Libraries that say “moments accountant” and libraries that say “RDP accountant” compute the same thing.
The identity itself is simple, so what was new in 2016? The contribution of Abadi et al. was a bound on \(K(\lambda)\) for the subsampled Gaussian step of DP-SGD, where each step uses a random fraction of the data. Amplification by subsampling derives it in RDP form.
There is also a statistical reading. The log of a moment generating function is called the cumulant generating function: its derivatives at 0 are the mean, the variance and the higher cumulants of the variable. So \(K_M(\lambda)\) is the cumulant generating function of the privacy loss of the worst pair (more precisely, the supremum over neighbours of their cumulant generating functions). If the loss is normal, all cumulants beyond the variance vanish, \(K\) is a quadratic in \(\lambda\), and the RDP curve is linear in \(\alpha\), as for the Gaussian.


27.7.5 Example: the Gaussian privacy loss
Take the Gaussian pair \(P = \mathcal N(0, 1)\), \(Q = \mathcal N(\mu, 1)\). The log-ratio of the two densities is \(-\frac{y^2}{2} + \frac{(y - \mu)^2}{2} = \frac{\mu^2}{2} - \mu y\), so the privacy loss \(L(Y) = \frac{\mu^2}{2} - \mu Y\) with \(Y \sim P\) is a linear function of a standard normal. It is therefore normal, with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu^2\) (Divergences). The log-MGF of a normal variable with mean \(m\) and variance \(v\) is \(m\lambda + v\lambda^2/2\), so \[K(\lambda) = \lambda\frac{\mu^2}{2} + \frac{\lambda^2\mu^2}{2} = \lambda\cdot\frac{(\lambda + 1)\mu^2}{2} = \lambda\,\varepsilon(\lambda + 1), \tag{27.16}\] with \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha\mu^2/2\), as Equation 27.15 says. At \(\mu = 1\), the formula gives \(K(1) = \frac12 + \frac12 = 1.0000\) and \(K(2) = 1 + 2 = 3.0000\). Averaging \(e^{\lambda L}\) over a million draws of \(Y\) gives 1.0000 and 3.0003.


27.7.6 Check yourself

A mechanism has \(K_M(\lambda) = \lambda(\lambda + 1)/8\). What is its RDP curve? (\(\varepsilon(\alpha) = K(\alpha - 1)/(\alpha - 1) = (\alpha - 1)\alpha/(8(\alpha - 1)) = \alpha/8\), a Gaussian with \(\sigma = 2\).)
Why does Abadi et al.’s composability theorem need no new proof once you know Equation 27.10? (Multiplying Equation 27.10 at order \(\lambda + 1\) by \(\lambda > 0\) gives it.)

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.8 From RDP to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)

27.8.1 Context
After composing, you hold a curve. What you report is an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair, because that is the guarantee with a direct meaning for an event: no set of outputs becomes more than \(e^\varepsilon\) times likelier, up to an additive \(\delta\) (Definition). The conversion rests on one observation. Outputs whose privacy loss is at most some threshold \(c\) already satisfy the \(e^c\) bound, so only the outputs with loss above \(c\) can break it, and their total probability can be charged to \(\delta\). That probability is a tail of the privacy loss, and a Chernoff bound controls a tail with an exponential moment, which is exactly what each point of the RDP curve provides. Every order gives a valid \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), and you pick the best one.


27.8.2 Statement
Mironov’s conversion (Mironov 2017, Proposition 3). The converted \(\varepsilon\) is the RDP value plus a tail term, which pays for \(\delta\) and shrinks as the order grows. If \(M\) is \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP, then for every \(0 < \delta < 1\) it is \((\varepsilon_\delta, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon_\delta = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{27.17}\] If you hold the whole curve, take the best order: \(\varepsilon_\delta = \min_\alpha\big[\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\big]\). For the Gaussian curve \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\), the first term grows with \(\alpha\) and the second falls, and over all real \(\alpha > 1\) the minimum is where they balance: \[\alpha^* = 1 + \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}, \qquad \varepsilon_\delta = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}}{\sigma}. \tag{27.18}\]


27.8.3 Derivation
The conversion. The plan is to split every event into outputs with small loss, which satisfy the \(e^c\) bound, and outputs with large loss, whose probability is the tail, then bound the tail with Chernoff. Fix neighbours, with privacy loss \(L\), and a threshold \(c\) to be chosen.

Split any event \(S\) by the size of the loss: \(P(S) = P(S \cap \{L \le c\}) + P(S \cap \{L > c\})\).
Bound each part. On \(\{L \le c\}\), \(\ln(p/q) \le c\), so \(p \le e^c q\) by the definition of \(L\). Integrating over \(S \cap \{L \le c\}\), the first term is at most \(e^cQ(S)\). The second term is at most \(P[L > c]\), since \(S \cap \{L > c\}\) is a subset of \(\{L > c\}\).
Chernoff on the loss. Apply Fact 4 with \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\) and then Fact 1, which says \(\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}] = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)}\): \(P[L > c] \le e^{-(\alpha-1)c}\,\mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big] = e^{(\alpha - 1)(D_\alpha(P\|Q) - c)} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - c)}\).
Choose \(c\) to make the tail \(\delta\). Setting \((\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - c) = \ln\delta\) gives \(c = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\). Then \(P(S) \le e^cQ(S) + \delta\) for every \(S\) and every pair of neighbours, which is \((c, \delta)\)-DP.

Mironov proves the same bound by a different route, through Hölder’s inequality (“probability preservation”).
The Gaussian optimum. The plan is to minimize the converted \(\varepsilon\) over the order with calculus. Write \(a = \alpha - 1 > 0\) and \(\ell = \ln(1/\delta)\). Substituting the Gaussian curve \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2) = (a + 1)/(2\sigma^2)\) into Equation 27.17 gives \(\varepsilon_\delta(a) = \frac{a + 1}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\ell}{a}\).

Set the derivative to zero: \(\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{\ell}{a^2} = 0\), so \(a^2 = 2\sigma^2\ell\) and \(a = \sigma\sqrt{2\ell}\). The function is convex in \(a > 0\) (a line plus \(\ell/a\), whose second derivative \(2\ell/a^3\) is positive), so this is the minimum.
Substitute: \(\frac{a}{2\sigma^2} = \frac{\sqrt{2\ell}}{2\sigma}\) and \(\frac{\ell}{a} = \frac{\ell}{\sigma\sqrt{2\ell}} = \frac{\sqrt{2\ell}}{2\sigma}\). The two terms that depend on \(a\) are equal at the optimum, and they add to \(\sqrt{2\ell}/\sigma\). With the constant \(\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\), this is Equation 27.18.



27.8.4 Interpretation
The conversion gives something away in two places. Step 2 charges the whole tail \(P[L > c]\) to \(\delta\). The exact smallest \(\delta\) at level \(c\) is the hockey-stick divergence, which can be written as an average over outputs, \(\delta(c) = \mathbb E_P\big[(1 - e^{c - L})_+\big]\): factoring \(p\) out of \((p - e^cq)_+\) leaves \((1 - e^{c - L})_+\). So the exact \(\delta\) charges an output with loss \(L > c\) only the fraction \(1 - e^{c - L}\) of its probability, not all of it. Step 3 then bounds the tail with a Chernoff bound, which overestimates it. From RDP to (ε, δ) and to tests removes much of both losses with sharper conversions.
The order trades two terms against each other. Small orders make the curve small but the tail term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) large; large orders do the opposite (Figure 27.4, left). The optimum moves to smaller orders as the composed curve grows, because a steeper curve makes large orders more expensive. By Equation 27.18 with \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)} = 4.7985\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), one Gaussian step with \(\sigma = 20\) wants \(\alpha \approx 1 + 20 \times 4.7985 \approx 97\), while 1000 steps, with composed noise multiplier \(20/\sqrt{1000} = 0.6325\), want \(\alpha \approx 1 + 0.6325 \times 4.7985 \approx 4\). That is why the grid runs from 1.1 to 512.
For many Gaussian steps the conversion reproduces the square-root growth of advanced composition. For \(k\) steps, Equation 27.18 with \(\sigma/\sqrt k\) in place of \(\sigma\) gives \(\varepsilon_\delta = \frac{k}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)}}{\sigma}\). The second term grows like \(\sqrt k\), the same shape as advanced composition, but with constants derived from the Gaussian curve instead of from a worst-case \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\) point.


27.8.5 Example: one Gaussian step, and many
One step, \(\sigma = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Here \(\ln(1/\delta) = 11.5129\) and \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)} = \sqrt{23.0259} = 4.7985\). The curve is \(\alpha/2\), and Equation 27.17 adds \(11.5129/(\alpha - 1)\). Three orders show the trade-off:

\(\alpha = 2\): \(1.0000 + 11.5129 = 12.5129\);
\(\alpha = 5.8\): \(2.9000 + 2.3985 = 5.2985\);
\(\alpha = 20\): \(10.0000 + 0.6059 = 10.6059\).

At the small order the tail term dominates, at the large order the curve does, and in between they nearly balance. The grid’s best order is 5.8, next to the continuous optimum \(\alpha^* = 1 + 4.7985 = 5.7985\), and both give \(\varepsilon = 5.2985\).
To see how good this is, compare it with the exact \(\varepsilon\) of the Gaussian mechanism at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The exact privacy curve of a Gaussian pair whose means are \(\mu = 1/\sigma\) standard deviations apart is \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) \tag{27.19}\] (Balle & Wang 2018; Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, \(\Phi(t)\) being the probability that a standard normal variable is below \(t\). It is the hockey-stick divergence \(P(S) - e^\varepsilon Q(S)\) evaluated on the set \(S\) of outputs whose privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\): since the loss is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and standard deviation \(\mu\) under \(P\) (and mean \(-\mu^2/2\) under \(Q\)), each of \(P(S)\) and \(Q(S)\) is a normal tail, which gives the two \(\Phi\) terms. Solving \(\delta(\varepsilon) = 10^{-5}\) for \(\varepsilon\) by bisection gives 4.3772. The conversion is 21% too large (\(5.2985/4.3772 = 1.21\)). Read the other way, the mechanism at \(\varepsilon = 5.2985\) actually has \(\delta = 1.300 \times 10^{-7}\), 76.9 times smaller than the conversion promises (\(10^{-5}/(1.300 \times 10^{-7}) = 76.9\)).
\(k\) steps, \(\sigma = 20\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Table 27.7 compares four ways to account for \(k\) Gaussian steps. The exact value is available because \(k\) steps are one Gaussian with \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\). The two generic routes from Part 3 first turn each step into one \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\) point of its exact curve, then compose the points. Basic composition adds the per-step guarantees, both the \(\varepsilon\)s and the \(\delta\)s, so it spends \(\delta/k\) per step and reports \(k\varepsilon_0\). Advanced composition treats the total privacy loss as a sum of \(k\) independent bounded terms and bounds its tail. It spends a fraction \(s\) of \(\delta\) on the \(k\) per-step slacks, \(\delta_0 = s\delta/k\) each, and the rest, \(\delta' = (1 - s)\delta\), on the tail of the sum, and it gives \[\varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2). \tag{27.20}\] The first term is the size of a fluctuation of the summed loss that is exceeded with probability at most \(\delta'\), from Azuma’s inequality for a sum of \(k\) terms each between \(-\varepsilon_0\) and \(\varepsilon_0\). The second term is a bound on the mean of the summed loss: \(k\) times the largest mean loss of one step, \(\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\). The script picks the best \(s\) on the grid Part 3 uses, the powers \(10^{-1/4}, 10^{-2/4}, \dots, 10^{-10}\); at every \(k\) in Table 27.7 it lands on \(s = 10^{-1/4} \approx 0.56\).
The second term is the sharper form from Part 3. The textbook form, \(k\varepsilon_0(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\) (Dwork & Roth 2014, Theorem 3.20), would give 105.86 at \(k = 1000\) instead of 68.01.

Advanced composition is loose, and it gets looser as \(k\) grows: it is 5 to 9 times the exact value, because each step’s curve was collapsed to one point before composing. For one step it is even worse than basic composition, since the factor \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta')}\) is paid even when \(k = 1\), when there is no sum to concentrate.
RDP is 18% to 57% above exact in this table, and it gets tighter as \(k\) grows. At \(k = 1\) the best order on the continuous scale would be 97.0 (giving 0.241), but the grid jumps from 63 to 128, so the grid’s answer 0.251 is a little worse. For \(k \ge 10\) the grid optimum agrees with Equation 27.18 to within 0.001 (0.771 at 31.3, 2.524 at 10.6, and 8.838 on the grid against 8.837 at \(\alpha^* = 4.03\)). The remaining gap to the exact value is the conversion’s slack, which the next chapter reduces.
That slack depends on the composed \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\), the distance between the two composed Gaussians in standard deviations. At the continuous optimum, Mironov’s conversion is 1.07 times exact at \(\mu = 10\), 1.21 at \(\mu = 1\), 1.42 at \(\mu = 0.1\) and 1.76 at \(\mu = 0.01\). Weak composed mechanisms pay the most, because as \(\mu \to 0\) the exact \(\varepsilon\) falls faster than the Chernoff bound does.

The converted \(\varepsilon\) (black) is the sum of the RDP curve (dashed) and the tail term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) (dotted). Its minimum over the grid, 8.84 at \(\alpha = 4\), sits above the exact value 7.51 (green). Right: total \(\varepsilon\) against the number of steps \(k\) on log axes, for advanced composition, RDP with Mironov’s conversion, and the exact value.





27.8.6 Check yourself

A mechanism is \((10, 0.5)\)-RDP. What \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\)-DP does Equation 27.17 give at that order? (\(0.5 + 11.5129/9 = 1.7792\).)
In Table 27.7, why is the best order 4 for \(k = 1000\) steps but 128 for one step? (The composed curve is 1000 times steeper, so large orders cost more. In Equation 27.18, replacing \(\sigma\) by \(\sigma/\sqrt k\) shrinks \(\alpha^* - 1\) by \(\sqrt k\).)

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
section: 27.9 Code: check every curve and every conversion
text:
27.9 Code: check every curve and every conversion
The script code/renyi_dp.py computes every number in this chapter and draws every figure. The curves are small typed functions (gaussian_rdp, laplace_rdp, randomized_response_rdp). title: 28  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
28.1 Why this matters
Rényi differential privacy (RDP) is the quantity accountants track, because it composes by adding curves (previous chapter). Recall what the curve is. For two neighbouring datasets, which differ in one person’s record, a mechanism produces two output distributions, \(P\) on the dataset without your record and \(Q\) on the one with it. For each order \(\alpha > 1\), the Rényi divergence \(D_\alpha(P\|Q)\) measures how far apart they are: it is a logarithmic average of the likelihood ratio \(p/q\) raised to the power \(\alpha - 1\), so larger orders weigh the outputs where \(P\) is much more likely than \(Q\) more heavily. The RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) bounds that divergence, over all neighbouring pairs, at every order. When mechanisms run one after another, their curves add.
The curve is not the quantity anyone reports. A paper, a model card or a regulator asks for \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differential privacy (DP), or for a statement about attacks: how much better than guessing can a test tell whether your record was used? So every RDP analysis ends with a conversion, and the conversion decides the number you publish. This chapter answers three questions: how much the standard conversion loses, and where; what the best \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) is that you can claim from an RDP curve, and which order to use for it; and what an RDP curve says about tests, and what it can never say.
One idea organizes all three answers: an RDP curve is a summary of the privacy loss distribution, and converting it asks for the largest \(\delta\) consistent with that summary. The privacy loss of an output is the logarithm of how much more likely that output is under \(P\) than under \(Q\). Drawn at random from the mechanism, it is the privacy loss random variable (PRV), and \(\delta\) is a particular average over it. The RDP curve records the moment generating function (MGF) of the PRV, the average of \(e^{\lambda L}\) for a loss \(L\), at the points \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\), and nothing else. A conversion has to bound the average that defines \(\delta\) using only those MGF values. Mironov’s conversion does this with Markov’s inequality and throws away most of what the summary says. The improved conversion, and the hypothesis-testing view behind it, recover almost all of it: for the Gaussian mechanism the improved conversion agrees to three decimals with the best any method could do with the curve alone. What remains, 5 to 10% of \(\varepsilon\), is not a defect of any formula. A two-outcome mechanism has an RDP curve no larger than the Gaussian’s and a larger \(\delta\), so no conversion that sees only the curve can do better. Table 28.1 lists the results.
Conventions. \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\) are the output distributions of the mechanism \(M\) on neighbouring datasets \(D\) and \(D'\), with densities \(p\) and \(q\). As in Part 3, \(D'\) is the dataset that holds your record and \(D\) the one without it. A guarantee must hold for every ordered pair of neighbours, so every bound below holds just as well with the roles of \(P\) and \(Q\) swapped. The privacy loss at an output \(y\) is \(L(y) = \ln(p(y)/q(y))\): positive when \(y\) is more likely under \(D\) than under \(D'\), negative when it is less likely. With \(Y \sim P\), the random number \(L(Y)\) is the PRV (composition). Throughout, \(\alpha\) is the Rényi order and never an error rate. A test of “the output came from \(P\)” against “it came from \(Q\)”, that is, of “your record was not used” against “it was”, looks at the output and either accepts or rejects. It has type I error \(a\), the probability that it rejects although the output came from \(P\) (for a membership test, its false-positive rate: saying \(D'\) when the data were \(D\)), and type II error \(b\), the probability that it accepts although the output came from \(Q\), as in hypothesis testing, where they were called \(\alpha_\phi\) and \(\beta_\phi\). Its power \(1 - b\) is the probability that it correctly rejects when the output came from \(Q\).
The running example is the Gaussian mechanism. One step adds noise \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) to a query of sensitivity 1, where \(\sigma\) is the noise multiplier. After dividing the output by \(\sigma\), the two worlds are \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(\mathcal N(1/\sigma, 1)\). With \(k\) independent steps the outputs form a vector, and only its component along the direction of the shift differs between the worlds; that shift has length \(\sqrt{k}/\sigma\). So every quantity in this chapter depends only on \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\), and the composed mechanism is the pair \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\), \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\). Its RDP curve is \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha\mu^2/2\): one step has curve \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) (previous chapter), and \(k\) steps add \(k\) copies, \(k\alpha/(2\sigma^2) = \alpha\mu^2/2\). All numbers use \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and the part’s grid of 154 orders: 1.1 to 10.9 in steps of 0.1, every integer from 12 to 63, and then 128, 256 and 512.

title: 28  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
section: 28.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
28.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

28.2.1 Fact 1 — δ is an expectation over the privacy loss
\((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for the ordered pair \((P, Q)\) says \(P(S) \le e^\varepsilon Q(S) + \delta\) for every event \(S\) (definition): any set of outputs is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times more likely under \(D\) than under \(D'\), up to an additive slack \(\delta\). The smallest \(\delta\) that works is therefore the largest value of \(P(S) - e^\varepsilon Q(S)\) over all events. That largest value is reached by putting into \(S\) exactly the outputs with \(p > e^\varepsilon q\), because each such output adds a positive amount \(p - e^\varepsilon q\) and every other output would subtract. The result, \(\int (p - e^\varepsilon q)_+\), where \((x)_+ = \max(x, 0)\), is the hockey-stick divergence \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q)\) of divergences. Written in terms of the privacy loss, it is an average over the PRV: \[\delta(\varepsilon) = E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_P\big[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big] = P[L > \varepsilon] - e^\varepsilon Q[L > \varepsilon]. \tag{28.1}\]
The second form comes from factoring \(p\) out of the integrand. Where \(p > 0\), \((p - e^\varepsilon q)_+ = p\,(1 - e^\varepsilon q/p)_+\), and \(q/p = e^{-L}\), so this is \(p\,(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\); integrating \(p\) times a function of the output is taking its average under \(P\). The integrand is positive exactly where \(L > \varepsilon\), and integrating \(p - e^\varepsilon q\) over that set gives the last form.
The second form is the one to remember. Each output contributes to \(\delta\) only if its privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), and then only the fraction \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L}\) of its probability. An output with loss \(L = \varepsilon + \ln 2\) contributes half its probability, since \(1 - e^{-\ln 2} = 1 - \frac12\). An output with loss just above \(\varepsilon\) contributes almost nothing, and only an output with infinite loss contributes all of its probability.


28.2.2 Fact 2 — RDP is the MGF of the privacy loss
The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) is defined by \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\int p^\alpha q^{1 - \alpha}\). Write \(p^\alpha q^{1 - \alpha} = p\,(p/q)^{\alpha - 1}\) and \((p/q)^{\alpha - 1} = e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\): the integral is the average under \(P\) of \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\), which is the MGF of the PRV at the point \(\alpha - 1\). An RDP bound \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \varepsilon(\alpha)\) is therefore a bound on that MGF value: \[\mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big] = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}. \tag{28.2}\] This is Equation 3.12 of divergences, with the exponent multiplied out.
So knowing the RDP curve at the orders \(\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dots\) is knowing (an upper bound on) the MGF of the PRV at \(\alpha_1 - 1, \alpha_2 - 1, \dots\). That is the whole summary. Every conversion is a way of bounding the average in Equation 28.1 using only the averages in Equation 28.2.


28.2.3 Fact 3 — Data processing on a test
A test \(\phi\) maps the output to “reject” or “accept”, so its outcome is a coin. Under \(P\) the coin shows “reject” with probability \(a\); under \(Q\) it shows “reject” with probability \(1 - b\). Turning the output into this coin is post-processing, and post-processing cannot increase a Rényi divergence: this is the data processing inequality of divergences. The short reason is that merging outputs can only shrink the sum \(\int p^\alpha q^{1 - \alpha}\). The function \(x^\alpha y^{1 - \alpha}\) is convex for \(\alpha > 1\) and scales linearly when \(x\) and \(y\) are both multiplied by the same factor, and such a function satisfies \(g(x_1 + x_2, y_1 + y_2) \le g(x_1, y_1) + g(x_2, y_2)\); merging two outputs replaces the right side by the left. (A test that randomizes its decision is handled the same way; divergences gives the general proof.) So, writing \(\mathrm{Bern}(x)\) for “reject with probability \(x\)”, \[D_\alpha\big(\mathrm{Bern}(a)\,\|\,\mathrm{Bern}(1 - b)\big) \le D_\alpha(P\|Q). \tag{28.3}\] In words: a test cannot tell the two worlds apart better, in Rényi divergence, than the full output does.


28.2.4 Fact 4 — The Gaussian pair, exactly
For the running example everything can be computed in closed form, which is what lets this chapter measure each conversion against the truth. Take \(P = \mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(Q = \mathcal N(\mu, 1)\). The privacy loss is the difference of the two log densities, \(L(y) = -\frac{y^2}{2} + \frac{(y - \mu)^2}{2} = \frac{\mu^2}{2} - \mu y\). It is a linear function of \(y\), so under \(P\), where \(y\) is standard normal, the PRV is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and standard deviation \(\mu\): \(\mathcal N(\mu^2/2, \mu^2)\).
Now evaluate the last form of Equation 28.1. Write \(\Phi(x) = \Pr[Z \le x]\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function. Under \(P\), \(L > \varepsilon\) means \(y < \mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu\), which has probability \(\Phi(\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu)\). Under \(Q\), write \(y = \mu + z\) with \(z\) standard normal; then \(L = -\mu^2/2 - \mu z\), and \(L > \varepsilon\) means \(z < -\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu\). So \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big), \tag{28.4}\] the closed form already derived in divergences. It falls as \(\varepsilon\) grows, because the integrand \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\) does, so inverting it by bisection gives the exact \(\varepsilon\) at any \(\delta\). The script evaluates the second term in logarithms so that it stays accurate when \(e^\varepsilon\) overflows. As a check, at \(\mu = 1\) a Riemann sum of \(\mathbb E_P[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+]\) over the normal density gives \(1.2694\times10^{-1}\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(1.5372\times10^{-3}\) at \(\varepsilon = 3\), the same as the closed form to all printed digits.

text:
28.3 Where Mironov’s conversion loses

28.3.1 Context
Rényi DP derived Mironov’s conversion: an \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP mechanism, one whose Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) is at most \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), is \((\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1), \delta)\)-DP. It is easy to remember and easy to compute. This section rewrites that proof as two inequalities on the privacy loss and measures what each one costs on the Gaussian, so that you can see where the excess comes from.


28.3.2 Statement
The proof first replaces \(\delta\) by the probability that the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), and then bounds that probability with the MGF. For every order \(\alpha > 1\) and every \(\varepsilon\), \[\delta(\varepsilon) \;\overset{(1)}{\le}\; P[L > \varepsilon] \;\overset{(2)}{\le}\; e^{(\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon)}, \tag{28.5}\] and setting the right side equal to \(\delta\) gives Mironov’s conversion \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{28.6}\]


28.3.3 Derivation
The proof in Rényi DP has exactly these two steps. Written with Fact 1 and Fact 2:

Drop the fraction. Fact 1 says each output with \(L > \varepsilon\) contributes the fraction \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L}\) of its probability. Step 1 rounds that fraction up to 1: \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+ \le \mathbf 1[L > \varepsilon]\), because the left side is 0 when \(L \le \varepsilon\) and below 1 otherwise. Averaging under \(P\) gives inequality (1). This is the step that charges the whole tail \(P[L > \varepsilon]\) to \(\delta\).
Bound the tail by the MGF (Chernoff). Markov’s inequality says a nonnegative random variable exceeds a level \(t\) with probability at most its average divided by \(t\). Apply it to \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\), which exceeds \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}\) exactly when \(L > \varepsilon\): \(P[L > \varepsilon] \le \mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}]\,e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}\). Fact 2 bounds the average by \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\), which gives inequality (2).
Solve for ε. Setting \(e^{(\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon)} = \delta\) and taking logarithms gives \((\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon) = -\ln(1/\delta)\), which is Equation 28.6. DP also needs the inequality with the roles of the two datasets swapped, the pair \((Q, P)\). RDP bounds \(D_\alpha(Q\|P)\) by the same curve, because swapping two neighbours gives two neighbours, so the same argument applies.



28.3.4 Interpretation
The two steps lose in different places. Table 28.2 measures them on the Gaussian, converting each inequality of Equation 28.5 into an \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The first row is the exact \(\varepsilon\) from Equation 28.4. The second is the \(\varepsilon\) at which the tail \(P[L > \varepsilon] = \Phi(\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu)\) equals \(\delta\). Since \(\Phi(x) = 10^{-5}\) at \(x = -\Phi^{-1}(1 - 10^{-5}) = -4.2649\), where \(\Phi^{-1}\) is the inverse of \(\Phi\), this is \(\varepsilon = \mu^2/2 + 4.2649\,\mu\): \(0.5 + 4.2649 \approx 4.765\) at \(\mu = 1\) and \(50 + 42.649 = 92.649\) at \(\mu = 10\). The third row is Mironov’s \(\varepsilon'\) minimized over the grid.

Step 1 ignores how far past \(\varepsilon\) the loss goes. An output with \(L\) slightly above \(\varepsilon\) counts fully toward the tail but almost nothing toward \(\delta\). The density of the Gaussian PRV is falling steeply at \(\varepsilon\), which sits several standard deviations above its mean, so most of the tail sits just above \(\varepsilon\), and step 1 overcounts it.
Step 2 replaces a tail by an MGF, and that costs more. Markov’s inequality is tight only for a variable that puts all its mass on 0 and on the level \(t\); the Gaussian PRV is nothing like that, so the bound is far above the true tail at 4.765. At \(\mu = 10\) this step costs 5.377 of the \(98.026 - 91.817 = 6.209\) total excess (Table 28.2). Of that, 0.041 is the grid’s: over all real orders Mironov’s conversion gives 97.985 at \(\alpha = 1.480\), against 98.026 at the grid’s 1.5.
On the \(\delta\) side the losses are multiplicative. At Mironov’s \(\varepsilon = 5.299\) for \(\mu = 1\), the exact \(\delta\) is \(1.300\times10^{-7}\). The tail is \(7.992\times10^{-7}\), 6.1 times larger, and Mironov’s bound is \(1.000\times10^{-5}\), 12.5 times larger again. You pay for \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and get \(1.3\times10^{-7}\).


28.3.5 Example: one release of a mean
You release the mean of a bounded statistic with the Gaussian mechanism at noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1\), so \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/2\). Mironov’s conversion gives \(\alpha/2 + \ln(10^5)/(\alpha - 1)\) at each order. The first term grows with the order and the second shrinks, so there is a best order in between. Over the continuous range of orders the sum is smallest at \(\alpha = 5.799\), with \(\varepsilon' = 5.299\) (Section 28.6 derives both); the grid’s best order, 5.8, gives the same 5.299. The exact answer is 4.377. Reporting Mironov’s number overstates \(\varepsilon\) by 0.921, which means \(e^{0.921}\) more “allowed” likelihood ratio for every output.


28.3.6 Check yourself

Why does step 2 lose about ten times more at \(\mu = 10\) than at \(\mu = 1\)? (The PRV has mean \(\mu^2/2\) and standard deviation \(\mu\). At the best order, Mironov’s \(\varepsilon^* = \mu^2/2 + 2\sqrt{(\mu^2/2)\ln(1/\delta)} = \mu^2/2 + \mu\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\) sits \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)} \approx 4.799\) standard deviations above the mean, while the true tail point sits \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \delta) = 4.2649\) standard deviations above it. The gap is a fixed number of standard deviations, about 0.534, so in \(\varepsilon\) it grows like \(\mu\): 0.534 at \(\mu = 1\), about ten times that at \(\mu = 10\).)
Is step 1 ever tight? (Only when every output with \(L > \varepsilon\) has \(L = \infty\), where \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L} = 1\), such as a mechanism that sometimes reveals the record outright, with the pair ordered so that \(P\) is the output on the dataset that holds the record.)
