title: 29  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.5 From zCDP to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)

29.5.1 Context
Whatever you account in, you report \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). Fact 3 turns an RDP curve into \((\varepsilon, \delta)\): each order \(\alpha\) gives a valid \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\), and you take the best order. For a \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism the RDP curve is known in closed form, \(\rho\alpha\), so that optimization over \(\alpha\) can be done by hand. The result is the formula most papers quote. The improved conversion of Fact 3 has no closed form but is easy to minimize numerically.


29.5.2 Statement
Putting the line \(\rho\alpha\) into Mironov’s conversion and choosing the best order gives the simple conversion. A \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for every \(\delta \in (0, 1)\) with \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}, \tag{29.10}\] attained at \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/\rho}\) (Bun & Steinke 2016, Proposition 1.3). Putting the same line into the improved conversion (Canonne, Kamath & Steinke 2020, Proposition 12 and Corollary 13) gives a smaller \(\varepsilon\), as a minimum over orders that has to be computed numerically: \[\varepsilon = \min_{\alpha > 1}\left[\rho\alpha + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1} + \ln\Big(1 - \frac1\alpha\Big) - \frac{\ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\right]. \tag{29.11}\] For calibration you need the reverse: the largest \(\rho\) whose simple conversion stays within a target \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta\). Solving Equation 29.10 for \(\rho\), a target \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta\) is met by any \[\rho \le \Big(\sqrt{\varepsilon + \ln(1/\delta)} - \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}\Big)^2. \tag{29.12}\]


29.5.3 Derivation

Plug the line into Mironov’s conversion. By Fact 3 with \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \rho\alpha\), every \(\alpha > 1\) gives a valid \(\varepsilon\): \(g(\alpha) = \rho\alpha + \ell/(\alpha - 1)\), where \(\ell = \ln(1/\delta)\). The first term grows with the order and the second shrinks, so there is a best order in between.
Minimize. \(g'(\alpha) = \rho - \ell/(\alpha - 1)^2\) is zero at \(\alpha - 1 = \sqrt{\ell/\rho}\). Both terms of \(g\) are convex on \(\alpha > 1\) (a line, and a positive multiple of \(1/(\alpha - 1)\)), so \(g\) is convex and this stationary point is the minimum.
Evaluate. At \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{\ell/\rho}\), the first term is \(\rho\alpha^* = \rho + \rho\sqrt{\ell/\rho} = \rho + \sqrt{\rho\ell}\) and the second is \(\ell/\sqrt{\ell/\rho} = \ell\sqrt{\rho/\ell} = \sqrt{\rho\ell}\). Their sum is \(\rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ell}\), which is Equation 29.10. Bun and Steinke reach the same formula through the tail bound: by Equation 29.4 with \(\lambda = 2\sqrt{\rho\ell}\), \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon] \le e^{-4\rho\ell/(4\rho)} = \delta\) for this \(\varepsilon\), and a privacy loss that exceeds \(\varepsilon\) with probability at most \(\delta\) gives \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP (the argument of Fact 3; see also Composition).
The improved form is Fact 3’s improved conversion with \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \rho\alpha\). Its derivation is in From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests. The script minimizes it over a fine continuous grid of 20,001 log-spaced orders from \(1 + 10^{-4}\) to \(1 + 10^4\), and, for comparison, over the part’s grid ORDERS, the fixed list of orders on which this part’s accountants store RDP curves.
Inversion. Write \(x = \sqrt\rho\). Equation 29.10 reads \(x^2 + 2x\sqrt\ell = \varepsilon\). Adding \(\ell\) to both sides completes the square: \((x + \sqrt\ell)^2 = \varepsilon + \ell\). Take the positive root, \(x = \sqrt{\varepsilon + \ell} - \sqrt\ell\), and square it. Since the simple \(\varepsilon\) grows with \(\rho\), any smaller \(\rho\) also meets the target.



29.5.4 Interpretation
For a Gaussian, every bit of slack is in the conversion. Dividing the output of a Gaussian mechanism by \(\sigma\) changes nothing about privacy, because the map can be undone. After the division the two output distributions are \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) with \(\mu = \Delta/\sigma\), and \(\rho = \Delta^2/(2\sigma^2) = \mu^2/2\). So a \(\rho\)-zCDP Gaussian mechanism is the pair \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) vs \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) with \(\mu = \sqrt{2\rho}\), the \(\mu\) of \(\mu\)-Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) in f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy. For this pair the exact \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) trade-off is known. The privacy profile \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the smallest \(\delta\) for which the mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, the largest value of \(P(S) - e^\varepsilon Q(S)\) over sets of outputs \(S\). The best set is the outputs where the privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), so \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[L > \varepsilon]\). The privacy loss is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu^2\) under \(P\) (as in Section 29.3), and with mean \(-\mu^2/2\) under \(Q\), so each probability is a value of \(\Phi\) (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms): \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big). \tag{29.13}\] The zCDP line is exact for the Gaussian, so the gap between Equation 29.10 and the exact \(\varepsilon\) from Equation 29.13 is the price of the conversion alone. Figure 29.3 shows it. The simple formula is 21% too large at \(\rho = 0.5\) (ratio \(5.299/4.377 = 1.210\)), the improved conversion 8% (ratio \(4.728/4.377 = 1.080\)). Both gaps shrink, in relative terms, as \(\rho\) grows.
The grid hardly matters here. On ORDERS, the improved conversion agrees with the fine grid to within \(0.001\) for \(\rho \le 1\). At \(\rho = 50\) the best order on the fine grid is \(1.472\), between the grid points \(1.4\) and \(1.5\), and ORDERS gives \(96.116\) against \(96.035\).






Figure 29.3: Left: \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for a \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism, from the simple formula Equation 29.10, the improved conversion Equation 29.11, and the exact value for the Gaussian mechanism with \(\mu = \sqrt{2\rho}\). Right: each conversion divided by the exact Gaussian value.





29.5.5 Example: \(\varepsilon\) for \(k\) Gaussian steps
\(k\) Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 1\) are \((k/2)\)-zCDP, since each costs \(1/2\) and composition adds. Table 29.4 converts a range of \(\rho\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), where \(\ln(1/\delta) = 11.5129\). The row \(\rho = 0.5\) is one step of the part’s small example. For it the best order of the simple formula is \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{11.5129/0.5} = 5.799\), and the simple \(\varepsilon\) is \(0.5 + 2\sqrt{0.5 \times 11.5129} = 5.299\). 29.5.6 Check yourself

You have a budget of \(\rho = 1\) and spend \(0.5\) on one query. How much \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is left for the rest? (The question has no clean answer: \(\varepsilon\) does not add, because the conversion is a square root of \(\rho\), not a multiple of it. Budgets are kept in \(\rho\), which adds, and converted once at the end. The whole run is \(7.077\)-DP by the improved conversion whatever the split.)
Why does the simple formula’s best order \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/\rho}\) grow as \(\rho\) shrinks? (A small \(\rho\) makes the term \(\rho\alpha\) cheap, so the conversion can afford a high order, which shrinks the \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) term.)

title: 29  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.6 Group privacy

29.6.1 Context
A household, a user with many records, or a hospital contributes several records. Group privacy asks how the guarantee degrades for datasets that differ in \(m\) records. (This section writes \(m\) for the group size, because \(k\) is the number of steps in this part.) Two such datasets are joined by a chain of \(m\) neighbouring steps, each changing one record. For pure DP the answer is \(m\varepsilon\): each step multiplies probabilities by at most \(e^\varepsilon\), so \(m\) steps multiply them by at most \(e^{m\varepsilon}\) (Properties of DP). For \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, \(\delta\) blows up exponentially in \(m\), because each step’s \(\delta\) is multiplied by the \(e^\varepsilon\) factors of the later steps. For RDP the chain argument works only if you give up orders, because Rényi divergence has no triangle inequality: \(D_\alpha(P\|Q)\) is not bounded by \(D_\alpha(P\|R) + D_\alpha(R\|Q)\) at the same order. zCDP gets a clean answer because it constrains every order at once, so it can pay for the chain in higher orders.


29.6.2 Statement
The answer is that the slope grows with the square of the group size, exactly as it does for the Gaussian, where a group shifts the mean \(m\) times as far. If \(M\) is \(\rho\)-zCDP and \(D\), \(D'\) are joined by a chain of \(m\) neighbouring steps, then for every \(\alpha > 1\) \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big) \le m^2\rho\,\alpha, \tag{29.14}\] so \(M\) is \(m^2\rho\)-zCDP for groups of size \(m\) (Bun & Steinke 2016, Proposition 1.9). The Gaussian mechanism attains it. The tool is a triangle-like inequality for Rényi divergence (their Lemma 5.2). It lets you go from \(P\) to \(Q\) through an intermediate \(R\), at the price of using higher orders on the two legs and a factor slightly above 1 on the first: for distributions \(P\), \(Q\), \(R\) and \(m > 1\), \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \frac{m\alpha}{m\alpha - 1}D_{\frac{m\alpha - 1}{m - 1}}(P\|R) + D_{m\alpha}(R\|Q). \tag{29.15}\] For comparison, Mironov’s group bound for plain RDP gives up orders instead: an \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP mechanism is \((\alpha/2^c, 3^c\varepsilon)\)-RDP for groups of \(2^c\), when \(\alpha \ge 2^{c+1}\) (Mironov 2017, Proposition 2; see Rényi DP).


29.6.3 Derivation
The triangle-like inequality, by Hölder. Write \(P(y)\), \(Q(y)\), \(R(y)\) for the densities. The idea is to write the sum that defines \(D_\alpha(P\|Q)\) as an average under \(R\) of a product of two ratios, \(P/R\) and \(R/Q\), and then split the product with Hölder’s inequality. Each factor then becomes a Rényi divergence of one leg of the chain.

Insert \(R\). \(e^{(\alpha-1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} = \sum_y P(y)^\alpha Q(y)^{1-\alpha} = \mathbb E_R\big[(P/R)^\alpha\,(R/Q)^{\alpha - 1}\big]\), where the ratios are evaluated at \(Y \sim R\). To check it, multiply out one term: \(R \cdot P^\alpha R^{-\alpha} \cdot R^{\alpha - 1}Q^{1 - \alpha} = P^\alpha Q^{1 - \alpha}\). Rewriting a sum under one distribution as an average under another like this is a change of measure (Fact 1 of Divergences).
Hölder’s inequality. For positive random variables \(X\), \(Y\) and exponents \(u, v > 1\) with \(\frac1u + \frac1v = 1\), \(\mathbb E[XY] \le (\mathbb E[X^u])^{1/u}(\mathbb E[Y^v])^{1/v}\). Choose \(v\) so that the second factor becomes a divergence of order \(m\alpha\), the order the induction below can afford, and \(u\) to match: \(u = \frac{m\alpha - 1}{\alpha(m - 1)}\) and \(v = \frac{m\alpha - 1}{\alpha - 1}\), which satisfy \(\frac1u + \frac1v = \frac{\alpha(m-1) + \alpha - 1}{m\alpha - 1} = 1\). Then \[\mathbb E_R\big[(P/R)^\alpha(R/Q)^{\alpha-1}\big] \le \big(\mathbb E_R[(P/R)^{u\alpha}]\big)^{1/u}\big(\mathbb E_R[(R/Q)^{v(\alpha-1)}]\big)^{1/v}. \tag{29.16}\]
Recognize two Rényi divergences. By Fact 1 in its sum form, an average under \(R\) of a power of \(P/R\) is a Rényi divergence of \(P\) from \(R\): \(\mathbb E_R[(P/R)^{\beta}] = \sum_y R(y)^{1-\beta}P(y)^\beta = e^{(\beta-1)D_\beta(P\|R)}\) with \(\beta = u\alpha = \frac{m\alpha - 1}{m - 1}\). In the same way \(\mathbb E_R[(R/Q)^{\gamma - 1}] = \sum_y R(y)^{\gamma}Q(y)^{1-\gamma} = e^{(\gamma - 1)D_\gamma(R\|Q)}\) with \(\gamma = v(\alpha - 1) + 1 = m\alpha\).
Take logarithms and divide by \(\alpha - 1\). The left side becomes \(D_\alpha(P\|Q)\). The second factor contributes \(\frac1v\cdot v(\alpha - 1)D_{m\alpha}(R\|Q)/(\alpha - 1) = D_{m\alpha}(R\|Q)\). The first contributes \(\frac1u(u\alpha - 1)D_\beta(P\|R)/(\alpha - 1)\), a coefficient \(\frac{u\alpha - 1}{u(\alpha - 1)}\). Here \(u\alpha - 1 = \frac{m\alpha - 1 - (m - 1)}{m - 1} = \frac{m(\alpha - 1)}{m - 1}\), so the coefficient is \(\frac{m(\alpha-1)}{m-1}\cdot\frac{\alpha(m-1)}{(m\alpha - 1)(\alpha - 1)} = \frac{m\alpha}{m\alpha - 1}\). This is Equation 29.15.

Group privacy, by induction on \(m\). Now walk along the chain one record at a time, using the triangle-like inequality to add one step to a group of \(m - 1\).

Base case. \(m = 1\) is the definition.
Step. Let \(D \simeq_{m-1} \hat D \simeq D'\): \(\hat D\) is \(m - 1\) steps from \(D\) and one step from \(D'\). Apply Equation 29.15 with \(P = M(D)\), \(R = M(\hat D)\), \(Q = M(D')\). The first term involves the group of \(m - 1\), so by the induction hypothesis at order \(\beta = \frac{m\alpha - 1}{m - 1}\) it is at most \(\frac{m\alpha}{m\alpha - 1}(m-1)^2\rho\frac{m\alpha - 1}{m - 1} = m(m - 1)\rho\alpha\); the factor \(\frac{m\alpha - 1}{m - 1}\) from the order cancels the coefficient’s denominator. The second term is a single neighbouring step, so by \(\rho\)-zCDP at order \(m\alpha\) it is at most \(m\rho\alpha\). The sum is \((m^2 - m + m)\rho\alpha = m^2\rho\alpha\), which is Equation 29.14.
Tightness. For the Gaussian mechanism a group of \(m\) shifts the mean by \(m\Delta\), and the Gaussian Rényi divergence \(\alpha s^2/(2\sigma^2)\) with \(s = m\Delta\) (Equation 3.15) gives exactly \(\alpha m^2\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2) = m^2\rho\alpha\). Along the chain \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\), \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\), \(\mathcal N(2, 1)\), Equation 29.15 holds with equality: at \(\alpha = 3\), \(m = 2\), the left side is \(D_3\) for a shift of 2, \(3 \cdot 4/2 = 6\); on the right, the first leg has order \((6 - 1)/1 = 5\) and coefficient \(6/5\), giving \(\frac65 \cdot \frac52 = 3\), and the second leg has order 6, giving \(6/2 = 3\). Both sides are \(6\).



29.6.4 Interpretation
Quadratic in \(m\), and that is right. With \(\rho \approx \varepsilon^2/2\) for pure DP, \(m^2\rho \approx (m\varepsilon)^2/2\): zCDP’s group privacy matches pure DP’s \(m\varepsilon\) after the translation from \(\varepsilon\) to \(\rho\). The RDP route is weaker on two counts. It halves the order at each doubling of the group, so a curve known on all orders becomes a curve known only on orders up to \(\alpha/2^c\). And it multiplies \(\varepsilon\) by 3 per doubling, so the value \(\rho\alpha\) at order \(\alpha\) becomes \(3^c\rho\alpha\) at order \(\alpha' = \alpha/2^c\). In terms of the new order that is \(3^c 2^c\rho\alpha' = 6^c\rho\alpha'\): a slope of \(6^c\rho\), against zCDP’s \(m^2\rho = 4^c\rho\).
Strong group privacy is also a weakness. Bun and Steinke use exactly this property to prove lower bounds for zCDP that are as strong as those for pure DP. For example, stability-based algorithms, which are \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with sample sizes independent of the domain size, cannot be zCDP. That is the motivation for the next two sections: approximate zCDP and truncated CDP both weaken group privacy for large groups to escape these bounds.


29.6.5 Example: households under the Gaussian mechanism
Table 29.5 takes the Gaussian mechanism with \(\sigma = 1\) (\(\rho = 0.5\)) and groups of size \(m\). The RDP route starts from the curve at order 64, where \(\varepsilon(64) = 0.5 \times 64 = 32\). For a group of \(m = 2^c\) it gives order \(64/2^c\), \(\varepsilon = 3^c \times 32\), and slope \(6^c \times 0.5\): for \(m = 2\) that is order 32, \(\varepsilon = 96\) and slope 3.

A user contributes up to 4 records to a \(0.1\)-zCDP release. What \(\rho\) protects the user? (\(4^2 \times 0.1 = 1.6\).)
Why does the induction in step 6 need \(\rho\)-zCDP at order \(m\alpha\), larger than \(\alpha\)? (Hölder trades one divergence of order \(\alpha\) for two of higher orders. zCDP controls every order, so the trade is free; a bound known only up to some order would run out after a few steps, which is what happens to truncated CDP.)

title: 29  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.7 Approximate zCDP

29.7.1 Context
Some useful mechanisms are \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP but not zCDP at all. Propose-test-release and stability-based histograms check, privately, that the data are far from any dataset where the answer would change, release an exact answer when they are, and fail only with probability about \(\delta\). The group-privacy lower bound above shows they cannot be zCDP. You still want to compose them with Gaussian steps in one budget. Bun and Steinke’s answer is to allow zCDP to fail on an event of probability \(\delta\).


29.7.2 Statement
\(M\) is \(\delta\)-approximately \(\rho\)-zCDP if, after throwing away a bad event of probability at most \(\delta\) in each world, the rest is \(\rho\)-zCDP. Precisely: for all neighbours \(D \simeq D'\) there are events \(E\) (for \(M(D)\)) and \(E'\) (for \(M(D')\)), each of probability at least \(1 - \delta\), such that for every \(\alpha > 1\) \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)|_E\,\|\,M(D')|_{E'}\big) \le \rho\alpha \quad\text{and}\quad D_\alpha\big(M(D')|_{E'}\,\|\,M(D)|_E\big) \le \rho\alpha, \tag{29.17}\] where \(M(D)|_E\) is the output distribution conditioned on \(E\) (Bun & Steinke 2016, Definition 1.12). With \(\delta = 0\) the events are certain and this is \(\rho\)-zCDP.
Three more properties make it a usable ledger. First, it absorbs \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP: an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism is \(\delta\)-approximately \((\varepsilon^2/2)\)-zCDP (their Proposition 1.13 and Corollary 8.7). Second, it composes column by column: \(\delta_1\)-approximate \(\rho_1\)-zCDP followed by \(\delta_2\)-approximate \(\rho_2\)-zCDP is \((\delta_1 + \delta_2 - \delta_1\delta_2)\)-approximately \((\rho_1 + \rho_2)\)-zCDP (their Lemma 8.2). For many steps the failure probability is \(1 - \prod_i(1 - \delta_i) \le \sum_i\delta_i\). Third, it converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) by adding the failure probability to the conversion’s \(\delta\): a \(\delta_a\)-approximately \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta_a + (1 - \delta_a)\delta')\)-DP, where \(\varepsilon\) is any conversion of \(\rho\)-zCDP at \(\delta'\) (their Lemma 8.8, stated there with their own refinement of the conversion; the argument below works with any of them).


29.7.3 Derivation
This derives the conversion, which is what you use at the end. The idea: on the good event the mechanism is \(\rho\)-zCDP and the usual conversion applies; the bad event can add at most its probability. Let \(\Pr[E], \Pr[E'] \ge 1 - \delta_a\) and fix a set of outputs \(S\).

Split on the event. \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le \Pr[M(D) \in S \mid E]\Pr[E] + (1 - \Pr[E])\), because the probability of \(S\) on the complement of \(E\) is at most 1. Write \(a = \Pr[M(D) \in S \mid E]\); the right side is \(a\Pr[E] + 1 - \Pr[E] = 1 - \Pr[E](1 - a)\), which can only shrink as \(\Pr[E]\) grows. So its value at the smallest allowed \(\Pr[E]\) bounds it: it is at most \(a(1 - \delta_a) + \delta_a\).
Use the conditional zCDP. The conditioned pair is \(\rho\)-zCDP, so by any conversion, \(\Pr[M(D) \in S \mid E] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S \mid E'] + \delta'\).
Remove the conditioning on \(D'\). Dropping the outputs outside \(E'\) can only lower a probability: \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] \ge \Pr[M(D') \in S \mid E']\Pr[E'] \ge \Pr[M(D') \in S \mid E'](1 - \delta_a)\).
Combine. Put step 2 into step 1 and use step 3 for the term with \(e^\varepsilon\): \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le (1 - \delta_a)\big(e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S \mid E'] + \delta'\big) + \delta_a \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + (1 - \delta_a)\delta' + \delta_a\).

The other two properties have shorter reasons. The conversion from \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP comes from a decomposition of any \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP pair: with probability \(1 - \delta\) it behaves like an \(\varepsilon\)-DP pair, and Section 29.4 turns that into \(\varepsilon^2/2\). Composition holds because the conditioned mechanisms compose as zCDP (Fact 2), and the good events of both steps hold together with probability at least \((1 - \delta_1)(1 - \delta_2) = 1 - (\delta_1 + \delta_2 - \delta_1\delta_2)\).


29.7.4 Interpretation
Approximate zCDP is a way to keep one ledger with two columns, \(\rho\) and \(\delta_a\). The \(\rho\) column composes like zCDP, with its \(\sqrt k\) behaviour after conversion; the \(\delta_a\) column adds up, like \(\delta\) in basic composition. It is only worth using when some steps are genuinely \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) and not zCDP. For a step that is zCDP, putting it in the \(\delta_a\) column wastes \(\delta\).


29.7.5 Example: a pipeline with stability-based steps
A pipeline runs 10 stability-based steps, each \((0.5, 10^{-7})\)-DP, and 10 Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 1\). Each stability step enters the \(\rho\) column as \(0.5^2/2 = 0.125\) and the \(\delta_a\) column as \(10^{-7}\). The total is \(\rho = 10 \times 0.125 + 10 \times 0.5 = 6.25\) and \(\delta_a = 1 - (1 - 10^{-7})^{10} = 1.0000 \times 10^{-6}\). Converting with the improved conversion at \(\delta' = 10^{-5} - \delta_a\) gives \(\varepsilon = 22.100\) at total \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Without approximate zCDP you would convert the Gaussians alone (\(\varepsilon = 19.119\) at \(\delta = 9 \times 10^{-6}\)) and add the stability steps by basic composition (\(\varepsilon = 10 \times 0.5 = 5\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\)), for \(19.119 + 5 = 24.119\). The unified ledger saves about 2 because the \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) steps compose in \(\rho\) as \(\varepsilon^2/2\) each, not as \(\varepsilon\).


29.7.6 Check yourself

Is \((\varepsilon, 0)\)-DP the same as \(0\)-approximate \((\varepsilon^2/2)\)-zCDP? (No. \(\varepsilon\)-DP implies \((\varepsilon^2/2)\)-zCDP, but zCDP does not imply pure DP: the Gaussian is zCDP and not \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any finite \(\varepsilon\), because its privacy loss is normal and so unbounded.)
Why do the \(\delta_a\) add while the \(\rho\) add only under a square root in \(\varepsilon\)? (The \(\delta_a\) are failure probabilities of events and combine by the union bound. The \(\rho\) add, and the conversion turns \(\rho\) into \(\varepsilon \approx 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\).)

title: 29  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.8 Subsampling, and truncated CDP

29.8.1 Context
DP-SGD, the running example of this part, runs each step on a Poisson sample of the data: each record is used independently with probability \(q\). Subsampling makes a step much more private than the Gaussian it contains, because a record is usually not in the batch. Does zCDP see this? In this section \(q\) is the sampling rate, never a density.
Take add/remove neighbours (two datasets differ by one record being present or absent), sensitivity 1 and noise multiplier \(\sigma\), and reduce to one dimension. Without the record the step outputs \(Q = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\). With it, the record is in the sample with probability \(q\), shifting the output’s mean by 1, and absent otherwise, so the output is the mixture \(P = (1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). The RDP curve compares \(P\) against \(Q\); the other order, \(Q\) against \(P\), is never larger (both facts are derived in Amplification by subsampling, Equation 31.9). For integer orders the curve has a closed form, a binomial sum over how many of \(\alpha\) copies of the record’s contribution are present: \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln A_\alpha, \qquad A_\alpha = \sum_{j=0}^{\alpha}\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\exp\Big(\frac{j^2 - j}{2\sigma^2}\Big) \tag{29.18}\] (Mironov, Talwar & Zhang 2019). To see where it comes from, let \(r\) be the likelihood ratio of \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) to \(Q\). Then \(P/Q = 1 - q + q\,r\), and by Fact 1, \(A_\alpha = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} = \mathbb E_{Q}[(P/Q)^\alpha] = \mathbb E_Q[(1 - q + q\,r)^\alpha]\). Expand the power binomially. Each term needs \(\mathbb E_Q[r^j]\), which by Fact 1 is \(e^{(j - 1)D_j}\) for the pair \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\), \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\); with \(D_j = j/(2\sigma^2)\) (Equation 3.15 at order \(j\)) that is \(e^{(j^2 - j)/(2\sigma^2)}\).


29.8.2 Statement
No amplification for zCDP. For the Poisson-subsampled Gaussian with any \(q \in (0, 1]\), the smallest \(\rho\) with \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \le \rho\alpha\) for all \(\alpha\) is \(1/(2\sigma^2)\), the same as without subsampling.
Truncated CDP. Since the problem comes from large orders, ask for the line only on orders below a cut-off \(\omega\). A mechanism is \((\rho, \omega)\)-tCDP if for all neighbours and all \(\alpha \in (1, \omega)\) \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big) \le \rho\alpha \tag{29.19}\] (Bun, Dwork, Rothblum & Steinke 2018, Definition 1). \(\rho\)-zCDP is the case \(\omega = \infty\), that is \((\rho, \infty)\)-tCDP. Composition works as for zCDP on the orders both steps cover: \((\rho_1, \omega_1)\) and \((\rho_2, \omega_2)\) compose to \((\rho_1 + \rho_2, \min(\omega_1, \omega_2))\) (their Lemma 2). The conversion to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) is the simple zCDP conversion when its best order is below \(\omega\), and uses the order \(\omega\) itself otherwise (their Lemma 6): \[\varepsilon = \begin{cases}\rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)} & \text{if } \ln(1/\delta) \le (\omega - 1)^2\rho,\\[2pt] \rho\omega + \dfrac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\omega - 1} & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases} \tag{29.20}\] And, unlike zCDP, tCDP is amplified by subsampling (their Theorem 11): let \(\rho, s \in (0, 0.1]\) with \(\ln(1/s) \ge 3\rho(2 + \log_2(1/\rho))\), and let \(M\) be \((\rho, \omega')\)-tCDP with \(\omega' \ge \ln(1/s)/(2\rho) \ge 3\). Running \(M\) on a uniformly random subset of a fraction \(s\) of the records (fixed size, without replacement) is \((13s^2\rho,\ \omega)\)-tCDP with \(\omega = \ln(1/s)/(4\rho)\).


29.8.3 Derivation
No amplification for zCDP. Write \(\rho_0 = 1/(2\sigma^2)\), the slope of the Gaussian without subsampling. The plan is to show that \(\rho_0\) is enough (subsampling never hurts) and that nothing smaller is enough (at large orders, subsampling stops helping).

Upper bound, by convexity. \(1 - q + q\,r\) is an average of the values 1 and \(r\) with weights \(1 - q\) and \(q\). Since \(x \mapsto x^\alpha\) is convex, the power of an average is at most the average of the powers: \((1 - q + q\,r)^\alpha \le (1 - q) + q\,r^\alpha\). Take \(\mathbb E_Q\); with \(\mathbb E_Q[r^\alpha] = e^{(\alpha - 1)\alpha\rho_0}\) from the Gaussian curve, \(A_\alpha \le 1 - q + q\,e^{(\alpha - 1)\alpha\rho_0} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\alpha\rho_0}\), the last step because an average of 1 and a number at least 1 is at most that number. So \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \rho_0\alpha\). The other order obeys the same bound, by a convexity argument on pairs. For any pair \((A, B)\), \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(A\|B)} = \sum_y B(y)\,(A(y)/B(y))^\alpha\) is the perspective of the convex function \(x^\alpha\), which makes it jointly convex in \((A, B)\): the value at an average of pairs is at most the average of the values. Writing the pair \((Q, P)\) as the mixture \((1 - q)\,(Q, Q) + q\,(Q, \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2))\) gives \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(Q\|P)} \le (1 - q) + q\,e^{(\alpha - 1)\alpha\rho_0}\), the same bound. Subsampling never hurts.
Lower bound, by one term. Every term of Equation 29.18 is positive, so dropping terms gives a lower bound. Keep only \(j = \alpha\), the event that the record is present in all \(\alpha\) copies: \(A_\alpha \ge q^\alpha e^{(\alpha^2 - \alpha)\rho_0}\). Taking logs and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\), \[\varepsilon(\alpha) \ge \rho_0\alpha + \frac{\alpha\ln q}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{29.21}\]
Divide by \(\alpha\) and let \(\alpha \to \infty\). \(\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha \ge \rho_0 + \ln q/(\alpha - 1) \to \rho_0\): the penalty \(\ln q\) for the record being rarely sampled is fixed, while the Gaussian part grows with the order, so the penalty’s share of the slope vanishes. A line \(\rho\alpha\) above the whole curve needs \(\rho \ge \rho_0\), and by step 1, \(\rho_0\) suffices.

The tCDP conversion. This is the zCDP conversion of Section 29.5 with the orders restricted to \((1, \omega]\).

Restrict Mironov’s conversion. As in Section 29.5, every \(\alpha \in (1, \omega]\) gives a valid \(g(\alpha) = \rho\alpha + \ell/(\alpha - 1)\) with \(\ell = \ln(1/\delta)\). (The endpoint \(\omega\) is allowed: \(D_\alpha\) is non-decreasing in \(\alpha\) and lower semicontinuous, as a supremum over finite partitions of functions continuous in \(\alpha\), so \(D_\omega \le \lim_{\alpha \uparrow \omega}D_\alpha \le \rho\omega\).)
Constrained minimum of a convex function. The unconstrained minimizer is \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{\ell/\rho}\). If \(\alpha^* \le \omega\), that is \(\ell \le (\omega - 1)^2\rho\), use it and get Equation 29.10. Otherwise \(\alpha^*\) lies beyond \(\omega\); a convex function is decreasing to the left of its minimizer, so \(g\) is decreasing on \((1, \omega]\), the best allowed order is \(\omega\), and it gives \(\rho\omega + \ell/(\omega - 1)\).

The subsampling theorem has a longer proof (their Section 3): write the subsampled pair as mixtures \(sP + (1 - s)R\) and \(sQ + (1 - s)R\), expand \((1 + sZ)^\alpha\) with \(Z = (P - Q)/(sQ + (1 - s)R)\), and bound the second moment of \(Z\) through \(D_2\) and the higher moments through the tCDP bound at orders up to \(\omega'\). The second-moment term carries the factor \(s^2\) that gives the amplification. The truncation is essential: the higher-order terms are controlled only for \(\alpha\) up to about \(\ln(1/s)/\rho\).


29.8.4 Interpretation
The curve bends, and a line cannot. Figure 29.4 shows the curve of one DP-SGD step, \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), on integer orders. Up to \(\alpha = 8\) it is tiny and almost linear. Its slope there is close to \(q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)/2 = 10^{-4} \times 1.71828/2 = 8.5914 \times 10^{-5}\). That value comes from the first terms of Equation 29.18. If every exponential in the sum were 1, the sum would be \(((1 - q) + q)^\alpha = 1\); the \(j = 0\) and \(j = 1\) exponentials are exactly 1, so the excess over 1 starts at \(j = 2\), and for small \(q\) it is \(A_\alpha \approx 1 + \binom\alpha2q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\). Then \(\ln A_\alpha/(\alpha - 1) \approx \alpha q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)/2\). Between \(\alpha = 8\) and \(\alpha = 16\) the curve jumps by more than three orders of magnitude, from \(8.9364 \times 10^{-4}\) to \(3.0879\) (Table 29.6). Beyond that it follows the lower bound Equation 29.21, which turns positive where \(\rho_0(\alpha - 1) = \ln(1/q)\), at \(\alpha = 1 + 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q) = 1 + 2\ln 100 = 10.21\). At large orders the term \(j = \alpha\) dominates: it is the event that the record is in every one of \(\alpha\) imagined samples, rare but with the full Gaussian loss. A line through the origin above the whole curve must have the slope at infinity, \(\rho_0 = 0.5\). A line that only has to stay above the curve up to \(\omega = 8\) can have slope \(1.1171 \times 10^{-4}\), \(0.5/(1.1171 \times 10^{-4}) = 4476\) times smaller.
Small orders are what matter for DP-SGD. After \(k = 10{,}000\) steps the RDP curve is \(k\varepsilon(\alpha)\), and the conversion picks the order where \(k\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) is smallest. With per-step values around \(10^{-4}\), the first term is small at small orders (from \(10^4 \times 1.7181 \times 10^{-4} = 1.7181\) at order 2 to \(8.9364\) at order 8), and the order is pushed up only until the curve’s jump makes the first term expensive. That is a small order: on the integer orders of ORDERS the best is \(\alpha = 4\), for Mironov’s conversion and for the improved one. The large orders that set the zCDP slope are never used. So the right one-number summary of DP-SGD keeps \(\rho\) only on small orders, which is what \((\rho, \omega)\)-tCDP does. RDP accounting keeps the whole curve and does at least as well.
tCDP’s theorem is loose in its constant. Theorem 11 holds for every tCDP mechanism, so its constant 13 is generous. With \(\sigma = \sqrt5\) (\(\rho = 1/(2 \cdot 5) = 0.1\), so the theorem applies) and \(s = 0.01\), the side condition reads \(3\rho(2 + \log_2(1/\rho)) = 1.597 \le \ln(1/s) = 4.605\), and the theorem gives \((13 \times 0.01^2 \times 0.1,\ 4.605/0.4) = (1.300 \times 10^{-4},\ 11.51)\)-tCDP. The Poisson-subsampled Gaussian curve on integer orders up to \(11.51\) needs only \(\rho = 1.128 \times 10^{-5}\), about 11 times less. After \(10{,}000\) steps the theorem’s parameters convert to \(\varepsilon = 9.037\) by Equation 29.20, while RDP accounting of the Poisson curve on the integer orders of ORDERS, with the improved conversion, gives \(2.046\).
This comparison is only indicative. The theorem is for fixed-size sampling and replace-one neighbours, the curve for Poisson sampling and add/remove neighbours, and Amplification by subsampling explains why the two must not be mixed in an accountant.

29.8.6 Check yourself

Why do the largest orders decide zCDP’s \(\rho\) for a subsampled Gaussian, when no conversion ever uses them? (zCDP requires the line at every order. The ratio \(\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha\) keeps growing towards \(1/(2\sigma^2)\) as \(\alpha \to \infty\), so the limit sets the slope, and \(\rho = 1/(2\sigma^2)\).)
Two DP-SGD runs, one \((10^{-4}, 4)\)-tCDP per step and one \((10^{-5}, 20)\)-tCDP per step, are composed. What is the result? (\((\rho, \omega) = (1.1 \times 10^{-4}, 4)\) per pair of steps: \(\rho\) adds and \(\omega\) is the minimum, because the line is guaranteed for both steps only on the orders both cover.)

title: 30  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
30.1 Why this matters
Every privacy definition in this part answers the same question: how well can an adversary who sees the output of a mechanism \(M\) tell whether it ran on a dataset \(D\) or on a neighbour \(D'\) that differs from it in one record? Differential privacy (DP) in its \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) form answers with two numbers. Rényi differential privacy (RDP) answers with a curve over orders \(\alpha\) (Rényi DP), and concentrated DP with one number \(\rho\) (concentrated DP). But Part 1 already gave the complete answer to “how well can anyone tell \(P\) from \(Q\)”. It is the trade-off function \(T(P, Q)\): for each rate at which a test may wrongly reject \(P\) (its type I error), the smallest rate at which it can wrongly accept \(P\) when the truth is \(Q\) (its type II error) (Hypothesis testing, Section 4.5). This chapter makes that curve the privacy guarantee itself.
The organizing idea: the most informative description of a mechanism’s privacy is its whole trade-off curve between \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\), and every other notion is a lossy summary of it. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair is one straight line lying under the curve, an RDP curve is a set of moments of it, and both throw information away. Two facts make the curve practical rather than just complete. First, Gaussian mechanisms give a one-parameter family of curves \(G_\mu\) that is closed under composition: running a mechanism with curve \(G_{\mu_1}\) and then one with curve \(G_{\mu_2}\) gives the curve \(G_{\sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \mu_2^2}}\). Second, a central limit theorem (CLT) says that composing many mechanisms, each of which leaks little, gives a curve close to some \(G_\mu\), whatever the mechanisms were. Table 30.1 lists the results.
A clash of letters. The \(f\)-DP papers write \(\alpha\) for the type I error and \(\beta\) for the type II error, as Part 1 does. In this part \(\alpha\) is the Rényi order. So this chapter writes \(a\) for the type I error and \(b\) for the type II error of a test, and keeps \(\alpha\) for Rényi orders only.
Notation. Throughout, \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\) are the two output distributions, with densities \(p\) and \(q\). The one exception is Section 30.8, where \(q\) is a sampling rate and the densities are written \(P(y)\) and \(Q(y)\). A test \(\phi\) looks at the output \(y\) and “fires”, deciding that the data was \(D'\), with probability \(\phi(y)\). Its type I error is how often it fires when the data was \(D\), \(a = \mathbb E_P[\phi]\), and its type II error is how often it stays silent when the data was \(D'\), \(b = 1 - \mathbb E_Q[\phi]\). The privacy loss of an output \(y\) is the log of how much more likely \(y\) is under \(D\) than under \(D'\), \(L(y) = \ln\frac{p(y)}{q(y)}\). Drawing the output from \(P\) makes it random: \(L(Y)\) with \(Y \sim P\) is the privacy loss random variable (PRV) (composition).

section: 30.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses
text:
30.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses

30.2.1 Fact 1 — The curve is fixed by the law of the privacy loss
The trade-off curve is about the best tests, and the best tests only ever look at the privacy loss. The Neyman–Pearson lemma of Part 1 says that, at any type I error, the test with the smallest type II error fires on the outputs that are most typical of \(Q\) relative to \(P\), that is, where the likelihood ratio \(q/p\) is largest. Since \(q/p = e^{-L}\), these are the outputs where the privacy loss \(L\) is smallest. So every optimal test has the form “fire when \(L < l\)” (with a coin flip at \(L = l\) when \(L\) has an atom there), and its errors are the probabilities of the event \(\{L < l\}\) under \(P\) and under \(Q\). The curve \(T(P, Q)\) therefore depends on the pair only through the law of \(L\) under \(P\) and under \(Q\).
Those two laws are not independent of each other. To get a probability under \(Q\) from one under \(P\), weight each output by \(q/p = e^{-L}\). This is Part 1’s change of measure (Fact 2 of Hypothesis testing, where \(L\) names the ratio \(q/p\); here that ratio is \(e^{-L}\)): for any event \(A\) defined through \(L\), \[Q(A) = \mathbb E_P[e^{-L}\mathbf 1_A], \tag{30.1}\] when \(Q\) puts no mass where \(p = 0\). The reason is one line: \(\mathbb E_P[e^{-L}\mathbf 1_A] = \int_A p\cdot\frac{q}{p} = \int_A q\). So the law of the PRV under \(P\) alone fixes the curve.
The Gaussian pair shows this at work. Take \(P = \mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(Q = \mathcal N(\mu, 1)\), a unit-variance normal and the same normal shifted by \(\mu\). Taking the log of the ratio of the two densities, the \(y^2\) terms cancel and \[L(y) = \ln\frac{p(y)}{q(y)} = -\frac{y^2}{2} + \frac{(y - \mu)^2}{2} = \frac{\mu^2}{2} - \mu y. \tag{30.2}\] The loss is a linear function of a normal output, so it is normal. Under \(P\), \(y\) has mean 0 and variance 1, so \(L \sim \mathcal N(\frac{\mu^2}{2}, \mu^2)\). Under \(Q\), \(y\) has mean \(\mu\), so \(L \sim \mathcal N(\frac{\mu^2}{2} - \mu^2, \mu^2) = \mathcal N(-\frac{\mu^2}{2}, \mu^2)\). The change of measure with \(A\) = everything says \(\mathbb E_P[e^{-L}]\) should be \(Q(\text{everything}) = 1\). The moment generating function of a normal, \(\mathbb E[e^{tX}] = e^{tm + t^2v/2}\) for \(X \sim \mathcal N(m, v)\), with \(t = -1\), gives \(\mathbb E_P[e^{-L}] = e^{-\mu^2/2 + \mu^2/2} = 1\), as it must.
One consequence is used several times below: the slope of the curve is set by the loss at the threshold. Part 1 showed \(T'(a) = -q/p\) at the threshold of the test of size \(a\). The reason is that moving the threshold to include one more sliver of outputs near \(y\) raises the type I error by \(p(y)\,dy\) and lowers the type II error by \(q(y)\,dy\), so \(b\) changes by \(-q/p\) per unit of \(a\). In terms of the loss, this is the slope rule \[|T'(a)| = e^{-l(a)}, \tag{30.3}\] where \(l(a)\) is the threshold of the size-\(a\) test, the \(a\)-quantile of \(L\) under \(P\) (the test fires when \(L < l(a)\), which happens with probability \(a\) under \(P\)).


30.2.2 Fact 2 — The best “gain” of a test is a hockey-stick divergence
Suppose each correct detection of \(D'\) earns one unit and each false alarm costs \(\gamma\) units. A test’s net gain is then its power \(1 - b\) minus \(\gamma a\). The best gain over all tests is a divergence between \(P\) and \(Q\) that the book has already met: the hockey-stick divergence \(E_\gamma(Q\|P) = \sup_S\big(Q(S) - \gamma P(S)\big)\), the largest amount by which some event is more likely under \(Q\) than \(\gamma\) times its probability under \(P\) (Divergences). For any pair and any \(\gamma \ge 0\), \[\max_{a \in [0, 1]}\big(1 - T(P, Q)(a) - \gamma a\big) = \sup_S\big(Q(S) - \gamma P(S)\big) = E_\gamma(Q\|P). \tag{30.4}\]
To see why, write the gain of a test \(\phi\) as one integral: \(1 - b - \gamma a = \mathbb E_Q\phi - \gamma\mathbb E_P\phi = \int\phi\,(q - \gamma p)\). The integrand is positive exactly where \(q > \gamma p\), so the gain is largest when the test fires on those outputs and nowhere else, \(\phi = \mathbf 1[q > \gamma p]\). That test is the event \(S = \{q > \gamma p\}\), and its gain is \(\int(q - \gamma p)_+ = E_\gamma(Q\|P)\). The left side of Equation 30.4 reaches the same number in two stages: at each type I error \(a\) the largest power is \(1 - T(a)\) by the definition of \(T\), and maximizing over \(a\) then picks the best test overall.
At \(\gamma = 1\) the gain is \(1 - a - b\), the test’s advantage, and \(E_1(Q\|P)\) is the total variation (TV) distance. So Fact 2 contains Part 1’s statement that the best advantage of any test is the TV distance.


30.2.3 Fact 3 — A Gaussian shift in \(d\) dimensions is a Gaussian shift in one
When the output is a vector with independent unit-variance Gaussian noise, only the direction of the shift between the two means carries evidence; the noise in every perpendicular direction is the same under both hypotheses. So the \(d\)-dimensional problem is a one-dimensional one with shift equal to the length of the mean difference. For \(m \in \mathbb R^d\), \[T\big(\mathcal N(0, I_d), \mathcal N(m, I_d)\big) = G_{\|m\|_2}, \qquad G_\mu(a) = \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - a) - \mu\big). \tag{30.5}\] Here \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function, \(\Phi(t) = \Pr[Z \le t]\) for \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\), and \(\Phi^{-1}\) its inverse.
Start with \(d = 1\), which is Part 1’s Gaussian trade-off curve (Equation 4.10). For \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) the loss \(\frac{\mu^2}{2} - \mu y\) is small when \(y\) is large, so the best test fires when \(y > t\). Its type I error is \(a = \Pr[Z > t] = 1 - \Phi(t)\), so the threshold of the size-\(a\) test is \(t = \Phi^{-1}(1 - a)\). Its type II error is the chance that a draw from \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) stays below \(t\), \(b = \Phi(t - \mu)\). Substituting \(t\) gives \(G_\mu\).
For general \(d\), the likelihood ratio is \(\exp\big(\langle m, y\rangle - \frac12\|m\|^2\big)\), from the same cancellation of squares as in Fact 1. It depends on \(y\) only through the single number \(s = \langle m, y\rangle/\|m\|\), the length of the projection of \(y\) on the direction of the shift. By Neyman–Pearson, the optimal tests are thresholds on \(s\). Under \(\mathcal N(0, I)\), \(s \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\); under \(\mathcal N(m, I)\), \(s \sim \mathcal N(\|m\|, 1)\). Both hold because the inner product of a unit vector with a standard normal vector is a standard normal number (its variance is the squared length of the unit vector, 1), and the mean \(m\) contributes \(\langle m, m\rangle/\|m\| = \|m\|\). So every optimal test is a threshold test on \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(\|m\|, 1)\), whose curve is \(G_{\|m\|}\).
Figure 30.3 (left) shows the picture: 400 draws from each of \(\mathcal N(0, I_2)\) and \(\mathcal N((1, 1), I_2)\). The best boundary is the dashed line perpendicular to the shift. Nothing about the other direction helps.

title: 30  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
30.3 f-DP

30.3.1 Context
A definition of privacy should say what an adversary cannot do. In hypothesis-testing terms the strongest such statement is a lower bound on the adversary’s type II error at every type I error: however the adversary tunes its test, it must miss at least this often. That bound is a curve, so the definition takes a curve as its parameter.


30.3.2 Statement
Call \(f\) a trade-off function if it is the curve of some pair of distributions. Part 1 (Section 4.5) showed this means \(f\) is non-increasing, convex, continuous and satisfies \(f(a) \le 1 - a\) (a coin flip that fires with probability \(a\) already achieves \(b = 1 - a\)). A mechanism \(M\) is \(f\)-differentially private (\(f\)-DP) if no neighbouring pair is easier to tell apart than \(f\) allows, \[T\big(M(D), M(D')\big) \ge f \quad\text{for all neighbours } D \simeq D' \tag{30.6}\] (Dong, Roth & Su 2022, Definition 2.3; cited as Dong et al. from here on).
Two consequences follow. Because the neighbouring relation is symmetric, an \(f\)-DP mechanism is also \(\max(f, f^{-1})\)-DP, where \(f^{-1}(a) = \inf\{t \in [0, 1] : f(t) \le a\}\) is the inverse of \(f\), its graph reflected across the diagonal \(a = b\) (Dong et al., Proposition 2.4). A curve with \(f = f^{-1}\) is called symmetric. And the old definition is a special case: \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP is exactly \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\)-DP for the curve made of two straight lines, \[f_{\varepsilon,\delta}(a) = \max\big(0,\; 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon a,\; e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - a)\big), \tag{30.7}\] the curve that Part 3 derived in Section 18.7 (Equation 18.12; Wasserman & Zhou 2010; Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath 2015; Dong et al., Proposition 2.5).


30.3.3 Derivation

Swap the roles, then invert. Since \(D' \simeq D\) is also a neighbouring pair, \(f\)-DP gives \(T(M(D'), M(D)) \ge f\) as well. Now relate the curve of \((Q, P)\) to the curve of \((P, Q)\). Take a test \(\phi\) of \(P\) against \(Q\) with errors \((a, b)\) and use its opposite, \(1 - \phi\), as a test of \(Q\) against \(P\): it fires when the data was \(D'\) exactly when \(\phi\) stays silent, so its type I error is \(\mathbb E_Q[1 - \phi] = b\) and its type II error is \(1 - \mathbb E_P[1 - \phi] = a\). So the achievable error pairs of \((Q, P)\) are those of \((P, Q)\) with the coordinates swapped, and \(T(Q, P)\) is the inverse function of \(T(P, Q)\), in the generalized sense of \(f^{-1}\) above when the curve has flat stretches. Part 1 proves this as Exercise 2 of Hypothesis testing.
Reflecting keeps the order. A curve lying above \(f\) means its region of achievable errors sits inside the region above \(f\). Reflecting both regions across the diagonal keeps that inclusion, so \(T(M(D'), M(D)) \ge f\) turns into \(T(M(D), M(D')) \ge f^{-1}\). Together with \(T(M(D), M(D')) \ge f\) this gives \(\ge \max(f, f^{-1})\). The maximum of two convex, non-increasing functions is again convex and non-increasing, so this is a trade-off function.
\((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP is a curve. This is Part 3’s hypothesis-testing reading (Section 18.7), restated in this chapter’s letters. \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP says that for every event \(S\), \(Q(S) \le e^\varepsilon P(S) + \delta\) and \(P(S) \le e^\varepsilon Q(S) + \delta\). Read \(S\) as the region where a test fires, so \(a = P(S)\) and \(1 - b = Q(S)\). The first inequality becomes \(1 - b \le e^\varepsilon a + \delta\), that is \(b \ge 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon a\). The second, applied to the complement of \(S\), where \(P = 1 - a\) and \(Q = b\), becomes \(1 - a \le e^\varepsilon b + \delta\), that is \(b \ge e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - a)\). Together with \(b \ge 0\) these are the three pieces of Equation 30.7. A randomized test is a mixture of such region tests, so its errors obey the same linear bounds. Conversely, if every test has \(b \ge f_{\varepsilon,\delta}(a)\), then reading each event \(S\) as a test gives back the two DP inequalities. So \(T(P, Q) \ge f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) for every neighbouring pair exactly when \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.



30.3.4 Interpretation
\(f\)-DP contains \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP: with \(f = f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) you get back the old definition, and other curves express guarantees that no single \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair can.
The shape of \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) shows what the two parameters do. It has two straight pieces, with slopes \(-e^\varepsilon\) and \(-e^{-\varepsilon}\). They meet on the diagonal \(a = b\): setting \(a = 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon a\) gives \(a = \frac{1 - \delta}{1 + e^\varepsilon}\). The curve starts at \(1 - \delta\) on the \(b\)-axis, not at 1. That gap is what \(\delta\) means: a test may catch \(D'\) with probability \(\delta\) at no type I cost.
Post-processing comes for free. Processing the outputs can only make two distributions harder to tell apart, because any test on the processed output is also a test on the raw output, so the trade-off curve can only rise under processing (Part 3, Section 19.3; Dong et al., Lemma 2.9). So \(f\)-DP is closed under post-processing.
The curve is also the most informative summary there is. Blackwell’s theorem (Dong et al., Theorem 2.10) says that \(T(P, Q) \le T(P', Q')\) holds exactly when some randomized map sends \(P\) to \(P'\) and \(Q\) to \(Q'\) at the same time. So comparing curves is the same as asking whether one pair can be turned into the other by post-processing. Any quantity that respects post-processing, such as a divergence, can therefore only be a coarsening of the curve.


30.3.5 Example: three mechanisms with “\(\varepsilon = 1\)”
Binary randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 1\) reports the true bit with probability \(e/(1 + e) = 0.7311\) and flips it otherwise (randomized response; as a mechanism it protects one person’s bit under replace-one neighbours, and here it serves as a pair of distributions). If the bit is 0 under \(D\) and 1 under \(D'\), the output distributions are \(P = (0.7311, 0.2689)\) and \(Q = (0.2689, 0.7311)\) over the outputs (0, 1). The only useful test is “fire when the output is 1”, with \(a = 0.2689\) and \(b = 0.2689\); mixing it with “never fire” and “always fire” fills in the straight lines to \((0, 1)\) and \((1, 0)\). So the curve has a single interior corner at \((0.2689, 0.2689)\). That is exactly \(f_{1,0}\), whose corner is at \(1/(1 + e) = 0.2689\) by the formula \(\frac{1 - \delta}{1 + e^\varepsilon}\) above. The Laplace mechanism with sensitivity 1 and scale \(1/\varepsilon\) is also \((1, 0)\)-DP, and the Gaussian mechanism with \(\sigma = 1\) is shown for comparison.

30.3.6 Check yourself

Why must \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) be symmetric, \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta} = f_{\varepsilon,\delta}^{-1}\)? (Its two pieces are reflections of each other across the diagonal: solving \(b = 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon a\) for \(a\) gives \(a = e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - b)\), which is the second piece with \(a\) and \(b\) swapped. This mirrors the two DP inequalities, one for each order of \(D, D'\).)
The Laplace curve in Table 30.2 coincides with \(f_{1,0}\) for small \(a\) and lies above it in the middle. Is \(\varepsilon = 1\) the smallest \(\varepsilon\) with \(\delta = 0\) it satisfies? (Yes. Near \(a = 0\) both curves are \(1 - e\,a\), and any \(f_{\varepsilon,0}\) with \(\varepsilon < 1\) is \(1 - e^\varepsilon a\) there, which lies above the Laplace curve.)

title: 30  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
30.4 Gaussian differential privacy

30.4.1 Context
The Gaussian mechanism is the workhorse of private machine learning. By Fact 3, its curve is a Gaussian trade-off curve \(G_\mu\), which has one parameter. Using that family as the yardstick gives a one-number definition that is exact for the Gaussian mechanism.


30.4.2 Statement
A mechanism is \(\mu\)-GDP if it is \(G_\mu\)-DP, with \(G_\mu\) as in Equation 30.5 (Dong et al., Definition 2.6): no test can separate its neighbouring outputs better than one can separate \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) from \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\). The Gaussian mechanism adds noise to a query \(g\), \(M(D) = g(D) + \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2\Delta_2^2 I)\), where \(\Delta_2\) is the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity of \(g\) (the largest Euclidean distance \(\|g(D) - g(D')\|_2\) over neighbours) and \(\sigma\) the noise multiplier (the noise standard deviation in units of \(\Delta_2\)). It is \[\mu\text{-GDP with } \mu = \frac{1}{\sigma}, \tag{30.8}\] and this is tight: when the sensitivity is attained by some neighbouring pair, that pair has trade-off curve exactly \(G_{1/\sigma}\). \(\mu\)-GDP is closed under post-processing.


30.4.3 Derivation
The plan is to turn the two output distributions, by invertible maps that cannot change any test’s errors, into the standard pair of Fact 3, and then read off the shift.

Standardize. Divide the output by \(\sigma\Delta_2\). The map is invertible, so any test on the scaled output is a test on the original and vice versa, and no error changes. After it, the noise has identity covariance: \(P = \mathcal N(g(D)/(\sigma\Delta_2), I)\) and \(Q = \mathcal N(g(D')/(\sigma\Delta_2), I)\).
Reduce to one dimension. Subtract \(g(D)/(\sigma\Delta_2)\) from both, another invertible map, so that \(P\) is centred at 0. Fact 3 then gives \(T(P, Q) = G_\nu\) with \(\nu = \|g(D) - g(D')\|_2/(\sigma\Delta_2)\), the length of the remaining shift.
Bound the shift. By the definition of sensitivity, \(\|g(D) - g(D')\|_2 \le \Delta_2\), so \(\nu \le 1/\sigma\).
A bigger shift is easier to detect. \(G_\mu(a) = \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1 - a) - \mu)\) decreases as \(\mu\) grows, because \(\Phi\) is increasing. So \(G_\nu \ge G_{1/\sigma}\) for every neighbouring pair, which is the statement that the mechanism is \(1/\sigma\)-GDP. A pair with \(\|g(D) - g(D')\|_2 = \Delta_2\) has \(\nu = 1/\sigma\) and gives equality.
Post-processing. It is the special case \(f = G_\mu\) of the post-processing property of \(f\)-DP in Section 30.3.



30.4.4 Interpretation
For the Gaussian mechanism, \(\mu\)-GDP is not a bound with slack; it is the curve. Every other guarantee for this mechanism, in particular every \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair, follows from \(\mu\) (Section 30.5).
\(\mu\) has a direct reading: it is the distance between the two output means in units of the noise standard deviation. Part 1’s Table 4.4 gives a feel for it. At a 5% false-alarm rate the threshold is \(\Phi^{-1}(0.95) = 1.6449\), so at \(\mu = 1\) the best test misses with probability \(\Phi(1.6449 - 1) = 0.7405\) and has power \(1 - 0.7405 = 0.2595\); at \(\mu = 2\) it misses with probability \(\Phi(-0.3551) = 0.3612\) and has power 0.6388. Dong et al. suggest that \(\mu \le 0.5\) is a reasonable guarantee and \(\mu \ge 6\) promises almost nothing (their discussion of Figure 3, after Definition 2.6).
The guarantee is set by the worst pair. A pair whose outputs differ by half the sensitivity has curve \(G_{0.5}\) at \(\sigma = 1\), more private than the guarantee \(G_1\), which comes from the pairs that attain the full sensitivity.


30.4.5 Example: one noisy query
A count query has \(\Delta_2 = 1\), since adding or removing one record changes the count by 1. Released with \(\sigma = 1\), it is 1-GDP; with \(\sigma = 4\), it is 0.25-GDP. For \(\sigma = 1\), Table 30.3 evaluates \(G_1\) at three type I errors, each by setting the threshold \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - a)\) and subtracting the shift 1. For example, at \(a = 0.01\) the threshold is \(\Phi^{-1}(0.99) = 2.3263\) and \(G_1(0.01) = \Phi(1.3263) = 0.9076\).

30.4.6 Check yourself

A query has \(\ell_2\) sensitivity 3 and you add \(\mathcal N(0, 6^2 I)\). What is \(\mu\)? (The noise multiplier is the noise standard deviation in units of the sensitivity, \(\sigma = 6/3 = 2\), so \(\mu = 1/\sigma = 0.5\).)
Why is it enough to look at the one-dimensional statistic \(\langle m, y\rangle/\|m\|\) when the query returns a vector? (Fact 3: the likelihood ratio depends on \(y\) only through it, so by Neyman–Pearson no test can do better than thresholding it.)

title: 30  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
30.5 Duality with (ε, δ)

30.5.1 Context
Regulators, papers and libraries report \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). So you need to turn a curve into \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pairs without losing anything, and you need the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) profile of \(\mu\)-GDP in closed form.


30.5.2 Statement
The idea is geometric. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee is the line \(b = 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon a\) (and its mirror image), and a curve satisfies it when the curve lies above the line. For a given slope \(-e^\varepsilon\), the smallest \(\delta\) that works is the one where the line just touches the curve. Doing this for every slope gives the function \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), and since a convex curve is the upper envelope of the lines that touch it, these lines together carry all of the curve.
The tool that computes “the line of slope \(y\) that just touches \(f\)” is the convex conjugate \(f^*(y) = \sup_{a}\big(ya - f(a)\big)\): for each slope \(y\) it gives (minus) the intercept of the touching line. In these terms: for a symmetric trade-off function \(f\), a mechanism is \(f\)-DP if and only if it is \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\)-DP for every \(\varepsilon \ge 0\), with \[\delta(\varepsilon) = 1 + f^*(-e^\varepsilon), \qquad f^*(y) = \sup_{a \in [0, 1]}\big(ya - f(a)\big), \tag{30.9}\] (Dong et al., Proposition 2.12). For \(f = G_\mu\) the touching point can be found in closed form, and \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} + \frac{\mu}{2}\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} - \frac{\mu}{2}\Big) \tag{30.10}\] (Dong et al., Corollary 2.13). This is the exact privacy profile of the Gaussian mechanism, the same formula that Part 3 derived as a hockey-stick divergence (Equation 20.17 in Section 20.6; Balle & Wang 2018, Theorem 8). Here it comes out of the curve by convex duality.


30.5.3 Derivation of the duality

One \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair is one line. By Equation 30.7, \(f \ge f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) requires in particular \(f(a) \ge 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon a\) for all \(a\). Rearranged, \(\delta \ge 1 - f(a) - e^\varepsilon a\) for every \(a\), so the smallest \(\delta\) that works is \(\sup_a\big(1 - f(a) - e^\varepsilon a\big)\). With \(y = -e^\varepsilon\) in the definition of the conjugate, this is \(1 + f^*(-e^\varepsilon)\), the quantity in Equation 30.9. The other piece of \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) is the mirror image of this line across the diagonal, and \(f\) is its own mirror image (it is symmetric), so the other piece gives the same condition.
So \(f\)-DP implies every \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\). If \(T(M(D), M(D')) \ge f\) and, by step 1 with the smallest \(\delta\), \(f \ge f_{\varepsilon,\delta(\varepsilon)}\), then \(T(M(D), M(D')) \ge f_{\varepsilon,\delta(\varepsilon)}\).
Conversely, the lines rebuild the curve. A convex function is the supremum of the lines that touch it from below. For each \(\varepsilon \ge 0\) the line \(1 - \delta(\varepsilon) - e^\varepsilon a\) touches \(f\) where the slope of \(f\) is \(-e^\varepsilon\). As \(\varepsilon\) runs over \([0, \infty)\) the slopes run over every value from \(-1\) down, which covers the part of the curve left of the diagonal (a symmetric curve has slope \(-1\) where it crosses the diagonal and is steeper to the left). The mirror pieces cover the rest by symmetry. So \(\sup_{\varepsilon \ge 0} f_{\varepsilon,\delta(\varepsilon)} = f\), and a mechanism that is \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\)-DP for all \(\varepsilon\) has \(T \ge f_{\varepsilon,\delta(\varepsilon)}\) for every \(\varepsilon\), hence \(T \ge f\) (Dong et al., Proposition 2.11).
The conjugate is a hockey-stick divergence. When \(f = T(P, Q)\), Fact 2 (Equation 30.4) with \(\gamma = e^\varepsilon\) says \(1 + f^*(-e^\varepsilon) = \max_a(1 - f(a) - e^\varepsilon a) = E_{e^\varepsilon}(Q\|P)\). So \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the familiar privacy profile \(\delta(\varepsilon) = E_{e^\varepsilon}\) of composition, the smallest \(\delta\) that goes with each \(\varepsilon\). For a symmetric pair the two orders, \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(Q\|P)\) and \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q)\), agree.



30.5.4 Derivation of the Gaussian profile through the conjugate
To evaluate \(1 + G_\mu^*(-e^\varepsilon) = \max_a\big(1 - G_\mu(a) - e^\varepsilon a\big)\), find the test where the curve has slope \(-e^\varepsilon\), then read off its two errors.

Find the touching point. The expression \(1 - G_\mu(a) - e^\varepsilon a\) is concave in \(a\), because \(G_\mu\) is convex, so its maximum is where its derivative vanishes, \(G_\mu'(a) = -e^\varepsilon\). By the slope rule (Fact 1), the slope at the size-\(a\) threshold \(t = \Phi^{-1}(1 - a)\) is minus the likelihood ratio there. For \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) that ratio is \(q(t)/p(t) = e^{\mu t - \mu^2/2}\). Setting it equal to \(e^\varepsilon\) gives \(\mu t - \mu^2/2 = \varepsilon\), so \(t = \frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} + \frac{\mu}{2}\).
Read off the errors. The test fires when \(y > t\). Its type I error is \(a^* = 1 - \Phi(t) = \Phi\big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} - \frac{\mu}{2}\big)\), using \(1 - \Phi(t) = \Phi(-t)\). Its power is the chance a draw from \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) exceeds \(t\), \(1 - b^* = 1 - \Phi(t - \mu) = \Phi\big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} + \frac{\mu}{2}\big)\).
Substitute into \(\delta = 1 - b^* - e^\varepsilon a^*\) to get Equation 30.10.
Agreement with Part 3. By Fact 2 this route computes \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(Q\|P)\). Part 3 instead computed \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = P[L > \varepsilon] - e^\varepsilon Q[L > \varepsilon]\) from the Gaussian law of the loss (Fact 1: \(L \sim \mathcal N(\frac{\mu^2}{2}, \mu^2)\) under \(P\) and \(\mathcal N(-\frac{\mu^2}{2}, \mu^2)\) under \(Q\)). The two agree because the Gaussian pair is symmetric: reflecting the line \(y \mapsto \mu - y\) swaps \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\), so swapping \(P\) and \(Q\) changes nothing.



30.5.5 Interpretation
The duality is lossless both ways. Reporting the whole profile \(\varepsilon \mapsto \delta(\varepsilon)\) loses nothing, because the lines rebuild the curve. Reporting one point, such as \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), keeps one touching line and drops the rest of the curve (Figure 30.2, right).
At \(\varepsilon = 0\) the profile is the TV distance. The line of slope \(-1\) touches a symmetric curve on the diagonal, at the test with the best advantage \(1 - a - b\). For \(G_\mu\) that test has threshold \(t = \mu/2\), halfway between the means, and Equation 30.10 at \(\varepsilon = 0\) gives \(\delta(0) = \Phi(\mu/2) - \Phi(-\mu/2) = 2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\), Part 1’s best advantage.
Small \(\delta\) costs \(\varepsilon\), in proportion to \(\mu\). To make \(\delta\) small, the first term of Equation 30.10, a Gaussian tail \(\Phi(-x)\) with \(x = \frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} - \frac{\mu}{2}\), must be small. A normal tail falls roughly like \(e^{-x^2/2}\), so reaching \(\delta\) needs \(x\) of about \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\), and \(\varepsilon\) grows roughly like \(\mu\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\). Each further factor of ten in \(\delta\) therefore costs extra \(\varepsilon\), a little less with each decade (a square root grows ever more slowly), and about \(\mu\) times as much as at \(\mu = 1\). At \(\mu = 1\), going from \(\delta = 10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-5}\) to \(10^{-6}\) raises \(\varepsilon\) from 3.8044 to 4.3772 to 4.8866 (steps of 0.57 and 0.51); at \(\mu = 2\), from 8.8769 to 9.9973 to 10.9972 (steps of 1.12 and 1.00, about twice as large). Figure 30.2 (left) and Table 30.4 show the same growth.


30.5.6 Example: reading \(\delta(1)\) of 1-GDP off the curve
At \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\) the touching threshold is \(t = \frac{1}{1} + \frac{1}{2} = 1.5000\). The best test where the slope is \(-e\) has type I error \(a^* = \Phi(-1.5) = 0.066807\) and power \(1 - b^* = \Phi(1 - 1.5) = \Phi(-0.5) = 0.308538\), so \(\delta(1) = 0.308538 - e \times 0.066807 = 0.308538 - 0.181601 = 0.126937\). These are the numbers of Part 3’s Table 20.6, read in a new way. There, 0.3085 was the probability of the bad event \(\{L > 1\}\), where the privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), and 0.1816 its correction. Here they are the power of the best test and the price of its type I error at the exchange rate \(e\). As a check on step 1, maximizing \(1 - G_1(a) - e\,a\) over a grid of 20,001 values of \(a\) gives the same 0.126937, at \(a = 0.0668\).
Going the other way, from a target \(\delta\) to \(\varepsilon\), has no closed form, but \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) decreases in \(\varepsilon\), so the function gdp_eps finds the \(\varepsilon\) where it equals the target by bisection. At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\):

From Figure 30.2 (right), which part of \(G_1\) does the \(\varepsilon = 0\) line describe? (The point where the slope is \(-1\), on the diagonal at \(a = b = \Phi(-1/2) = 0.3085\): the best-advantage test. Larger \(\varepsilon\) describe points closer to the axes.)
Is “1-GDP” the same guarantee as “\((4.3772, 10^{-5})\)-DP”? (No. 1-GDP implies it, but the single curve \(f_{4.3772, 10^{-5}}\) allows far more power: at \(a = 0.1\) its second piece allows \(b = e^{-4.3772}(1 - 10^{-5} - 0.1) = 0.0113\), while \(G_1(0.1) = 0.6109\).)

title: 30  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
30.6 Composition

30.6.1 Context
Training runs a mechanism thousands of times on the same data. Composing \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantees directly is lossy (composition). Composing curves is exact, and for Gaussian curves it is a one-line formula.


30.6.2 Statement
When an adversary sees the outputs of two mechanisms run with independent randomness, it faces the pair of joint distributions: \(P \times P'\) (both outputs drawn on \(D\)) against \(Q \times Q'\) (both drawn on \(D'\)). The curve of that joint pair defines the composition of curves. The tensor product of two trade-off functions \(f = T(P, Q)\) and \(g = T(P', Q')\) is \[f \otimes g = T(P \times P', Q \times Q'), \tag{30.11}\] the curve of the pair of product distributions. It does not depend on which pairs are used to represent \(f\) and \(g\) (Dong et al., Definition 3.1). If each mechanism \(M_i\) is \(f_i\)-DP, even when it is chosen adaptively from earlier outputs, then the composition \((M_1, \dots, M_k)\) is \(f_1 \otimes \dots \otimes f_k\)-DP, and no better bound holds in general (Dong et al., Theorem 3.2). For Gaussian curves the product is again Gaussian, with the shifts adding like the sides of a right-angled triangle: \[G_{\mu_1} \otimes G_{\mu_2} \otimes \dots \otimes G_{\mu_k} = G_\mu, \qquad \mu = \sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \dots + \mu_k^2} \tag{30.12}\] (Dong et al., Corollary 3.3).


30.6.3 Derivation

Non-adaptive composition through Blackwell. Suppose \(T(P_i, Q_i) \ge f_i = T(\tilde P_i, \tilde Q_i)\), where \((\tilde P_i, \tilde Q_i)\) is some pair whose curve is exactly \(f_i\). By Blackwell’s theorem (Dong et al., Theorem 2.10), a curve lies above another exactly when its pair can be produced from the other pair by post-processing, so some randomized map \(K_i\) sends \(\tilde P_i \mapsto P_i\) and \(\tilde Q_i \mapsto Q_i\). Apply the maps coordinatewise and independently: \((K_1, \dots, K_k)\) sends \(\prod\tilde P_i \mapsto \prod P_i\) and \(\prod\tilde Q_i \mapsto \prod Q_i\). Post-processing cannot help a test, so \(T(\prod P_i, \prod Q_i) \ge T(\prod\tilde P_i, \prod\tilde Q_i) = \bigotimes f_i\).
Adaptive composition. When \(M_2\) depends on the output of \(M_1\), the second coordinate is not independent of the first, and step 1 does not apply. Dong et al. prove the same bound with the Neyman–Pearson lemma alone, conditioning on the first output (their Theorem 3.2 and Appendix C). This chapter uses the result without re-proving it.
Tightness. If the mechanisms ignore each other’s outputs and some neighbouring pair attains each \(f_i\), the composed pair is exactly the product pair, so its curve is exactly \(\bigotimes f_i\).
Gaussian curves. \(G_{\mu_i} = T(\mathcal N(0, 1), \mathcal N(\mu_i, 1))\), so \(\bigotimes G_{\mu_i}\) is the curve of \(k\) independent coordinates, \(T(\mathcal N(0, I_k), \mathcal N(m, I_k))\) with \(m = (\mu_1, \dots, \mu_k)\). By Fact 3, this is \(G_{\|m\|_2}\), and \(\|m\|_2 = \sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \dots + \mu_k^2}\), which is Equation 30.12.



30.6.4 Interpretation
Under composition, the quantity that adds up is \(\mu^2\), just as variances of independent noises add. With \(k\) identical steps, \(\mu\) grows like \(\sqrt k\). Full-batch noisy gradient descent with clipped gradients and noise multiplier \(\sigma\) for \(k\) steps is a composition of \(k\) Gaussian mechanisms, each \(1/\sigma\)-GDP, so it is \(\sqrt{k/\sigma^2} = \sqrt k/\sigma\)-GDP. By step 3 it is in the worst case no better: no accountant can improve on it, and none needs to do more.
Concentrated DP is the same arithmetic. In zero-concentrated DP the Gaussian mechanism has \(\rho = \mu^2/2\), and \(\rho\) adds under composition (concentrated DP), which is the same as \(\mu^2\) adding. The difference is what you can read off at the end: \(\mu\)-GDP gives the exact curve, \(\rho\) only an RDP bound on it (Section 30.9).
For other curves the tensor product is hard. For \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) the product is a supremum of many \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\) curves, which is the optimal composition theorem of Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath. Computing it exactly is #P-complete, a class of counting problems believed to have no efficient algorithm, when the \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\) differ from step to step (Murtagh & Vadhan 2016; Part 3, Section 21.5). So numerical accountants compute \(\bigotimes f_i\) another way: since the composed privacy loss is the sum of the independent per-step losses, they discretize the PRV and convolve its law with itself. These are the privacy loss distribution (PLD) and PRV accountants of numerical accounting.


30.6.5 Example: two concrete products
Gaussian. By Equation 30.12, two 1-GDP releases compose to \(G_{\sqrt 2} = G_{1.4142}\); three releases with \(\mu = (0.5, 0.5, 1)\) to \(G_{\sqrt{0.25 + 0.25 + 1}} = G_{1.2247}\); four 1-GDP releases to \(G_{\sqrt 4} = G_2\); and 100 releases with \(\sigma = 10\) each, so \(\mu_i = 0.1\), to \(G_{\sqrt{100 \times 0.01}} = G_1\). A simulation of the projected test in two dimensions, \(\mu = (1, 1)\), at \(a = 0.05\) with 1,000,000 draws per hypothesis gives \(\hat a = 0.0497\) and \(\hat b = 0.5913\), against \(G_{\sqrt2}(0.05) = 0.5912\). The composed release sits strictly between one release, \(G_1(0.05) = 0.7405\), and a single release with twice the shift, \(G_2(0.05) = 0.3612\) (Figure 30.3).
Randomized response twice. This shows the tensor product for curves that are not Gaussian. Run randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 1\) on the same bit twice, independently. Part 3 tabulated the same product at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) as a sum of privacy losses (Table 21.2); here it is read as a curve. Each run keeps the bit with probability 0.7311. Under \(P\) (bit 0) and \(Q\) (bit 1) the four output pairs have the probabilities of Table 30.5; for example, 00 has probability \(e^2/(1 + e)^2 = 0.5344\) under \(P\) (both runs keep the bit) and \(1/(1 + e)^2 = 0.0723\) under \(Q\) (both runs flip it).

7.3891






By Neyman–Pearson, the best tests add outcomes to the firing region in decreasing order of the likelihood ratio \(q/p\) (Table 30.5): first 11 (\(q/p = e^2\)), then the two mixed pairs (\(q/p = 1\)), then 00 (\(e^{-2}\)). Each addition raises \(a\) by the outcome’s \(p\) and lowers \(b\) by its \(q\). Firing on 11 alone gives \((a, b) = (0.0723, 1 - 0.5344) = (0.0723, 0.4656)\); adding one mixed pair gives \((0.2689, 0.2689)\); adding both gives \((0.4656, 0.0723)\). So the curve \(f_{1,0}\otimes f_{1,0}\) is the polygon through \((0, 1)\), \((0.0723, 0.4656)\), \((0.2689, 0.2689)\), \((0.4656, 0.0723)\) and \((1, 0)\), with straight segments in between from randomizing at the boundary outcome. Its slopes are minus the likelihood ratios, \(-e^2\), \(-1\) and \(-e^{-2}\). An \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) curve has only two slopes, so this curve is not \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) for any pair. It is the supremum of two such curves: \(f_{2,0}\), whose first line \(1 - e^2a\) is the steep segment, and \(f_{0,0.4621}\), whose line \(1 - \delta - a\) is the middle segment, with \(\delta = 1 - 0.0723 - 0.4656 = 0.4621\), which equals \(\tanh(1/2)\) (Exercise 3). This is the smallest instance of the fact that composed \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantees are a family of pairs, not one pair.
Composing points loses. Four 1-GDP releases are 2-GDP, so Table 30.4 gives \(\varepsilon = 9.9973\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Suppose instead you first turn each release into one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) point, giving each a quarter of the \(\delta\) budget, \((4.6902, 2.5\times10^{-6})\), and then compose the points with basic composition, which adds the \(\varepsilon\)’s and the \(\delta\)’s. You get \(\varepsilon = 18.7607\) at \(\delta = 4 \times 2.5\times10^{-6} = 10^{-5}\): almost twice as large. Even optimal composition of the points loses, because each point has already dropped most of its curve; Part 3’s Figure 21.4 shows by how much for many steps.






Figure 30.3: Left: 400 draws each from \(\mathcal N(0, I_2)\) and \(\mathcal N((1, 1), I_2)\), the outputs of two Gaussian releases on \(D\) and \(D'\). The best test thresholds the projection on the shift (arrow); the dashed line is its boundary at \(a = 0.05\). Right: \(G_1\) for one release, \(G_{\sqrt 2}\) for two, and simulated errors of the projected test (crosses, 20,000 draws per point).





30.6.6 Check yourself

You may release a vector query with \(\Delta_2 = 1\) either once with \(\sigma = 1\) or twice, independently, with \(\sigma = \sqrt2\) each. Which is more private? (Neither: each of the two releases is \(1/\sqrt2\)-GDP, and \(\sqrt{(1/\sqrt2)^2 + (1/\sqrt2)^2} = 1\), the same \(G_1\).)
Why does the product of two \(f_{\varepsilon,0}\) curves have a segment of slope \(-1\)? (Outcomes with equal likelihood under \(P\) and \(Q\), here the mixed pairs 01 and 10, carry no evidence; adding them to the firing region trades type I for type II error one for one.)
