section: 30.7 The central limit theorem for composition
text:
30.7 The central limit theorem for composition

30.7.1 Context
Most mechanisms are not Gaussian, so Equation 30.12 does not apply directly. But the privacy loss of a composition is the sum of the independent per-step losses, because the densities of independent outputs multiply and logs turn products into sums. Sums of many small independent terms are nearly normal, and by Fact 1 a normal privacy loss means a Gaussian curve. The CLT for \(f\)-DP turns this into a statement about curves.


30.7.2 Statement
To use the CLT you need the mean, the variance and a third-moment size of the privacy loss. Dong et al. write them as functionals of the curve itself, through its slope: by the slope rule of Fact 1, \(-\ln|f'(a)|\) is the threshold loss \(l(a)\), so averaging powers of it over \(a \in [0, 1]\) averages powers of the loss (the derivation makes this precise). For a trade-off function \(f = T(P, Q)\) define (Dong et al., §3.2) \[\mathrm{kl}(f) = -\int_0^1\ln|f'(a)|\,da, \quad \kappa_2(f) = \int_0^1\ln^2|f'(a)|\,da, \quad \kappa_3(f) = \int_0^1\big|\ln|f'(a)|\big|^3da, \quad \bar\kappa_3(f) = \int_0^1\big|\ln|f'(a)| + \mathrm{kl}(f)\big|^3da. \tag{30.13}\] In words: \(\mathrm{kl}\) is the mean of the loss, \(\kappa_2\) its second moment, \(\kappa_3\) its third absolute moment and \(\bar\kappa_3\) its third absolute moment about the mean.
Berry–Esseen form (Dong et al., Theorem 3.4). For \(k\) curves, collect each functional into a vector, \(\mathrm{kl} = (\mathrm{kl}(f_1), \dots, \mathrm{kl}(f_k))\) and so on, and write \(\|\cdot\|_1\) for the sum of the entries and \(\|\cdot\|_2^2\) for the sum of their squares. Then \(\|\mathrm{kl}\|_1\) is the mean of the summed loss and \(\|\kappa_2\|_1 - \|\mathrm{kl}\|_2^2\) its variance. The theorem matches the composition to the Gaussian curve whose loss has the same ratio of mean to standard deviation, and bounds the error by the Berry–Esseen ratio of third moment to variance\(^{3/2}\). Let \(f_1, \dots, f_k\) be symmetric with \(\kappa_3(f_i) < \infty\), and put \[\mu = \frac{2\|\mathrm{kl}\|_1}{\sqrt{\|\kappa_2\|_1 - \|\mathrm{kl}\|_2^2}}, \qquad \gamma = \frac{0.56\,\|\bar\kappa_3\|_1}{\big(\|\kappa_2\|_1 - \|\mathrm{kl}\|_2^2\big)^{3/2}}. \tag{30.14}\] If \(\gamma < \frac12\), then for all \(a \in [\gamma, 1 - \gamma]\) the composed curve lies in a band around \(G_\mu\) of width \(\gamma\) in both directions: \[G_\mu(a + \gamma) - \gamma \le f_1 \otimes \dots \otimes f_k(a) \le G_\mu(a - \gamma) + \gamma. \tag{30.15}\]
Limit form (Dong et al., Theorem 3.5). As the number of curves grows and each one leaks less, the band shrinks to zero. Precisely, for a triangular array \(f_{k1}, \dots, f_{kk}\) of symmetric curves (a fresh list of \(k\) curves for each \(k\)) with \(\sum_i\mathrm{kl}(f_{ki}) \to K \ge 0\), \(\max_i\mathrm{kl}(f_{ki}) \to 0\), \(\sum_i\kappa_2(f_{ki}) \to s^2 > 0\) and \(\sum_i\kappa_3(f_{ki}) \to 0\), the composition converges uniformly to \(G_{2K/s}\). For \((\varepsilon_i, 0)\)-DP mechanisms with \(\sum_i\varepsilon_{i}^2 \to \mu^2\) and \(\max_i\varepsilon_i \to 0\), the limit is \(G_\mu\) (Dong et al., Theorem 3.6).


30.7.3 Derivation (the idea; the proof is in Dong et al., Appendix D)

The functionals are moments of the PRV. By the slope rule (Fact 1), \(-\ln|f'(a)| = l(a)\), the \(a\)-quantile of \(L\) under \(P\). Now use the quantile transform: if \(U\) is uniform on \([0, 1]\), then \(l(U)\) has the law of \(L\), just as feeding uniform random numbers into the inverse of a distribution function produces samples from that distribution. So \(\int_0^1 g(l(a))\,da = \mathbb E[g(l(U))] = \mathbb E_P[g(L)]\) for any function \(g\). Taking \(g(x) = x\), \(x^2\) and \(|x - \mathbb E_PL|^3\) gives \[\mathrm{kl}(f) = \mathbb E_P[L] = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q), \quad \kappa_2(f) = \mathbb E_P[L^2], \quad \bar\kappa_3(f) = \mathbb E_P\big|L - \mathbb E_PL\big|^3. \tag{30.16}\] The first is the Kullback–Leibler divergence, the expected log likelihood ratio. And \(\kappa_2 - \mathrm{kl}^2\) is the second moment minus the squared mean, the variance of the PRV.
Composition adds independent losses. For product distributions the densities multiply, so the composed loss is \(L_1 + \dots + L_k\) with independent terms. Means add and, for independent terms, variances add. So under \(P\) the composed loss has mean \(K = \|\mathrm{kl}\|_1\) and variance \(V = \|\kappa_2\|_1 - \|\mathrm{kl}\|_2^2\).
The ordinary CLT. When no term dominates, the sum is close to \(\mathcal N(K, V)\). The Berry–Esseen theorem says how close: the distribution function of a sum of independent terms differs from that of the matching normal by at most a constant times the summed third absolute central moments divided by \(V^{3/2}\). Here that is \(\|\bar\kappa_3\|_1/V^{3/2}\), and with the constant 0.56 it is the \(\gamma\) of Equation 30.14.
Match a Gaussian pair. By Fact 1 the pair behind \(G_\mu\) has PRV \(\mathcal N(\frac{\mu^2}{2}, \mu^2)\) under \(P\), whose mean-to-standard-deviation ratio is \(\frac{\mu^2/2}{\mu} = \mu/2\). Matching that ratio to \(K/\sqrt V\) gives \(\mu = 2K/\sqrt V\), Equation 30.14.
Why match the ratio and not the variance alone. A normal law \(\mathcal N(m, v)\) is the law of some PRV only if \(\mathbb E_P[e^{-L}] = 1\) (the change of measure of Fact 1 with \(A\) = everything). By the normal moment generating function, \(\mathbb E[e^{-L}] = e^{-m + v/2}\), so the condition is \(m = v/2\), as in the Gaussian pair, where \(m = \mu^2/2\) and \(v = \mu^2\). Sums of small losses satisfy this only approximately, so at finite \(k\) different matches give slightly different \(\mu\); matching the ratio is Dong et al.’s choice. In the limit the two agree: \(K = s^2/2\), and then \(2K/s = s\). Dong et al. observe this in all their examples, and for symmetric curves it follows in a few lines. Symmetry means the law of the summed loss under \(Q\) is the mirror image of its law under \(P\), so if \(L \to \mathcal N(K, s^2)\) under \(P\), then \(L \to \mathcal N(-K, s^2)\) under \(Q\). For every \(c > 0\) the change of measure gives \(\mathbb E_P[e^{-L}\mathbf 1\{L > -c\}] = Q[L > -c]\). The integrand on the left is bounded by \(e^c\) and jumps only at \(-c\), a point of probability 0 under the normal limit, so both sides pass to the limit: \(\mathbb E[e^{-Z}\mathbf 1\{Z > -c\}] = \Pr[Z' > -c]\) with \(Z \sim \mathcal N(K, s^2)\) and \(Z' \sim \mathcal N(-K, s^2)\). Letting \(c \to \infty\) gives \(\mathbb E[e^{-Z}] = 1\), that is \(e^{-K + s^2/2} = 1\), so \(K = s^2/2\).
From the law of the loss to the curve. By Fact 1 the curve is a functional of the law of the loss under \(P\). Since that law is close to the Gaussian pair’s, so is the curve.



30.7.4 Interpretation
This is why GDP is the natural family. The limit of many small compositions is always some \(G_\mu\), and the family is closed under composition. The \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) family is not: two runs of randomized response already leave it (Table 30.5).
For \(\varepsilon\)-DP pieces, \(\mu\) is the root sum of squares, \(\mu = \sqrt{\sum\varepsilon_i^2}\), in the limit. That is the \(\sqrt k\) behaviour of advanced composition, with the exact constant.
The CLT is an approximation, not a bound. The Berry–Esseen band \(\gamma\) is a bound, but it is wide: 0.0562 at \(k = 100\) in the example below. The point estimate \(G_\mu\) can be above or below the true curve, and the error is largest in the tails. That is where small \(\delta\) lives, because a small \(\delta\) is decided by rare, large values of the loss, and a CLT controls the bulk of a distribution much better than its tails.


30.7.5 Example: composing randomized response and Laplace
Take \(k\) mechanisms, each \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP with \(\varepsilon_0 = 1/\sqrt k\), so that \(\sum\varepsilon_i^2 = k \cdot \frac1k = 1\) and the limit is \(G_1\). To judge the CLT you need the true \(\delta(1)\) of the composition, and that requires the exact law of the summed loss.
For randomized response this law is simple. Under \(P\) each run reports the true bit with probability \(e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\), giving loss \(+\varepsilon_0\), and flips it otherwise, giving \(-\varepsilon_0\). If \(B \sim \mathrm{Bin}(k, e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0}))\) counts the truthful runs, the summed loss is \(\varepsilon_0 B - \varepsilon_0(k - B) = \varepsilon_0(2B - k)\). The profile is the hockey-stick divergence \(\int(p - e^\varepsilon q)_+\), which after dividing inside by \(p\) is \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E_P[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+]\), an exact finite sum over the \(k + 1\) values of \(B\). For the Laplace mechanism the loss has two atoms at \(\pm\varepsilon_0\) and a continuous part in between. The script rounds the continuous part down, and then up, to a lattice of spacing \(\varepsilon_0/400\), convolves \(k\) copies by the fast Fourier transform, and reports both values. Since \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) only grows when any loss grows, the two values bracket the exact one.

text:
30.8 The subsampled Gaussian and DP-SGD

30.8.1 Context
DP-SGD (subsampling) composes \(k\) steps. Each step forms a batch by Poisson subsampling, which includes each record independently with probability \(q\), clips each gradient to norm at most the sensitivity, and adds Gaussian noise with noise multiplier \(\sigma\) to their sum. Each step leaks little when \(q\) is small, because the target record is usually not even in the batch, so the CLT applies. Under add/remove neighbours, where \(D'\) is \(D\) with one record added, one subsampled Gaussian step reduces to the pair of step 1 below: a Gaussian against a two-component mixture (subsampling derives it). The reason is short: the other records contribute the same to both outputs and can be subtracted, and the added record’s clipped gradient, at worst a shift of one sensitivity, is present with probability \(q\) and absent otherwise. So the derivation here stands on its own. In this section \(q\) is the sampling rate; the two output densities of one step are \(P(y)\) and \(Q(y)\).


30.8.2 Statement
Under add/remove neighbours, if \(k \to \infty\) and \(q\sqrt k \to c\) with \(\sigma\) fixed, \(k\) steps of the Poisson-subsampled Gaussian mechanism are asymptotically \(\mu\)-GDP with \[\mu = q\sqrt{k\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big)} \tag{30.17}\] (Bu, Dong, Long & Su 2020, Section 3, proved as their Theorem 5; Dong et al., Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 5.4, prove the analogous limit for their fixed-size batches under replace-one, with a different constant). This is a limit, used in practice as an approximation at finite \(k\).


30.8.3 Derivation (heuristic, through Equation 30.14)
The plan is to compute the mean and variance of one step’s privacy loss for small \(q\), add them over \(k\) steps, and plug them into \(\mu = 2K/\sqrt V\) from the CLT.

One step. Work in units of the sensitivity, so a present record shifts the mean by 1. The pair is \(P = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) (the record is absent) and \(Q = (1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) (present, so with probability \(q\) it is in the batch). The ratio of the \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) density to the \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) density is \(e^{(2y - 1)/(2\sigma^2)} = e^{(y - 1/2)/\sigma^2}\), from the same cancellation of squares as in Fact 1. So the likelihood ratio is \[\frac{Q(y)}{P(y)} = 1 - q + q\,e^{(y - 1/2)/\sigma^2} = 1 + qW(y), \qquad W(y) = e^{(y - 1/2)/\sigma^2} - 1. \tag{30.18}\] Writing it as \(1 + qW\) isolates the small parameter \(q\): \(W\) measures how much the output favours “the record was in the batch”, and \(q\) scales it down.
Moments of \(W\) under \(P\). The mean is 0: \(\mathbb E_P[W] = \mathbb E_P[\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\text{-density}/P(y)] - 1 = 1 - 1 = 0\), because averaging a density ratio under the denominator integrates the numerator density, which is 1. For the second moment, use the moment generating function of \(Y \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), \(\mathbb E[e^{tY}] = e^{t^2\sigma^2/2}\), with \(t = 2/\sigma^2\): \(\mathbb E_P[e^{2(Y - 1/2)/\sigma^2}] = e^{2/\sigma^2}e^{-1/\sigma^2} = e^{1/\sigma^2}\). Expanding the square, \(\mathbb E_P[W^2] = \mathbb E_P[(W + 1)^2] - 2\,\mathbb E_P[W + 1] + 1 = e^{1/\sigma^2} - 2 + 1 = e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\). This is the \(\chi^2\) divergence between the two Gaussians, the mean squared deviation of their density ratio from 1.
Expand the loss. The loss is \(L = \ln\frac{P(y)}{Q(y)} = -\ln(1 + qW)\). For small \(q\), the Taylor series \(\ln(1 + x) = x - \frac{x^2}{2} + O(x^3)\) gives \(L = -qW + \frac{q^2W^2}{2} + O(q^3W^3)\). Taking moments under \(P\) with step 2: the first term has mean 0, so \(\mathbb E_P[L] \approx \frac{q^2}{2}\mathbb E_P[W^2] = \frac{q^2}{2}(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\), and to leading order the variance is that of \(-qW\), \(\mathrm{Var}_P[L] \approx q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\).
Sum over \(k\) steps. Means and variances of independent losses add, so \(K \approx \frac{kq^2}{2}(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\) and \(V \approx kq^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\). Then \(\mu = 2K/\sqrt V = kq^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)/\big(q\sqrt{k(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\big) = q\sqrt{k(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\), Equation 30.17.
The regime. With \(q\sqrt k \to c\), each step’s moments are \(O(q^2) = O(1/k)\), so \(K\) and \(V\) converge to finite limits, \(\max_i\mathrm{kl} \to 0\), and \(\sum\kappa_3 = O(kq^3) \to 0\). These are the conditions of the limit form of the CLT. The other order of \(P\) and \(Q\) gives the same leading terms.



30.8.4 Interpretation
Subsampling buys a factor of about \(q\). Full-batch training (\(q = 1\)) for \(k\) steps is \(\sqrt k/\sigma\)-GDP. Dividing Equation 30.17 by \(\sqrt k/\sigma\), subsampling multiplies this by about \(q\sqrt{e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1}\cdot\sigma\), which for \(\sigma = 1\) is \(q \times 1.3108\).
It is an approximation, not a bound. Two approximations stack: the CLT itself, and the expansion in step 3 (the exact per-step moments are smaller than the leading terms). Neither is controlled in the tail, which is where \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) lives. Gopi, Lee & Wutschitz (2021) showed that the CLT value can lie below the true \(\varepsilon\) of DP-SGD. The example below confirms it for the running example; numerical accounting computes certified values and choosing an accountant compares all the accountants on this example.
Watch the neighbouring relation. Corollary 5.4 of Dong et al. analyses fixed-size batches under replace-one neighbours, where \(D'\) swaps one record of \(D\) for another, and gets a different constant (\(\mu = 1.7101\) at \(k = 10{,}000\) in the running example). Do not mix the two (subsampling explains why).


30.8.5 Example: the running DP-SGD example
The running example has sampling rate \(q = 0.01\), noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1\) and target \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Then \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1 = 1.7183\) and \(\sqrt{1.7183} = 1.3108\), so Equation 30.17 gives \(\mu = 0.01 \times 1.3108\sqrt k\); at \(k = 100\), for example, \(\mu = 0.01 \times 1.3108 \times 10 = 0.1311\). Table 30.8 turns each \(\mu\) into \(\varepsilon\) with Equation 30.10 and compares it with a numerical accountant.

The bracket in Table 30.8 comes from the same lattice-and-convolve method as the Laplace example, applied to the per-step loss on a lattice of spacing \(h = 10^{-5}\), taking the worse of the two orders of neighbours. Rounding each step’s loss down or up by at most \(h\) moves the composed loss by at most \(kh\), so the bracket’s width is \(kh\) by construction (0.0010, 0.0100 and 0.1000), and the informative number is its lower end. That lower end is exact up to the quadrature error in the per-step weights. In all three rows the CLT value lies below the lower end of the bracket. The ratio of the CLT value to that lower end is 0.638 at \(k = 100\), 0.887 at \(k = 1{,}000\) and 0.979 at \(k = 10{,}000\), where \(q\sqrt k\) is largest and the CLT regime fits best.

In the order of the derivation (\(P = \mathcal N(0, 1)\), the record absent), the mean of the loss is \(8.1890\times10^{-5}\) against the leading term \(q^2(e - 1)/2 = 8.5914\times10^{-5}\), and the variance \(1.6009\times10^{-4}\) against \(q^2(e - 1) = 1.7183\times10^{-4}\). Plugging the exact moments into Equation 30.14 gives \(\mu = 1.2944\) at \(k = 10{,}000\) and \(\varepsilon = 5.9184\). The other order (the record present in \(D\)) gives \(\mu = 1.2795\) and \(\varepsilon = 5.8379\). Both are below the CLT’s 6.0071, and further below the lower end 6.1377. So a smaller “more exact” \(\mu\) is not more conservative; only a certified accountant is.

Figure 30.5 shows how quickly \(\varepsilon\) grows with \(k\) once \(\mu\) passes 1, and how strongly it depends on \(\sigma\): \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\) is 3.7707 at \(\sigma = 0.8\), 1.7183 at \(\sigma = 1\) and 0.5596 at \(\sigma = 1.5\).


30.8.6 Check yourself

At fixed \(q\) and \(\sigma\), how does the CLT \(\mu\) scale with the number of epochs \(E = kq\)? (As \(\sqrt k\), so as \(\sqrt{E/q}\): ten times more epochs multiplies \(\mu\) by \(\sqrt{10}\).)
Why can you not report “\(\varepsilon = 6.0071\)” for the running example at \(k = 10{,}000\) as a DP guarantee? (It is an asymptotic approximation with no error bound, and a numerical accountant shows the true \(\varepsilon\) is at least 6.1377, up to quadrature error.)

title: 30  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
section: 30.9 RDP as a lossy summary of the curve
text:
30.9 RDP as a lossy summary of the curve

30.9.1 Context
Rényi DP tracks \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = D_\alpha(P\|Q)\) over orders \(\alpha > 1\), where the Rényi divergence \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_P\big[(p/q)^{\alpha - 1}\big]\) is a log-moment of the likelihood ratio. Conversions (Section 28.5) turned an RDP curve into the region of test errors it allows, with lower boundary \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\), and showed that each point of that boundary is attained by a two-outcome pair. This section reads that construction in the language of \(f\)-DP. What kind of guarantee is \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\), and where does it sit between the true curve and a single \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair?


30.9.2 Statement
The construction rests on one observation: a test turns any pair into a pair of coins. Its output is “fire” with probability \(a\) under \(P\) and \(1 - b\) under \(Q\), so it maps \(P\) to \(\mathrm{Bern}(a)\) and \(Q\) to \(\mathrm{Bern}(1 - b)\), and processing cannot increase a Rényi divergence. So the test’s errors must keep these two coins within the RDP budget at every order. The lowest type II error that passes this check at each \(a\) is \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\).
Let \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) be an RDP curve, known at the orders of the part’s grid (the fixed list of orders that the accountants of this part evaluate) and in both orders of neighbours, and let \[f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(a) = \min\big\{b : D_\alpha\big(\mathrm{Bern}(a)\,\big\|\,\mathrm{Bern}(1 - b)\big) \le \varepsilon(\alpha) \text{ and } D_\alpha\big(\mathrm{Bern}(1 - b)\,\big\|\,\mathrm{Bern}(a)\big) \le \varepsilon(\alpha) \text{ for every order } \alpha \text{ of the grid}\big\} \tag{30.19}\] be the lowest type II error it allows (Equation 28.11). Then:

The trade-off curve of a pair determines its RDP curve.
\(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is a symmetric trade-off function, and a mechanism with this RDP curve is \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\)-DP. At each \(a\), no higher value follows from the RDP values alone.
The best \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) that the RDP values certify is the privacy profile of \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\): \(\delta_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\varepsilon) = 1 + f_{\mathrm{RDP}}^*(-e^\varepsilon)\), which is the optimal conversion Equation 28.12 of Conversions.

For the Gaussian pair, \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha\mu^2/2\) (Part 1). At \(\mu = 1\), \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) lies below \(G_1\) at every \(a\) the script computed.


30.9.3 Derivation

The curve determines the Rényi divergence. By Fact 1 the curve fixes the law of \(L\) under \(P\). Since \(p/q = e^L\), the Rényi divergence is \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}]\), a functional of that law (Divergences).
RDP implies \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\)-DP. A test with errors \((a, b)\) maps \(P\) to \(\mathrm{Bern}(a)\) and \(Q\) to \(\mathrm{Bern}(1 - b)\). By data processing for Rényi divergence (post-processing cannot increase it), the two Bernoullis satisfy the constraints whenever \(P\) and \(Q\) do. So every point of the true curve is feasible, and \(T(P, Q) \ge f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\).
\(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is a trade-off function. Each constraint is convex in \((a, b)\), because each term of the Bernoulli divergence has the form \(x^\alpha y^{1 - \alpha}\), which is jointly convex for \(\alpha > 1\) (“Computing it” in Conversions). So the feasible set is convex and its lower boundary \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is convex. The point \((a, 1 - a)\) is feasible, because two equal Bernoullis have divergence 0, so \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(a) \le 1 - a\) and \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(1) = 0\). A convex function on \([0, 1]\) whose minimum is at \(a = 1\) is non-increasing: for \(a < a' < 1\), write \(a' = \lambda a + (1 - \lambda)\cdot 1\), and then \(f(a') \le \lambda f(a) + (1 - \lambda)f(1) \le f(a)\). Swapping \(a\) and \(b\) swaps the two constraints (the coins \(\mathrm{Bern}(a)\) and \(\mathrm{Bern}(1 - b)\) trade places after relabelling their outcomes), so the feasible set is symmetric about the diagonal and \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}} = f_{\mathrm{RDP}}^{-1}\).
No higher value at any \(a\). For each feasible \((a, b)\) the pair \((\mathrm{Bern}(a), \mathrm{Bern}(1 - b))\) is itself a mechanism that satisfies the constraints at every order of the grid, and its test “fire on outcome 1” has errors \((a, b)\), so its curve passes through \((a, b)\) (step 5 of the derivation in Conversions). So at each \(a\) some pair consistent with the RDP values reaches \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(a)\). Different values of \(a\) need different pairs.
The optimal conversion is the conjugate. Equation 28.12 writes the best certified \(\delta\) as \(\max_a\big[1 - a - e^\varepsilon f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(a)\big]\), with the roles of \(a\) and \(b\) the other way round from the duality of Section 30.5. Because \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is symmetric, its graph contains \((b, a)\) whenever it contains \((a, b)\), so swapping the roles changes nothing: the maximum equals \(\max_a\big[1 - f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(a) - e^\varepsilon a\big] = 1 + f_{\mathrm{RDP}}^*(-e^\varepsilon)\), the duality of Equation 30.9 applied to \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\).
Below \(G_1\). The script computes \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) for \(\mu = 1\) by bisection on \(b\) over the grid of orders, and finds it below \(G_1\) everywhere it looked. This is a numerical observation, not a proof. More orders impose more constraints and can only raise \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\), but not by much: at \(a = \Phi(-1/2) = 0.3085\), a dense set of orders in \([1.01, 3000]\) raises it from 0.2201 to 0.2219, still far below \(G_1(0.3085) = 0.3085\).



30.9.4 Interpretation
The results form a ladder of summaries. For the Gaussian mechanism, \(G_\mu\) is the exact curve, \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is what its RDP curve keeps, and an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair is one touching line of \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\). So the slack of an RDP conversion has two parts: the gap between the line and \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\), which the optimal conversion removes, and the gap between \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) and the true curve, which no conversion removes (Section 28.7).
RDP loses because it keeps only the exponential moments \(\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}]\) at a few orders. Different laws of the loss share them, and \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) has to allow the worst of those laws. The absolute gap in \(b\) is largest in the bulk. Relative to the attacker’s power \(1 - b\), though, the RDP curve allows roughly the same factor more power than the Gaussian has from the bulk down to \(a = 10^{-6}\) (Table 28.5), so the loss is not confined to the bulk.


30.9.5 Example: what 1-GDP’s RDP curve forgets
Table 30.9 compares \(G_1\) with \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) computed from \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/2\). The third row is the best advantage, which for a symmetric curve sits at the diagonal point \(a = b\), where it equals \(1 - a - b = 1 - 2a\); for \(G_1\) that is \(1 - 2 \times 0.3085 = 0.3829\). The last row is the duality of Section 30.5 applied to each curve.

30.9.6 Check yourself

If a mechanism’s RDP curve is no larger than the Gaussian’s at every order of the grid, must its trade-off curve lie on or above \(G_\mu\)? (No. By step 4, for each \(a\) the two-outcome pair through \((a, f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(a))\) satisfies the Gaussian’s RDP curve at every order of the grid, yet its curve passes below \(G_\mu\) at \(a\).)
Why is GDP accounting for full-batch noisy gradient descent strictly better than RDP accounting for it? (Both compose exactly, but GDP keeps the whole curve \(G_{\sqrt k/\sigma}\), while RDP keeps only \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha k/(2\sigma^2)\), from which only \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\), which lies below \(G_{\sqrt k/\sigma}\), can be recovered.)

Dong, Roth & Su, “Gaussian Differential Privacy” (Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B, 2022; arXiv:1905.02383): the source of \(f\)-DP and GDP. Definition 2.3 (\(f\)-DP), Proposition 2.4 (symmetrization), Proposition 2.5 (\(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\)), Propositions 2.11–2.12 and Corollary 2.13 (duality), Theorem 2.14 (group privacy), Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3 (composition), Theorems 3.4–3.6 (CLTs), Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 5.4 (CLT for their fixed-size subsampling under replace-one, NoisySGD). The discussion sections are a good read on why the curve is the right object.
Bu, Dong, Long & Su, “Deep Learning with Gaussian Differential Privacy” (Harvard Data Science Review, 2020): the Poisson-subsampling CLT of Equation 30.17 (Section 3, proved as Theorem 5 in the appendix) and its use for DP-SGD, with experiments.
Wasserman & Zhou, “A Statistical Framework for Differential Privacy” (Journal of the American Statistical Association, 2010): the hypothesis-testing reading of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP behind Equation 30.7.
Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath, “The Composition Theorem for Differential Privacy” (ICML 2015): optimal composition of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP through testing regions and Blackwell’s theorem; the tensor product of \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) curves in other words.
Balle & Wang, “Improving the Gaussian Mechanism for Differential Privacy: Analytical Calibration and Optimal Denoising” (ICML 2018): Theorem 8 is the exact \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) profile of the Gaussian mechanism, Equation 30.10, and its use to calibrate \(\sigma\).

Murtagh & Vadhan, “The Complexity of Computing the Optimal Composition of Differential Privacy” (TCC 2016): exact optimal composition of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantees is #P-complete when the \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\) differ, which is why accountants discretize.

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
text:
31.1 Why this matters
Differential privacy (DP) for deep learning would be useless without one trick. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, runs ten thousand steps or more. Each step is a Gaussian mechanism: it clips every example’s gradient, sums them and adds Gaussian noise whose standard deviation is the noise multiplier \(\sigma\) times the clipping norm. Composing ten thousand such steps with \(\sigma = 1\), and paying for every record at every step, gives \(\varepsilon = 5425.5\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), as Rényi DP computes: a privacy loss nobody would report.
The trick is that each step only looks at a small random batch. If a record is in the batch only with probability \(q\), an adversary who sees the step’s output must first guess whether the record was used at all. That uncertainty is worth a lot. With \(q = 0.01\), it turns a step that costs \(\varepsilon = 1\) into one that costs about \(0.017\). In the language of Rényi differential privacy (RDP), which describes a mechanism by a curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) giving its privacy cost at each order \(\alpha > 1\), it turns the curve of a Gaussian step from \(\alpha/2\) into something of order \(10^{-4}\alpha\) for small orders.
This chapter answers three questions. How much privacy does random sampling buy, exactly? Which sampling scheme does the answer hold for? And how do you compute it for the Gaussian steps of DP-SGD?
Notation. In this chapter \(q\) is always the sampling rate, never a density. Output distributions are capital letters, as in the rest of this part, and the same letter names a distribution and its density. \(P_0\) is a step’s output without the record and \(P_1\) its output with it. For the subsampled Gaussian, \(P_0 = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), \(P_1 = \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\), and the output with the record sampled at rate \(q\) is the mixture \(P_q = (1 - q)P_0 + qP_1\): with probability \(1 - q\) the record is left out and the output is drawn from \(P_0\), with probability \(q\) it is used and the output is drawn from \(P_1\). The mixture lemma of the toolkit uses three generic distributions \(R\), \(P\), \(P'\) and a mixing weight \(\eta\); the letter \(\gamma\) is taken, because it is the parameter of the hockey-stick divergence \(E_\gamma\) defined in Fact 1. An output is \(y\).

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
text:
31.1.1 The one idea: the output is a mixture, and mixtures are closer
Fix a dataset \(D\) and add one record \(x\) to get \(D' = D \cup \{x\}\). Under Poisson sampling, each record enters the batch independently with probability \(q\), by its own coin flip. Condition on which records of \(D\) were drawn. On \(D\), the mechanism then outputs some distribution \(P_0\). On \(D'\), it outputs \(P_1\) if \(x\) was drawn and \(P_0\) otherwise. Since \(x\) is drawn with probability \(q\), the output on \(D'\) is the mixture, compared with the output on \(D\): \[(1 - q)P_0 + qP_1 \quad\text{against}\quad P_0. \tag{31.1}\] With probability \(1 - q\) the two runs are identical. The difference between the runs is diluted by a factor \(q\), and every likelihood ratio, the ratio of the two densities at an output \(y\) that measures how much more likely \(y\) is in one run than in the other, is pulled toward 1. Divide the mixture by \(P_0\) to see it: the ratio \(P_1/P_0\) becomes \((1 - q) + q\,P_1/P_0\), a weighted average of 1 and the old ratio. All of DP-SGD’s privacy rests on this dilution, and the dilution depends on how the batch was drawn. A different sampling scheme gives a different mixture, and an accountant that assumes one scheme while the training code runs another reports a number that does not apply.

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
section: 31.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses
text:
31.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses

31.2.1 Fact 1 — \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) is a statement about events, and averaging preserves it
A mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP when, for every pair of neighbouring datasets taken in both orders, the output distributions \(P\) and \(Q\) satisfy \(P(A) \le e^\varepsilon Q(A) + \delta\) for every event \(A\) (Definition): no set of outputs becomes more than \(e^\varepsilon\) times more likely, except for a slack \(\delta\). The hockey-stick divergence packs this into one number. It is the largest amount by which \(P\) exceeds \(\gamma\) times \(Q\) on any event, \(E_\gamma(P\|Q) = \max_A[P(A) - \gamma Q(A)]\), so the DP condition for the pair is exactly \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) \le \delta\).
Because the condition is a bound on each event separately, it survives averaging. Suppose \(P = \sum_t w_tP_t\) and \(Q = \sum_t w_tQ_t\) are averages with the same weights \(w_t\), for instance over some random choice \(t\) that both runs share. For every event the excess is the average of the excesses, \(P(A) - \gamma Q(A) = \sum_tw_t[P_t(A) - \gamma Q_t(A)]\). If each bracket is at most \(\delta\), so is their weighted average. So \(E_\gamma(P\|Q) \le \max_tE_\gamma(P_t\|Q_t)\). This is joint convexity of \(E_\gamma\), restricted to a shared mixing variable.
The subsampled mechanism is exactly such an average, over which other records were drawn. Fact 1 lets you fix those records and prove the bound for one draw.


31.2.2 Fact 2 — The mixture lemma
This is the fact that does the amplifying. Picture two runs whose outputs are mixtures with the same weight \(\eta\): with probability \(1 - \eta\) both draw from a common distribution \(R\), where the runs agree, and with probability \(\eta\) the first draws from \(P\) and the second from \(P'\), where they may differ. Where they agree the likelihood ratio is 1; where they differ it is at most about \(e^\varepsilon\). The mixture’s ratio should then be at most the weighted average \((1 - \eta)\cdot 1 + \eta e^\varepsilon = 1 + \eta(e^\varepsilon - 1)\), and the slack \(\delta\), which only enters through the differing part, should shrink to \(\eta\delta\). The lemma makes this precise, with one subtlety: \(P\) must be close not only to \(P'\) but also to \(R\), because a high-probability event of \(P\) could otherwise be one that \(R\) never produces.
Let \(R\), \(P\), \(P'\) be three distributions, \(\varepsilon \ge 0\), \(\delta \in [0, 1]\) and \(\eta \in [0, 1]\). Suppose that for every event \(A\), \[P(A) \le e^\varepsilon P'(A) + \delta \qquad\text{and}\qquad P(A) \le e^\varepsilon R(A) + \delta. \tag{31.2}\] Then for every event \(A\), \[(1 - \eta)R(A) + \eta P(A) \le e^{\varepsilon'}\big[(1 - \eta)R(A) + \eta P'(A)\big] + \eta\delta, \qquad e^{\varepsilon'} = 1 + \eta(e^\varepsilon - 1). \tag{31.3}\]
So the \(\varepsilon\) shrinks to \(\varepsilon'\) and the \(\delta\) to \(\eta\delta\). This is an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) form of what Balle, Barthe & Gaboardi (2018, Theorem 2) call advanced joint convexity.
Proof. The plan is to treat the three probabilities of \(A\) as unknowns, see that the gap between the two sides gets larger only when \(P'(A)\) and \(R(A)\) get smaller, and push them down to the smallest values the assumptions allow. Fix \(A\) and write \(a = P(A)\), \(b = P'(A)\), \(c = R(A)\), and \(F\) for the left side minus the right side without the \(\eta\delta\). The claim is \(F \le \eta\delta\).

Expand. The \((1-\eta)c\) on the left and the \(e^{\varepsilon'}(1 - \eta)c\) on the right combine to \((1 - \eta)c(1 - e^{\varepsilon'})\), and \(1 - e^{\varepsilon'} = -\eta(e^\varepsilon - 1)\). So \[F = \eta a - \eta(1 - \eta)(e^\varepsilon - 1)\,c - \eta\big(1 + \eta(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big)\,b. \tag{31.4}\]
Signs. The coefficients of \(b\) and \(c\) are negative, so \(F\) is largest when \(b\) and \(c\) are as small as the assumptions allow. Solving each assumption for the smaller side gives \(b \ge e^{-\varepsilon}(a - \delta)\) and \(c \ge e^{-\varepsilon}(a - \delta)\), and both are also \(\ge 0\), being probabilities. Which of the two lower bounds binds depends on whether \(a\) exceeds \(\delta\).
Case \(a \le \delta\). Drop the negative terms: \(F \le \eta a \le \eta\delta\).
Case \(a > \delta\). Put \(b = c = e^{-\varepsilon}(a - \delta)\) into step 1. The two coefficients add up to \((1 - \eta)(e^\varepsilon - 1) + 1 + \eta(e^\varepsilon - 1) = e^\varepsilon\), so \(F \le \eta a - \eta e^{-\varepsilon}(a - \delta)e^\varepsilon = \eta\delta\).

The script checks the lemma on random examples. It draws 20,000 random triples \((R, P, P')\) on four outcomes, computes the smallest \(\delta\) for which the two assumptions hold in both directions at \(\varepsilon = 1\), and checks Equation 31.3 with \(\eta = 0.1\). For each triple it divides the left side’s excess over \(e^{\varepsilon'}\) times the bracket by \(\eta\delta\). The largest value of this ratio is 1.0000: the lemma holds, and some triples meet it with equality to four digits, so it cannot be improved.


31.2.3 Fact 3 — Group privacy
A guarantee for datasets one record apart also covers datasets two records apart, at a price. If a mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for datasets one step apart, apply the definition twice along the chain \(D_0, D_1, D_2\): \(P_0(A) \le e^\varepsilon P_1(A) + \delta \le e^\varepsilon\big(e^\varepsilon P_2(A) + \delta\big) + \delta = e^{2\varepsilon}P_2(A) + (1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta\). So it is \((2\varepsilon, (1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta)\)-DP for datasets two steps apart (Properties). Replacing a record is a removal followed by an addition, so a guarantee for add/remove neighbours gives one for replace-one neighbours at this price.

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
section: 31.3 Amplification for (ε, δ)-DP under Poisson sampling
text:
31.3 Amplification for (ε, δ)-DP under Poisson sampling

31.3.1 Context
You have a mechanism \(M\) that is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for add/remove neighbours, datasets that differ by one record being present in one and absent from the other. You run it on a Poisson sample of the data, each record kept with probability \(q\). What are the privacy parameters of the combined mechanism? This is the oldest amplification result. Kasiviswanathan et al. (2008) used it to learn privately from a sample, and the tight form below is due to Li, Qardaji & Su (2012) and Balle, Barthe & Gaboardi (2018).


31.3.2 Statement
The answer is the mixture lemma with the sampling rate as the weight: the likelihood ratio becomes a weighted average of 1 and \(e^\varepsilon\), and \(\delta\) is paid only when the record is drawn. Let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for add/remove neighbours and let \(M \circ S_q\) run \(M\) on a Poisson sample with rate \(q\). Then \(M \circ S_q\) is \((\varepsilon', \delta')\)-DP for add/remove neighbours with \[\varepsilon' = \ln\big(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big), \qquad \delta' = q\delta. \tag{31.5}\] The bound is tight: for every \(\varepsilon\) and \(q\) some mechanism attains it (Balle, Barthe & Gaboardi 2018, Theorems 8 and 13).


31.3.3 Derivation
The idea is to fix every random choice except whether \(x\) is drawn, apply the mixture lemma once for each order of the pair, and then average the fixed choices back in with Fact 1. Let \(D' = D \cup \{x\}\).

Condition on the rest of the sample. Let \(T\) be the Poisson sample of \(D\). Because each record has its own coin, the sample of \(D'\) is \(T\) or \(T \cup \{x\}\), the second with probability \(q\), independently of \(T\). Given \(T\), write \(P_0 = M(T)\) and \(P_1 = M(T \cup \{x\})\). Then \(M \circ S_q(D)\) given \(T\) is \(P_0\), and \(M \circ S_q(D')\) given \(T\) is \((1 - q)P_0 + qP_1\).
Direction “\(D'\) against \(D\)”. Here the mixture is on the left. Apply the mixture lemma (Fact 2) with \(R = P_0\), \(P = P_1\), \(P' = P_0\) and \(\eta = q\). Both of its assumptions then read \(P_1(A) \le e^\varepsilon P_0(A) + \delta\), which holds because \(T\) and \(T \cup \{x\}\) are neighbours and \(M\) is DP. The right side of Equation 31.3 becomes \(e^{\varepsilon'}[(1 - q)P_0(A) + qP_0(A)] + q\delta = e^{\varepsilon'}P_0(A) + q\delta\). This is the remove direction in the naming of Numerical accounting: the dataset with the record comes first, and its neighbour is obtained by removing \(x\).
Direction “\(D\) against \(D'\)”. Now the mixture is on the right. Apply the lemma with \(R = P_0\), \(P = P_0\), \(P' = P_1\). The assumptions are \(P_0(A) \le e^\varepsilon P_1(A) + \delta\), which is DP of \(M\) again, and \(P_0(A) \le e^\varepsilon P_0(A) + \delta\), which is always true. The left side is \((1 - q)P_0(A) + qP_0(A) = P_0(A)\) and the right side \(e^{\varepsilon'}[(1 - q)P_0(A) + qP_1(A)] + q\delta\). This is the add direction.
Average over \(T\). Both bounds hold for every \(T\) with the same \((\varepsilon', q\delta)\), and both runs average over \(T\) with the same weights, so they hold for the averages over \(T\) (Fact 1).

Tightness. To show \(\varepsilon'\) cannot be smaller, you need a mechanism whose likelihood ratio actually reaches \(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\). Randomized response does it. It reports a bit truthfully with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) and flipped otherwise (Randomized response), so the probability of any report changes by a factor of exactly \(e^\varepsilon\) when the true bit changes. Let \(M\) apply it to the bit “the sample contains a flagged record”. Take \(D\) with no flagged record and \(x\) flagged. Then the bit is 0 whenever \(x\) is not drawn and 1 whenever it is, so \(P_0\) and \(P_1\) are the same for every \(T\), and \(P_1(1)/P_0(1) = e^\varepsilon\). The likelihood ratio of the mixture to \(P_0\) at the output “1” is \[\frac{(1 - q)P_0(1) + qP_1(1)}{P_0(1)} = (1 - q) + q\frac{P_1(1)}{P_0(1)} = 1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1). \tag{31.6}\] With \(\delta = 0\) the event \(\{1\}\) forces \(e^{\varepsilon'} \ge 1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\), so \(\varepsilon'\) in Equation 31.5 cannot be improved.


31.3.4 Interpretation
The formula behaves differently for small and large \(\varepsilon\). For small \(\varepsilon\), amplification is linear in \(q\). When \(\varepsilon \ll 1\), \(e^\varepsilon - 1 \approx \varepsilon\) and \(\ln(1 + y) \approx y\) for small \(y\), so \(\varepsilon' \approx q\varepsilon\). A 1% sample makes each step a hundred times cheaper.
For large \(\varepsilon\), amplification only subtracts. When \(qe^\varepsilon \gg 1\), the 1 inside the logarithm is negligible and \(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1) \approx qe^\varepsilon\), so \(\varepsilon' \approx \ln(qe^\varepsilon) = \varepsilon - \ln(1/q)\). Sampling can never remove more than \(\ln(1/q)\) nats, because in the worst case the record was drawn, and that happens with probability \(q\). At \(q = 0.01\) and \(\varepsilon = 10\), Table 31.3 gives 5.3993, close to \(10 - \ln 100 = 5.395\). Figure 31.1 shows the switch between the two regimes around \(\varepsilon \approx \ln(1/q)\), where \(qe^\varepsilon\) reaches 1.
The \(\delta\) always shrinks by \(q\), because the failure event of \(M\) only matters when the record was drawn. Finally, Equation 31.5 is a statement about one step, and it is tight for one step. Composing per-step \((\varepsilon', \delta')\) pairs is not tight, and the running example shows by how much (Section 31.7).






Figure 31.1: The subsampled \(\varepsilon'\) against the base \(\varepsilon\) for three sampling rates, with the small-\(\varepsilon\) approximation \(q\varepsilon\) dotted and no sampling dashed. Amplification is a factor \(q\) for small \(\varepsilon\) and only a shift by \(\ln(1/q)\) for large \(\varepsilon\).





31.3.5 Example: randomized response, sampled at 10%
Take \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(q = 0.1\), and the randomized-response mechanism of the tightness argument. When the record is not drawn the true bit is 0, which is reported as 0 with probability \(e/(1 + e) = 0.7311\) and as 1 with probability \(1/(1 + e) = 0.2689\); when it is drawn the two probabilities swap. The mixture weights these by 0.9 and 0.1: for the output 1, \(0.9 \times 0.2689 + 0.1 \times 0.7311 = 0.3152\). Table 31.2 shows both outputs and the likelihood ratios in both directions.

31.3.6 Check yourself

At \(q = 0.01\), roughly how large must \(\varepsilon\) be before amplification stops being a factor of 100? (Around \(\ln(1/q) = 4.6\), where \(q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\) reaches 1. At \(\varepsilon = 5\), Table 31.3 gives \(\varepsilon' = 0.9059\), not 0.05.)
Why does the derivation need \(T\) and \(x\) to be drawn independently? (So that, given \(T\), the record is included with probability exactly \(q\). The mixture weights must not depend on the rest of the sample.)

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
section: 31.4 The sampling scheme must match the neighbouring relation
text:
31.4 The sampling scheme must match the neighbouring relation

31.4.1 Context
Poisson sampling gives batches of random size. Most training code draws fixed-size batches: either a random batch of \(m\) out of \(n\) records at each step, or a random permutation of the data cut into \(n/m\) consecutive batches per epoch (shuffle and partition). Does the amplification of Equation 31.5 still apply? Only if you change what you compare. A fixed batch size pairs naturally with replace-one neighbours, datasets of the same size that differ in one record’s value, because with a fixed batch size adding a record would change the size. Accounting for one scheme while running another is a bug that can multiply \(\varepsilon\) several times over.


31.4.2 Statement
Fixed-size batches, replace-one. A uniformly random batch of \(m\) out of \(n\) contains a given record with probability \(m/n\), so \(m/n\) plays the role of \(q\), and the same formula holds, as long as the base guarantee is for replace-one neighbours. Draw a uniformly random batch of \(m\) records from \(n\), and let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for replace-one neighbours on datasets of size \(m\). Then the subsampled mechanism is \((\varepsilon', \delta')\)-DP for replace-one neighbours on datasets of size \(n\), with \[\varepsilon' = \ln\Big(1 + \frac mn(e^\varepsilon - 1)\Big), \qquad \delta' = \frac mn\delta \tag{31.7}\] (Balle, Barthe & Gaboardi 2018, Theorem 9). The formula is that of Equation 31.5 with \(q = m/n\), but the base guarantee is a different one.
The matching rule. Each combination of sampling scheme and neighbouring relation produces its own pair of output distributions, and needs its own base guarantee. Table 31.4 lists them. Its last column applies them to DP-SGD’s noisy gradient sum, where every gradient is clipped to norm \(C\) and the noise has standard deviation \(\sigma C\); what matters is how far one record can move the sum, measured in units of the noise. The zero-out relation in the last row compares a dataset with the same dataset in which the target’s gradient is set to 0.

31.4.3 Derivation
Equation 31.7 by a coupling. A fixed-size batch is not drawn record by record, so there is no independent coin for the differing record. The trick, called a coupling, is to build the batch in a way that has such a coin, and then to use the same coin and the same other records for both datasets. Let \(D\) and \(D'\) differ in record \(i\): \(x\) in \(D\), \(x'\) in \(D'\).

Build a batch that avoids \(i\) in two stages. Draw \(B\), a uniform \((m-1)\)-subset of the other \(n - 1\) records, then \(z\), a uniform record from the \((n - 1) - (m - 1) = n - m\) others not in \(B\). The batch \(B \cup \{z\}\) is a uniform \(m\)-subset that avoids \(i\): each such subset arises from \(m\) choices of which element is \(z\), equally often.
Write both outputs as mixtures over \((B, z)\). A uniform \(m\)-subset of \(n\) contains \(i\) with probability \(\eta = m/n\). Given that it does, the rest of it is a uniform \((m-1)\)-subset of the others, which is \(B\); given that it does not, it is a uniform \(m\)-subset avoiding \(i\), which is \(B \cup \{z\}\). So flip an independent coin with probability \(\eta\): on heads the batch is \(B \cup \{x\}\) in \(D\) and \(B \cup \{x'\}\) in \(D'\), on tails it is \(B \cup \{z\}\) in both. Given \((B, z)\), the outputs are \((1 - \eta)R + \eta P\) and \((1 - \eta)R + \eta P'\) with \(R = M(B\cup\{z\})\), \(P = M(B\cup\{x\})\), \(P' = M(B\cup\{x'\})\).
Check the lemma’s assumptions. The three batches \(B\cup\{x\}\), \(B\cup\{x'\}\), \(B\cup\{z\}\) have size \(m\) and differ pairwise in one element, so they are pairwise replace-one neighbours. Hence \(P \le e^\varepsilon P' + \delta\) and \(P \le e^\varepsilon R + \delta\) on every event, and the same with \(P\) and \(P'\) swapped.
Apply the mixture lemma and average. Fact 2 with weight \(\eta\) gives the bound in one direction, and again with \(P\) and \(P'\) swapped in the other. Both runs average over \((B, z)\) with the same weights, so Fact 1 carries the bound to the full mechanism.

The Gaussian column. For a sum of gradients clipped to norm \(C\), adding or removing a record moves the sum by at most \(C\), and replacing one moves it by up to \(2C\): the old gradient leaves and a new one, possibly pointing the opposite way, comes in. A Gaussian mechanism’s privacy depends only on the shift divided by the noise’s standard deviation, and \(2C/(\sigma C) = C/((\sigma/2)C)\), so noise \(\sigma C\) with shift \(2C\) is the same as shift \(C\) with noise multiplier \(\sigma/2\). Lebeda, Regehr, Kamath & Steinke (2024, Proposition 9) show, using Zhu, Dong & Wang (2022, Theorem 11), that for fixed-size batches this shift of \(2C\) is the worst case under the add relation and under the remove relation, each taken separately, because a record entering the batch pushes another one out.
Poisson with replace-one. Given the rest of the sample \(T\), the target is drawn with probability \(q\) in both runs, so the outputs are \((1 - q)R + qP\) and \((1 - q)R + qP'\) with \(R = M(T)\), \(P = M(T\cup\{x\})\), \(P' = M(T\cup\{x'\})\). The pair \((P, R)\) is one add/remove step apart, but \((P, P')\) is two: remove \(x\), then add \(x'\). The mixture lemma needs one guarantee for both pairs, so use the weaker one. Fact 3 gives the base guarantee \((2\varepsilon, (1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta)\) for both, and Fact 2 then gives \(\varepsilon' = \ln(1 + q(e^{2\varepsilon} - 1))\) and \(\delta' = q(1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta\). For small \(q\) both logarithms are close to their arguments’ excess over 1, and since \(e^{2\varepsilon} - 1 = (e^\varepsilon - 1)(e^\varepsilon + 1)\), this bound is about \(e^\varepsilon + 1\) times the add/remove value.
The bound is not tight: the pair \((P, R)\) is only one step apart, but the lemma charges it the two-step guarantee. For pure DP (\(\delta = 0\)) the exact value follows from likelihood ratios. Pure DP of \(M\) says that every likelihood ratio between neighbours lies in \([e^{-\varepsilon}, e^\varepsilon]\), so both \(P/R\) and \(P'/R\) do. Divide the two mixtures by \(R\): their ratio is \(\frac{(1 - q) + qP/R}{(1 - q) + qP'/R}\). It is largest when the numerator is largest and the denominator smallest, that is with \(P/R = e^\varepsilon\) and \(P'/R = e^{-\varepsilon}\), which gives at most \(\frac{1 - q + qe^\varepsilon}{1 - q + qe^{-\varepsilon}}\). Taking the logarithm, and writing \(1 - q + qe^{-\varepsilon} = 1 - q(1 - e^{-\varepsilon})\), \[\varepsilon' = \ln\big(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big) - \ln\big(1 - q(1 - e^{-\varepsilon})\big). \tag{31.8}\] The Laplace mechanism on a sum attains it (Exercise 3). For small \(\varepsilon\) each of the two logarithms is about \(q\varepsilon\), so the value is about twice the add/remove value. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(q = 0.01\) it is 0.02338, against 0.06193 for the group-privacy bound and 0.01704 for add/remove: a ratio of 1.37, not 3.64.


31.4.4 Interpretation
Why mixing them is a bug. Each row of Table 31.4 is correct on its own. The bug is to train with one row and report the number from another. Two cases are common.
The first is fixed-size sampled batches with a Poisson accountant. The accountant assumes a shift of \(C\); the training run has a shift of \(2C\). You are reporting the privacy of twice as much noise as you added. Lebeda et al. (2024, Table 1) give an example with \(q = 0.001\), \(\sigma = 0.8\) and 10,000 steps: at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) they report \(\varepsilon = 0.80\) for Poisson sampling and \(\varepsilon = 12.98\) for fixed-size batches, from a numerical accountant. (The tight privacy-loss-distribution accountants of the dp_accounting and prv_accountant libraries give 0.78 for Poisson sampling; that value comes from those libraries, not from this chapter’s script.) The RDP accountant of this chapter reproduces the gap: 1.38 against 15.30.
The second is shuffle and partition with a Poisson accountant, and it is worse, because the mechanism of amplification is missing altogether. In one epoch the record is in exactly one batch, never absent, so no step’s output is a mixture with “not used”. The only uncertainty is which batch held the record, and the other records can give that away.
Chua et al. (2024) build a bad case. Every other record has gradient \(-1\), the target has \(+1\), and the neighbouring dataset zeroes the target out. Recentre each batch sum by adding the batch size, which removes the \(-1\) contributions of a full batch of other records. Batches without the target then output \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\). The target’s batch has one \(-1\) fewer and a \(+1\) instead, so it outputs \(\mathcal N(2, \sigma^2)\), or \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) when the target is zeroed. You don’t know which batch holds it, so with \(b\) batches the epoch’s output is a mixture, over the batch index \(t\), of \(\mathcal N(2e_t, \sigma^2I)\) against the same mixture of \(\mathcal N(e_t, \sigma^2I)\), where \(e_t\) is the vector with 1 in position \(t\) and 0 elsewhere.
A natural test looks at the largest of the \(b\) batch outputs and says “target present” when it exceeds a threshold \(\tau\). The largest output stays below \(\tau\) only if every batch output does, and the batches are independent. The target’s batch stays below \(\tau\) with probability \(\Phi(\frac{\tau-2}\sigma)\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function, and each of the \(b - 1\) others with probability \(\Phi(\frac\tau\sigma)\). This does not depend on which batch holds the target, so mixing over \(t\) changes nothing, and the test fires with probability \(1 - \Phi(\frac{\tau-2}\sigma)\Phi(\frac\tau\sigma)^{b-1}\) under the first distribution and \(1 - \Phi(\frac{\tau-1}\sigma)\Phi(\frac\tau\sigma)^{b-1}\) under the second. Recall that \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), the smallest \(\delta\) that works with a given \(\varepsilon\), is the largest value of \(P(A) - e^\varepsilon Q(A)\) over events \(A\) (Fact 1). Any one event, such as “the largest output exceeds \(\tau\)”, gives a value no larger, so it gives a lower bound on \(\delta(\varepsilon)\). Maximizing over \(\tau\) gives the best such lower bound, and the smallest \(\varepsilon\) it does not rule out at a given \(\delta\) is a lower bound on the true \(\varepsilon\).
This is the zero-out relation, not add/remove. Under zero-out, a Poisson step’s clipped sum also moves by at most \(C\), as under add/remove, so the Poisson accountant’s number applies to the same relation, and the comparison below is like with like.
The script reproduces Chua et al.’s headline check: with \(\sigma = 0.4\) and \(b = 10{,}000\) batches, the test gives \(\delta(4) \ge 0.226\) for shuffling, against \(\delta(4) = 0.244\) for a fixed, non-random batch order. They report that a Poisson accountant gives \(\delta(4) \le 1.18 \times 10^{-5}\) for the same parameters.


31.4.5 Example: one epoch of the running example
Take \(q = 0.01\), so one epoch is \(b = 100\) batches, and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Table 31.5 compares three batch samplers for one epoch. With deterministic batches the record is used once, in a known batch, so the epoch is a plain Gaussian mechanism and its \(\varepsilon\) is exact. For shuffle and partition the table gives the lower bound from the test above, and for Poisson sampling the upper bound from the RDP accountant of Section 31.7.

At the running example’s \(\sigma = 1\), shuffled training has \(\varepsilon \ge 4.06\) after one epoch, while the Poisson accountant reports at most 1.21. Shuffling buys almost nothing over a fixed order (4.38). The gap closes as \(\sigma\) grows (Figure 31.2). At \(\sigma = 3\) the shuffled lower bound falls below the Poisson upper bound, which says only that this particular test is too weak there to show a gap. For fixed-size sampled batches over many epochs, the running example gives \(\varepsilon = 47.42\) after 10,000 steps against 6.71 for Poisson (both by RDP; the first uses noise multiplier \(\sigma/2 = 0.5\)).

31.4.6 Check yourself

Your code draws a fresh random batch of exactly 256 out of 25,600 records at each step. Which noise multiplier should you give a Poisson-sampling RDP accountant with \(q = 0.01\)? (Half of the one you use, \(\sigma/2\): the base mechanism’s shift is \(2C\).)
Why can’t the mixture lemma be applied to one step of shuffled training? (Given the other records’ positions, the record’s batch is fixed, so the step’s output on \(D'\) is not a mixture of “used” and “not used”. The randomness is only in which step uses it.)

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
text:
31.5 RDP of the Poisson-subsampled Gaussian

31.5.1 Context
Per-step \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) amplification composes badly (Section 31.7). RDP composes better. A mechanism is \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP when the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) between its outputs on any two neighbouring datasets is at most \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\). The Rényi divergence \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_{y\sim Q}\big[(P(y)/Q(y))^\alpha\big]\) is a log-average of a power of the likelihood ratio; a larger order \(\alpha\) weights large ratios more heavily. Under composition the RDP curves of the steps simply add (Rényi DP), so you want the RDP curve of one subsampled Gaussian step. That is a Rényi divergence between a Gaussian mixture and a Gaussian. It has no closed form, but it has an exact series for integer orders and a stable numerical integral for the rest. Figure 31.3 shows the pair and its privacy loss, the logarithm of the likelihood ratio at each output.






Figure 31.3: Left: one subsampled Gaussian step with \(q = 0.1\). The output with the record is the mixture (dashed), barely distinguishable from \(P_0\). Right: the privacy loss \(\ln\big((1 - q) + q\,P_1/P_0\big)\). Where the record is unlikely to have been used it is flat near \(\ln(1 - q)\); in the far right tail it runs parallel to the unsubsampled loss, \(\ln(1/q)\) lower.





31.5.2 Statement
The statement reduces the whole problem to one dimension and one direction. Whatever the data, the worst case is a single coordinate in which the record moves the sum by the full sensitivity, and of the two orders of the pair the one with the mixture first is always the larger. That divergence is the average under \(P_0\) of the mixture’s likelihood ratio raised to the power \(\alpha\), and for integer \(\alpha\) the binomial theorem expands it into a finite sum.
Let \(P_0 = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), \(P_1 = \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) and \(P_q = (1 - q)P_0 + qP_1\). The Poisson-subsampled Gaussian mechanism with \(\ell_2\) sensitivity 1 (one record moves the sum by Euclidean length at most 1) and noise multiplier \(\sigma\) is \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP for add/remove neighbours with \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \max\big\{D_\alpha(P_q\|P_0),\ D_\alpha(P_0\|P_q)\big\} = D_\alpha(P_q\|P_0) = \frac{\ln A_\alpha}{\alpha - 1}, \tag{31.9}\] \[A_\alpha = \mathbb E_{y\sim P_0}\Big[\Big((1 - q) + q\frac{P_1(y)}{P_0(y)}\Big)^\alpha\Big], \qquad \frac{P_1(y)}{P_0(y)} = e^{(2y - 1)/(2\sigma^2)}. \tag{31.10}\] For integer \(\alpha\), \[A_\alpha = \sum_{j=0}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\exp\Big(\frac{j^2 - j}{2\sigma^2}\Big). \tag{31.11}\] The first direction, \(D_\alpha(P_q\|P_0)\), puts the dataset with the record first: it is the remove direction of Section 31.3 and of Numerical accounting. The reduction to one dimension is Mironov, Talwar & Zhang (2019, Theorem 4), the dominance of the first direction their Theorem 5 and Corollary 7, and Equation 31.11 their Section 3.3.


31.5.3 Derivation
The derivation first removes everything except the one coordinate along which the record moves the output, then evaluates the divergence of the remaining one-dimensional pair.

Condition on the rest of the sample (Mironov, Talwar & Zhang 2019, Theorem 4). Let \(f\) be the clipped gradient sum, divided by \(C\) so that the sensitivity is 1. Condition on the rest of the sample \(T\). The outputs are \(\mathcal N(f(T), \sigma^2I)\) and the mixture \((1 - q)\mathcal N(f(T), \sigma^2I) + q\mathcal N(f(T\cup\{x\}), \sigma^2I)\), and both runs average these over \(T\) with the same weights.
Averaging cannot increase the divergence. This is the RDP counterpart of Fact 1. For \(\alpha > 1\), \(e^{(\alpha-1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} = \int P(y)^\alpha Q(y)^{1-\alpha}\,dy\). Write the integrand as \(Q\,(P/Q)^\alpha\). The function \(t^\alpha\) is convex, and a function of the form \(Q\,g(P/Q)\) with \(g\) convex, called the perspective of \(g\), is jointly convex in the pair \((P, Q)\): the value at an average of pairs is at most the average of the values. So for averages with shared weights \(w_t\), \(\int(\sum_tw_tP_t)^\alpha(\sum_tw_tQ_t)^{1-\alpha} \le \sum_tw_t\int P_t^\alpha Q_t^{1-\alpha} \le \max_t\int P_t^\alpha Q_t^{1-\alpha}\), in either order of the pair. The divergence of the averages over \(T\) is at most the largest divergence for one \(T\). This is the quasi-convexity of the Rényi divergence (van Erven & Harremoës 2014, Theorem 13).
Shift, rotate and rescale. Moving both distributions by the same amount or rotating both does not change any likelihood ratio, so it does not change the divergence. Shift by \(f(T)\) and rotate so the difference \(f(T\cup\{x\}) - f(T)\) lies along the first axis. The other coordinates have the same distribution in both runs and are independent of the first, and the Rényi divergence of independent coordinates is the sum of theirs (additivity, Divergences), so the identical ones contribute 0 and drop out. A difference of length \(c < 1\) is, after rescaling by \(1/c\), the same as length 1 with noise \(\sigma/c > \sigma\). That pair is the length-1 pair with extra independent noise added, and no processing of the outputs can increase a divergence (data processing), so it cannot be worse. What is left is the pair \((P_q, P_0)\) in both orders.
Write the first direction as an expectation under \(P_0\). By the definition of \(D_\alpha\) given in the context, \(D_\alpha(P_q\|P_0) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_{P_0}[(P_q/P_0)^\alpha]\), and dividing the mixture by \(P_0\) gives \(P_q/P_0 = (1 - q) + q\,P_1/P_0\). This is Equation 31.10. The ratio \(P_1/P_0\) is the Gaussian likelihood ratio: the normalizing constants cancel and \(\exp\big(\frac{-(y-1)^2 + y^2}{2\sigma^2}\big) = e^{(2y-1)/(2\sigma^2)}\).
Expand for integer \(\alpha\). Write \(r = P_1/P_0\). The binomial theorem gives \((1 - q + qr)^\alpha = \sum_j\binom\alpha j(1-q)^{\alpha-j}q^jr^j\), and the expectation of a sum is the sum of the expectations, so \(A_\alpha\) is this sum with each \(r^j\) replaced by \(\mathbb E_{P_0}[r^j]\).
Compute each moment. \(\mathbb E_{P_0}[r^j] = \mathbb E[e^{j(2y-1)/(2\sigma^2)}]\) for \(y \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\). The moment generating function of this normal is \(\mathbb E[e^{sy}] = e^{s^2\sigma^2/2}\), and with \(s = j/\sigma^2\) it gives \(e^{j^2/(2\sigma^2)}\). Multiplying by the constant factor \(e^{-j/(2\sigma^2)}\), the \(j\)-th moment is \(e^{(j^2 - j)/(2\sigma^2)}\), which gives Equation 31.11. Equivalently, \(\mathbb E_{P_0}[(P_1/P_0)^j] = e^{(j-1)D_j(P_1\|P_0)}\) by the definition of \(D_j\), and \(D_j(P_1\|P_0) = j/(2\sigma^2)\) for two Gaussians with unit shift (Divergences, Equation 3.15).
Fractional \(\alpha\): integrate numerically. For non-integer \(\alpha\) the binomial sum does not terminate, so compute Equation 31.10 as an integral. Its integrand is \(P_0(y)\) times a power of the mixture ratio. Huge and tiny factors would overflow, so work with its logarithm, \(\ln P_0(y) + \alpha\,\mathrm{logaddexp}\big(\ln(1-q), \ln q + \frac{2y-1}{2\sigma^2}\big)\), where \(\mathrm{logaddexp}(u, v) = \ln(e^u + e^v)\) is computed without forming \(e^u\) or \(e^v\). Sum on a grid of step \(\sigma/100\) with log-sum-exp, the same trick for a sum of many exponentials. The integrand has a bump near \(y = 0\) and, for large \(\alpha\), a second one near \(y = \alpha\). The second comes from the part \(q^\alpha e^{\alpha(2y-1)/(2\sigma^2)}\): multiplied by \(P_0(y) \propto e^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), it gives an exponent \((-y^2 + 2\alpha y)/(2\sigma^2)\), a Gaussian centred at \(y = \alpha\) (the tilted distributions of Divergences). So the grid runs from \(-12\sigma\) to \(\alpha + 12\sigma\).
The other direction. By the definition, \(D_\alpha(P_0\|P_q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_{P_q}[(P_0/P_q)^\alpha]\). Changing the expectation from \(P_q\) to \(P_0\) multiplies the integrand by \(P_q/P_0\), which turns \((P_0/P_q)^\alpha\) into \((P_0/P_q)^{\alpha - 1}\), so \(D_\alpha(P_0\|P_q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_{P_0}[(P_q/P_0)^{-(\alpha-1)}]\). The power is negative, so there is no finite binomial sum; integrate it numerically. Mironov, Talwar & Zhang (2019, Theorem 5) prove \(D_\alpha(P_q\|P_0) \ge D_\alpha(P_0\|P_q)\) for every \(\alpha \ge 1\). Their argument uses the reflection \(y \mapsto 1 - y\), which swaps \(P_0\) and \(P_1\). The script computes both and takes the larger, which is always the first. This dominance is for Rényi divergences. For \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), Section 32.7 computes both directions, because neither dominates in general.

Walk-through at \(\alpha = 2\). With \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\), Equation 31.11 has three terms, one for each possible number \(j\) of factors \(r\) (Table 31.6).

Without the exponential factors the three coefficients add up to \((1 - q + q)^2 = 1\). The exponential factor only changes the last term, from \(q^2\) to \(q^2e^{1/\sigma^2}\), so the terms sum to \(A_2 = 1 + q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1) = 1 + 0.0001 \times 1.71828 = 1.00017183\), and \(\varepsilon(2) = \ln A_2/(2 - 1) = 1.7181 \times 10^{-4}\). Without sampling, \(\varepsilon(2) = 2/(2\sigma^2) = 1\). Only the \(j = 2\) term carries any privacy cost, because the terms \(j = 0\) and \(1\) have the same factor 1 that a mixture of identical distributions would have.


31.5.4 Interpretation
Two regimes. Figure 31.4 shows the curve for \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\). Up to about \(\alpha = 8\) the curve stays within 30% of the small-\(q\) line, the \(j = 2\) term alone, worked out in Section 31.6 (1.30 times it at \(\alpha = 8\), Table 31.8): \(\varepsilon(8) = 8.9364 \times 10^{-4}\), against 4 without sampling. Between \(\alpha = 8\) and 16 it climbs steeply: \(\varepsilon(16) = 3.0879\) and \(\varepsilon(32) = 11.246\), against 8 and 16 without sampling. The reason is in the right panel of Figure 31.3. Low orders average the privacy loss over the bulk, where sampling flattens it. High orders look at the far tail, where the loss is the unsubsampled one minus \(\ln(1/q)\). In the tail, sampling saves only \(\ln(1/q)\), as for \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) at large \(\varepsilon\). The one-term lower bound Equation 29.21 of Concentrated DP makes this precise. Every term of Equation 31.11 is positive, so \(A_\alpha\) is at least its last term, \(q^\alpha e^{\alpha(\alpha - 1)/(2\sigma^2)}\), and dividing its logarithm by \(\alpha - 1\) gives \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \ge \frac{\alpha\ln q}{\alpha - 1} + \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}\): the unsubsampled curve minus about \(\ln(1/q)\).
Which orders matter. An accountant turns the RDP curve into an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee by a conversion that holds at every order, such as \(\varepsilon = k\,\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) for \(k\) steps, and it only uses the order that makes this smallest. For long DP-SGD runs that order sits in the quadratic regime. For a few steps it sits at the foot of the steep rise, where \(k\,\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is still small next to the conversion term (Section 31.7).






Figure 31.4: The RDP curve of the Poisson-subsampled Gaussian with \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) (black), against the unsubsampled Gaussian \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\), the small-\(q\) term \(\alpha q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)/2\) and the leading term of Abadi et al.’s bound. The vertical line marks where Abadi et al.’s bound stops applying. The dashed vertical line marks \(\alpha = 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q)\), where the quadratic expansion breaks. The exact curve stays near the quadratic term up to about \(\alpha = 8\), then rises toward the unsubsampled line.

Comparing them where both exist tests the integral. Table 31.7 does this at integer orders, and also compares the two directions at several orders, for \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\).

At \(\alpha = 32\) it is nearly four orders of magnitude smaller (\(1.6923 \times 10^{-3}\) against 11.246), because it raises the mixture ratio to a negative power and so looks at the left tail, where the ratio \(P_0/P_q\) is bounded by \(1/(1-q)\): the mixture always keeps at least \(1 - q\) of \(P_0\). The script also checks every order of the grid for \(\sigma = 0.5\) and \(\sigma = 2\): the largest excess of the reverse direction is negative in both cases (\(-5.09 \times 10^{-4}\) and \(-5.67 \times 10^{-8}\)).


31.5.6 Check yourself

In Equation 31.11, why do the terms \(j = 0\) and \(j = 1\) never cost privacy? (Their exponential factor is \(e^0 = 1\). They are the terms in which the record’s influence enters at most linearly, and a linear term averages to the same value under both distributions, since \(\mathbb E_{P_0}[P_1/P_0] = 1\).)
Why does the numerical grid for \(D_\alpha(P_q\|P_0)\) extend to \(y = \alpha + 12\sigma\), far beyond where \(P_0\) has any mass? (For large \(\alpha\) the integrand is dominated by \(q^\alpha P_0(y)e^{\alpha(2y-1)/(2\sigma^2)}\), which is a Gaussian bump centred at \(y = \alpha\). Cutting the grid at \(12\sigma\) would miss it.)

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
section: 31.6 Small q and the moments accountant
text:
31.6 Small q and the moments accountant

31.6.1 Context
Abadi et al. (2016) introduced DP-SGD together with the moments accountant. Its central quantity is built from the privacy loss, \(L = \ln\big(P(y)/Q(y)\big)\) for an output \(y\) drawn from \(P\): the log-likelihood ratio of the output, which is large when the output gives the record away. The accountant tracks the logarithm of the moment generating function of \(L\), which Abadi et al. call \(\alpha_M(\lambda)\) and Rényi DP renames \(K_M(\lambda) = \ln\mathbb E[e^{\lambda L}]\), because \(\alpha\) is our order. It adds \(K_M\) over steps and converts the total to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) with a tail bound.
This is RDP in disguise, as Rényi DP shows. Since \(e^{\lambda L} = (P/Q)^\lambda\), the expectation under \(P\) is \(\mathbb E_P[(P/Q)^\lambda] = \mathbb E_Q[(P/Q)^{\lambda + 1}] = e^{\lambda D_{\lambda+1}(P\|Q)}\), so \(K_M(\lambda) = \lambda\,\varepsilon(\lambda + 1)\). The tail bound is Markov’s inequality applied to \(e^{\lambda L}\): \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon] \le \mathbb E[e^{\lambda L}]e^{-\lambda\varepsilon}\), which gives \(\delta = \min_\lambda e^{K_M(\lambda) - \lambda\varepsilon}\), Mironov’s conversion. Abadi et al. did not have Equation 31.11 in general. They proved an asymptotic bound for small \(q\). How good is it, and where does it stop holding?


31.6.2 Statement
When \(q\) is small, the walk-through at \(\alpha = 2\) generalizes: the terms \(j = 0\) and \(1\) of Equation 31.11 cost nothing, every term from \(j = 3\) on carries \(q^3\) or a higher power, and the \(j = 2\) term dominates. For \(q \to 0\) at fixed \(\alpha\) and \(\sigma\), the leading term of the subsampled Gaussian’s RDP curve is \[\varepsilon(\alpha) \approx \frac{\alpha q^2\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big)}{2} \approx \frac{\alpha q^2}{2\sigma^2}\quad\text{for large }\sigma. \tag{31.12}\] Abadi et al. (2016, Lemma 3) prove a bound of the same shape, under conditions that limit the order. For \(\sigma \ge 1\), \(q < 1/(16\sigma)\) and integer \(\lambda \le \sigma^2\ln\frac{1}{q\sigma}\), \[K_M(\lambda) \le \frac{q^2\lambda(\lambda + 1)}{(1 - q)\sigma^2} + O\Big(\frac{q^3\lambda^3}{\sigma^3}\Big), \quad\text{that is}\quad \varepsilon(\alpha) \lesssim \frac{q^2\alpha}{(1 - q)\sigma^2}\ \text{ for }\ \alpha \le 1 + \sigma^2\ln\frac{1}{q\sigma}. \tag{31.13}\] The second form divides by \(\lambda\) and substitutes \(\alpha = \lambda + 1\).


31.6.3 Derivation

Subtract what costs nothing. Without the exponential factors, Equation 31.11 is \(\sum_j\binom\alpha j(1-q)^{\alpha-j}q^j = (1 - q + q)^\alpha = 1\) by the binomial theorem. Subtracting this 1 from \(A_\alpha\) leaves each term multiplied by its exponential factor minus 1: \[A_\alpha = 1 + \sum_{j=2}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\big(e^{(j^2 - j)/(2\sigma^2)} - 1\big). \tag{31.14}\] The \(j = 0\) and \(j = 1\) terms are gone, because their factor is \(e^0 - 1 = 0\).
Keep the lowest power of \(q\). The \(j = 2\) term is \(\binom\alpha2q^2(1-q)^{\alpha-2}(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\). Every other term carries \(q^3\) or more, so for small \(q\) it is negligible next to this one.
Take the logarithm. For small \(y\), \(\ln(1 + y) = y + O(y^2)\), and \((1 - q)^{\alpha - 2} = 1 + O(q)\). So \((\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha) = \ln A_\alpha = \frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)}{2}q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1) + O(q^3)\).
Divide by \(\alpha - 1\) to get Equation 31.12. For large \(\sigma\), \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1 \approx 1/\sigma^2\), since \(e^u \approx 1 + u\) for small \(u\).
Where does the expansion break? The expansion assumes the \(j = 2\) term dominates, so look at how the terms change with \(j\). Going from \(j\) to \(j + 1\), the binomial coefficient is multiplied by \(\frac{\alpha - j}{j + 1}\), the power of \(q\) by \(q\), and the exponential by \(e^{((j+1)^2 - (j+1) - j^2 + j)/(2\sigma^2)} = e^{j/\sigma^2}\). So the terms first fall, and grow once \(q\,e^{j/\sigma^2}\) passes 1, near \(j \approx \sigma^2\ln(1/q)\). The expansion fails only later, when the last term, \(q^\alpha e^{\alpha(\alpha-1)/(2\sigma^2)}\), overtakes the \(j = 2\) term, about \(q^2e^{1/\sigma^2}\). Ignoring the binomial coefficient and comparing logarithms, that happens when \(\alpha\ln q + \frac{\alpha(\alpha - 1)}{2\sigma^2} > 2\ln q + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\). Move everything to one side: the terms in \(\ln q\) give \(-(\alpha - 2)\ln\frac1q\), and the others give \(\frac{\alpha^2 - \alpha - 2}{2\sigma^2}\). Since \(\alpha^2 - \alpha - 2 = (\alpha - 2)(\alpha + 1)\), the condition is \((\alpha - 2)\big(\frac{\alpha + 1}{2\sigma^2} - \ln\frac1q\big) > 0\), that is \(\alpha > 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q) - 1\). So the expansion holds up to about \[\alpha \approx 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q), \tag{31.15}\] and the curve leaves the quadratic regime abruptly there. At \(q = 0.01\), \(\ln(1/q) = 4.605\), so this is 9.2 for \(\sigma = 1\) and 147.4 for \(\sigma = 4\). The exact curve first exceeds twice the leading term at 8.9 and 147.4 (Table 31.8). Abadi et al.’s condition \(\lambda \le \sigma^2\ln\frac{1}{q\sigma}\) has the same form with about half the constant, so it is conservative.



31.6.4 Interpretation
The first thing to notice is that the cost is quadratic, not linear, in \(q\). The \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) amplification of Section 31.3 gives a per-step \(\varepsilon'\) linear in \(q\). In RDP the cost per step is quadratic in \(q\), about \(\alpha q^2/(2\sigma^2)\). Since \(k = E/q\) steps make \(E\) epochs, the total RDP after \(E\) epochs is about \((E/q) \times \alpha q^2/(2\sigma^2) = E\,q\,\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\). It shrinks as batches get smaller at a fixed number of epochs.
Abadi et al.’s bound is about twice the leading term for large \(\sigma\): \(q^2\alpha/\sigma^2\) against \(q^2\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\). It is a valid but loose upper bound, and it is the source of the “\(\varepsilon(\alpha) \approx q^2\alpha/\sigma^2\)” you will see quoted.
The real limit of the expansion is not its constant but its order range. Up to \(\alpha = \sigma^2\ln(1/q)\) the leading term is within 8% (1.08 at \(\alpha = 4.6\) for \(\sigma = 1\), 1.05 at \(\alpha = 73.7\) for \(\sigma = 4\)). Beyond \(\alpha \approx 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q)\) (Equation 31.15) it is wrong by orders of magnitude, 2246 times too small at \(\alpha = 16\) for \(\sigma = 1\), and an accountant that uses it there under-reports \(\varepsilon\).


31.6.5 Example: where the expansion breaks
Table 31.8 compares the exact curve with Equation 31.12 and Equation 31.13 at \(q = 0.01\). For instance, at \(\alpha = 2\) and \(\sigma = 1\) the Abadi column is \(q^2\alpha/((1 - q)\sigma^2) = 0.0002/0.99 = 2.0202 \times 10^{-4}\).
