title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 41.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
41.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

41.2.1 Fact 1 — DP-SGD’s guarantee depends on the clipped sum, not on which weights it updates
Each step of DP-SGD releases \(\sum_{i \in S_t}\bar g_i + \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I)\), where \(\bar g_i\) is record \(i\)’s gradient clipped to length at most \(C\) and \(S_t\) is a Poisson-sampled batch. Adding or removing one record changes the sum by one clipped gradient, of length at most \(C\), so the noise is \(\sigma\) times the sensitivity, and the accountant composes the steps into \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) from \(q\), \(\sigma\) and \(T\) alone (DP-SGD). Nothing in this argument depends on what the gradient is a gradient of: all weights, the last layer, the factors of a low-rank update, or a projection of the gradient onto a fixed subspace. The clipping simply applies to the vector of trainable coordinates, whatever it is. With \(q = 0.01\) and \(T = 10{,}000\), the accountant gives \(\sigma = 7.72\), 4.13, 2.28 and 0.917 for \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), 1, 2 and 8 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).


41.2.2 Fact 2 — A Gaussian vector’s length grows like the square root of its dimension, and a projection keeps it Gaussian
If \(\xi \sim \mathcal N(0, s^2I_k)\), then \(\mathbb E\|\xi\|^2 = ks^2\), a sum of \(k\) squared coordinates each with mean \(s^2\), and \(\|\xi\|\) concentrates near \(s\sqrt k\) (Concentration inequalities). If \(P\) is the orthogonal projection onto a fixed \(m\)-dimensional subspace, then \(P\xi\) is again Gaussian, with standard deviation \(s\) along each of \(m\) orthonormal directions of the subspace and nothing outside it. The reason is rotation invariance: the density of \(\xi\) depends only on \(\|\xi\|\), so in any orthonormal basis its coordinates are independent \(\mathcal N(0, s^2)\), and the projection keeps \(m\) of them. So noise restricted to a subspace has length about \(s\sqrt m\).


41.2.3 Fact 3 — Public data is free, and so is anything computed from it
DP bounds how the output’s distribution changes when one private record changes. A computation that reads only public data, such as pretraining, choosing a subspace from public gradients or tuning on a public validation set, produces a fixed object as far as the private data are concerned, and using it as the starting point or a hyperparameter of a private algorithm costs nothing. In the DP-SGD proof this enters as the condition that the initial weights \(w_0\) are chosen independently of the private data (DP-SGD). Anything computed afterwards from the private algorithm’s output is post-processing (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).


41.2.4 Fact 4 — A dense layer’s per-example gradient is an outer product
For a layer that maps an input \(a \in \mathbb R^{d_{\text{in}}}\) to \(Wa\), the gradient of record \(i\)’s loss with respect to \(W\) is \(\delta_ia_i^\top\), where \(\delta_i\) is the gradient with respect to the layer’s output, and its length is \(\|\delta_i\|\,\|a_i\|\), because the squared entries \(\delta_{ij}^2a_{il}^2\) sum to \((\sum_j\delta_{ij}^2)(\sum_l a_{il}^2)\). Clipping can therefore compute each record’s gradient norm without forming the gradient, ghost clipping (DP-SGD).

41.3 Why dimension costs, and when it does not

41.3.1 Context
Every bound on private learning in this part grows with the dimension. Private empirical risk minimization shows that the best excess risk achievable under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP grows like \(\sqrt d\) for convex Lipschitz losses and like \(d\) for strongly convex ones, and that a matching lower bound holds. The noise in DP-SGD has length \(\sigma C\sqrt k/B\), growing with the number of trainable weights. Yet large pretrained language models with hundreds of millions of weights are fine-tuned privately with good results. How much does each trainable direction really cost, and what decides it?


41.3.2 Statement
The noise on the averaged gradient, restricted to the \(k\) trainable coordinates, has length \[\|\xi_t\|/B \approx s\sqrt k = \frac{\sigma C\sqrt k}{B}. \tag{41.1}\] Near the starting point, model the loss as a quadratic with curvature \(H\). Then \(T\) steps of noisy gradient descent with step size \(\eta\) and noise of standard deviation \(s\) per coordinate raise the expected loss, compared with the same steps without noise, by \[\Delta = \sum_{j=1}^k\frac{\eta s^2}{2(2 - \eta h_j)}\Big(1 - (1 - \eta h_j)^{2T}\Big) \approx \frac{\eta s^2}{4}\,d_{\text{eff}}, \qquad d_{\text{eff}} = \sum_{j=1}^k\Big(1 - (1 - \eta h_j)^{2T}\Big), \tag{41.2}\] where \(h_j\) are the eigenvalues of \(H\) restricted to the trainable coordinates, \(0 \le h_j < 2/\eta\), and the approximation assumes \(\eta h_j \ll 1\). The effective dimension \(d_{\text{eff}}\) satisfies \[d_{\text{eff}} \le \min\Big(k,\ 2\eta T\operatorname{tr}H\Big). \tag{41.3}\]


41.3.3 Derivation
The idea is to follow the noise separately from the signal. On a quadratic, the dynamics are linear, so the noise’s contribution to the weights is a sum of independent Gaussian kicks, each shrunk by the curvature. Directions with high curvature forget old kicks quickly and reach a steady state; directions with almost no curvature keep accumulating kicks but charge very little for them.

Separate the noise. On the quadratic \(J(w) = J(w_*) + \frac12(w - w_*)^\top H(w - w_*)\) the gradient is \(H(w - w_*)\). Let \(w_t\) follow the noisy steps \(w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta(H(w_t - w_*) + \xi_t)\) and \(\bar w_t\) the same steps without noise, from the same start. Their difference \(e_t = w_t - \bar w_t\) obeys \(e_{t+1} = (I - \eta H)e_t - \eta\xi_t\) with \(e_0 = 0\), because the terms with \(w_*\) are the same for both and cancel. So \(e_t\) is a linear function of the noise alone, a Gaussian with mean zero.
The loss increase. Expanding the quadratic around \(\bar w_T\), \(J(w_T) = J(\bar w_T) + \nabla J(\bar w_T)^\top e_T + \frac12e_T^\top He_T\). The middle term has mean zero, because \(e_T\) has mean zero and is independent of the deterministic \(\bar w_T\). So \(\Delta = \frac12\mathbb E[e_T^\top He_T]\).
One direction at a time. In the eigenbasis of \(H\) the coordinates decouple, and by Fact 2 each coordinate of the noise is still \(\mathcal N(0, s^2)\), independently. Along an eigenvector with curvature \(h\), the coordinate \(e\) of the error obeys \(e_{t+1} = (1 - \eta h)e_t - \eta\xi\), so after \(T\) steps it is \(-\eta\sum_{t<T}(1 - \eta h)^{T - 1 - t}\xi_t\), with variance \[v_T = \eta^2s^2\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}(1 - \eta h)^{2t} = \eta^2s^2\,\frac{1 - (1 - \eta h)^{2T}}{1 - (1 - \eta h)^2}, \tag{41.4}\] a geometric sum.
Its cost. The direction contributes \(\frac12hv_T\) to \(\Delta\). Since \(1 - (1 - \eta h)^2 = \eta h(2 - \eta h)\), this is \(\frac{\eta s^2}{2(2 - \eta h)}(1 - (1 - \eta h)^{2T})\), and summing over the directions gives Equation 41.2. With \(\eta h \ll 1\) the first factor is \(\eta s^2/4\).
Two limits. For \(2\eta hT \gg 1\) the bracket is 1: the direction is at its steady state, the case Private empirical risk minimization analyses, and it costs \(\eta s^2/4\) whatever its curvature (stiffer directions wander less but charge more per unit of wandering). For \(2\eta hT \ll 1\) the bracket is about \(2\eta hT\), by \((1 - x)^{2T} \approx 1 - 2Tx\), and the direction costs about \(\frac{\eta s^2}{4}\cdot 2\eta hT\): the noise has random-walked a distance of variance \(T\eta^2s^2\), charged at rate \(h/2\), which is small when the direction is flat.
The bound. Each bracket is at most 1, which gives \(d_{\text{eff}} \le k\). And \(1 - (1 - x)^{2T} \le 2Tx\) for \(0 \le x \le 1\) (Bernoulli’s inequality, \((1 - x)^{2T} \ge 1 - 2Tx\)), so \(d_{\text{eff}} \le 2\eta T\sum_jh_j = 2\eta T\operatorname{tr}H\).



41.3.4 Interpretation
The count of trainable weights is an upper bound, not the price. Equation 41.2 says that noise in a direction the loss does not care about, \(h_j \approx 0\), costs nothing, however long it is. What you pay for is roughly the number of directions whose curvature exceeds \(1/(2\eta T)\), the directions the noise has time to fill. A large pretrained model whose loss is curved in only a few directions near the pretrained weights can be fine-tuned in all its weights at a cost set by those few. This is the explanation Li, Liu, Hashimoto, Inan, Kulkarni, Lee & Thakurta (2022) give for why private fine-tuning of large language models does not suffer from their size: the optimal rates of Private empirical risk minimization are worst cases over all losses with a given Lipschitz constant, and they replace the dimension \(d\) by a quantity that measures how the gradients spread over directions.
Fewer trainable weights still help, for two reasons. Freezing weights removes their directions from the sum, so \(d_{\text{eff}}\) can only fall. And clipping happens to the trainable gradient: with fewer coordinates, per-example gradients are shorter, fewer are clipped, and the average clipped gradient, the signal, can be longer. Both effects appear in the example below. Against them stands the bias of freezing: if the task needs a direction that is frozen, no amount of private data can move it.
The step size and the number of steps are part of the dimension. \(d_{\text{eff}}\) grows with \(\eta T\): a longer or more aggressive run fills more flat directions with noise. This is one reason private fine-tuning works best with smaller step sizes than private training from scratch, as Section 41.7 finds.
How good is the model? The quadratic is a local model, accurate while fine-tuning stays near its starting point; the loss of a network is not quadratic far from it. And the loss increase is not an accuracy loss: accuracy changes only when noise flips predictions. Use Equation 41.2 to compare strategies, not to predict accuracy.






Figure 41.1: Left: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (\(\sigma = 4.13\), \(B = 100\), \(C = 0.5\)), the noise length \(\sigma C\sqrt k/B\) (line) against the number of trainable weights \(k\), and the length of the average clipped gradient at the pretrained model (points) for the last layer, low-rank adapters of ranks 1 to 16, and all weights. Right: their ratio. The noise grows like \(\sqrt k\) while the signal shrinks, because longer gradient vectors are clipped more.





41.3.5 Example: the running example after pretraining
Table 41.2 gives the noise length Equation 41.1 for the three trainable sets of Section 41.7, with \(B = 100\) and \(C = 0.5\).

The signal is the average clipped gradient over the private records at the start of fine-tuning. From the pretrained weights its length is 0.0130 when all weights are trained, 0.0207 for the adapter and 0.0250 for the last layer alone (Figure 41.1). The last layer’s 65 coordinates carry a longer average clipped gradient than all 3,329 coordinates together, because each record’s gradient restricted to 65 coordinates is shorter and less often clipped. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the noise is 92.0 times the signal for all weights, 22.9 times for the adapter and 6.7 times for the last layer. By the break-even argument of DP-SGD, a signal of constant direction outgrows a random walk of noise after \((\text{noise}/\text{signal})^2\) steps: 8,455, 523 and 44 steps. From a random initialization the signal is 0.0618, five times longer than from the pretrained weights, because a random network gets many records wrong and their gradients are long; but it shrinks quickly as training proceeds, to 0.026 after 1,000 steps in DP-SGD.
The curvature tells a less pessimistic story. Take the Gauss–Newton curvature of the private loss at the pretrained weights: the Hessian of the logistic loss with the network replaced by its linearization around the current weights, the average over records of \(\pi_i(1 - \pi_i)\nabla f_i\nabla f_i^\top\), with \(f_i\) the network’s output on record \(i\) and \(\pi_i\) its predicted probability. It is positive semi-definite, and near a good fit it is close to the full Hessian, which is what the quadratic model needs. Estimated from 2,000 private records, it has largest eigenvalue 0.723 and trace 16.310 over all weights; for the last layer alone the largest eigenvalue is 0.142 and the trace 0.681. With \(\eta = 0.1\) and \(T = 10{,}000\), only 406 of the 3,329 directions have curvature above \(1/(2\eta T) = 5 \times 10^{-4}\), and \(d_{\text{eff}} = 451\); for the last layer, \(d_{\text{eff}} = 60.2\) of 65. The full model’s noise is \(\sqrt{3{,}329/65} = 7.2\) times longer than the last layer’s, but by Equation 41.2 it costs only \(451/60.2 = 7.5\) times more, not \(3{,}329/65 = 51\) times. At \(\varepsilon = 1\), where \(s = 0.0206\), Equation 41.2 predicts a loss increase of 0.0048 for all weights at \(\eta = 0.1\), against 0.0355 if every direction had reached its steady state, and 0.00064 for the last layer alone.


41.3.6 Check yourself

You double the number of steps at the same \(\sigma\) (ignoring that this would raise \(\varepsilon\)). Which directions’ noise cost changes? (Only the flat ones, \(2\eta hT \lesssim 1\), whose cost doubles roughly; directions already at their steady state cost the same.)
Why does \(d_{\text{eff}} \le 2\eta T\operatorname{tr}H\) not help much in the running example? (Because \(2\eta T\operatorname{tr}H = 2 \times 0.1 \times 10{,}000 \times 16.31 = 32{,}620\), far above \(k = 3{,}329\). The trace is dominated by a few large eigenvalues; the bound is useful only when the total curvature is small compared with \(1/(\eta T)\).)

section: 41.4 Good features: the last layer as private convex ERM
text:
41.4 Good features: the last layer as private convex ERM

41.4.1 Context
The simplest way to use a pretrained model is to freeze everything except the last layer and train a linear classifier on the frozen features, linear probing. For the running example that is logistic regression on the 64 hidden activations plus a bias, 65 weights. It turns private deep learning back into the convex problem of Private empirical risk minimization, where the rates and the methods are known. Tramèr & Boneh (2021) showed that this simple recipe beats end-to-end private training of convolutional networks on standard image benchmarks at moderate budgets, even with handcrafted features (the ScatterNet wavelet transform), and that features learned on public data do better still. What does the private part of a linear probe cost, and what limits it?


41.4.2 Statement
Let \(\phi(x) \in \mathbb R^k\) be the frozen features, computed from public data only, and \(\ell(w, (x, y)) = \ln(1 + e^{-y\langle w, \phi(x)\rangle})\). Then:

The per-record gradient has length at most \(\|\phi(x)\|\). For \(k - 1\) tanh features and a constant 1, \(\|\phi(x)\| \le \sqrt k\), so the loss is \(\sqrt k\)-Lipschitz in \(w\) and clipping is optional.
The excess risk of a private probe splits into a feature gap and a privacy cost: \[R(\tilde w) - R_{\text{best}} = \underbrace{R(w^\phi) - R_{\text{best}}}_{\text{features}} + \underbrace{R(\tilde w) - R(w^\phi)}_{\text{privacy}}, \tag{41.5}\] where \(R\) is the risk, \(R_{\text{best}}\) the best risk of any model, and \(w^\phi\) the best linear model on the features \(\phi\). The first term does not depend on \(n\) or \(\varepsilon\). The second is private convex ERM in \(k\) dimensions, whose best rate for losses that are \(L\)-Lipschitz over a ball of radius \(R_w\) is \(\tilde\Theta\big(LR_w\sqrt{k\ln(1/\delta)}/(n\varepsilon)\big)\) (Bassily, Smith & Thakurta 2014).



41.4.3 Derivation

The gradient bound. \(\nabla_w\ell = \ell'(m)\,y\,\phi(x)\) with \(m = y\langle w, \phi(x)\rangle\) the margin and \(\ell'(m) = -1/(1 + e^m) \in (-1, 0)\). So \(\|\nabla_w\ell\| \le \|\phi(x)\|\). Each tanh activation lies in \((-1, 1)\), so \(\|\phi(x)\|^2 < (k - 1) + 1 = k\).
The split. Add and subtract \(R(w^\phi)\). The first difference compares two non-private quantities and contains no noise.
The privacy term. By Fact 3, \(\phi\) is a fixed function, so the probe is an ordinary convex ERM problem on the transformed records \((\phi(x_i), y_i)\), with dimension \(k\) and Lipschitz constant \(\sqrt k\) or the clipping norm. The rate is the one Private empirical risk minimization states, proved by Bassily, Smith & Thakurta (2014), and noisy gradient descent attains it. The Lipschitz constant and the dimension enter through the noise \(\propto L\sqrt k\) that every private method must add.



41.4.4 Interpretation
Features cap accuracy; privacy only decides how close you get to the cap. The feature gap is the price of freezing, paid even with infinite data and no privacy. The privacy cost falls like \(\sqrt k/(n\varepsilon)\). With few features and good ones, both are small; with few features and poor ones, the probe is private, cheap and bad. This is the trade-off behind the title of Tramèr & Boneh’s paper: private learning needs better features, or much more data. End-to-end training can eventually beat a probe, because it can learn better features, but it pays for every one of its weights to do so, and at small \(\varepsilon\) and small \(n\) it does not catch up.
Why linear probing is the safe first baseline. The problem is convex, so the optimizer cannot wander into a bad region, and the theory of Private empirical risk minimization applies: output perturbation, objective perturbation and noisy gradient descent all work, with known rates and no clipping bias if you use the Lipschitz bound. It has few hyperparameters, and with very few weights it can even be run full-batch. If a probe on public features is already within your accuracy target, there is little reason to fine-tune more.
Clipping below the Lipschitz bound still pays. The bound \(\sqrt k\) is a worst case: it is reached only by a record with every activation saturated and a large negative margin. Most records’ gradients are much shorter, because a record classified with a wide margin has \(|\ell'(m)|\) close to 0. Clipping at a smaller \(C\) biases the gradient of the few long ones and divides the noise by \(\sqrt k/C\); Exercise 3 compares the two on the running example.


41.4.5 Example: the ceiling and the cost on the running example
The pretrained network’s 64 hidden units plus a constant give \(k = 65\) features; the largest feature norm on the private training records is 7.035, below the bound \(\sqrt{65} = 8.062\). The pretrained network itself, with its public last layer, labels 0.9035 of the private test inputs correctly (the report half, Section 41.7). Fitting the last layer exactly and non-privately on the 10,000 private records, by Newton’s method, raises this to 0.9536: that is the probe’s ceiling, \(w^\phi\) in Equation 41.5. A network trained non-privately on the private data from scratch reaches 0.9606, so the feature gap is 0.007 in accuracy. The private probe reaches 0.9478 at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and 0.9514 at \(\varepsilon = 8\) (Table 41.5): at every budget it is within 0.006 of its ceiling, and at no budget can it pass it.


41.4.6 Check yourself

The public features are replaced by 650 features of the same quality (same ceiling). What happens to the privacy cost of the probe? (The noise length grows by \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2\) at the same \(\sigma\), so the privacy term of Equation 41.5 grows by about that factor at a fixed \(n\varepsilon\); you need about 3.2 times more data for the same cost.)
Is the probe private if the features were computed by a network pretrained on data that included some of the private records? (The probe is private with respect to the private dataset given the features; but the features themselves are a function of those records and were not trained privately, so the released model as a whole has no guarantee for them. See Section 41.8.)

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.5 Low-rank adapters

41.5.1 Context
The last layer is often not enough: the features of a model pretrained on one task are not exactly right for another, and the probe stops at its ceiling. Training all weights fixes the features but pays for every weight. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) sits in between: it freezes each pretrained weight matrix \(W_0\) and learns a low-rank correction, \(W = W_0 + UV^\top\) with \(U \in \mathbb R^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}\) and \(V \in \mathbb R^{d_{\text{in}} \times r}\) (Hu et al. 2022). Yu et al. (2022) showed that private fine-tuning of language models with LoRA and similar parameter-efficient methods matches or beats private full fine-tuning at a fraction of the cost. How many weights does it train, what are its per-example gradients, and in which directions can it move \(W\)?


41.5.2 Statement
A rank-\(r\) adapter on a \(d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}\) matrix has \[k = r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}}) \tag{41.6}\] trainable weights, against \(d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\) for the matrix. With \(\delta_i\) the gradient of record \(i\)’s loss with respect to the layer’s output and \(a_i\) its input, the per-example gradients are outer products, \[\nabla_U\ell_i = \delta_i\,(V^\top a_i)^\top, \qquad \nabla_V\ell_i = a_i\,(U^\top\delta_i)^\top, \tag{41.7}\] with lengths \(\|\delta_i\|\|V^\top a_i\|\) and \(\|a_i\|\|U^\top\delta_i\|\), so ghost clipping applies. One step with noisy gradient sums \(G_U = \sum_i\overline{\nabla_U\ell_i} + \xi_U\) and \(G_V = \sum_i\overline{\nabla_V\ell_i} + \xi_V\) and step \(\eta/B\) changes \(W\) by \[\Delta W = -\frac\eta B\big(G_UV^\top + UG_V^\top\big) + O\Big(\frac{\eta^2}{B^2}\Big). \tag{41.8}\] In particular, from the usual start \(U = 0\), the first step’s change has rank at most \(r\), and to first order its rows lie in the span of the columns of \(V\). The privacy guarantee is that of DP-SGD with the same \(q\), \(\sigma\) and \(T\) (Fact 1).


41.5.3 Derivation

Counting. \(U\) has \(d_{\text{out}}r\) entries and \(V\) has \(d_{\text{in}}r\).
The chain rule through the product. By Fact 4 the gradient with respect to \(W\) is \(G_i = \delta_ia_i^\top\), and the loss depends on \(U\) and \(V\) only through \(W\). A small change \(dU\) changes \(W\) by \(dU\,V^\top\), which changes the loss by \(\operatorname{tr}(G_i^\top dU\,V^\top) = \operatorname{tr}(V^\top G_i^\top dU) = \langle G_iV, dU\rangle\), using the cyclic property of the trace. So \(\nabla_U\ell_i = G_iV = \delta_i(a_i^\top V) = \delta_i(V^\top a_i)^\top\). In the same way a change \(dV\) changes \(W\) by \(U\,dV^\top\) and the loss by \(\operatorname{tr}(G_i^\top U\,dV^\top) = \langle G_i^\top U, dV\rangle\), so \(\nabla_V\ell_i = G_i^\top U = a_i(\delta_i^\top U) = a_i(U^\top\delta_i)^\top\). This is Equation 41.7.
Norms. Each is an outer product of two vectors, so its length is the product of their lengths, as in Fact 4. The norm of record \(i\)’s whole gradient is the square root of the sum of the squared norms over \(U\), \(V\) and the other trainable layers, computed from vectors of length \(d_{\text{out}}\), \(d_{\text{in}}\) and \(r\) without forming any matrix.
The step. After the step, \(W' = W_0 + (U - \frac\eta BG_U)(V - \frac\eta BG_V)^\top\). Expanding the product, \(W' - W = -\frac\eta B(G_UV^\top + UG_V^\top) + \frac{\eta^2}{B^2}G_UG_V^\top\), which is Equation 41.8.
From \(U = 0\). Then \(\nabla_V\ell_i = 0\) for every record, so \(G_V = \xi_V\) is pure noise, and \(\Delta W = -\frac\eta BG_UV^\top + \frac{\eta^2}{B^2}G_U\xi_V^\top\). The first term is a \(d_{\text{out}} \times r\) matrix times \(V^\top\), of rank at most \(r\), with rows that are combinations of the columns of \(V\). The second term is of order \(\eta^2/B^2\) and tilts those rows slightly. The whole \(\Delta W\) is a product of a \(d_{\text{out}} \times r\) and an \(r \times d_{\text{in}}\) matrix, so its rank is at most \(r\) exactly.



41.5.4 Interpretation
An adapter is DP-SGD in a smaller, moving space. The noise of DP-SGD on \((U, V)\) lives in \(k = r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})\) coordinates, so Equation 41.1 applies with that \(k\). Seen from \(W\), each step moves the matrix within a set of dimension about \(k\): the directions \(XV^\top + UY^\top\) for arbitrary \(X\) and \(Y\), which change as \(U\) and \(V\) change. The adapter restricts the update to that set; noise in the other \(d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}} - k\) directions of \(W\) never arises.
What the restriction costs. At the start, with \(U = 0\) and \(V\) random, the update is the true gradient \(G\) multiplied on the right by \(VV^\top\), which for a random \(V\) with small \(r\) is close to a multiple of the projection onto the span of its columns: the gradient is projected onto a random \(r\)-dimensional subspace of the inputs. Random subspaces capture a fraction of about \(r/d_{\text{in}}\) of a fixed vector’s energy, which for small \(r\) is little. As \(V\) moves (its gradient is no longer zero once \(U \neq 0\)) the subspace aligns with the useful directions. Low-rank adaptation works when the change from the pretrained weights that the new task needs is itself close to low rank, as Hu et al. (2022) observed for language models. The rank \(r\) trades bias against noise like the number of trainable weights does.
Full fine-tuning is not ruled out. Li, Tramèr, Liang & Hashimoto (2022) fine-tuned all the weights of pretrained language models with DP-SGD and matched or beat the parameter-efficient methods, once the hyperparameters were right: large batches, a learning rate tuned for private training, and a fine-tuning objective aligned with pretraining. Equation 41.2 explains why this can work: what full fine-tuning pays is \(d_{\text{eff}}\), not \(p\). Whether an adapter or full fine-tuning wins is an empirical question that depends on the model, the data and the tuning, and the published evidence goes both ways. The adapter’s advantages that do not depend on accuracy are certain: it stores and communicates only \(k\) numbers per task, and it computes and clips much smaller gradients.


41.5.5 Example: counting, and checking the gradients
The running example’s first layer maps 51 inputs (50 features and a constant) to 64 hidden units: 3,264 weights. A rank-4 adapter trains \(4 \times (51 + 64) = 460\) of them, plus the 65 weights of the last layer, \(k = 525\); rank 1 gives 180 and rank 16 gives 1,905. For a \(768 \times 768\) projection of a transformer, rank 8 trains \(8 \times 1{,}536 = 12{,}288\) weights instead of 589,824, a factor of 48 fewer, so the noise is \(\sqrt{48} = 6.9\) times shorter. On 256 private records, the ghost norms of Equation 41.7 agree with explicitly formed per-example gradients of the adapter to a relative difference of \(3.3 \times 10^{-16}\). Exercise 4 checks the rank of the first step.


41.5.6 Check yourself

Why does LoRA start with \(U = 0\) rather than both factors random? (So that \(W = W_0\) at the start: the fine-tuned model begins exactly at the pretrained one. With both random, the first forward pass would use a randomly perturbed matrix.)
An adapter of rank \(r = \min(d_{\text{in}}, d_{\text{out}})\) can represent any change of \(W\). Does it then have the same noise as training \(W\) directly? (No, more: it has \(r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})\) coordinates, more than \(d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\) when \(r\) is this large. Adapters save noise only at small rank.)

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.6 Gradients near a public subspace

41.6.1 Context
Section 41.3 says the noise costs little in directions the loss does not use. If you knew the directions the private gradients do use, you could add noise only there. Public data gives an estimate: compute per-example gradients on public records at the current or pretrained weights, find their top principal directions, and project the private gradients onto them. Zhou, Wu & Banerjee (2021) do this as projected DP-SGD, and Yu, Zhang, Chen & Liu (2021) as gradient embedding perturbation, which also releases the residual outside the subspace with separate noise. Li et al. (2022) measured that the gradients of private fine-tuning are dominated by a few principal components. How much does a projection save, and what does it lose?


41.6.2 Statement
Let \(P_m\) be the orthogonal projection onto an \(m\)-dimensional subspace computed from public data only. Releasing \[P_m\Big(\sum_{i \in S_t}\bar g_i\Big) + \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2P_m) \tag{41.9}\] (noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) along each of \(m\) orthonormal directions of the subspace) at every step has the same \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) as DP-SGD with the same \(q\), \(\sigma\) and \(T\). If \(\bar m\) is the average clipped gradient and \(f_m = \|P_m\bar m\|^2/\|\bar m\|^2\) the fraction of its energy that the subspace captures, the kept signal has length \(\sqrt{f_m}\|\bar m\|\), the noise on the averaged gradient has length about \(s\sqrt m\), and signal outgrows noise after about \[T_{\text{even}}(m) = \Big(\frac{s\sqrt m}{\sqrt{f_m}\,\|\bar m\|}\Big)^2 \tag{41.10}\] steps, against \((s\sqrt p/\|\bar m\|)^2\) without projection. The lost fraction \(1 - f_m\) of the signal is a bias that no number of steps recovers.


41.6.3 Derivation

Sensitivity. A projection never lengthens a vector: \(\|P_mx\| \le \|x\|\), because \(x = P_mx + (x - P_mx)\) with the two parts orthogonal, so \(\|x\|^2 = \|P_mx\|^2 + \|x - P_mx\|^2\). Adding or removing one record changes the projected sum by \(P_m\bar g\), of length at most \(C\).
The mechanism. In an orthonormal basis of the subspace, Equation 41.9 is \(m\) coordinates of a vector of sensitivity at most \(C\) plus independent \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2)\) noise on each: a Gaussian mechanism with ratio \(1/\sigma\), exactly as in DP-SGD, and Poisson sampling makes it the same subsampled Gaussian. The subspace is fixed before the private data are read (Fact 3), so it is a public parameter of the mechanism. Equivalently, Equation 41.9 is the projection of the ordinary DP-SGD release onto the subspace (Fact 2), and projection is post-processing.
Signal and noise. Dividing by \(B\), the kept signal is \(P_m\bar m\), of length \(\sqrt{f_m}\|\bar m\|\) by the definition of \(f_m\), and the noise has \(m\) coordinates of standard deviation \(s\), length about \(s\sqrt m\) (Fact 2).
Break-even. As in DP-SGD, over \(j\) steps a signal of constant direction adds up to \(j\) times its length and independent noise to \(\sqrt j\) times; they are equal at Equation 41.10.



41.6.4 Interpretation
A projection trades bias for variance, and public data sets the exchange rate. The noise falls by \(\sqrt{p/m}\), the signal by \(\sqrt{f_m}\). If the private gradients lie near the public subspace, \(f_m\) is close to 1 for \(m \ll p\) and the trade is excellent. If the public data are unrelated, the subspace is no better than a random one, \(f_m \approx m/p\), and the projection removes as much signal as noise, gaining nothing. The quality of the public data appears here directly as \(f_m\).
A fixed subspace is a cap; methods refresh it or add the residual. Since \(P_m\) removes the part \(1 - f_m\) of the signal at every step, training with a fixed projection can only move the weights within the subspace. Projected DP-SGD recomputes the subspace from public gradients as training proceeds; gradient embedding perturbation releases the residual \(\bar g - P_m\bar g\) too, with its own noise, so the bias disappears at the price of a little more noise. LoRA, in this light, chooses a subspace by structure (low-rank changes of each matrix) and lets training move it.
Why this explains full fine-tuning. The same concentration that makes a public subspace useful makes \(d_{\text{eff}}\) small in Equation 41.2: gradients near a low-dimensional subspace are gradients of a loss curved in few directions. Projection makes the saving explicit and certain; full fine-tuning gets part of it implicitly, if the step size and number of steps are small enough that flat directions do not fill up with noise.






Figure 41.2: Left: eigenvalues of the Gauss–Newton curvature of the private loss at the pretrained weights, estimated from 2,000 private records, on log scales, with the thresholds \(1/(2\eta T)\) for \(\eta = 0.1\) and \(0.5\) and \(T = 10{,}000\); directions below a threshold contribute little noise cost. Right: the fraction of the energy of the private average clipped gradient that lies in the top \(m\) principal directions of 500 public per-example gradients (solid), and in \(m\) random directions (dashed).





41.6.5 Example: how concentrated the running example’s gradients are
At the pretrained weights the average clipped private gradient has length 0.0130. The top principal directions of 500 clipped public per-example gradients capture Table 41.3’s fractions of its energy; random subspaces of the same dimension capture about \(k/p\).

At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the kept signal outgrows the noise after 222 steps in the 64-dimensional subspace, against 8,455 steps for all weights. 41.6.6 Check yourself

The public subspace is computed from the private data instead, by a non-private principal component analysis. Is Equation 41.9 still \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP? (No. The subspace then depends on the private records, the projection is no longer a fixed public map, and the subspace itself leaks information about them; it must be computed privately, at a cost in budget, or from public data.)
When does projection onto \(m\) public directions not shorten the break-even time? (When \(f_m \le m/p\) or close to it, so that the signal shrinks as much as the noise: for public data unrelated to the private task, or for a subspace computed at weights far from where training now is.)

41.7 Pretraining and fine-tuning the running example

41.7.1 Context
How much does a related public dataset buy on the running example, at each budget, and which part of the model should be fine-tuned?


41.7.2 Statement
The public task. The private teacher has a first layer \(W_1^{\text{priv}}\) (8 hidden units, 51 inputs) and an output layer \(w_2^{\text{priv}}\). The public teacher has first layer \(W_1^{\text{priv}} + 0.15Z\) and output layer \(\cos(0.3)\,w_2^{\text{priv}} + \sin(0.3)\,z\), where \(Z\) and \(z\) are fixed standard normal draws: the same hidden units, each slightly perturbed, read out with weights turned by 0.3 radians toward a random vector. It labels 50,000 inputs drawn from the private input distribution. The design makes pretraining useful but not sufficient: the public student must learn features close to the ones the private task needs, but cannot learn the private task itself. The public teacher agrees with the private one on 0.9004 of the private test inputs.
Pretraining. The 64-unit student is trained on the public data by non-private SGD, 10,000 steps with batches of 100 and step size 0.5, to 0.9861 training accuracy on the public task. On the private task it reaches 0.9035 without any private data.
Fine-tuning. From the pretrained weights, DP-SGD with \(q = 0.01\), \(C = 0.5\) and \(T = 10{,}000\) trains: all 3,329 weights (full); the last layer, \(k = 65\) (last layer); a rank-4 adapter \(W_1 = W_1^{\text{pre}} + UV^\top\) and the last layer, \(k = 525\) (adapter). The baseline trains all weights from a random initialization (scratch), the setting of DP-SGD. The private test set of 20,000 records is split in half: the step size of each method is chosen from three values on the first half at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (Table 41.4) and used at every budget, and accuracy is reported on the second half.

41.7.3 Derivation
Each entry is a measurement, and each method’s privacy follows from Fact 1 and Fact 3: the pretrained weights and the adapter’s random \(V\) are fixed before the private data are read, the clipped sum of each step has sensitivity \(C\) in the method’s trainable coordinates, and the accountant gives \(\sigma = 7.72\), 4.13, 2.28 and 0.917 for the four budgets, the same for every method because \(q\) and \(T\) are the same. The step sizes were chosen by looking at private data, the validation half, without paying for it; Hyperparameter tuning shows how to do that privately, and the comparison here is of methods at their best, as in DP-SGD.


41.7.4 Interpretation
Pretraining is worth about a factor of eight in \(\varepsilon\). Every fine-tuning method at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) (0.9395 to 0.9478) beats training from scratch at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (0.9246), and the best of them comes within 0.004 of training from scratch at \(\varepsilon = 2\) (0.9518). The adapter at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (0.9616) matches training from scratch at \(\varepsilon = 8\) (0.9611) and the non-private model trained from scratch (0.9606), and full fine-tuning at \(\varepsilon = 2\) (0.9663) beats both. The public data carry information about the private task that 10,000 private records do not, and that information is free.
Which weights to train depends on the budget. At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) the last layer is best: with 65 trainable weights its noise is \(\sqrt{3{,}329/65} = 7.2\) times shorter than full fine-tuning’s, and its ceiling, 0.9536, is not yet binding. From \(\varepsilon = 1\) on, the last layer is stuck near its ceiling (0.9497 to 0.9519) while the adapter and full fine-tuning keep improving: they can correct the features, and the noise is now small enough to let them. The adapter, with 525 weights, is never more than 0.0022 below the best method at any budget: the middle choice is the robust one. Full fine-tuning is behind at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), by 0.0083, but not far behind elsewhere once its step size is right, as Li et al. (2022) found for language models; at \(\varepsilon = 2\) and 8 it is the best, by 0.0010 and 0.0022. Figure 41.3, a separate set of single runs, shows the same overall picture, with the order of the three pretrained methods at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and 1 changed: differences of a few thousandths between them are within run-to-run variation.
Step sizes matter as much as the method. In Table 41.4 full fine-tuning loses 1.3 points at a step size three times too large, and the adapter 1.5 points. The best step size for full fine-tuning and the adapter, 0.1, is 2.5 times smaller than for training from scratch. That is the effective-dimension argument of Section 41.3 at work: a larger \(\eta\) fills more flat directions with noise and undoes what pretraining provided.
What the run-to-run spread says. The standard deviations over two runs are small for the pretrained methods, 0.0013 or less, but two runs estimate a spread only roughly: the rank sweep below repeats the adapter at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and finds a standard deviation of 0.0023, and a mean of 0.9624 against the table’s 0.9616. Differences between the pretrained methods smaller than about 0.005 should not be read as rankings.






Figure 41.3: Test accuracy of the four strategies against \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), one run each with the step sizes of Table 41.4 and a different seed from Table 41.5, with the pretrained model’s accuracy before fine-tuning (dotted). The pretrained methods are far ahead of training from scratch at small budgets; the last layer stays near its ceiling from \(\varepsilon = 1\) on, and training from scratch passes it at larger budgets.





41.7.5 Example: the adapter’s rank
At \(\varepsilon = 1\), with the adapter’s step size 0.1, two runs each give \(0.9590 \pm 0.0038\) at rank 1 (\(k = 180\)), \(0.9624 \pm 0.0023\) at rank 4 (\(k = 525\)) and \(0.9586 \pm 0.0031\) at rank 16 (\(k = 1{,}905\)). Rank 4 is best, but the differences are about the size of the run-to-run spread. Two forces pull in opposite directions: a higher rank lets the update follow more of the directions the task needs, and it adds noise, whose length grows like \(\sqrt k\) (Figure 41.1). On this problem neither dominates over a sixteenfold range of ranks, so the rank is a cheap hyperparameter to get roughly right.


41.7.6 Check yourself

Why is the last layer’s accuracy at \(\varepsilon = 8\) (0.9514) not higher than at \(\varepsilon = 2\) (0.9519)? (It is at its ceiling, the best linear model on the frozen features, 0.9536 non-privately. Less noise cannot help a model that cannot represent a better classifier.)
If the public teacher were identical to the private one, which strategy would you expect to win at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), and why? (The last layer, or no fine-tuning at all: the pretrained model would already be close to perfect, so there would be nothing for the extra weights to learn and only noise for them to collect. Exercise 5 measures it.)

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 41.8 What public data does not buy
text:
41.8 What public data does not buy

41.8.1 Context
Everything so far treated the public data as free. Formally that is right: the guarantee of a private fine-tuning run does not depend on what the public data are. But “public” is a label someone chose, and the guarantee says nothing about the records under that label. Tramèr, Kamath & Carlini (2024) argue that the field’s reliance on large web-scraped pretraining data needs scrutiny on several counts. What exactly is guaranteed, and what is not?


41.8.2 Statement
Let \(\mathcal A(D_{\text{pub}}, D)\) pretrain on \(D_{\text{pub}}\) without privacy and fine-tune on \(D\) with an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP algorithm. Then for every fixed \(D_{\text{pub}}\), the map \(D \mapsto \mathcal A(D_{\text{pub}}, D)\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. There is no guarantee of any kind with respect to \(D_{\text{pub}}\). A person with a record \(x\) in both datasets is protected only for the copy in \(D\): removing it from \(D\) changes the output’s distribution by at most \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), while the copy in \(D_{\text{pub}}\) can be revealed completely.


41.8.3 Derivation

Fixed public data. With \(D_{\text{pub}}\) fixed, pretraining produces fixed weights \(w_0\) (or a fixed distribution over them, if pretraining is randomized, independent of \(D\)). The DP-SGD proof of DP-SGD holds for any \(w_0\) chosen independently of the private data (Fact 3), so it holds conditionally on \(w_0\), and therefore for the mixture over \(w_0\).
Nothing for the public data. Changing one record of \(D_{\text{pub}}\) can change \(w_0\) arbitrarily, and the fine-tuned model inherits whatever \(w_0\) encodes; non-private training can memorize individual records (Memorization and extraction). No noise was calibrated to that change.
A record in both. The neighbouring datasets that DP compares are \(D\) and \(D\) without \(x\), with \(D_{\text{pub}}\) the same in both. A test of whether \(x\) was in \(D\) has true positive rate at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times its false positive rate plus \(\delta\) (The definition). A test of whether \(x\) is in the training data at all can use the copy in \(D_{\text{pub}}\), which nothing bounds.



41.8.4 Interpretation
Overlap and contamination. Web-scale “public” datasets contain personal data: posts, profiles, documents put online by others, data that leaked. A private fine-tuning set of medical notes or emails may overlap with them, and the people whose records appear in both are protected only as well as the pretraining protects them, that is, not at all. Calling the resulting model “differentially private” is accurate about \(D\) and misleading about those people. Tramèr, Kamath & Carlini (2024) argue for this reason that the label should be used with care, and that the privacy of pretraining data deserves its own consideration.
Distribution shift. Public data help as much as they resemble the private task. Benchmarks in which the “private” set is a standard dataset whose distribution is close to well-curated public data, for example two collections of natural images, can overstate what the method will do on genuinely sensitive data, which is often unlike anything public: medical images, rare languages, internal logs. Table 41.5 used a public task close to the private one by design; Exercise 5 shows the gain shrinking, and for the last layer turning into a loss against training from scratch, as the public teacher drifts away.
Public is not the same as non-sensitive. Even when every pretraining record is public, a model trained on them can reproduce them, link them, or make inferences about people that the original publication did not allow. And large pretrained models are often too large to fine-tune locally, so the private data are sent to whoever has the compute, which is a trust question DP does not address (Trust models).
What to report. State what the public data are, how they were obtained, whether overlap with the private data was checked (deduplication against the private set is the minimum), and that the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) covers the private dataset given the pretrained model. Any choice made by looking at private data, such as which public model to start from or the step size, is part of the private computation and must be accounted for.


41.8.5 Example: one record, two copies
At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), any test of whether a record was in the private fine-tuning set that has false positive rate 0.01 has true positive rate at most \(e \times 0.01 + 10^{-5} = 0.0272\). If the same record is also in the public set, a membership test against the pretrained model, such as the likelihood-ratio attack of Membership inference, is bounded by nothing; it may still fail in practice, but no theorem says it will. If the record appears twice in the private set, group privacy gives \((2\varepsilon, 2e^\varepsilon\delta) = (2, 5.44 \times 10^{-5})\) for the pair (Post-processing, group privacy and composition), a weaker but real guarantee. A copy in the public set is worse than a duplicate in the private set.


41.8.6 Check yourself

You choose between three public pretrained models by fine-tuning each privately and keeping the one with the best private validation accuracy. What have you spent? (Three private training runs plus a selection on private data: the budget of all three, composed, or a private selection procedure from Hyperparameter tuning. Choosing by public validation data would have been free.)
A company deduplicates its private dataset against the public pretraining corpus by exact string matching. What can still go wrong? (Near-duplicates and paraphrases of the same personal information survive exact matching, and records about the same person need not be duplicates at all; the deduplication protects copies, not people.)

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.10 References

Tramèr & Boneh, “Differentially Private Learning Needs Better Features (or Much More Data)” (ICLR 2021). Linear models on handcrafted ScatterNet features beat end-to-end private networks at moderate budgets; features from public data do better. The source of Section 41.4.
Hu, Shen, Wallis, Allen-Zhu, Li, Wang, Wang & Chen, “LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models” (ICLR 2022). The adapter of Section 41.5, without privacy.
Yu, Naik, Backurs, Gopi, Inan, Kamath, Kulkarni, Lee, Manoel, Wutschitz, Yekhanin & Zhang, “Differentially Private Fine-tuning of Language Models” (ICLR 2022). Private fine-tuning with LoRA and other parameter-efficient methods; reports, for example, 87.8% accuracy on a language-inference benchmark at \(\varepsilon = 6.7\) against 90.2% without privacy, for a large RoBERTa model.
Li, Tramèr, Liang & Hashimoto, “Large Language Models Can Be Strong Differentially Private Learners” (ICLR 2022). Full fine-tuning with the right hyperparameters matches parameter-efficient methods; ghost clipping for sequence models.
Li, Liu, Hashimoto, Inan, Kulkarni, Lee & Thakurta, “When Does Differentially Private Learning Not Suffer in High Dimensions?” (NeurIPS 2022). Dimension-free bounds when gradients concentrate in few directions, and the measurement that fine-tuning gradients are dominated by a few principal components. The background of Section 41.3.
Zhou, Wu & Banerjee, “Bypassing the Ambient Dimension: Private SGD with Gradient Subspace Identification” (ICLR 2021). Projected DP-SGD with a subspace estimated from public gradients.
Yu, Zhang, Chen & Liu, “Do Not Let Privacy Overbill Utility: Gradient Embedding Perturbation for Private Learning” (ICLR 2021). Projection onto a public anchor subspace plus a separately noised residual.
Tramèr, Kamath & Carlini, “Position: Considerations for Differentially Private Learning with Large-Scale Public Pretraining” (ICML 2024). What the public-pretraining paradigm does and does not protect, and how benchmarks can mislead. The source of Section 41.8.
Bassily, Smith & Thakurta, “Private Empirical Risk Minimization: Efficient Algorithms and Tight Error Bounds” (FOCS 2014). The rates for private convex ERM used in Section 41.4.
De, Berrada, Hayes, Smith & Balle, “Unlocking High-Accuracy Differentially Private Image Classification through Scale” (arXiv 2022). Private fine-tuning of image models pretrained on large public datasets, among other practices.

Rules of thumb

Start from a model pretrained on public data that resembles the private task. On the running example this is worth about a factor of eight in \(\varepsilon\).
At very small budgets, train the last layer: few weights, a convex problem, a known ceiling. Measure that ceiling non-privately on public data to know what is at stake.
At moderate budgets, train a low-rank adapter or all weights; the adapter is the robust middle choice. Tune the step size, smaller than from scratch, on public data.
Count the trainable weights, but think in effective dimension: noise in directions the loss does not use is cheap; noise in directions it does use is what you pay for.

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
text:
42.1 Why this matters
Every differential privacy (DP) guarantee in this part so far protects one record. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, clips each record’s gradient, adds noise scaled to that clip, and reports \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for the part’s running example: an adversary who sees the trained model learns little about whether any single training example was used. But the people behind the data do not contribute one record each. A user of a messaging app contributes hundreds of messages, a patient dozens of visits, a photographer thousands of photos. Each of those records is protected by DP, and the person is not, because what the adversary learns about all of a person’s records together can be much larger than what they learn about one.
This chapter asks two questions. What does a record-level \(\varepsilon\) say about a person who contributed \(k\) records? And how do you train a model with a guarantee for the person instead?

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
text:
42.1.1 The one idea: the neighbouring relation is the privacy unit
A DP guarantee compares the outputs on two neighbouring datasets, and whatever differs between neighbours is what is protected. If neighbours differ in one record, records are protected; if they differ in all of one person’s records, people are. Nothing else in the definition changes. The work is to bound how much the unit, now a person, can move the computation, and to account for that bound.
There are two ways to get a guarantee for a person. The first keeps the record as the unit and pays for the person afterwards, by group privacy or by an accountant that knows the person has \(k\) records. It is cheap to implement and expensive in privacy, because the noise was calibrated to one record while the person moves the output by up to \(k\). The second makes the person the unit from the start: sample people instead of records, bound each person’s total contribution by clipping it, and run the usual accountant with people in place of records. On the running example the first route gives a useless model at any reasonable budget, and the second gives one within a few points of the non-private model.
Table 42.1 lists the results and where each is used.



Table 42.1: The results of this chapter and where each is used.

Notation. The training set has \(n\) records belonging to \(U\) users; user \(u\) owns \(n_u\) records. Two datasets are example-level neighbours if they differ by adding or removing one record, and user-level neighbours if they differ by adding or removing all the records of one user. \(k\) is the number of records a user contributes, or the cap on it. In a batch drawn by Poisson sampling at rate \(q\), \(M\) is the number of a given user’s records that are drawn. As in DP-SGD, \(C\) is the clipping norm, \(\sigma\) the noise multiplier, \(T\) the number of steps and \(B\) the expected batch size, now counted in whichever unit is sampled.
The running example. The part’s network (one hidden layer of 64 tanh units, 3,329 weights) learns labels produced by a fixed teacher network from 10,000 training records of 50 features, and is tested on 20,000 more. This chapter assigns the 10,000 records to \(U = 1{,}000\) users. Each user gets one record, and the other 9,000 are spread over users with probabilities proportional to log-normal weights, so user sizes are very uneven: the mean is 10 records, the median 4, and the largest user holds 348 (Figure 42.1). A user’s records are a nearest-neighbour cluster around a random record, so they resemble each other the way one person’s messages do: the label balance \(|\bar y|\) is 0.21 on average in the ten largest users, against 0.06 in the whole set. The population is fixed, like the dataset.






Figure 42.1: Left: the number of records per user in the running example’s population of 1,000 users, on log–log axes; 193 users have one record and the largest has 348. Right: the share of all records held by the largest users. The largest 10 users hold 17.9% of the records and the smallest half of the users 10.3%.



How to read this chapter. The toolkit restates three facts from earlier parts. Section 42.3 and Section 42.4 say what a record-level guarantee gives a person; the second has the chapter’s main derivation, the accountant for a user with \(k\) records. Section 42.5 and Section 42.6 are the two ways to train with a user-level guarantee, Section 42.7 asks what they do to heavy users, and Section 42.8 compares everything on the running example.

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
section: 42.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses
text:
42.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses

42.2.1 Fact 1 — Group privacy
If a mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for neighbours that differ in one record, then for two datasets that differ in \(k\) records it satisfies, for every event \(S\), \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{k\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D'') \in S] + \delta_k, \qquad \delta_k = \delta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e^{j\varepsilon} = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}. \tag{42.1}\] The reason is a chain: \(D\) and \(D''\) are joined by a path of \(k\) steps, each between neighbouring datasets. Applying the one-record guarantee once per link multiplies the probability bound by \(e^\varepsilon\) each time, and each link’s slack \(\delta\) is then multiplied by the \(e^\varepsilon\) of every later link, which is where the geometric sum comes from. The bound is attained by some mechanisms, so no better one holds for every \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). For Rényi differential privacy (RDP) the chain is weaker still, because the Rényi divergence has no triangle inequality: an \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP mechanism is \((\alpha/2^c, 3^c\varepsilon)\)-RDP for groups of \(2^c\) records, when \(\alpha \ge 2^{c+1}\) (Mironov 2017; Rényi DP). Each doubling of the group halves the order and triples \(\varepsilon\).


42.2.2 Fact 2 — The accountant of DP-SGD
One step of DP-SGD adds Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to a sum of clipped per-example gradients computed on a Poisson batch: each record enters independently with probability \(q\). In units of \(C\), the worst case for one record is the pair \(P_0 = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), the output without the record, and the mixture \((1 - q)P_0 + q\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\), the output with it. Its RDP curve at order \(\alpha\), the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) between the two, is \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln A_\alpha\), and for integer \(\alpha\) \[A_\alpha = \sum_{j=0}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\exp\Big(\frac{j^2 - j}{2\sigma^2}\Big). \tag{42.2}\] The sum comes from expanding \(\big((1 - q) + q\,r\big)^\alpha\), with \(r\) the Gaussian likelihood ratio, by the binomial theorem and averaging each power \(r^j\) under \(P_0\) (Amplification by subsampling). RDP curves add over the \(T\) steps, even when each step depends on earlier outputs, and the total converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) at the best order: \[\varepsilon = \min_\alpha\Big[T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}\alpha - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\Big]. \tag{42.3}\] The terms \(j = 0\) and \(1\) carry no privacy cost, since their exponential factor is 1. For small \(q\) and moderate orders only the \(j = 2\) term matters beyond them, so \(A_\alpha \approx 1 + \binom\alpha2q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\) and \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) \approx \frac\alpha2q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\).


42.2.3 Fact 3 — The Gaussian moment generating function
If \(Y \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), then \(\mathbb E[e^{sY}] = e^{s^2\sigma^2/2}\) for every real \(s\) (Distributions). Every Rényi divergence between Gaussians with the same variance reduces to it, because their likelihood ratio is the exponential of a linear function of the output: for \(P_m = \mathcal N(m, \sigma^2)\), \[\frac{P_m(y)}{P_0(y)} = \exp\Big(\frac{-(y - m)^2 + y^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big) = \exp\Big(\frac{2my - m^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big). \tag{42.4}\]

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
text:
42.3 The privacy unit

42.3.1 Context
A model trained with record-level DP-SGD at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) is released. One of the people in the training set contributed \(k\) of its records. What, exactly, does the guarantee promise that person? The question has to be answered before a deployment can say “your data are protected”, because the promise is about whatever the neighbouring relation changes, and that relation was chosen by the engineer, not by the person.


42.3.2 Statement
A mechanism is user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP if for every pair of datasets \(D\), \(D'\) that differ by adding or removing all the records of one user, and every event \(S\), \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{42.5}\] It is example-level DP if the same holds for datasets that differ in one record. A mechanism that is example-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP is user-level \((k\varepsilon, \delta_k)\)-DP for users with at most \(k\) records, with \(\delta_k\) from Equation 42.1. Without more information about the mechanism, nothing better can be said.


42.3.3 Derivation

User-level neighbours are \(k\) example-level steps apart. If \(D'\) is \(D\) plus the \(k\) records of one user, add them one at a time. The datasets \(D, D \cup\{x_1\}, D\cup\{x_1, x_2\}, \dots, D'\) form a chain in which each is an example-level neighbour of the next.
Apply group privacy. Fact 1 along this chain gives Equation 42.1 with \(D'' = D'\), in both directions, since the chain can be walked either way.
Nothing better holds in general. The bound is attained by a mechanism built for the purpose, which outputs an alarm with probabilities chosen so that every link’s inequality is an equality (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). A guarantee that is only known as “\((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP” could come from that mechanism.



42.3.4 Interpretation
The definition is the same; the unit is not. User-level DP is not a new privacy notion. It is DP with a coarser neighbouring relation, so every property proved for DP holds for it: post-processing, composition and the accountants of Part 4. The only thing that changes is the sensitivity: how far one unit can move the computation. Records, users, households, devices and organizations are all possible units, and the choice should follow the question “whose participation do I want to hide?” A deployment that says “DP” without naming the unit leaves that question open, and Choosing an accountant lists the unit among the things a guarantee must report.
Group privacy is linear in \(\varepsilon\) and exponential in \(\delta\). For pure DP a user with \(k\) records gets \(k\varepsilon\), already weak: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) per record, a user with 10 records gets \(\varepsilon = 10\), a likelihood ratio of \(e^{10} \approx 22{,}000\). With \(\delta > 0\) it is worse. In Equation 42.1 each \(\delta\) is multiplied by up to \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\), so to keep the user’s \(\delta_k\) at \(10^{-5}\) the per-record \(\delta\) must be tiny, and a smaller \(\delta\) means a larger per-record \(\varepsilon\). For DP-SGD this trade can be made at any \(\delta\), because the accountant’s RDP curve converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) at every \(\delta\): choose the per-record \(\delta\) so that \(\delta_k = 10^{-5}\) exactly.
For DP-SGD it can fail altogether. The per-record \(\varepsilon\) grows as the per-record \(\delta\) shrinks, so \(\delta_k = \delta\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}\) is a race between a falling \(\delta\) and a rising \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\). For small \(k\) the falling \(\delta\) wins. For larger \(k\) the rising \(\varepsilon\) wins at every \(\delta\), and no choice brings \(\delta_k\) down to \(10^{-5}\). Group privacy then gives no \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\) guarantee at all (Exercise 2 traces the race).


42.3.5 Example: the running example’s users
The running example’s model is example-level \((6.71, 10^{-5})\)-DP. Read naively as a user-level statement, a user with two records gets \(\varepsilon = 2 \times 6.71 = 13.42\) with \(\delta_2 = 10^{-5}(1 + e^{6.71}) = 0.0082\): a probability of almost one in a hundred that the guarantee fails outright, which is no guarantee. Re-converting the accountant’s RDP curve at a smaller per-record \(\delta\) does better. The per-record \(\delta\) that makes \(\delta_2 = 10^{-5}\) gives a per-record \(\varepsilon\) of 9.30, so the user gets \((18.61, 10^{-5})\). For five records the same procedure gives a per-record \(\varepsilon\) of 23.62 and a user-level \(\varepsilon\) of 118.12. For ten records it gives nothing: no per-record \(\delta\) makes \(\delta_{10}\) as small as \(10^{-5}\). In the running example’s population, 244 of the 1,000 users have at least ten records (the median is 4), and 30 have at least 50.


42.3.6 Check yourself

A dataset has one row per hospital visit, and a mechanism is \(0.2\)-DP (pure) at the visit level. What does a patient with 7 visits get? (\(1.4\)-DP, by group privacy with \(k = 7\); for pure DP the bound is just \(k\varepsilon\).)
Why does a user-level guarantee still compose and survive post-processing? (Because it is DP with a different neighbouring relation, and those proofs hold for any fixed relation: they never use what a neighbour is.)

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
section: 42.4 A user with k records in example-level DP-SGD
text:
42.4 A user with k records in example-level DP-SGD

42.4.1 Context
Group privacy treats DP-SGD as a black box. It is not one: we know exactly how a user with \(k\) records enters each step. Each of the user’s records is drawn into the batch independently with probability \(q\), so in each step a random number of them, between 0 and \(k\), contributes to the noisy sum. An accountant that knows this can compute the user’s guarantee directly, as Amplification by subsampling did for one record. How large is that guarantee, and how does it grow with \(k\)?


42.4.2 Statement
Let \(M \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(k, q)\) be the number of the user’s records in a Poisson batch, and \(b_m = \binom km q^m(1 - q)^{k - m}\) its probabilities. In units of \(C\), one step of example-level DP-SGD compares \[P_0 = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) \qquad\text{and}\qquad P_{(k)} = \sum_{m=0}^k b_m\,\mathcal N(m, \sigma^2), \tag{42.6}\] the output without the user and with the user, whose drawn records all push the sum by the full \(C\) in the same direction. Charles et al. (2024, Theorem 3) prove that this pair, composed over the \(T\) steps, bounds the user’s privacy loss, and that the bound is attained by a loss for which the user’s gradients are aligned. The user’s RDP curve is therefore \(\varepsilon_{k}(\alpha) = \max\{D_\alpha(P_{(k)}\|P_0), D_\alpha(P_0\|P_{(k)})\}\). The first divergence is \(\frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln A_\alpha\) with \[A_\alpha = \mathbb E\Big[\exp\Big(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{1\le i<j\le\alpha}M_iM_j\Big)\Big], \qquad M_1, \dots, M_\alpha \text{ independent copies of } M, \tag{42.7}\] for integer \(\alpha\). For small \(kq\) the curve is close to that of a single record sampled at rate \(kq\): \[\varepsilon_k(\alpha) \approx \frac\alpha2(kq)^2\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big). \tag{42.8}\] The user’s \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) after \(T\) steps is Equation 42.3 applied to \(T\varepsilon_k(\alpha)\).


42.4.3 Derivation
The derivation follows the one for a single record: find the distribution of one step’s output with and without the user, write the Rényi divergence as an average of a power of the likelihood ratio, and evaluate the average. The new ingredient is that the power of a mixture over \(m\) becomes a product of independent copies of \(M\), which makes the average computable by Fact 3.

How many of the user’s records are drawn. Poisson sampling draws each record independently with probability \(q\), so the number of the user’s \(k\) records in the batch is a sum of \(k\) independent coins: \(M \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(k, q)\), independent of which other records are drawn.
What they do to the sum. Fix the other records’ contribution, which is the same with and without the user. Given \(M = m\), the user adds \(m\) clipped gradients, each of length at most \(C\), so their sum has length at most \(mC\), with equality when they all point the same way. In units of \(C\) and along that direction, the output is \(\mathcal N(m, \sigma^2)\) with probability \(b_m\): the mixture of Equation 42.6. That the aligned case is the worst over all configurations of the user’s gradients, and that the reduction to one dimension is valid, is the content of Charles et al.’s Theorem 3; the intuition is that gradients pointing in different directions add in squares rather than in length, and spread the user’s influence over several coordinates where it is harder to detect.
The divergence as an average. By the definition of the Rényi divergence, \(e^{(\alpha-1)D_\alpha(P_{(k)}\|P_0)} = \mathbb E_{y\sim P_0}\big[(P_{(k)}(y)/P_0(y))^\alpha\big]\). Dividing the mixture by \(P_0\) term by term with Equation 42.4, \[\frac{P_{(k)}(y)}{P_0(y)} = \sum_m b_m\exp\Big(\frac{2my - m^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big) = \mathbb E_M\Big[\exp\Big(\frac{2My - M^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big)\Big], \tag{42.9}\] an average over the number of drawn records.
The power of an average is an average over independent copies. For integer \(\alpha\), \((\mathbb E_M[f(M)])^\alpha = \mathbb E[f(M_1)f(M_2)\cdots f(M_\alpha)]\) with \(M_1, \dots, M_\alpha\) independent copies of \(M\): multiplying out \(\alpha\) copies of the sum \(\sum_mb_mf(m)\) gives one term for every choice \((m_1, \dots, m_\alpha)\), with weight \(b_{m_1}\cdots b_{m_\alpha}\), which is the joint distribution of independent copies. The product of exponentials is the exponential of the sum, so with \(S = M_1 + \dots + M_\alpha\), \[\Big(\frac{P_{(k)}(y)}{P_0(y)}\Big)^\alpha = \mathbb E\Big[\exp\Big(\frac{2Sy - \sum_iM_i^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big)\Big]. \tag{42.10}\]
Average over \(y\). Exchange the two averages, which is allowed because everything is positive. For fixed copies, Fact 3 with \(s = S/\sigma^2\) gives \(\mathbb E_{y\sim P_0}[e^{Sy/\sigma^2}] = e^{S^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), so \[A_\alpha = \mathbb E\Big[\exp\Big(\frac{S^2 - \sum_iM_i^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big)\Big]. \tag{42.11}\] Expanding the square, \(S^2 = \sum_iM_i^2 + 2\sum_{i<j}M_iM_j\), and the squares cancel: this is Equation 42.7. Only products of different copies remain.
Check against one record. For \(k = 1\), each \(M_i\) is a coin, 0 or 1. If \(J\) of the \(\alpha\) coins are 1, the sum \(\sum_{i<j}M_iM_j\) counts the pairs among them, \(\binom J2 = (J^2 - J)/2\), and \(J \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(\alpha, q)\). The average of \(e^{(J^2 - J)/(2\sigma^2)}\) over \(J\) is Equation 42.2.
Small \(kq\). When \(kq\) is small, most copies are 0. The terms of Equation 42.7 with at most one non-zero copy have \(\sum_{i<j}M_iM_j = 0\) and contribute their probability times 1. The first term that costs privacy has exactly two copies equal to 1, the most likely way for a product to be non-zero: there are \(\binom\alpha2\) pairs of copies, each copy is 1 with probability about \(kq\), and the factor is \(e^{1/\sigma^2}\). So \(A_\alpha \approx 1 + \binom\alpha2(kq)^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\), the same as Equation 42.2’s first three terms with \(q\) replaced by \(kq\). Taking \(\ln(1 + x) \approx x\) and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) gives Equation 42.8.
Other orders and the other direction. For non-integer \(\alpha\), and for \(D_\alpha(P_0\|P_{(k)})\), there is no finite expansion. Compute both as one-dimensional integrals of \(P_0(y)\) times a power of the mixture ratio of step 3, on a grid of step \(\sigma/10\) wide enough to contain the bump near \(y = \alpha k\) that large orders create, with log-sum-exp to avoid overflow, exactly as for one record.



42.4.4 Interpretation
A user with \(k\) records looks like one record sampled \(k\) times as often. Equation 42.8 says that, in the regime where amplification works well, the only thing that matters is the probability that some record of the user is in the batch, about \(kq\). Halving the sampling rate exactly compensates doubling the user’s records. Since the per-step RDP grows like \((kq)^2\), and \(\varepsilon\) after conversion grows roughly like the square root of the RDP slope, the user’s \(\varepsilon\) grows roughly linearly in \(k\) while \(kq\) is small.
Beyond that regime it grows faster. Two things break the approximation. First, \(kq\) is no longer small: for \(k = 50\) and \(q = 0.01\), half of all steps include one of the user’s records, and subsampling, which helps only because the unit is usually absent, stops helping. Second, the higher terms of Equation 42.7 grow like \(e^{M_iM_j/\sigma^2}\), and \(M_iM_j\) can be as large as \(k^2\). A step that draws all \(k\) records shifts the sum by \(kC\), a mechanism with noise multiplier \(\sigma/k\), whose privacy loss has a tail that no amount of rarity can hide at high orders. The accountant then uses orders close to 1, where the conversion is expensive.
Group privacy is the wrong tool for DP-SGD. It ignores both the structure of the mechanism and the fact that the RDP curve is known. The direct accountant gives a smaller \(\varepsilon\) for every \(k\) and a finite one for every \(k\).
The accountant is a worst case over gradients, not over users. It assumes the user’s drawn records push the sum in the same direction by the full \(C\). Real users’ gradients are partly aligned, which is precisely why their records are correlated, and the theorem says some loss attains the bound. An auditor should therefore treat it as the guarantee, not as a pessimistic estimate.






Figure 42.2: The user-level \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) of the running example’s DP-SGD (\(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), 10,000 steps; \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) per record) for a user with \(k\) records. The direct accountant of Equation 42.6 (black) is close to a single record sampled at rate \(kq\) (blue, dotted) and grows faster than linearly (grey). Group privacy from the record-level guarantee (red, dashed) is larger, and gives no guarantee at all for \(k = 10\) and above.
