The first column checks the accountant: with one record it is the DP-SGD accountant, 6.72 against 6.71, the difference coming from the coarser grid of orders this chapter’s script uses (its best order is 4, against 4.1 on the finer grid). At \(\alpha = 4.1\) the two curves agree to all printed digits, \(3.733633 \times 10^{-4}\). For \(k = 2\) and 5 at \(\alpha = 2\), the numerical integral and the exact formula Equation 42.7, \(A_2 = \mathbb E[e^{M_1M_2/\sigma^2}]\), agree to seven digits (\(6.992273 \times 10^{-4}\) and \(4.626224 \times 10^{-3}\)), and the reverse direction is smaller (\(6.119238 \times 10^{-4}\) and \(3.412123 \times 10^{-3}\)).
Already at two records, the person behind them is protected at \(\varepsilon = 15.54\), more than twice the record’s 6.71. At ten, \(\varepsilon = 146.20\) means no protection at all. The rate-\(kq\) approximation is within 1.5% at \(k = 2\) (15.32 against 15.54) and 8% at \(k = 10\) (134.50 against 146.20), so it is a quick estimate of the user’s exposure: rerun the record-level accountant with \(q\) replaced by \(kq\). In every row it errs on the low side, because it drops the terms in which several of the user’s records are drawn together.


42.4.6 Check yourself

Your model was trained with example-level DP-SGD at \(q = 0.001\), and its heaviest user has 20 records. Which single-record accountant run gives a quick estimate of that user’s \(\varepsilon\), and in which direction is it off? (The run with \(q = 0.02\) and the same \(\sigma\) and \(T\). It underestimates slightly, because it ignores steps that draw several of the user’s records at once.)
In Equation 42.7, why do only products of different copies appear? (Because the \(\sum_iM_i^2\) in the exponent of the likelihood ratio cancels the squares in \(S^2\) after the Gaussian average. Each copy alone averages to a ratio whose expectation under \(P_0\) is 1, as for one record.)

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
text:
42.5 User-level DP-SGD

42.5.1 Context
Accounting for users after the fact charges a heavy user for every one of their records. The alternative changes the algorithm, so that the unit DP-SGD samples, clips and accounts for is the user. The idea is due to McMahan, Ramage, Talwar & Zhang (2018), who used it to train a language model with federated learning, where each user’s device computes an update on its own data and the server only sees the updates. What does the algorithm compute, and what does it guarantee?


42.5.2 Statement
Start from weights \(w_0\) chosen independently of the data. For \(t = 0, \dots, T - 1\):

Sample users. Put each user in the set \(S_t\) independently with probability \(q\).
Per-user update. For each \(u \in S_t\), compute one vector from user \(u\)’s records alone, for example the average gradient \(\bar g_u = \frac1{n_u}\sum_{i \in u}\nabla_w\ell(w_t, z_i)\), or the change in weights after a few local steps of SGD on those records.
Clip per user. \(\tilde g_u = \bar g_u\min(1, C/\|\bar g_u\|)\).
Noisy sum. \(G_t = \sum_{u\in S_t}\tilde g_u + \xi_t\) with \(\xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I)\).
Step. \(w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta\,G_t/(qU)\).

Releasing \(w_1, \dots, w_T\) is user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\varepsilon\) given by Equation 42.3 for the curve \(T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\) of Fact 2: exactly the accountant of example-level DP-SGD, with users in place of records and \(q\) the user sampling rate.
A common variant replaces steps 2 and 3 by per-record clipping and a cap: keep at most \(k\) records per user, clip each record’s gradient to \(C\), and sum them. One user then moves the sum by at most \(kC\), and the guarantee is that of noise multiplier \(\sigma/k\): \[A_\alpha = \sum_{j=0}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\exp\Big(\frac{k^2(j^2 - j)}{2\sigma^2}\Big), \tag{42.12}\] Equation 42.2 with \(\sigma\) replaced by \(\sigma/k\).


42.5.3 Derivation
The proof of DP-SGD used four properties of the clipped sum. Each holds with users in place of records.

One user moves the clipped sum by at most \(C\). Fix the weights \(w_t\) and the other sampled users. Each \(\tilde g_v\) is computed from user \(v\)’s records alone, so adding user \(u\) to the dataset leaves every other term unchanged and adds \(\tilde g_u\), of length at most \(C\) by step 3. However many records \(u\) has, they enter only through \(\tilde g_u\).
One step is a subsampled Gaussian mechanism over users. User \(u\) enters \(S_t\) with probability \(q\), independently of the other users. So the step’s output with \(u\) is a mixture: with probability \(1 - q\) the same as without \(u\), with probability \(q\) shifted by \(\tilde g_u\). After rescaling by \(C\) and rotating the shift onto one axis, the worst case is the pair of Fact 2, and the step’s RDP curve is \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\).
Dividing by \(qU\) is post-processing, since the number of users \(U\) is treated as public, as \(n\) is in example-level DP-SGD.
Compose and convert. RDP composition over the \(T\) adaptive steps and Equation 42.3 finish the proof, as before.
The capped-sum variant. With per-record clipping, user \(u\)’s contribution is a sum of at most \(k\) vectors of length at most \(C\), so its length is at most \(kC\), and the user is still sampled as a whole with probability \(q\). In units of \(C\) the pair is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) against \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\mathcal N(k, \sigma^2)\). Dividing the output by \(k\), an invertible map that changes no divergence, gives the pair with shift 1 and noise \(\sigma/k\), whose curve is Equation 42.2 with \(\sigma/k\): that is Equation 42.12. The script checks it at \(k = 2\), \(\alpha = 3\): both give \(8.219438 \times 10^{-2}\).



42.5.4 Interpretation
The count that matters is the number of units. User-level DP-SGD has the privacy of example-level DP-SGD on a dataset of \(U\) records. To keep the same expected batch of \(B\) units, the sampling rate must be \(B/U\), larger than \(B/n\) by the average number of records per user, and amplification is correspondingly weaker. On the running example, with 1,000 steps and an expected batch of 100 units, a record-level \(\varepsilon = 4\) needs \(\sigma = 0.778\) at \(q = 0.01\), and a user-level \(\varepsilon = 4\) needs \(\sigma = 3.78\) at \(q = 0.1\). The noise on the averaged update, \(\sigma C/B\), is 0.0189 against 0.00389, about five times larger. This is the honest price of protecting people: there are ten times fewer of them than records, and DP’s cost per unit is fixed.
Records inside a user are free. The guarantee does not depend on \(n_u\). A user’s records can be averaged, used for several local steps, or subsampled, all without changing \(\varepsilon\), as long as the result is one clipped vector computed from that user’s data alone. More records per user make each \(\bar g_u\) a better estimate of the user’s gradient, so the signal improves while the noise stays fixed. Levy et al. (2021) show that, when each user’s records come from the same distribution, user-level private learning gains from having more records per user.
Average, or sum then clip? Averaging before clipping gives every user a vector of the same kind regardless of size, which keeps the clipping norm meaningful across users. Clipping each record and summing at most \(k\) of them uses per-example gradient code that already exists, but pays a factor \(k\) in noise multiplier (Equation 42.12). Summing all of a user’s records and then clipping the sum is also valid (sensitivity \(C\)), and gives heavy users more weight than averaging does, as Section 42.7 shows.
What the proof assumes. Step 1 needs every user’s contribution to be computed from that user alone, which rules out cross-user normalization and requires that one user’s records are not spread across several “users” in the data. If one person has several accounts, the unit is the account, and the person is again a group. Step 2 needs users to be Poisson-sampled; an implementation that iterates over users in a fixed shuffled order is a different mechanism, as for records.


42.5.5 Example: the noise each strategy needs
Table 42.3 fixes 1,000 steps with an expected batch of 100 sampled units and gives the noise multiplier for four user-level budgets. The column “record-level” is not a user-level guarantee; it shows the noise the same schedule would need to protect only records. Column (a) is example-level DP-SGD on all 10,000 records (\(q = 0.01\)), accounted for the largest user with \(k = 348\) by Equation 42.6; (b) is user-level DP-SGD (\(q = 0.1\)); (c) keeps at most 2 records per user, 1,807 records in all, and runs example-level DP-SGD on them with \(q = 100/1{,}807 = 0.0553\), accounted for \(k = 2\) (Section 42.6).

Why does user-level DP-SGD on 1,000 users need more noise than example-level DP-SGD on 10,000 records, at the same expected batch, steps and \(\varepsilon\)? (To keep the batch at 100 units it must sample at rate 0.1 instead of 0.01. Amplification by subsampling is weaker at a higher rate, so the same \(\varepsilon\) needs a larger \(\sigma\).)

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
text:
42.6 Contribution bounding

42.6.1 Context
User-level DP-SGD needs a data pipeline that groups records by user and computes one vector per user. Many training pipelines are built around records: shuffled files of examples, per-example gradient code, fixed-length batches. Can you keep that pipeline and still protect users? You can, if you limit how many records each user contributes. The question is what limit to choose, because the limit trades the noise the accountant requires against the data you throw away.


42.6.2 Statement
Contribution bounding keeps at most \(k\) records of each user, chosen without looking at other users’ data, for example at random, and discards the rest. Run example-level DP-SGD on the \(n_k = \sum_u\min(n_u, k)\) remaining records with sampling rate \(q\). The result is user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\varepsilon\) given by the accountant of Equation 42.6 for a user with \(k\) records. The trade-off:

the noise grows with \(k\): in the small-\(kq\) regime the user’s RDP is that of a record sampled at rate \(kq\) (Equation 42.8), so the noise multiplier must grow roughly in proportion to \(k\) at a fixed \(q\);
the bias shrinks with \(k\): the training set loses \(n - n_k\) records, all of them from users with more than \(k\) records, so the data are both smaller and reweighted toward light users.



42.6.3 Derivation

Bounding is applied per user. Write the bounded dataset as \(\Pi(D) = \bigcup_u\pi(D_u)\), where \(D_u\) is user \(u\)’s records and \(\pi\) keeps at most \(k\) of them using randomness that is independent of everything else. Adding user \(u\) to \(D\) adds \(\pi(D_u)\) to \(\Pi(D)\) and changes nothing else, so user-level neighbours map to datasets that differ in at most \(k\) records, all of one user.
Account for those records. Example-level DP-SGD on \(\Pi(D)\) sees the user’s at most \(k\) records, each drawn independently with probability \(q\). By Section 42.4, the pair for one step is Equation 42.6 with \(k\). A user with fewer records is covered too: they are a \(k\)-record user some of whose clipped gradients happen to be 0, and the worst case of Section 42.4 is over all gradients of length at most \(C\), including 0. Composition and conversion are as before.
The noise grows with \(k\). At fixed \(q\), Equation 42.8 depends on \(k\) and \(q\) through \(kq\) only. Keeping the user’s RDP fixed while \(k\) doubles therefore requires either halving \(q\), which halves the batch, or raising \(\sigma\). In the regime where the per-step RDP is about \(\frac\alpha2(kq)^2/\sigma^2\), holding it fixed means \(\sigma \propto kq\).
The bias. Before bounding, the expected update of DP-SGD averages over all \(n\) records; after it, over \(n_k\) records in which each user has weight \(\min(n_u, k)/n_k\) instead of \(n_u/n\). A user with \(n_u > k\) loses weight, and their records beyond \(k\) are not used at all.



42.6.4 Interpretation
Choosing \(k\) is a bias–variance trade-off. Amin, Kulesza, Muñoz Medina & Vassilvitskii (2019) studied exactly this choice for private empirical risk minimization, and showed that the best cap depends on the distribution of user sizes: a cap above most users’ sizes buys little data at a large noise cost, and a cap below them throws away most of the data. Their framing is the same as that of choosing the clipping norm in Beyond global sensitivity: a smaller bound means less noise and more distortion of what is computed. Because the cap depends on the data, it should be chosen from public knowledge of the population or privately; choosing it by trying several caps and looking at test accuracy, as the example below does to show the trade-off, spends privacy that the accountant does not see (Hyperparameter tuning).
Which records to keep matters. Random selection keeps the proof simple. Chua et al. (2024) compare selection rules for fine-tuning language models under contribution bounding and report that keeping each user’s longest records worked best on one of their datasets. Any rule that looks only at the user’s own records is allowed, by step 1.
Bounding plus user-level DP-SGD. The two techniques combine: cap each user at \(k\) records to bound compute, then compute one clipped vector per user. With user sampling, the cap no longer costs noise, only data, and users can contribute their full records again by subsampling them inside each step.

Why must the cap be applied with randomness independent of other users’ data? (The derivation needs adding one user to change only that user’s kept records. If, say, the cap kept the \(k\) records most similar to the rest of the dataset, adding a user could change which records other users keep, and neighbours would differ in more than \(k\) records.)
In Table 42.4, \(kq\) rises from 0.100 to 0.593 as the cap goes from 1 to 50. What does Equation 42.8 predict for the noise multiplier, and why is the actual one smaller? (Proportionality to \(kq\) predicts about \(3.78 \times 5.93 = 22.4\). The rule is only approximate: it holds where \(\sigma\) is large and \(kq\) small, and at \(kq = 0.593\) neither the rate-\(kq\) approximation nor the large-\(\sigma\) law is accurate, so the accountant’s 21.8 differs from it.)

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
text:
42.7 Heterogeneous users

42.7.1 Context
User sizes are rarely equal. In the running example’s population, 30 users with at least 50 records each hold 30.6% of the records, while the smallest half of the users hold 10.3% (Figure 42.1). Example-level training weights each user by their number of records; user-level training does not. What objective does user-level DP-SGD optimize, and what does that mean for heavy users?


42.7.2 Statement
Averaged over the user sampling and the noise, the update direction of user-level DP-SGD is \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{qU}\Big] = \frac1U\sum_{u=1}^U\min\Big(1, \frac{C}{\|\bar g_u\|}\Big)\bar g_u, \tag{42.13}\] a sum in which each user has weight at most \(1/U\) whatever their number of records. Example-level DP-SGD gives user \(u\) weight \(n_u/n\) in its expected update, \(\frac1n\sum_u\sum_{i\in u}\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)g_i\).


42.7.3 Derivation

Average over the sampling. User \(u\) is in \(S_t\) with probability \(q\), so \(\mathbb E\sum_{u\in S_t}\tilde g_u = q\sum_u\tilde g_u\). The noise has mean zero.
Divide by \(qU\). The \(q\) cancels, leaving \(\frac1U\sum_u\tilde g_u\), which is Equation 42.13 by the definition of \(\tilde g_u\).
The weight of one user. \(\|\tilde g_u\| \le C\) for every user, so each term has length at most \(C/U\), and the share of any group of users in the update is at most their share of the users.
Example-level. The same computation for DP-SGD over records (DP-SGD) gives each record weight \(1/n\), so user \(u\)’s records together have weight \(n_u/n\).



42.7.4 Interpretation
User-level training changes the objective, not only the noise. With averaged per-user gradients, the model minimizes (a clipped version of) the average over users of each user’s average loss, \(\frac1U\sum_u\frac1{n_u}\sum_{i\in u}\ell(w, z_i)\), rather than the average over records. Whether that is what you want depends on the application. For a keyboard model, weighting people equally keeps a few very active users from defining everyone’s suggestions. For a model meant to fit the overall distribution of records, it under-weights heavy users’ content, and the bias can matter when heavy users differ from light ones, for example by language, topic or device.
Clipping caps heavy users twice. A heavy user’s average gradient is a good estimate, typically short when the model already fits their data, and is rarely clipped. But if the user’s data are unusual, their gradient is long and is clipped to \(C\), so their influence is capped at that of any other user. This is the user-level analogue of what clipping does to records with large gradients (Disparate impact).
Sum-then-clip sits in between. Summing a user’s gradients before clipping makes a heavy user’s vector up to \(n_u\) times longer than one record’s, so heavy users are clipped first, and their influence rises with \(n_u\) until it reaches \(C\). It interpolates between record weighting, for users whose sum stays below \(C\), and user weighting, for those above it (Exercise 5).


42.7.5 Example: heavy users in the running example
The 30 users with at least 50 records hold 30.6% of the records, and so 30.6% of the weight in the expected example-level update. Under user-level DP-SGD their weight is at most \(30/1{,}000 = 3.0\%\). Does that hurt the model where heavy users’ data are? The script splits the test set by the owner of each test point’s nearest training record. Because a heavy user’s records were chosen as the nearest neighbours of one seed in 50 dimensions, they spread widely, and 68.3% of test points have a heavy user’s record as their nearest neighbour. At user-level \(\varepsilon = 4\), user-level DP-SGD reaches 0.9361 on those points and 0.9319 on the others; the non-private model, 0.9607 and 0.9622. On this task, down-weighting heavy users costs nothing measurable, because one teacher network labels every record, so the light users’ records teach the same function. On data where heavy users’ records follow their own patterns, the same reweighting would cost accuracy on those patterns.


42.7.6 Check yourself

A user-level model will be used to predict for each record equally, and you know that heavy users’ records differ from light users’. What can you change without changing \(\varepsilon\)? (How each user’s vector is computed: summing instead of averaging before clipping, or a larger \(C\) relative to typical averaged gradients. Both are inside the per-user computation and leave the sensitivity at \(C\).)
Why is each user’s share of the user-level update at most \(1/U\) rather than exactly \(1/U\)? (Because a user’s clipped vector has length at most \(C\); users whose average gradient is shorter than \(C\), typically those the model already fits, contribute less.)

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
section: 42.8 Comparing the strategies on the running example
text:
42.8 Comparing the strategies on the running example

42.8.1 Context
Three ways to train the running example with a user-level guarantee are now on the table: (a) example-level DP-SGD on all records, with the user accountant for the heaviest user; (b) user-level DP-SGD; (c) contribution bounding to two records per user, then example-level DP-SGD. At the same user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), which model is best?


42.8.2 Statement
Table 42.5 trains each strategy for 1,000 steps with an expected batch of 100 units, \(C = 0.5\) and \(\eta = 0.5\), at the noise multipliers of Table 42.3, one run each.

42.8.3 Derivation
Each strategy’s guarantee was derived above: (a) and (c) by the accountant of Section 42.4 with \(k = 348\) and \(k = 2\), and (b) by Section 42.5. The cap \(k = 2\) is the best cap at \(\varepsilon = 4\) in Table 42.4, tied with \(k = 1\); choosing it from test accuracy is a leak that a real deployment would have to pay for. Run-to-run variation is of the order of a point at these budgets: the cap \(k = 1\) and user-level DP-SGD restricted to one random record per user are the same algorithm with the same \(\sigma\), and two runs of it gave 0.8917 and 0.9070.


42.8.4 Interpretation
Keeping the record as the unit fails. Strategy (a) is at chance, between 0.53 and 0.57, at every budget up to \(\varepsilon = 8\). The heaviest user dictates the noise for everyone: \(\sigma\) between 70.3 and 449 drowns every gradient. That is the practical meaning of Figure 42.2: an example-level pipeline on data with heavy users needs either an enormous \(\varepsilon\) or a cap.
Changing the unit wins. User-level DP-SGD is the best strategy at every budget, 0.9347 at \(\varepsilon = 4\) against 0.9612 for the non-private model. It needs a little less noise than the cap of 2 (Table 42.3) and, unlike the cap, it uses every record, through the per-user average. Its advantage is largest at small budgets: 9.8 points at \(\varepsilon = 1\), 1.1 points at \(\varepsilon = 8\). Its cost is compute: each step processes all the records of about 100 users, about 1,000 records, ten times what the example-level strategies process.
Bounding is the fallback. Strategy (c) keeps the example-level pipeline and loses 5 to 10 points against (b) below \(\varepsilon = 8\). It comes close at \(\varepsilon = 8\), where the noise is small enough that the discarded data, not the noise, limits accuracy.
These findings agree with published comparisons on language models, which use different data, models and accountants. Chua et al. (2024) compare contribution bounding with group-privacy accounting (“Group Privacy”) against user-level DP-SGD with per-user averaging (“User-wise DP-SGD”) for fine-tuning, and report that user-wise DP-SGD generally does better, especially at small budgets. Charles et al. (2024), who call the two sampling schemes example-level and user-level sampling, report that user-level sampling usually does better when each user’s data are varied and when strong privacy is required, and that example-level sampling sometimes wins. Note that Chua et al. account for the cap with the generic group privacy of Equation 42.1; the direct accountant of Section 42.4 would give them less noise.






Figure 42.3: Test accuracy of the running example against the user-level \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), for the three strategies (1,000 steps, expected batch 100, one run each; the runs differ from Table 42.5 in their random seeds). User-level DP-SGD is best at every budget; example-level DP-SGD on all records, accounted for its heaviest user, stays near chance.





42.8.5 Example: what the user-level guarantee costs
At \(\varepsilon = 4\) the running example loses 2.7 points to protect users (0.9347 against 0.9612). The record-level model of DP-SGD at the same \(\varepsilon\), trained for 10,000 steps, reached 0.9548, and this chapter’s 1,000-step schedule would need only \(\sigma = 0.778\) for a record-level guarantee (Table 42.3). The difference is the price of the unit: 1,000 people instead of 10,000 records, and a guarantee that now covers the person with 348 records as well as the one with a single record.


42.8.6 Check yourself

Strategy (a) uses every record and the tightest available accountant. Why does it do worst? (Because the guarantee must hold for the heaviest user, whose 348 records put about 3.5 of them into every batch; the noise has to hide a shift of several clipping norms in almost every step, which takes \(\sigma\) in the hundreds.)
Would strategy (a) look better if the heaviest user were removed from the data? (Only a little: the accountant would be for the next-largest user, who has 258 records, so about 2.6 of them would still be in every batch. Removing a user because of their size is itself a data-dependent choice that must be made with public information or paid for, and it is a crude form of contribution bounding.)

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
section: 42.9 Code: check every number by computation
text:
42.9 Code: check every number by computation
The script code/user_level.py builds the user population, implements the user accountant of Equation 42.6 by numerical integration and checks it against Equation 42.7 and Equation 42.2, compares it with group privacy, and trains the three strategies with the part’s network. It imports the model, DP-SGD and the record-level accountant from code/dp_sgd.py. From the repository root:
uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/user_level.py

What to take from it. The record-level accountant answers the wrong question when people contribute many records, and asking it the right question, about a user with \(k\) records, gives answers that grow faster than \(k\). The fix is in the algorithm, not the accountant: make the person the unit that is sampled and clipped. Implementation needs only a per-user aggregation before clipping; the accountant is unchanged.

Rules of thumb

Name the privacy unit with every \(\varepsilon\). A record-level \(\varepsilon\) says little about a person with many records.
To estimate what an example-level model gives a user with \(k\) records, rerun the accountant at rate \(kq\), and expect the truth to be a little worse.
Don’t use group privacy for DP-SGD; account for the user’s records directly, or better, sample and clip users.
Prefer user-level DP-SGD with per-user averaging. It pays for the number of people, not their records, and uses all their data.
If the pipeline must stay record-based, cap records per user, choose the cap from public knowledge, and account for the cap with the user accountant.
Decide deliberately how heavy users should count: averaging weights people equally, summing before clipping weights records until the clip.

Practice. Exercises for this chapter, each with a worked solution, are in the exercise book.

title: 43  Disparate impact
text:
43.1 Why this matters
The chapter on private gradient descent showed that training the part’s running example with differential privacy (DP) at \(\varepsilon = 4\) costs less than one point of test accuracy: 0.9548 against 0.9610 without privacy. That number is an average over the test set. It says nothing about who loses the point. Bagdasaryan, Poursaeed & Shmatikov (2019) asked that question and found an uncomfortable answer: when a network is trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, the accuracy it loses is concentrated on the classes and subgroups that are under-represented in the training data. In their gender classifier, for example, the drop in accuracy was much larger on Black faces than on white faces, and the gap between groups that the non-private model already had grew under DP. They called this the disparate impact of DP on model accuracy.
This matters in two ways. A model that is “less than a point worse” can be ten points worse on a group of people, and an average hides it. And the groups that pay are often the ones a privacy guarantee is meant to protect: small populations, rare conditions, unusual records. This chapter explains why it happens, from the two ingredients of DP-SGD, measures it on the running example, and asks what can be done about it.

title: 43  Disparate impact
text:
43.1.1 The one idea: every record gets the same budget of influence, and every group gets the same noise
DP-SGD caps each record’s pull on the update at \(C\), then adds noise whose size depends only on \(C\) and \(\sigma\), not on the data. Both rules are blind to groups, and that is exactly why they are not neutral. A group’s pull on the expected update is at most its share of the records times \(C\), however badly the model fits it, so a group whose gradients are large is cut back more than a group whose gradients are small: that is the clipping mechanism. And the noise is the same for everyone, while a group’s signal is proportional to its size, so a small group’s signal-to-noise ratio is smaller by its share: that is the noise mechanism. Small groups and groups the model finds hard suffer from both, and the two compound, because clipping shrinks a group’s effective share and the noise then acts on the shrunk share.
Table 43.1 lists the results and where each is used.



Table 43.1: The results of this chapter and where each is used.





Result
Where it is used

Deciding whether a group is large enough to train on privately

Notation. As in DP-SGD, \(n\) records \(z_i = (x_i, y_i)\) train a model with weights \(w\), \(g_i\) is record \(i\)’s gradient, \(C\) the clipping norm, \(\sigma\) the noise multiplier, \(q\) the sampling rate, \(B = qn\) the expected batch size, \(T\) the number of steps and \(\eta\) the step size. The records are split into groups \(g = 1, \dots, K\); group \(g\) has \(n_g\) records and share \(s_g = n_g/n\). A record’s clipping weight is \(\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\), the factor clipping multiplies its gradient by, and a group’s clipping weight \(w_g\) is its average over the group’s records. \(\mathrm{acc}_g\) is a model’s accuracy on test records of group \(g\). A subscript \(i\) always names a record and a subscript \(g\) or \(h\) a group, so \(g_i\) is a record’s gradient and \(\bar g_g\), defined below, a group’s average gradient.
The running example. The part’s running example classifies 50-dimensional inputs with a two-layer network (DP-SGD). This chapter adds a minority group. Of the \(n = 10{,}000\) training records, 9,500 are the first records of the running example’s fixed training set: standard normal inputs, labelled by the random teacher network. The other 500, a share of 5%, come from a different region and follow a different rule. Their inputs are \(x = 8u + z\), where \(u\) is a fixed unit vector and \(z\) is standard normal in a fixed 15-dimensional subspace orthogonal to \(u\), and their label is the sign of one coordinate of \(z\). So the minority’s records lie far from the majority’s, have larger inputs (average length 8.89 against 7.04), and need a rule that the majority does not teach. The non-private model learns both: it reaches 0.9529 on the majority and 0.9411 on the minority. Each group is tested on 20,000 fresh records of its own, so that the test error is small compared with the effects being measured. DP-SGD runs with the running example’s settings: \(q = 0.01\), \(C = 0.5\), \(\eta = 0.5\), \(T = 10{,}000\) steps and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).
How to read this chapter. Section 43.3 defines what to measure and shows the effect. Section 43.4 and Section 43.5 explain it, one mechanism each; they are the core of the chapter. Section 43.6 is about measuring per-group accuracy honestly, and applies to any model. Section 43.7 discusses what can be done and what each fix costs.

title: 43  Disparate impact
section: 43.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
43.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

43.2.1 Fact 1 — The expected update is a reweighted average gradient
Each DP-SGD step adds up the clipped gradients of a Poisson batch, adds Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to each coordinate, and divides by the public expected batch size \(B = qn\). Each record is in the batch with probability \(q\), so the expected sum is \(q\) times the sum over all records, and dividing by \(qn\) gives \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{B}\Big] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\min\Big(1, \frac C{\|g_i\|}\Big)g_i, \tag{43.1}\] the average gradient with each record weighted by its clipping weight (DP-SGD). The noise on the averaged update has standard deviation \(\tau = \sigma C/B\) per coordinate, whatever the data. In the running example at \(\varepsilon = 4\), \(\sigma = 1.36\) and \(\tau = 1.36 \times 0.5/100 = 0.0068\).


43.2.2 Fact 2 — A drift beats a random walk after (noise/signal)² steps
Suppose each step moves the weights by a signal of length \(\ell_{\text{sig}}\) that keeps pointing the same way, plus independent noise of length \(\ell_{\text{noise}}\). After \(k\) steps the signals add up to length \(k\ell_{\text{sig}}\). The noise vectors are independent with mean zero, so their squared lengths add, and their sum has length about \(\ell_{\text{noise}}\sqrt k\). The signal is longer once \(k\ell_{\text{sig}} > \ell_{\text{noise}}\sqrt k\), that is after \[k > \Big(\frac{\ell_{\text{noise}}}{\ell_{\text{sig}}}\Big)^2 \tag{43.2}\] steps. DP-SGD uses this to explain why training works when every step’s noise is ten times longer than its signal: at \(\varepsilon = 4\) the noise on the averaged gradient has length \(\tau\sqrt p\) for \(p = 3{,}329\) weights, and the signal emerges after a few hundred steps.


43.2.3 Fact 3 — A shrinking recursion with noise settles at a fixed variance
Let a number evolve as \(x_{t+1} = (1 - a)x_t + e_t\), where \(0 < a < 2\) and the \(e_t\) are independent with mean zero and variance \(v\). Each step shrinks \(x\) toward zero by the factor \(1 - a\) and adds fresh noise. Because the noise is independent of the current value, variances add: \(\operatorname{Var}x_{t+1} = (1 - a)^2\operatorname{Var}x_t + v\). Since \((1 - a)^2 < 1\), this converges, and the limit \(V\) solves \(V = (1 - a)^2V + v\): \[V = \frac{v}{1 - (1 - a)^2} = \frac{v}{a(2 - a)}. \tag{43.3}\] For example, with \(a = 0.1\) and \(v = 1\) the variance settles at \(1/(0.1 \times 1.9) = 5.26\): a weak pull toward zero lets the noise accumulate to more than five times one step’s variance. Halving the pull roughly doubles the stationary variance. The number of steps to forget the starting point is about \(1/a\), since \((1 - a)^t \approx e^{-at}\).


43.2.4 Fact 4 — An accuracy measured on \(m\) records is a binomial proportion
If a model classifies each test record of a group correctly with probability \(p\), independently, then the number correct out of \(m\) is binomial with mean \(mp\) and variance \(mp(1 - p)\), and the measured accuracy \(k/m\) has standard deviation \(\sqrt{p(1 - p)/m}\). The Clopper–Pearson interval (Hypothesis testing) inverts the binomial distribution exactly: at the 95% level its upper end \(u\) is the accuracy at which \(k\) or fewer correct answers would have probability 0.025, and its lower end \(l\) the accuracy at which \(k\) or more would have probability 0.025. It covers the true accuracy with probability at least 0.95. The smaller the group, the wider the interval, in proportion to \(1/\sqrt m\).

title: 43  Disparate impact
text:
43.3 Disparate impact, measured

43.3.1 Context
What exactly should you measure to say that DP hurts one group more than another, and does it happen on the running example? An accuracy gap between groups is not enough, because the non-private model may already have one. The question is how much privacy adds to each group’s error.


43.3.2 Statement
The privacy cost of group \(g\) is the accuracy the group loses when the same training recipe is made private: \[\pi_g = \mathrm{acc}_g(\text{non-private}) - \mathbb E\big[\mathrm{acc}_g(\text{private})\big], \tag{43.4}\] where the expectation is over the randomness of private training (Esipova et al. 2023 use this definition; Bagdasaryan et al. 2019 compare the same differences). DP has disparate impact when the privacy costs of groups differ, \(\pi_a \ne \pi_b\), and the privacy cost gap \(|\pi_a - \pi_b|\) measures how much.

43.3.3 Derivation
This statement is a definition and a measurement, so its “derivation” is the experiment’s design, and each choice in it is there to make the comparison fair.

Same data, same recipe. Every row trains on the same 10,000 records with the same sampling rate, step size and number of steps. The only differences are the clipping (absent in the non-private row) and the noise multiplier, which the accountant of DP-SGD sets for each \(\varepsilon\).
Large test sets. Each group is tested on 20,000 records, so by Fact 4 a measured accuracy near 0.9 has a standard deviation of \(\sqrt{0.9 \times 0.1/20{,}000} = 0.0021\). The differences in the table are much larger than that.
Several runs. Private training is random, and its spread differs between groups. Each row averages three runs and reports their standard deviation; the privacy cost subtracts the average private accuracy from the average non-private accuracy.
A non-private model that serves both groups. The minority’s non-private accuracy, 0.9411, is within 1.2 points of the majority’s, 0.9529. Any large gap in the private rows is therefore caused by privacy, not inherited from the data.



43.3.4 Interpretation
The minority pays almost all of it. At \(\varepsilon = 4\) the majority loses 0.59 points of accuracy and the minority 9.34, 15.7 times as much. At \(\varepsilon = 8\), a budget at which DP-SGD found the running example nearly as accurate as non-private training, the majority loses nothing (its accuracy is 0.20 points higher) and the minority loses 8.58 points. The ratio is smaller at \(\varepsilon = 1\), 4.6, only because there the majority starts to lose too: 7.07 points against the minority’s 32.78. An average over a test set drawn like the training set, 95% majority, would report a loss of \(0.95 \times 0.0059 + 0.05 \times 0.0934 = 0.0103\) at \(\varepsilon = 4\), about one point.
Both mechanisms are visible. The clipping-only row has no noise at all, yet the minority loses 4.04 points while the majority gains 0.51: clipping alone is disparate. Adding noise then widens the gap steadily as \(\varepsilon\) falls. The next two sections explain each part.
The minority’s runs also vary more. At \(\varepsilon = 4\) the standard deviation over runs is 0.0211 for the minority and 0.0037 for the majority. A single private run says less about a small group than about a large one, a point Section 43.6 returns to.






Figure 43.1: Test accuracy of each group of the running example against \(\varepsilon\) (log scale, one run per point, \(\delta = 10^{-5}\)), with each group’s non-private accuracy dashed. The majority is close to its non-private accuracy down to \(\varepsilon = 2\); the minority falls far below it at every budget.





43.3.5 Example: what the published experiments found
Bagdasaryan, Poursaeed & Shmatikov (2019) trained classifiers with DP-SGD on images and text and found the same pattern: the under-represented classes and subgroups, and the more complex ones, lost the most accuracy, and an existing gap between groups grew. Esipova et al. (2023) report, for MNIST digits where class 8 was undersampled to about 1% of the training set, a privacy cost of 8.9 points for the typical class 2 and 57.9 points for class 8 under DP-SGD (their Table 2, \(\varepsilon = 5.90\)). On the running example, Figure 43.1 shows the same shape: the majority’s curve is the curve of DP-SGD, the minority’s lies far below it.


43.3.6 Check yourself

Why is the privacy cost a better measure than the gap between the private model’s group accuracies? (Because part of the gap may be inherited from non-private training, which DP did not cause. The privacy cost subtracts each group’s own non-private accuracy.)
At \(\varepsilon = 4\), a test set with the training proportions shows an overall loss of under one point. What would a test set with equal numbers of both groups show? (The average of the two privacy costs, \((0.0059 + 0.0934)/2 = 0.0497\): about five points. The overall number depends on the test set’s mix as much as on the model.)

title: 43  Disparate impact
text:
43.4 Clipping reweights the groups

43.4.1 Context
Clipping without noise changes nothing about privacy (without noise there is none), yet in Table 43.2 it costs the minority 4.04 points. How does a rule that treats every record the same way end up treating groups differently?


43.4.2 Statement
Split the expected update of Fact 1 by group. Write \(\bar g_g = \frac1{n_g}\sum_{i\in g}g_i\) for group \(g\)’s average gradient and \(m_g = \frac1{n_g}\sum_{i\in g}\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\,g_i\) for its average clipped gradient. Then \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{B}\Big] = \sum_gs_g\,m_g, \qquad \|s_g\,m_g\| \le s_g\,C: \tag{43.5}\] each group pulls with its share times its average clipped gradient, and that pull is never longer than its share times \(C\), however large the group’s gradients are.
When the records within each group have parallel gradients, each group’s average clipped gradient is its average gradient scaled by a number, and the expected update becomes the gradient of a reweighted mixture of the groups: \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{B}\Big] = \Big(\sum_hs_h\,c_h\Big)\sum_g\tilde s_g\,\bar g_g, \qquad \tilde s_g = \frac{s_g\,c_g}{\sum_hs_h\,c_h}, \tag{43.6}\] where \(c_g = \|m_g\|/\|\bar g_g\|\) is the fraction of the group’s average gradient that survives clipping and \(\tilde s_g\) is its effective share. When all of a group’s records have the same norm, \(c_g\) is the group’s clipping weight \(w_g\).


43.4.3 Derivation

Split the sum. Fact 1’s expected update is \(\frac1n\sum_i\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)g_i\). Group the records: \(\frac1n\sum_g\sum_{i\in g}(\cdots) = \sum_g\frac{n_g}n\cdot\frac1{n_g}\sum_{i\in g}(\cdots) = \sum_gs_gm_g\).
Bound the pull. Each clipped gradient has length at most \(C\), and the length of an average is at most the average of the lengths (the triangle inequality), so \(\|m_g\| \le C\) and \(\|s_gm_g\| \le s_gC\).
Parallel gradients. If every \(g_i\) in group \(g\) points along the same unit vector \(e_g\), then \(g_i = \|g_i\|e_g\) and \(\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)g_i = \min(\|g_i\|, C)e_g\). Averaging, \(m_g\) and \(\bar g_g\) both point along \(e_g\), so \(m_g = c_g\bar g_g\) with \(c_g = \|m_g\|/\|\bar g_g\|\).
Factor out the total. \(\sum_gs_gc_g\bar g_g = (\sum_hs_hc_h)\sum_g\frac{s_gc_g}{\sum_hs_hc_h}\bar g_g\), which is Equation 43.6. The effective shares are non-negative and add up to 1.
Equal norms. If all of group \(g\)’s records also have the same norm \(\nu_g\), then \(c_g = \min(\nu_g, C)/\nu_g = \min(1, C/\nu_g) = w_g\).



43.4.4 Interpretation
Two errors: length and direction. Equation 43.6 separates what clipping does into two parts. The factor \(\sum_hs_hc_h\) shortens the update, which a larger step size can undo. The effective shares change which mixture of the groups is being descended, and no step size undoes that. Esipova et al. (2023) make this distinction for a whole batch: they compare training with the clipped batch gradient’s length but the true direction against the true length but the clipped direction, and find the direction error far more harmful, especially to the under-represented class (their Table 1). In Figure 43.2, clipping shortens the update and also turns it toward the majority.
Which groups are cut back. A group’s effective share falls when its clipping weight falls, that is when its gradients are long compared with \(C\). Gradients are long for two reasons. The model fits the group badly: for the logistic loss, the derivative with respect to the output is \(-y\,\mathrm{sigmoid}(-yf)\), close to 1 in size for a misclassified record and close to 0 for a record classified with a wide margin. And the group’s inputs are large: a dense layer’s per-example gradient is the outer product of the back-propagated error and the layer’s input, whose norm is the product of the two norms (DP-SGD), so at the same error a record with a longer input has a longer gradient. Tran, Dinh & Fioretto (2021) identify both factors, gradient norms and the input norms behind them, as the source of the clipping part of disparate impact. A small group the model has not yet learned has both.
A feedback loop. Early in training every record is clipped and every group has a similar weight. As the majority is learned, its gradients shrink below \(C\) and its weight rises toward 1, while the minority, not yet learned, keeps long gradients and a low weight. Its effective share falls below its true share, so it is learned more slowly, so its gradients stay long. The loop ends only when the minority’s gradients fall below \(C\) too.
Where training stops. Clipped gradient descent stops where the expected update is zero, \(\sum_gs_gm_g = 0\), not where the true average gradient \(\sum_gs_g\bar g_g\) is zero. If the groups’ gradients conflict, the stopping point is that of the reweighted objective, which has moved toward the majority.






Figure 43.2: The clipping example in two dimensions: 95 majority records with gradient (0.2, 0) and 5 minority records with gradient (0, 4). Without clipping the two groups pull about equally hard (black); clipping at C = 0.5 cuts the minority’s pull eightfold and turns the update toward the majority (red). Scaling every gradient by the same factor 1/8 instead keeps the direction (blue).





43.4.5 Example: two dimensions, then the running example
Take 95 majority records whose gradient is \((0.2, 0)\), already short, and 5 minority records whose gradient is \((0, 4)\), long because the model fits them badly. Without clipping the average gradient is \((0.95 \times 0.2, 0.05 \times 4) = (0.19, 0.2)\), of length 0.2759: the five minority records pull as hard as the ninety-five others, and the minority’s component is a fraction \(0.2/0.39 = 0.513\) of the sum of the two components. Clip at \(C = 0.5\). The majority’s gradients are untouched; the minority’s shrink to length 0.5. The average becomes \((0.19, 0.05 \times 0.5) = (0.19, 0.025)\), of length 0.1916, and the minority’s fraction falls to 0.116. The update has turned by 39.0 degrees toward the majority. Here \(c_{\text{maj}} = 1\) and \(c_{\text{min}} = 0.5/4 = 0.125\), and Equation 43.6 gives the minority an effective share of \(0.05 \times 0.125/(0.05 \times 0.125 + 0.95) = 0.0065\) instead of 0.05. Scaling every gradient by \(C/Z\) with \(Z = 4\), the largest norm, instead gives \((0.0238, 0.0250)\): eight times shorter, but at an angle of 0.0 degrees to the true average.

Why does a larger clipping norm reduce the clipping part of disparate impact? (It raises the clipping weights of the groups with long gradients more than those of groups whose gradients are already below \(C\), whose weight is already 1, so the effective shares move back toward the true shares.)

title: 43  Disparate impact
section: 43.5 The noise floor of a small group
text:
43.5 The noise floor of a small group

43.5.1 Context
Noise is added to the sum, the same for everyone. Why should it hurt a small group more than a large one? Because what the noise competes with is each group’s signal, and a group’s signal in the sum is proportional to its size.


43.5.2 Statement
A drift that is a fraction of the population’s. If the part of the expected update that serves group \(g\) is a fraction \(s_g\) of what the whole population’s signal would be, and the noise is unchanged, Fact 2 says that group’s signal emerges from the noise only after \[k_g = \frac1{s_g^2}\Big(\frac{\ell_{\text{noise}}}{\ell_{\text{sig}}}\Big)^2 \tag{43.7}\] steps, \(1/s_g^2\) times as many as for a signal the whole population shares.
A quadratic model of the noise floor. Suppose group \(g\)’s loss depends on its own block of \(k\) weights, which the other groups’ losses do not touch, as \(L_g = \frac\lambda2\|w_g - w_g^*\|^2\), and the training objective is the share-weighted average \(\sum_gs_gL_g\). Run gradient descent with noise of standard deviation \(\tau\) per coordinate on the averaged gradient, as DP-SGD adds. Then group \(g\)’s excess loss settles at \[\mathbb E[L_g] = \frac{k\,\eta\,\tau^2}{2\,s_g\,(2 - \eta s_g\lambda)} \approx \frac{k\,\eta\,\tau^2}{4\,s_g}, \tag{43.8}\] and it takes about \(1/(\eta s_g\lambda)\) steps to get there. With clipping, \(s_g\) is replaced by \(s_gc_g\), the group’s share times the fraction of its gradient that survives clipping; when the majority is hardly clipped, this is close to the effective share \(\tilde s_g\) of Equation 43.6.


43.5.3 Derivation

The group’s gradient. The objective’s gradient with respect to \(w_g\) is \(s_g\lambda(w_g - w_g^*)\): only group \(g\)’s loss depends on these weights, and it enters with weight \(s_g\).
One step. With \(x = w_g - w_g^*\) and noise \(\tau\xi\) on the averaged gradient, \(\xi\) standard normal, the update \(w_g \leftarrow w_g - \eta(s_g\lambda x + \tau\xi)\) gives \(x \leftarrow (1 - \eta s_g\lambda)x - \eta\tau\xi\), coordinate by coordinate.
Stationary variance. This is Fact 3 with \(a = \eta s_g\lambda\) and \(v = \eta^2\tau^2\): each coordinate settles at variance \(\eta^2\tau^2/(a(2 - a)) = \eta\tau^2/(s_g\lambda(2 - \eta s_g\lambda))\).
Excess loss. \(L_g = \frac\lambda2\sum_jx_j^2\) over the \(k\) coordinates, so its expectation is \(\frac\lambda2k\) times the variance, which is Equation 43.8. For a small group \(\eta s_g\lambda\) is small and \(2 - \eta s_g\lambda \approx 2\).
Time scale. By Fact 3 the starting point is forgotten after about \(1/a = 1/(\eta s_g\lambda)\) steps.
The break-even law. If the population’s signal has length \(\ell_{\text{sig}}\) per step, the part that serves group \(g\) has length \(s_g\ell_{\text{sig}}\) and the noise length is still \(\ell_{\text{noise}}\); Fact 2 with \(s_g\ell_{\text{sig}}\) in place of \(\ell_{\text{sig}}\) gives Equation 43.7.
With clipping. By Equation 43.6, with parallel gradients within the group, group \(g\)’s term in the expected update is \(s_gc_g\bar g_g\) instead of \(s_g\bar g_g\), while the noise is unchanged. Treating \(c_g\) as constant over the steps considered, steps 1 to 6 apply with \(s_gc_g\) in place of \(s_g\). If the majority’s \(c\) is close to 1, then \(\sum_hs_hc_h\) is close to 1 and \(s_gc_g\) is close to \(\tilde s_g\).



43.5.4 Interpretation
The floor scales like one over the share. A group with a twentieth of the records sits at about twenty times the excess loss of a group with all of them. The curvature \(\lambda\) cancels: a group whose loss is sharper is pulled back harder, but each unit of noise also costs it more, and the two effects balance. What does not cancel is the share, because the noise is not scaled by it. It also takes the small group \(1/s_g\) times longer to reach even that floor.
Why waiting does not help. At a fixed budget, more steps require more noise per step. Under the small-\(q\) law of DP-SGD, multiplying the number of steps by \(m\) multiplies the noise variance per step by about \(m\), so the break-even count of Equation 43.7 grows as fast as the run (Exercise 3).
The two mechanisms compound. Clipping lowers a group’s pull from \(s_g\) to \(s_gc_g\); the noise floor scales like one over the pull. A group that is 5% of the data and whose gradients clipping halves pays the floor of a group of 2.5%.
How good is the model. The quadratic model is exact for what it assumes, as the simulation below confirms, but a network is not quadratic and its groups do not use disjoint weights. Where the minority’s task overlaps the majority’s, the majority’s gradient does part of the minority’s work, and the penalty is smaller. Tran, Dinh & Fioretto (2021) derive a related per-step decomposition for DP-SGD without assuming disjoint weights: the expected change in a group’s loss has a clipping term, driven by the group’s gradient norms, and a noise term proportional to \(\eta^2\sigma^2C^2\) times the trace of the group’s loss Hessian, which they relate to the group’s distance to the decision boundary and its input norms. The quadratic model makes the role of the share explicit, which their per-step terms leave implicit.

Right: the stationary excess loss of a group in the quadratic model, Equation 43.8, against its share, with the noise of \(\varepsilon = 4\), compared with simulation.

(By a factor of 4, since it is proportional to \(\tau^2\), for every group alike. Why does the curvature \(\lambda\) drop out of the approximate noise floor? (The pull toward the optimum and the cost of a displacement are both proportional to \(\lambda\); the stationary variance falls like \(1/\lambda\) and the loss per unit of variance rises like \(\lambda\).)

title: 43  Disparate impact
text:
43.6 Measuring per-group accuracy

43.6.1 Context
Every number so far was measured on 20,000 test records per group. Real evaluations are not so generous: a test split of 2,000 records with a 5% minority holds 100 minority records. How precisely can a group’s accuracy, and the gap between two groups, be measured, and how much does a single training run say?


43.6.2 Statement
The test-set error of a group’s accuracy is binomial (Fact 4): with \(k\) correct of \(m\) records, report the Clopper–Pearson interval. For the gap between two groups measured on disjoint test records, the two estimates are independent and their variances add, so an approximate 95% interval is \[(\hat p_a - \hat p_b) \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_a(1 - \hat p_a)}{m_a} + \frac{\hat p_b(1 - \hat p_b)}{m_b}}, \tag{43.9}\] with \(\hat p_g\) the measured accuracies and \(m_g\) the numbers of test records. Training randomness is a second, separate source of variation: a group’s accuracy varies from run to run, more for small groups, and is estimated only by training several times.


43.6.3 Derivation

One group. Each test record is classified correctly or not, independently given the model, with probability equal to the group’s true accuracy \(p_g\). The count is binomial, and Clopper–Pearson inverts it exactly (Hypothesis testing).
The gap. The two counts come from disjoint test records, so they are independent given the model. The variance of a difference of independent estimates is the sum of their variances, \(p_a(1 - p_a)/m_a + p_b(1 - p_b)/m_b\). For large counts the difference is approximately normal by the central limit theorem, and 1.96 standard deviations on each side cover 95%.
Two sources. Conditional on the trained model, the spread comes from the test set alone. Over training runs, the model itself varies; by the law of total variance the spread of a single run’s measured accuracy is the test-set variance plus the run-to-run variance of the true accuracy. Only repeated training estimates the second.



43.6.4 Interpretation
Small groups need intervals. The width of the Clopper–Pearson interval falls like \(1/\sqrt m\) (Figure 43.5). A 5-point gap between groups can be seen only with a few hundred minority test records, and a 1-point gap only with thousands (Exercise 4). Report the interval, not only the point estimate, for every group.
Report the spread over runs. In Table 43.2 the run-to-run standard deviation at \(\varepsilon = 4\) is 0.0211 for the minority against 0.0037 for the majority, almost six times as large. A comparison of two training recipes on one run each can easily be reversed for the small group. This is the same lesson as for the overall accuracy of private models (DP-SGD), sharper for small groups.
The evaluation leaks too. Per-group accuracies computed on private test data are statistics of that data. If they are published, they need their own privacy analysis, which Choosing ε and the selection mechanisms of Hyperparameter tuning address.






Figure 43.5: Width of the 95% Clopper–Pearson interval for a group’s accuracy against the number of test records in the group, for observed accuracies 0.95 and 0.7, on log scales. The width falls like one over the square root of the number of records.

The true accuracy is inside it, as it should be 95% of the time, and the non-private model’s 0.9411 from Table 43.2 lies only just above its upper end, 0.936: on this test set alone the minority’s privacy cost could be anywhere from about half a point to fourteen points. With 500 records the interval is 6.5 points wide and still contains the true value. The majority’s interval, from 1,900 records at a higher accuracy, is 2 points wide. 43.6.6 Check yourself

A report gives a private model’s accuracy as 0.84 on a subgroup of 60 test records and 0.85 non-private on the same records. What can you conclude? (Almost nothing about this subgroup. Each accuracy’s 95% interval is about \(2 \times 1.96\sqrt{0.84 \times 0.16/60} = 0.19\) wide, nineteen times the one-point difference. Because both models were tested on the same records, the difference could be measured more precisely from the records on which they disagree, but the report does not say how many there are.)
Why doesn’t a larger test set fix the run-to-run variation? (It removes the test-set error for the model at hand, but a different training run produces a different model. Only repeated training estimates how much a group’s accuracy varies with the training noise.)

title: 43  Disparate impact
text:
43.7 Mitigations and what they cost

43.7.1 Context
Both mechanisms come from DP-SGD’s two knobs. Can you choose the knobs, or change the algorithm, so that small groups pay less, without spending more privacy? Each fix in this section moves cost around rather than removing it, and it is worth knowing where to.


43.7.2 Statement
Global scaling is a large clipping norm. Scaling every per-example gradient by \(C/Z\), where no gradient is longer than \(Z\), and adding noise \(\sigma C\), is the same algorithm as DP-SGD with clipping norm \(Z\), the same noise multiplier and step size \(\eta C/Z\): \[\frac\eta B\Big(\frac CZ\sum_{i\in S_t}g_i + \sigma C\xi\Big) = \frac{\eta C/Z}B\Big(\sum_{i\in S_t}g_i + \sigma Z\xi\Big). \tag{43.10}\]
Oversampling a group costs that group’s privacy. If group \(g\)’s records are sampled at rate \(vq\) instead of \(q\), its pull on the update grows by the factor \(v\), and each of its records has the privacy of the subsampled Gaussian at rate \(vq\): \[\varepsilon_g = \varepsilon_{\text{acct}}(vq, \sigma, T, \delta) \;>\; \varepsilon_{\text{acct}}(q, \sigma, T, \delta), \tag{43.11}\] where \(\varepsilon_{\text{acct}}\) is the accountant of DP-SGD. The algorithm’s guarantee is the largest over records, so a fixed target \(\varepsilon\) requires the noise multiplier for rate \(vq\).


43.7.3 Derivation

Global scaling. Factor \(C/Z\) out of the left-hand side: \(\frac CZ\sum_ig_i + \sigma C\xi = \frac CZ(\sum_ig_i + \sigma Z\xi)\). With clipping norm \(Z\) and no gradient longer than \(Z\), DP-SGD’s clipped sum is \(\sum_ig_i\) and its noise \(\sigma Z\xi\), which is the right-hand side. Both have sensitivity-to-noise ratio \(1/\sigma\), so the same accountant applies (Exercise 6).
Oversampling: the pull. The expected clipped sum is \(\sum_iq_i\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)g_i\), with \(q_i\) record \(i\)’s sampling rate. With \(q_i = vq\) for group \(g\) and division by the public \(B = qn\), group \(g\)’s term becomes \(vs_gm_g\).
Oversampling: the privacy. The add/remove analysis of record \(x\) in DP-SGD compares the output with and without \(x\); the mixture depends only on \(x\)’s own inclusion probability, because the other records’ terms are the same in both. A record sampled at rate \(vq\) therefore has the privacy of the subsampled Gaussian at rate \(vq\). The sampling rate may depend on the record’s own group, which is part of the record, but the rule must be fixed in advance, not chosen by looking at the data.
The guarantee. \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP must hold for every record, so it is the largest of the per-record values, which is Equation 43.11’s.



43.7.4 Interpretation
Global scaling trades direction for noise. By Equation 43.10, scaling all gradients by the same factor is the large-\(C\) end of the clipping-norm curve of DP-SGD with \(\eta C\) fixed: nothing is clipped, so the update points in the true direction (the blue arrow of Figure 43.2), but the noise \(\sigma Z\) is as large as possible relative to the gradients. Esipova et al. (2023) propose a version that clips the rare gradients above \(Z\) instead of discarding them and adapts \(Z\) during training from a privately estimated count of how many gradients exceed it; they report that it reduces the privacy cost gap and improves accuracy compared with DP-SGD and with earlier mitigations on MNIST, CelebA and two tabular datasets. Because it treats every record alike, it needs no group labels.
Group-aware methods need group labels. Xu, Du & Wu (2021) adjust each group’s contribution according to how much that group is being clipped, giving groups that are clipped more a larger clipping bound, so that the groups’ clipping biases are equalized. Tran, Dinh & Fioretto (2021) add to the training objective penalties on the differences between groups in the quantities their decomposition identifies. Both need each training record’s group, which is itself sensitive and may not be available or lawful to collect, and the per-group statistics they use must be computed privately.
Oversampling buys little at a fixed budget. Fixed at \(\varepsilon = 4\) for every record, sampling the minority four times as often requires \(\sigma = 4.71\) instead of 1.36: the minority’s pull grows by 4 and the noise by \(4.71/1.36 = 3.46\). Its signal-to-noise ratio improves by only \(4/3.46 = 1.16\), while the majority’s falls by 3.46, and the majority’s records are then far more private than the target, \(\varepsilon = 0.86\), which is wasted budget (Exercise 5). Oversampling without changing \(\sigma\) would silently give the minority \(\varepsilon = 20.96\): the group that is already disadvantaged in accuracy would also get the weakest privacy.
Some of the cost is unavoidable. Learning a group’s own rule privately is, in part, a private estimation problem on that group’s \(n_g\) records, and private estimation has a price that no algorithm avoids. Lower bounds proves it for the simplest case: releasing \(d\) attribute means with constant accuracy under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP needs at least about \(\sqrt d/(e^\varepsilon - 1)\) records, by the fingerprinting argument, whatever the mechanism. Put differently, the error that \(n_g\) records allow shrinks only like \(1/(n_g\varepsilon)\), and the Gaussian mechanism, with error about \(\sqrt{d\ln(1/\delta)}/(n_g\varepsilon)\), is close to the best possible. A smaller group is a smaller dataset, and no clever clipping makes it larger. Feldman (2020) argues the deeper point for any learner: when the data have a long tail of small subpopulations, fitting them well requires memorizing their few examples, which is exactly what DP forbids. What helps is more data from the group, a larger \(\varepsilon\) (with its own costs), or a starting point that already serves the group, such as a public pretrained model (Public data and private fine-tuning).

None of the three changes helps the minority. A ten times smaller clipping norm clips the minority more, and its accuracy falls by 1.64 points while the majority’s rises by 0.71: the clipping mechanism of Section 43.4 at work. A ten times larger one clips almost nothing, so the update’s direction is right, but with \(\eta C\) fixed the noise in each step, \(\eta\sigma C/B\), is unchanged while the step along every gradient shorter than 0.5 is ten times smaller: the noise is ten times larger relative to that part of the signal, and the minority falls by 3.44 points: the noise mechanism of Section 43.5 at work. 43.7.6 Check yourself

Why does oversampling a group require more noise, while upweighting its loss does not? (Upweighting leaves every record’s contribution bounded by \(C\) and its sampling rate at \(q\), so the accountant is unchanged, but clipping undoes it. Oversampling raises the group’s sampling rate, which the subsampled Gaussian’s privacy depends on.)
A team proposes to fix disparate impact by setting \(C\) to the largest per-example gradient norm observed in the training data. What is wrong? (The clipping norm then depends on the data, and the sensitivity argument of DP-SGD assumes it is fixed in advance. A data-dependent \(C\) must itself be chosen privately, as in Esipova et al.’s adaptive threshold, and the estimate charged to the budget.)

Neither knob of DP-SGD removes the effect at a fixed budget; it only moves it between the groups and between the two mechanisms.

title: 43  Disparate impact
text:
43.9 References

Bagdasaryan, Poursaeed & Shmatikov, “Differential Privacy Has Disparate Impact on Model Accuracy” (NeurIPS 2019). The observation this chapter explains: DP-SGD’s accuracy loss falls on under-represented and complex groups, and existing gaps grow.
Tran, Dinh & Fioretto, “Differentially Private Empirical Risk Minimization under the Fairness Lens” (NeurIPS 2021). Per-step decompositions of a group’s excess risk into clipping and noise terms, for output perturbation and DP-SGD, and the role of gradient norms, input norms, the loss Hessian and the distance to the decision boundary.
Esipova, Ghomi, Luo & Cresswell, “Disparate Impact in Differential Privacy from Gradient Misalignment” (ICLR 2023). Separates clipping’s direction error from its length error, finds the direction error the main cause, and proposes global scaling with an adaptive threshold.
Xu, Du & Wu, “Removing Disparate Impact on Model Accuracy in Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent” (KDD 2021). Group-dependent clipping that equalizes the groups’ clipping bias.
Feldman, “Does Learning Require Memorization? A Short Tale about a Long Tail” (STOC 2020). Why fitting small subpopulations well requires memorizing their examples, and so conflicts with privacy.
Clopper & Pearson, “The use of confidence or fiducial limits illustrated in the case of the binomial” (Biometrika, 1934). The exact interval of Section 43.6.

Rules of thumb

Always report accuracy per group, with Clopper–Pearson intervals and the spread over several training runs, next to the non-private model’s.
Expect the privacy cost of a group to grow like one over its share of the data, and faster for groups with long gradients: large inputs or a rule the rest of the data does not teach.
Clipping alone is disparate. A larger clipping norm (with \(\eta C\) fixed) reduces the clipping part and raises the noise part.
Do not upweight a group’s loss to help it: clipping undoes it. Do not oversample a group without accounting at its higher sampling rate.
When a group is too small to learn privately, get more data from it or start from a public model that already serves it.

title: 44  Choosing ε
text:
44.1 Why this matters
Every model trained with differential privacy (DP) ships with a number, its budget \(\varepsilon\). DP is the guarantee that one record changes the probability of any output by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), up to a slack \(\delta\). Chapter 37 trained the part’s running example, a small neural network on 10,000 records, with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) made private by per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, at five budgets, and measured what each costs in accuracy: test accuracy 0.9175 at \(\varepsilon = 1\), 0.9441 at \(\varepsilon = 2\), 0.9548 at \(\varepsilon = 4\) and 0.9604 at \(\varepsilon = 8\), against 0.9610 without privacy, all at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). That is half of a decision. The other half is what each budget means for the people in the data: what an attacker who sees the model can learn about one of them, and how sure it can be. Without that half, the choice of \(\varepsilon\) is made by habit (“everyone uses 8”) or by the accuracy curve alone, and neither survives a reviewer, a regulator or a data subject who asks what the number promises.
This chapter supplies the privacy half. It reads the guarantee in three operational ways: as a bound on any membership test, as a bound on how far an attacker’s belief can move, and as a bound on reconstructing a record. For each it compares two numbers: what the single pair \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) promises, and what the actual training algorithm, DP-SGD, really allows. It then turns to \(\delta\), to the budgets that real deployments have published and the units they are stated in, and to a procedure for choosing and defending a number.

title: 44  Choosing ε
text:
44.1.1 The one idea: ε is one line under a curve
An attacker who wants to know whether a record was in the training set runs a test, and every test has two error rates. The definition of DP is equivalent to a straight-line bound on those rates: at false positive rate \(\alpha\), the true positive rate is at most \(e^\varepsilon\alpha + \delta\). But a training algorithm has a whole trade-off curve, the best true positive rate at every false positive rate, and \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) is only one line that lies above it, touching it at one point. Far from that point, the line can be useless: at \(\varepsilon = 8\) it allows a test that catches every member while almost never accusing a non-member, while the curve of DP-SGD at the same \(\varepsilon\) caps the true positive rate at 0.0589 when the false positive rate is \(10^{-3}\). Choosing \(\varepsilon\) well means computing and reporting the curve, not just the line, and reading it at the error rates that matter for your threat.
Table 44.1 lists the results and where each is used.

Notation. A membership test sees the trained model (or the whole sequence of iterates) and says “member” or “non-member” about a target record \(z\). Its false positive rate (FPR) \(\alpha\) is the probability that it says “member” when \(z\) was not in the training set, and its true positive rate (TPR) is the probability that it says “member” when \(z\) was. \(Q\) is the distribution of the output when \(z\) is in the data, \(P\) the distribution when it is not, and \(L = \ln(Q(y)/P(y))\) is the privacy loss of an output \(y\). \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the smallest \(\delta\) for which a mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP at a given \(\varepsilon\), its privacy profile. For DP-SGD, \(q\) is the sampling rate, \(\sigma\) the noise multiplier and \(T\) the number of steps. The running example has \(q = 0.01\), \(T = 10{,}000\) and \(n = 10{,}000\) records, and its noise multiplier is the one the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant of DP-SGD requires for each target \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).
How to read this chapter. The toolkit and Section 44.3 restate what The definition of differential privacy proves, in the form this chapter needs. Section 44.4 is the core: the curve of DP-SGD against the line. Section 44.5 and Section 44.6 read the same curve as beliefs and as reconstruction. Section 44.7, Section 44.8 and Section 44.9 are about practice and can be read on their own.

title: 44  Choosing ε
section: 44.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
44.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

44.2.1 Fact 1 — A membership attacker is a test, and DP bounds the probability of every event
Fix the training set without the target, \(D^-\), and the target record \(z\). The attacker sees an output \(y\), drawn from \(Q = M(D^- \cup \{z\})\) if \(z\) is a member and from \(P = M(D^-)\) if not, and says “member” on some set \(S\) of outputs. Then \(\mathrm{FPR} = P(S)\) and \(\mathrm{TPR} = Q(S)\): both error rates are probabilities of one event. A mechanism \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP when, for every pair of neighbouring datasets and every event \(S\), in both orders, \[Q(S) \le e^\varepsilon P(S) + \delta. \tag{44.1}\] So DP is a statement about tests before it is a statement about anything else. This chapter uses add/remove neighbours, as DP-SGD with Poisson sampling does (DP-SGD). An attacker that randomizes, saying “member” with probability \(\phi(y)\), has \(\mathrm{TPR} = \mathbb E_Q[\phi]\) and \(\mathrm{FPR} = \mathbb E_P[\phi]\), and the same bound holds for it, because a randomized test is an average of events (The definition of differential privacy).


44.2.2 Fact 2 — The best test thresholds the privacy loss
Among all tests with a given FPR, the one with the largest TPR says “member” when the likelihood ratio \(Q(y)/P(y)\) is large, that is, when the privacy loss \(L(y)\) exceeds a threshold \(t\), randomizing at the threshold if needed. This is the Neyman–Pearson lemma (Hypothesis testing). The reason is an exchange argument: if a test said “member” on an output with a low ratio and “non-member” on one with a higher ratio, swapping the two (in equal amounts of \(P\)-probability) would keep its FPR and raise its TPR.
Two consequences follow. First, the best TPR at FPR \(\alpha\) depends only on the distribution of \(L\). Write \(\omega\) for the distribution of \(L\) when \(y \sim Q\), the privacy loss distribution (PLD). Then the best test with threshold \(t\) has \[\mathrm{TPR}(t) = Q[L > t], \qquad \mathrm{FPR}(t) = P[L > t] = \mathbb E_Q\big[e^{-L};\ L > t\big], \tag{44.2}\] where the second form is a change of measure: \(P(y) = e^{-L(y)}Q(y)\) by the definition of \(L\), so the \(P\)-probability of any event is the \(Q\)-average of \(e^{-L}\) over it. Second, the best achievable pairs \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{TPR})\) form a region whose upper boundary, the trade-off curve written here as \(\mathrm{TPR}^*(\alpha)\), is increasing and concave: increasing because a test with a higher FPR can always say “member” more often, concave because randomizing between two tests reaches every point of the segment between them.


44.2.3 Fact 3 — Beliefs multiply by the likelihood ratio
An attacker who believes beforehand that \(z\) is a member with probability \(p\), the prior, and then sees \(y\), believes afterwards \[\frac{\Pr[\text{member} \mid y]}{\Pr[\text{non-member} \mid y]} = \frac{p}{1 - p}\cdot\frac{Q(y)}{P(y)} = \frac{p}{1 - p}e^{L(y)}. \tag{44.3}\] This is Bayes’ rule in odds form: the posterior odds are the prior odds times the likelihood ratio, and the likelihood ratio is \(e^L\). Converting odds \(o\) back to a probability, \(o/(1 + o)\), gives the posterior \(p e^L/(p e^L + 1 - p)\).


44.2.4 Fact 4 — DP-SGD’s worst case is one pair of distributions, composed
Each step of DP-SGD adds Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to a sum of per-example gradients clipped to length \(C\), over a batch that contains each record independently with probability \(q\). DP-SGD showed that, for the target record, the worst case over models, data and directions is a one-dimensional pair in units of \(C\): without the record the step’s output is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), with it the output is the mixture \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). The privacy loss of one step is \(\ell(y) = \ln\big((1 - q) + q\,e^{(2y - 1)/(2\sigma^2)}\big)\), and \(T\) steps release \(T\) outputs whose losses add, so the PLD of the whole run is the distribution of a sum of \(T\) such losses. Three accountants summarize it (Choosing an accountant):

the RDP accountant bounds the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) by \(R(\alpha) = T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\) and converts it to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\); it is a valid upper bound, and it is what DP-SGD used to set \(\sigma\);
the numerical PLD accountant discretizes the one-step loss on a grid of spacing \(h\), rounding each loss up (pessimistic) or down (optimistic), and composes by fast Fourier transform (FFT) convolution; the truth lies between the two answers, which differ by at most a shift of \(Th\) in the total loss (Numerical accounting);
the Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) central limit theorem (CLT) approximates the run by a single Gaussian pair \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) with \(\mu = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\); it is an approximation, not a bound (f-DP and Gaussian DP).

title: 44  Choosing ε
section: 44.3 What one (ε, δ) pair says about a membership test
text:
44.3 What one (ε, δ) pair says about a membership test

44.3.1 Context
A model card says “trained with \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (8, 10^{-5})\)”. Taken alone, what does that number forbid an attacker to do? This is the question to answer first, because it is the only one you can answer for a model whose algorithm you have not seen.


44.3.2 Statement
If \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, every membership test, against every target, satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le \min\big\{1,\ e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta,\ 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \mathrm{FPR})\big\}, \tag{44.4}\] and its advantage, \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\), the amount by which it beats guessing, satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} \le \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1 + 2\delta}{e^\varepsilon + 1}. \tag{44.5}\]


44.3.3 Derivation

The first line. Apply the definition (Fact 1) with \(D^- \cup \{z\}\) first and the event \(S\) on which the test says “member”: \(Q(S) \le e^\varepsilon P(S) + \delta\), that is \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\).
The second line. Apply it in the other order to the complement \(S^c\), where the test says “non-member”: \(P(S^c) \le e^\varepsilon Q(S^c) + \delta\), that is \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} \le e^\varepsilon(1 - \mathrm{TPR}) + \delta\). Solving for TPR gives \(\mathrm{TPR} \le 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \mathrm{FPR})\). A probability is at most 1, which is the third term of Equation 44.4.
The advantage. \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\) is largest where the two lines of steps 1 and 2 cross, because below the crossing the first line rises faster than the diagonal (slope \(e^\varepsilon \ge 1\)) and above it the second line rises more slowly (slope \(e^{-\varepsilon} \le 1\)). Setting \(e^\varepsilon\alpha + \delta = 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \alpha)\) and multiplying by \(e^\varepsilon\) gives \(\alpha(e^{2\varepsilon} - 1) = e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta - \delta e^\varepsilon\), so \(\alpha = (1 - \delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\). There the TPR is \(e^\varepsilon(1 - \delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1) + \delta\), and subtracting \(\alpha\) gives Equation 44.5.



44.3.4 Interpretation
The bound has three regimes. At small FPR the line \(e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\) binds, and the ratio TPR/FPR is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) plus \(\delta/\mathrm{FPR}\). Below \(\mathrm{FPR} \approx \delta e^{-\varepsilon}\) the \(\delta\) term dominates, and the guarantee rests on \(\delta\) alone. At large FPR the second line binds. And once \(e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta \ge 1\), which at \(\varepsilon = 8\) happens from \(\mathrm{FPR} = (1 - 10^{-5})e^{-8} = 3.35\times10^{-4}\) on, the bound allows a perfect true positive rate: the pair says nothing at all at the false positive rates where attacks are usually evaluated.
Low FPR is where it matters. Membership inference evaluates attacks by their TPR at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) or below, because an attack that flags members while almost never flagging non-members is one that confidently identifies people. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the pair caps that TPR at \(e \times 10^{-3} + 10^{-5} = 0.002728\), a real constraint. At \(\varepsilon = 4\) the cap is 0.05461, at \(\varepsilon = 8\) it is 0.9997.
The advantage is an average, and DP’s guarantee is not about averages. Equation 44.5 bounds the advantage at a single point of the curve, the one with equal error rates. It is 0.4621 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 0.9640 at \(\varepsilon = 4\), numbers that make \(\varepsilon = 4\) sound hopeless. They are tight only for the worst mechanism with this \(\varepsilon\), randomized response, whose curve is exactly the two lines. DP-SGD is not that mechanism, as the next section shows.

Table 44.3 evaluates Equation 44.4 and Equation 44.5 for the six budgets of the running example. For \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.01\), the first line gives \(e \times 0.01 + 10^{-5} = 0.02719\).
